concepts.title: Arabic groups words into three parts of speech
concepts.rule: Use the Arabic categories: اِسْمٌ، فِعْلٌ، حَرْفٌ.

examples.arabic:
الِاسْمُ: كِتَابٌ، هُوَ، أَنَا، هَذَا، قَبْلَ
الْفِعْلُ: كَتَبَ، يَكْتُبُ، اُكْتُبْ، لَيْسَ
الْحَرْفُ: مَا، لَا، نَعَمْ، لَمْ، سَـ
examples.translation:
Ism: book, he, I, this, before
Fil: he wrote, he writes, write!, is not
Harf: ma, la, yes, lam, future sa-
examples.explanation: The Arabic category اِسْمٌ is broader than the everyday English idea of a naming noun: it includes pronouns and demonstratives. A فِعْلٌ is a verb, including the past, present-future and command forms shown. A حَرْفٌ is a particle with a grammatical function; here the term does not mean a single alphabet letter.

concepts.title: Sun letters borrow the lām sound
concepts.rule: Keep الـ in writing; double the sun letter in speech.

examples.arabic: الشَّمْسُ
examples.translation: The sun
examples.explanation: This is pronounced “ash-shamsu,” rather than “al-shamsu.” The ل stays in the spelling. A shaddah on ش marks the doubled sound. The book also gives النَّجْمُ (the star), الدِّيكُ (the rooster), الرَّجُلُ (the man), and السَّمَكُ (the fish).

concepts.note: The ل stays in writing but is not heard. The sun letter doubles.

concepts.title: Moon letters let the lām be heard
concepts.rule: With a moon letter, keep the “l” sound of al.

examples.arabic: الْقَمَرُ
examples.translation: The moon
examples.explanation: Read this as “al-qamaru.” Arabic has 14 sun letters and 14 moon letters. The sun letters are ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن; the remaining letters are moon letters. Compare الشَّمْسُ with الْقَمَرُ to hear the difference.

concepts.note: A moon letter keeps the l sound of al.

concepts.title: Let words flow into الـ
concepts.rule: The spelling stays; the opening vowel joins smoothly to the previous word.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ   ←   وَالْبَيْتُ
examples.translation: The house → and the house
examples.explanation: Read الْبَيْتُ on its own as “al-baytu.” With وَ before it, read وَالْبَيْتُ as “wal-baytu.” The alif remains in writing. This connecting initial vowel is called hamzat al-wasl; the sign ٱ can mark it.

concepts.note: The alif stays in writing; in speech the opening vowel drops.

concepts.title: A shorter vowel when فِي meets الـ
concepts.rule: Write فِي الْبَيْتِ; connect it in speech as “fil-bayti.”

examples.arabic:
فِي بَيْتٍ
فِي الْبَيْتِ
examples.translation:
In a house
In the house
examples.explanation: In فِي بَيْتٍ, keep the long vowel of fi. In فِي الْبَيْتِ, read the connection as “fil-bayti.” You already learned that the initial vowel of الـ drops after a preceding word; here the long vowel of فِي is shortened too. The spelling stays the same.

concepts.note: The long vowel of فِي shortens before الـ.

concepts.title: A connecting vowel beyond الـ
concepts.rule: Hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech in اِسْمٌ and اِبْنٌ too.

examples.arabic:
اِسْمُ الْوَلَدِ بِلَالٌ، وَاسْمُ الْبِنْتِ آمِنَةُ
أَيْنَ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ؟
examples.translation:
The boy’s name is Bilal, and the girl’s name is Aminah.
Where is Hamid’s son?
examples.explanation: At the start of speech, pronounce the initial “i” in ism or ibn. When another word comes before it, omit that vowel in connected speech: وَاسْمُ is read “wasmu,” and أَيْنَ ابْنُ is connected as “ayna-bnu.” The initial alif stays in writing.

concepts.note: Hamzat al-wasl drops after another word.

concepts.title: A final ى can sound like alif
concepts.rule: Read the final dotless ى in this word as a long “ā.”

examples.arabic: الْمُسْتَشْفَى
examples.translation: The hospital
examples.explanation: The Key highlights this spelling in its vocabulary. This final letter is called alif maqsura. Unlike ي, it has no two dots underneath. Connect it with the previous card: the word ends in a long “ā,” not a visible changing short-vowel ending.

concepts.note: Dotless final ى is read as a long ā.

concepts.title: When لِـ meets الـ, drop the alif
concepts.rule: لِـ + الـ becomes لِلـ in writing, and the noun is majrur.

examples.arabic:
الْإِمَامُ ← لِلْإِمَامِ
الْمُدَرِّسُ ← لِلْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
The imam → belonging to the imam
The teacher → belonging to the teacher
examples.explanation: The written connection begins لِلْ, not لِالْ. Since لِـ is a preposition, the following noun is also majrur: notice the final kasrah. This extends Chapter 6’s introduction to لِـ with the general spelling rule for nouns with الـ.

concepts.note: No extra alif is written: لِلْ, never لِالْ.

concepts.title: A short “i” connects ذَهَبَتْ to الـ
concepts.rule: Before الـ, connect ذَهَبَتْ with a short “i”: ذَهَبَتِ الْبِنْتُ.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبَتِ الْبِنْتُ
examples.translation: The girl went.
examples.explanation: Notice ذَهَبَتِ rather than ذَهَبَتْ in this connected example. Read it as “dhahabatil-bintu.” The short “i” lets the words join when the initial vowel of الـ drops. This is still the “she went” form; it is not the “you went” ending.

concepts.note: A short i joins the verb to الـ.

concepts.title: An extra alif with this “an” ending
concepts.rule: Write كِتَابًا with ا; write سَيَّارَةً without an extra ا.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابٌ ← كِتَابًا
سَيَّارَةٌ ← سَيَّارَةً
examples.translation:
A book → a book (mansub)
A car → a car (mansub)
examples.explanation: The extra alif in كِتَابًا is not a separate pronounced vowel when reading the tanwin in connected speech. سَيَّارَةً carries the tanwin on ة without adding ا. These are the spelling patterns illustrated by the Key.

concepts.note: The extra alif goes on كِتَابًا, but not after ة.

concepts.title: “Son of” between two names has a special spelling
concepts.rule: In بِلَالُ بْنُ حَامِدٍ, write بْنُ and omit Bilal’s tanwin.

examples.arabic: بِلَالُ بْنُ حَامِدٍ
examples.translation: Bilal, son of Hamid
examples.explanation: Compare the separate word اِبْنٌ from Book 1 with بْنُ in this naming phrase. حَامِدٍ remains the majrur owner after “son.” Keep this spelling change tied to the naming construction; it does not mean every اِبْن loses its alif.

concepts.note: Write بْنُ; Bilal has no tanwin.

concepts.title: Tanwin gets a linking “i” before hamzat al-wasl
concepts.rule: A linking sound can change pronunciation without changing grammatical case.

examples.arabic:
شَرِبَ حَامِدٌ الْمَاءَ
سَأَلَ بِلَالٌ ابْنَهُ
سَمِعَ فَيْصَلٌ الْأَذَانَ
examples.translation:
Hamid drank water.
Bilal asked his son.
Faisal heard the adhan.
examples.explanation: The first is connected as “shariba Hamidun-i-l-maʾa.” The extra short vowel avoids the two unvowelled sounds meeting. The Key calls that meeting الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. The linking vowel does not make حَامِدٌ majrur; it remains the subject.

concepts.note: A linking i follows tanwin before wasl.

concepts.title: A linking “u” follows these final مْ forms
concepts.rule: Before wasl here, connect the final مْ with “u.”

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُكُمُ الْجَدِيدُ
أَرَأَيْتُمُ الْإِمَامَ؟
كِتَابُهُمُ الْقَدِيمُ
أَسَأَلْتُمُ ابْنَهُ؟
examples.translation:
Your new house
Did you see the imam?
Their old book
Did you ask his son?
examples.explanation: Connect with a short “u”: baytukum-u-l-jadidu. Compare the linking kasrah after tanwin in Chapter 5: different endings use different connecting vowels. The noun’s case is not changed by this sound adjustment.

concepts.note: A linking u follows these final مْ forms.

concepts.title: Questioning مَا loses its alif after a preposition
concepts.rule: Drop the alif of questioning مَا after these prepositions.

examples.translation:
With what? · for what/why?
From what? · about what?
examples.explanation: مِنْ + مَا becomes مِمَّ, and عَنْ + مَا becomes عَمَّ: the ن blends into the م, producing shaddah. This also explains the earlier لِمَ, “why?” The rule here concerns questioning مَا.

concepts.note: Questioning مَا loses its alif after a preposition.

concepts.title: Question أَ becomes a long آ before الـ here
concepts.rule: Question أَ directly before الـ is written and read differently from أَهَذَا.

examples.arabic:
آلْمُدَرِّسُ قَالَ لَكَ؟
آلْيَوْمَ رَأَيْتَهُ؟
أَهَذَا الطَّالِبُ سَأَلَكَ؟
examples.translation:
Did the teacher tell you?
Did you see him today?
Did this student ask you?
examples.explanation: The first two begin with a long “ā” sound where question أَ meets الـ. In the third, the particle stands before هَذَا instead, so it stays a short أَ. Look at the word immediately after the question particle.

concepts.note: Question أَ becomes آ only right before الـ.

concepts.title: A final ى changes spelling before an attached pronoun
concepts.rule: Before these attached pronouns, final long-ā ى is written ا.

examples.arabic:
مَعْنًى ← مَعْنَاهُ
كَوَى ← كَوَاهُ
examples.translation:
A meaning → its meaning
He ironed → he ironed it
examples.explanation: The first is a noun with an attached owner pronoun, while the second is a verb with an attached object pronoun. In both, the long “ā” sound remains, but its written shape changes before the suffix.

concepts.note: Final ى is written ا before an attached pronoun.

concepts.title: Why “I eat” begins with آ
concepts.rule: Write آكُلُ, آخُذُ and آمُرُ with the long opening آ.

examples.arabic:
أَأْكُلُ ← آكُلُ
أَأْخُذُ ← آخُذُ
أَأْمُرُ ← آمُرُ
examples.translation:
Underlying combination → I eat
Underlying combination → I take
Underlying combination → I command
examples.explanation: The first hamza is the “I” prefix; the next belongs to the root and has sukun. The Key shows their combination becoming the long opening ā, written آ with maddah. The forms on the left illustrate the underlying combination, not the spelling to use in an ordinary sentence.

concepts.note: Two hamzas merge into a long ā.

concepts.title: The silent waw in عَمْرٌو
concepts.rule: Write the silent waw in عَمْرٌو, but omit it in عَمْرًا.

examples.arabic:
عَمْرٌو · عُمَرُ
سَأَلْتُ عَمْرًا.
سَأَلْتُ عُمَرَ.
examples.translation:
Amr · Umar
I asked Amr.
I asked Umar.
examples.explanation: In the mansub form عَمْرًا, the distinguishing waw is omitted. The tanwin alif already makes its spelling different from عُمَرَ. Amr has tanwin here; Umar is a diptote and has none. Do not pronounce the extra written waw as a long ū.

concepts.note: The silent waw is written in عَمْرٌو only.

concepts.title: Write ibn between names with care
concepts.rule: The spelling depends on both the name construction and the written line.

examples.arabic:
مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ وِلْيَمَ
الْحَسَنُ ابْنُ الْإِمَامِ عَلِيٍّ
بِلَالُ بْنُ حَامِدٍ
examples.translation:
Muhammad son of William
Hasan son of Imam Ali
Bilal son of Hamid
examples.explanation: The Key omits the alif between a son’s and father’s names only when the father’s name has no preceding title and all three words are on the same written line. Retain alif with a title or a line break. The name before ibn loses tanwin in this construction.

concepts.note: Alif is omitted only with no title and one written line.

concepts.title: Question hamza replaces wasl hamza
concepts.rule: The remaining hamza asks the question; it is not the original wasl.

examples.arabic:
أَنْفَتَحَ الْبَابُ؟
أَنْقَلَبَتِ السَّيَّارَةُ؟
examples.translation:
Did the door open?
Did the car overturn?
examples.explanation: Adding interrogative أَ to a wasl-initial verb omits the helping hamza. The resulting opening may resemble another verb form, so identify the root and the question context.

concepts.note: The question hamza replaces the wasl hamza.

concepts.title: Form VIII drops wasl after question hamza too
concepts.rule: Do not add a second helping hamza after the question.

examples.arabic:
أَنْتَظَرْتَنِي؟
أَصْطَفَى الْبَنَاتِ عَلَى الْبَنِينَ؟
examples.translation:
Did you wait for me?
Has he preferred daughters to sons?
examples.explanation: Interrogative hamza replaces the opening hamzat al-wasl. Internal Form VIII assimilation remains, as in اصطفى. Identify both the question prefix and the derived stem.

concepts.note: No second helping hamza after the question.

concepts.title: Recognize an indefinite noun
concepts.rule: For ordinary nouns such as كِتَابٌ, tanwin accompanies an indefinite meaning: “a book.”

examples.arabic: كِتَابٌ   ·   بَيْتٌ   ·   مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation: A book · a house · a mosque
examples.explanation: This ending is called tanwin. Here, the double vowel mark ٌ is read “un.” It tells you that the noun is indefinite: a book, rather than a particular book. Later, you will see tanwin on other kinds of words too.

concepts.title: Make a noun definite with الـ
concepts.rule: Add الـ and remove tanwin: بَيْتٌ becomes الْبَيْتُ.

examples.arabic: بَيْتٌ ← الْبَيْتُ
examples.translation: A house → the house
examples.explanation: When الـ is added, the tanwin ending goes away. Compare بَيْتٌ, ending in “un,” with الْبَيْتُ, ending in “u.” Do not keep both الـ and tanwin on the same noun in this pattern.

concepts.title: A common feminine ending: ة
concepts.rule: Look for a short “a” before the feminine ending ة.

examples.arabic: مُدَرِّسٌ ← مُدَرِّسَةٌ
examples.translation: A male teacher → a female teacher
examples.explanation: The feminine form is read “mudarrisatun” when its ending is pronounced. The ة is called ta marbutah. This is a common pattern, not a way to change every noun: some words have a separate feminine form.

rows: A male teacher → a female teacher

concepts.title: Sometimes the feminine word is different
concepts.rule: Learn the gender with the word; ة is a useful clue, not a universal rule.

examples.arabic:
اِبْنٌ   ·   بِنْتٌ
أَخٌ   ·   أُخْتٌ
examples.translation:
Son · daughter
Brother · sister
examples.explanation: Learn each pair together. بِنْتٌ and أُخْتٌ are feminine even though neither ends in ة. A noun’s meaning and learned gender matter more than guessing from its last letter.

concepts.title: Gender is not always visible
concepts.rule: A feminine noun does not need a ة ending.

examples.arabic:
يَدٌ   ·   عَيْنٌ
رَأْسٌ   ·   أَنْفٌ
examples.translation:
Hand · eye (feminine)
Head · nose (masculine)
examples.explanation: The feminine examples are يَدٌ (hand), رِجْلٌ (leg), عَيْنٌ (eye), and أُذُنٌ (ear). The masculine examples are رَأْسٌ (head), أَنْفٌ (nose), فَمٌ (mouth), and وَجْهٌ (face). Treat this as a learning aid and learn each noun’s gender.

concepts.title: Some nouns keep their final long “ā”
concepts.rule: A noun’s grammatical role can change without a visible change at its end.

examples.arabic:
هَذِهِ أَمْرِيكَا
أَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِيكَا
هُوَ رَئِيسُ أَمْرِيكَا
examples.translation:
This is America.
I am from America.
He is the president of America.
examples.explanation: أَمْرِيكَا keeps the same visible form in all three examples. In the second sentence it follows a preposition; in the third it is a mudaf ilayhi. Those grammatical roles still exist, even though you do not see a changing final vowel on this word.

concepts.title: Ask “whose book?”
concepts.rule: Some words keep the same form even when their grammatical role changes.

examples.arabic: كِتَابُ مَنْ؟
examples.translation: Whose book?
examples.explanation: Here مَنْ occupies the place of the owner. Its grammatical role is majrur, but its ending does not visibly change. The book calls this word indeclinable: its form stays the same even when its job changes.

concepts.title: Do not translate every tanwin as “a”
concepts.rule: Tanwin is an ending, not an English word: مَفْتُوحٌ in this predicate means “open,” not “a open.”

examples.arabic:
الْبَابُ مَفْتُوحٌ
الْقَلَمُ مَكْسُورٌ
examples.translation:
The door is open.
The pen is broken.
examples.explanation: مَفْتُوحٌ describes something as “open,” and مَكْسُورٌ describes something as “broken.” Both have tanwin, but English does not say “a open” or “a broken” here. Translate the meaning of the whole sentence.

concepts.title: A name can be definite and have tanwin
concepts.rule: A proper name such as حَامِدٌ identifies a person and is definite even though it has tanwin.

examples.arabic: حَامِدٌ
examples.translation: Hamid
examples.explanation: You first saw tanwin in بَيْتٌ, “a house.” But حَامِدٌ is simply “Hamid,” never “a Hamid” in this lesson. Like the describing words from Chapter 3, names show why tanwin cannot always be translated as “a.”

concepts.title: Notice the endings of these feminine names
concepts.rule: The feminine names illustrated here take a single dammah, not tanwin, in the nominative. Their gender need not be shown by ة.

examples.arabic: فَاطِمَةُ   ·   زَيْنَبُ   ·   آمِنَةُ
examples.translation: Fatimah · Zaynab · Aminah
examples.explanation: Compare these names with حَامِدٌ. They have a single dammah here, rather than the double mark of tanwin. زَيْنَبُ also reminds you that a feminine name does not have to end in ة. Learn the forms in the lesson; detailed exceptions come later.

examples.arabic: آمِنَةُ   ·   زَيْنَبُ
examples.translation: Aminah · Zaynab
examples.explanation: You met this rule in Chapter 4. The names shown take a single dammah, not tanwin. One ends in ة and the other does not. This collected list gives the name mamnuʿ min al-sarf to the pattern; detailed exceptions are beyond this introductory list.

concepts.title: The “n” here is not tanwin
concepts.rule: In these فَعْلَان adjectives, the written ن is part of the word. The illustrated forms have no tanwin.

examples.arabic:
كَسْلَانُ   ·   جَوْعَانُ   ·   عَطْشَانُ
غَضْبَانُ   ·   مَلْآنُ
examples.translation:
Lazy · hungry · thirsty
Angry · full
examples.explanation: These words have a written ن as part of the word itself. Their ending here is a single dammah, “u,” not the double dammah of tanwin. Do not confuse the long “ān” inside the word with an added tanwin “n.”

examples.arabic: كَسْلَانُ   ·   مَلْآنُ
examples.translation: Lazy · full
examples.explanation: This collects the pattern introduced in Chapter 9, which also included جَوْعَانُ, عَطْشَانُ, and غَضْبَانُ. The final ن belongs to the word itself; the case form shown has a single dammah.

concepts.title: Notice the extra و in “your brother”
concepts.rule: Learn أَبُو and أَخُو in these examples, rather than treating them like كِتَابُ.

examples.arabic:
أَخُوكَ   ·   أَبُوهُ
أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ   ·   أَخُو مُحَمَّدٍ
examples.translation:
Your brother (one male person) · his father
Muhammad’s father · Muhammad’s brother
examples.explanation: Here the mudaf includes a و: أَخُوكَ and أَبُوهُ. You see it with a named owner too: أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ. This lesson introduces two members of a special group traditionally called the five nouns. Other case forms come later.

concepts.title: “My father” and “my brother” have no extra و
concepts.rule: For “my,” remember the short forms أَبِي and أَخِي.

examples.arabic: أَبِي   ·   أَخِي
examples.translation: My father · my brother
examples.explanation: Compare أَبُوهُ (“his father”) with أَبِي (“my father”), and أَخُوكَ (“your brother”) with أَخِي (“my brother”). The extra و shown in the previous card does not appear with the first-person possessive ending.

concepts.title: A masculine name can end in ة
concepts.rule: These masculine names end in ة but remain masculine; their illustrated nominative forms have no tanwin.

examples.arabic: حَمْزَةُ   ·   أُسَامَةُ   ·   مُعَاوِيَةُ
examples.translation: Hamzah · Usamah · Muawiyah
examples.explanation: The ending ة is a common feminine clue, but it does not determine the gender of every name. These masculine names have a single dammah here, like the feminine names introduced earlier, rather than tanwin.

examples.arabic: حَمْزَةُ   ·   أُسَامَةُ
examples.translation: Hamzah · Usamah
examples.explanation: These are male names, despite their ة ending. They have no tanwin in the forms shown. Connect this with Chapter 10: gender and declension need to be learned with a name.

concepts.title: Arabic adjectives have plurals too
concepts.rule: Learn the plural of the description as well as the thing described.

examples.arabic:
مُدَرِّسٌ ← مُدَرِّسُونَ
طَوِيلٌ ← طِوَالٌ
examples.translation:
A teacher → teachers
Tall (singular) → tall (plural)
examples.explanation: A sound plural adds an ending while keeping the main word recognisable. A broken plural changes the internal pattern. Unlike an English adjective such as “tall,” طَوِيلٌ itself has a plural form, طِوَالٌ, given in this chapter’s vocabulary. Learn a word’s plural with its singular.

concepts.title: A sound masculine plural in ـُونَ
concepts.rule: Recognise ـُونَ as the sound masculine plural ending in these examples.

examples.arabic:
مُسْلِمٌ ← مُسْلِمُونَ
مُدَرِّسٌ ← مُدَرِّسُونَ
examples.translation:
A Muslim man → Muslim men
A male teacher → male teachers
examples.explanation: The main part of each word stays the same. Replace the singular ending with ـُونَ in these forms. This is one plural pattern, not a rule for making every masculine noun plural. Other case endings are studied later.

concepts.title: A sound feminine plural in ـَاتٌ
concepts.rule: The plural has long “ā” and open ت: ـَاتٌ.

examples.arabic:
مُسْلِمَةٌ ← مُسْلِمَاتٌ
مُهَنْدِسَةٌ ← مُهَنْدِسَاتٌ
examples.translation:
A Muslim woman → Muslim women
A female engineer → female engineers
examples.explanation: The singular has a short “a” before ة; the plural has a long “ā” before the open ت. Compare muslimatun with muslimātun: only the latter has the long “ā” before ت. The written ا makes the length clear.

concepts.title: A broken plural changes the inside
concepts.rule: Broken plurals have recurring patterns, but learn each noun’s plural.

examples.arabic:
نَجْمٌ ← نُجُومٌ
كِتَابٌ ← كُتُبٌ
جَبَلٌ ← جِبَالٌ
examples.translation:
A star → stars
A book → books
A mountain → mountains
examples.explanation: These examples follow فُعُولٌ, فُعُلٌ, and فِعَالٌ. The pattern letters ف ع ل stand for the word’s main consonants. The Key’s numbered transliterations use 1, 2, and 3 for those consonants. Learn the actual word pairs alongside the pattern.

concepts.title: More broken-plural patterns
concepts.rule: Use the singular–plural pair as your vocabulary unit.

examples.arabic:
تَاجِرٌ ← تُجَّارٌ
قَلَمٌ ← أَقْلَامٌ
أَخٌ ← إِخْوَةٌ
examples.translation:
A merchant → merchants
A pen → pens
A brother → brothers
examples.explanation: These follow فُعَّالٌ, أَفْعَالٌ, and فِعْلَةٌ. Notice the doubled middle consonant in تُجَّارٌ and the opening hamzah in أَقْلَامٌ. A plural is not always longer in the same way, so avoid guessing one ending for every noun.

concepts.title: Some broken plurals have no tanwin
concepts.rule: Remember the ending along with the plural: زُمَلَاءُ and أَصْدِقَاءُ.

examples.arabic:
زَمِيلٌ ← زُمَلَاءُ
صَدِيقٌ ← أَصْدِقَاءُ
examples.translation:
A classmate → classmates
A friend → friends
examples.explanation: زُمَلَاءُ follows فُعَلَاءُ, and أَصْدِقَاءُ follows أَفْعِلَاءُ. Both have one dammah here, not tanwin. Chapter 22 collects these patterns with other groups that do not take tanwin.

concepts.title: Learn these less regular feminine plurals
concepts.rule: Remember بَنَاتٌ، أَخَوَاتٌ، فَتَيَاتٌ as complete plural forms.

examples.arabic:
بِنْتٌ ← بَنَاتٌ
أُخْتٌ ← أَخَوَاتٌ
فَتَاةٌ ← فَتَيَاتٌ
examples.translation:
A daughter → daughters
A sister → sisters
A young woman → young women
examples.explanation: These end in ات, but their singular bases change as well. Learn the whole pair rather than trying to build the plural by adding ات mechanically.

concepts.title: Many non-Arabic names have no tanwin
concepts.rule: Learn the name’s ending too: these examples have no tanwin.

examples.arabic:
لَنْدَنُ   ·   بَاكِسْتَانُ   ·   وِلْيَمُ
إِبْرَاهِيمُ   ·   إِسْمَاعِيلُ
examples.translation:
London · Pakistan · William
Ibrahim · Ismail
examples.explanation: These examples end in a single dammah here. The Key also lists آدَمُ, إِسْحَاقُ, and يَعْقُوبُ. This is a grammatical classification of the names’ origins, and it has an exception in the next card.

concepts.title: A short-name exception
concepts.rule: These short masculine names keep tanwin.

examples.arabic: نُوحٌ   ·   لُوطٌ   ·   جُرْجٌ   ·   خَانٌ
examples.translation: Nuh · Lut · George · Khan
examples.explanation: These meet all three conditions described by the Key: masculine, three written letters, and sukun on the middle letter. Do not extend the “no tanwin” rule to every foreign name.

concepts.title: A longer broken-plural pattern
concepts.rule: Learn مَفَاعِلُ plurals without tanwin.

examples.arabic:
مَسْجِدٌ ← مَسَاجِدُ
دَفْتَرٌ ← دَفَاتِرُ
examples.translation:
A mosque → mosques
A notebook → notebooks
examples.explanation: They follow مَفَاعِلُ. The Key’s numbered pattern has four consonant positions here. Notice the single dammah rather than tanwin; Chapter 22 brings this together with related plural patterns.

concepts.title: One noun can have more than one plural
concepts.rule: A word may have more than one accepted plural form.

examples.arabic: حِمَارٌ ← حُمُرٌ / حَمِيرٌ
examples.translation: A donkey → donkeys (two plural forms)
examples.explanation: Both حُمُرٌ and حَمِيرٌ are given as plural forms. Since they refer to animals, connect them to the basic non-human plural agreement rule from Chapter 16. Learn both forms rather than assuming every noun has exactly one plural.

concepts.title: Arabic has a special form for two
concepts.rule: Use the dual for exactly two.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتٌ ← بَيْتَانِ
يَدٌ ← يَدَانِ
examples.translation:
A house → two houses
A hand → two hands
examples.explanation: The long “āni” ending expresses two without a separate number word. These are the forms shown in this lesson; other case forms of the dual are taught later.

concepts.title: A vowel can change inside an ـات plural
concepts.rule: Notice رَكْـ in the singular and رَكَـ in the plural.

examples.arabic: رَكْعَةٌ ← رَكَعَاتٌ
examples.translation: One rakʿah (unit of prayer) → rakʿahs
examples.explanation: The ك has sukun in رَكْعَةٌ but fathah in رَكَعَاتٌ. This is a reminder to learn a word’s actual plural rather than adding an ending and assuming every internal vowel stays the same.

concepts.title: Sometimes tanwin disappears because of the construction
concepts.rule: No tanwin can result from a construction, not just a special word class.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابٌ ← الْكِتَابُ
كِتَابٌ ← كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ
أُسْتَاذٌ ← يَا أُسْتَاذُ
examples.translation:
A book → the book
A book → Bilal’s book
A teacher → O teacher!
examples.explanation: These are familiar contextual reasons for omitting tanwin. They differ from the word groups in the following cards, which are classified as mamnuʿ min al-sarf, often called diptotes. Keep the direct-address rule tied to the forms taught so far.

concepts.title: Masculine names ending in ـان
concepts.rule: Keep the written ن, but do not add tanwin to these names.

examples.arabic: عُثْمَانُ   ·   رَمَضَانُ
examples.translation: Uthman · Ramadan
examples.explanation: The ن is part of the name, not the extra n-sound of tanwin. Each name has a single dammah here. The rule concerns this kind of proper name; it is not a rule for every Arabic word containing ان.

concepts.title: Names on the أَفْعَل pattern
concepts.rule: Learn أَحْمَدُ and أَنْوَرُ without tanwin.

examples.arabic: أَحْمَدُ   ·   أَنْوَرُ
examples.translation: Ahmad · Anwar
examples.explanation: Look at the word’s shape as well as its meaning. The opening hamzah and the rest of this pattern distinguish the class illustrated here. The last chapter uses أَحْمَدُ to show a special majrur ending.

concepts.title: Adjectives on أَفْعَل
concepts.rule: These colour adjectives on أَفْعَل have no tanwin.

examples.arabic: أَسْوَدُ   ·   أَحْمَرُ
examples.translation: Black · red
examples.explanation: The chapter’s vocabulary adds أَزْرَقُ (blue), أَخْضَرُ (green), أَصْفَرُ (yellow), and أَبْيَضُ (white). Learn the colour meaning together with the no-tanwin form. This card identifies the pattern illustrated, rather than claiming every adjective behaves this way.

concepts.title: Review: non-Arabic proper names
concepts.rule: Connect the summary with the exception already learned in Chapter 14.

examples.arabic: وِلْيَمُ   ·   لَنْدَنُ   ·   بَاكِسْتَانُ
examples.translation: William · London · Pakistan
examples.explanation: This reviews Chapter 14. Keep its short-name exception in mind: masculine three-letter names with an unvowelled middle consonant, such as نُوحٌ, were taught with tanwin. The summary does not cancel that earlier qualification.

concepts.title: Two plural patterns ending in ـاء
concepts.rule: These two broken-plural patterns belong to the no-tanwin class.

examples.arabic:
أَصْدِقَاءُ   ·   أَغْنِيَاءُ   ·   أَقْوِيَاءُ
فُقَرَاءُ   ·   زُمَلَاءُ   ·   وُزَرَاءُ
examples.translation:
Friends · rich people · strong people
Poor people · classmates · ministers
examples.explanation: The first row follows أَفْعِلَاء, the second فُعَلَاء. Compare the patterns with their earlier examples from Chapter 13. The common visible clue here is the ending اء, but learn the whole pattern rather than treating every اء word alike.

concepts.title: Two longer plural patterns without tanwin
concepts.rule: Recognise both مَفَاعِل and مَفَاعِيل as no-tanwin plural patterns here.

examples.arabic:
مَسَاجِدُ   ·   فَنَادِقُ   ·   مَكَاتِبُ
مَنَادِيلُ   ·   مَفَاتِيحُ   ·   فَنَاجِينُ
examples.translation:
Mosques · hotels · tables/desks
Handkerchiefs · keys · cups
examples.explanation: The first row follows مَفَاعِل; the second has the longer “ī” of مَفَاعِيل. All have a single dammah here. Compare مَسَاجِدُ and دَفَاتِرُ from Chapter 16.

concepts.title: A doubled letter can hide the pattern
concepts.rule: A shaddah can reflect two consonants merging inside a pattern.

examples.arabic: أَطِبَّاءُ
examples.translation: Doctors
examples.explanation: The Key explains an underlying form أَطْبِبَاءُ: the two ب letters combine, producing the shaddah in أَطِبَّاءُ. This small change can make the pattern less obvious. The result still has no tanwin.

concepts.title: A majrur name can end in “a”
concepts.rule: With these names, majrur is shown by “a,” without tanwin.

examples.arabic:
مِنْ أَحْمَدَ   ·   كِتَابُ أَحْمَدَ
مِنْ إِبْرَاهِيمَ   ·   كِتَابُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ
examples.translation:
From Ahmad · Ahmad’s book
From Ibrahim · Ibrahim’s book
examples.explanation: أَحْمَدَ and إِبْرَاهِيمَ are majrur in these examples: either they follow مِنْ or they are the owner in an idafah. Their “a” ending does not make them objects. Compare ordinary بِلَالٍ. This lesson illustrates names without الـ; do not generalise the ending to every form of every diptote.

concepts.title: ذُو means “having” or “possessing”
concepts.rule: ذُو plus a majrur noun can describe a quality someone has.

examples.arabic: ذُو مَالٍ   ·   ذُو خُلُقٍ   ·   ذُو عِلْمٍ
examples.translation: Possessing wealth (wealthy) · manners (well-mannered) · knowledge (learned)
examples.explanation: ذُو is the mudaf. مَالٍ, خُلُقٍ, and عِلْمٍ are mudaf ilayhi, so they are majrur. This builds directly on Book 1’s idafah and special-noun forms.

concepts.title: ذُو has feminine and plural partners
concepts.rule: Match the possessing form to the person or group it describes.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ ذُو عِلْمٍ وَأُخْتُهُ ذَاتُ خُلُقٍ
هَؤُلَاءِ الطُّلَّابُ ذَوُو خُلُقٍ
هَؤُلَاءِ الطَّالِبَاتُ ذَوَاتُ خُلُقٍ
examples.translation:
Bilal is learned and his sister is well-mannered.
These male students are well-mannered.
These female students are well-mannered.
examples.explanation: Use ذُو for masculine singular and ذَاتُ for feminine singular; the plurals here are ذَوُو and ذَوَاتُ. The quality after each form stays in the mudaf-ilayhi relationship.

concepts.title: A kasrah-looking ending need not mean majrur
concepts.rule: Work out grammatical case from the role, not only the last visible mark.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا الْكِتَابُ غَالٍ
أَنَا مُحَامٍ
أَبِي قَاضٍ
هَذَا وَادٍ
examples.translation:
This book is expensive.
I am a lawyer.
My father is a judge.
This is a valley.
examples.explanation: These are words with an underlying final ي, such as غَالِي and قَاضِي. In the indefinite forms shown, the ي and its dammah are omitted. The tanwin remains on the preceding letter. Their role here is still marfuʿ; more about this noun class comes later.

concepts.title: A name for two familiar plural patterns
concepts.rule: A new grammar term can name a pattern you already know.

examples.arabic: فَنَادِقُ   ·   فَنَاجِينُ
examples.translation: Hotels · cups
examples.explanation: You met these no-tanwin plural patterns at the end of Book 1. This point supplies the technical name مُنْتَهَى الْجُمُوعِ. Keep the familiar examples in mind so the new term has a concrete meaning.

concepts.title: Make a ذُو description definite through its second noun
concepts.rule: Keep الـ off ذُو; make its linked noun definite to match a definite thing described.

examples.arabic:
رَجُلٌ ذُو لِحْيَةٍ
الرَّجُلُ ذُو اللِّحْيَةِ
الْكِتَابُ ذُو الْغِلَافِ الْجَمِيلِ غَالٍ
examples.translation:
A bearded man
The bearded man
The book with the beautiful cover is expensive.
examples.explanation: ذُو لِحْيَةٍ qualifies indefinite رَجُلٌ. With definite الرَّجُلُ, the description is ذُو اللِّحْيَةِ, with الـ on the mudaf ilayhi. In the cover example, الْجَمِيلِ describes الْغِلَافِ and matches its definiteness and case.

concepts.title: A sound feminine plural uses kasrah for mansub
concepts.rule: Kasrah can mark a mansub sound feminine plural, not just a majrur noun.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُ الْأَبْنَاءَ وَالْبَنَاتِ
قَرَأْتُ الْكُتُبَ وَالصُّحُفَ وَالْمَجَلَّاتِ
examples.translation:
I saw the sons and the daughters.
I read the books, newspapers, and magazines.
examples.explanation: Both nouns in the first sentence are objects. الْأَبْنَاءَ has the usual fathah, while الْبَنَاتِ has kasrah because it belongs to the ـات plural class. In the second sentence, the same contrast appears with الْمَجَلَّاتِ.

concepts.title: “My brother” and “a brother of mine” differ in definiteness
concepts.rule: Attached “my” gives a definite noun; أَخٌ لِي keeps the noun indefinite.

examples.arabic: أَخِي   ·   أَخٌ لِي
examples.translation: My brother · a brother of mine
examples.explanation: The attached owner in أَخِي makes it definite through idafah. In أَخٌ لِي, the noun has tanwin and is indefinite; لِي gives the relationship separately. A similar meaning in English can hide a different Arabic construction.

concepts.title: ذُو becomes ذَا when mansub
concepts.rule: Match ذُو / ذَا to the case of the noun it describes.

examples.arabic:
فِي فَصْلِنَا طَالِبٌ ذُو شَعْرٍ طَوِيلٍ.
رَأَيْتُ طَالِبًا ذَا شَعْرٍ طَوِيلٍ.
أُرِيدُ مُصْحَفًا ذَا حَرْفٍ كَبِيرٍ.
examples.translation:
In our class there is a student with long hair.
I saw a student with long hair.
I want a copy of the Quran with large print.
examples.explanation: ذُو describes the marfu طَالِبٌ in the first example. With the mansub طَالِبًا or مُصْحَفًا, use ذَا. The noun following it remains majrur as part of the idafah: شَعْرٍ or حَرْفٍ. This ذَا means “having”; it is not a demonstrative here.

concepts.title: Another group of names without tanwin
concepts.rule: For these names: no tanwin, and fathah in the illustrated majrur form.

examples.arabic:
زُحَلُ · زُفَرُ · هُبَلُ
خَرَجَ عُمَرُ.
سَأَلْتُ عُمَرَ.
كَتَبْتُ إِلَى عُمَرَ.
examples.translation:
Saturn · Zufar · Hubal
Umar went out.
I asked Umar.
I wrote to Umar.
examples.explanation: The Key calls this pattern of proper names مَعْدُولٌ. These names have no tanwin. عُمَرُ has dammah as the subject, while عُمَرَ has fathah both as the object and after إِلَى. The last is majrur in grammatical role, even though its visible ending is a fathah.

concepts.title: أَشْيَاءُ is a diptote
concepts.rule: Remember أَشْيَاءُ without tanwin.

examples.arabic: شَيْءٌ · أَشْيَاءُ
examples.translation: A thing · things
examples.explanation: The Key explicitly identifies أَشْيَاءُ as مَمْنُوعٌ مِنَ الصَّرْفِ. Its singular شَيْءٌ can have tanwin, but this plural does not. Record the plural with its own grammatical behaviour rather than assuming it follows the singular.

concepts.title: Dual nouns use two case endings
concepts.rule: Dual: ـَانِ for marfu; ـَيْنِ for both mansub and majrur.

examples.arabic:
هَذَانِ رِيَالَانِ.
أُرِيدُ رِيَالَيْنِ.
اشْتَرَيْتُهُ بِرِيَالَيْنِ.
examples.translation:
These are two riyals.
I want two riyals.
I bought it for two riyals.
examples.explanation: A normal singular noun can show u, a or i for its three cases. The dual instead changes the long ending: riyālāni when marfu, riyālayni when mansub or majrur. The final nun has kasrah in both endings; that small final vowel alone does not identify the case.

concepts.title: Recognise dual ـَيْنِ in different jobs
concepts.rule: The dual ending ـَيْنِ serves two cases; context tells you which one.

examples.arabic:
قَرَأْتُ كِتَابَيْنِ.
رَجَعْتُ بَعْدَ يَوْمَيْنِ.
سَمِعْتُ هَذَا الْخَبَرَ مِنْ إِذَاعَتَيْنِ.
examples.translation:
I read two books.
I returned after two days.
I heard this news from two radio stations.
examples.explanation: كِتَابَيْنِ is mansub as the object. يَوْمَيْنِ is majrur after the mudaf بَعْدَ, and إِذَاعَتَيْنِ is majrur after مِنْ. All end in ـَيْنِ. Work out the grammatical job from the sentence rather than assuming that this ending always means an object.

concepts.title: Say “one of them … the other”
concepts.rule: Masculine: أَحَدُهُمَا / الْآخَرُ; feminine: إِحْدَاهُمَا / الْأُخْرَى.

examples.arabic:
لِي أَخَوَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا طَبِيبٌ وَالْآخَرُ مُهَنْدِسٌ.
لِي أُخْتَانِ: إِحْدَاهُمَا مُدَرِّسَةٌ وَالْأُخْرَى مُمَرِّضَةٌ.
examples.translation:
I have two brothers: one is a doctor and the other is an engineer.
I have two sisters: one is a teacher and the other is a nurse.
examples.explanation: For the brothers, use أَحَدُهُمَا … وَالْآخَرُ. For the sisters, use إِحْدَاهُمَا … وَالْأُخْرَى. The attached هُمَا refers to the pair in both cases; the words meaning “one” and “the other” carry the gender distinction.

concepts.title: Sound masculine plurals change ـُونَ to ـِينَ
concepts.rule: Sound masculine plural: ūna when marfu, īna when mansub or majrur.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجَ الْمُدَرِّسُونَ.
رَأَيْتُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ.
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْمُدَرِّسِينَ.
هَذِهِ بُيُوتُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ.
examples.translation:
The teachers went out.
I saw the teachers.
I went to the teachers.
These are the teachers’ houses.
examples.explanation: The teachers are a subject, object, noun after a preposition, and mudaf ilayhi respectively. The last three jobs use ـِينَ. Do not confuse this īna ending with the dual ـَيْنِ (ayni); their vowels and grammatical number differ.

concepts.title: Father and brother have long-vowel case endings
concepts.rule: Learn أَبُو / أَبَا / أَبِي and أَخُو / أَخَا / أَخِي by their case roles.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ أَبُوكَ؟
أَعْرِفُ أَبَاكَ.
مَاذَا قُلْتَ لِأَبِيكَ؟
أَيْنَ ذَهَبَ أَخُوهَا؟
أَرَأَيْتَ أَخَاهَا؟
أَذَهَبْتَ إِلَى أَخِيهَا؟
examples.translation:
Where is your father?
I know your father.
What did you tell your father?
Where did her brother go?
Did you see her brother?
Did you go to her brother?
examples.explanation: The waw marks marfu, alif marks mansub and ya marks majrur. Notice that the attached possessor remains the same within each set: ـكَ or ـهَا. These examples concern the mudaf forms; do not apply the long-vowel pattern to every occurrence of أَب or أَخ.

concepts.title: Learn the فَعْلَى plural pattern
concepts.rule: Remember these فَعْلَى plurals without tanwin.

examples.arabic:
مَرِيضٌ ← مَرْضَى
قَتِيلٌ ← قَتْلَى
جَرِيحٌ ← جَرْحَى
أَسِيرٌ ← أَسْرَى
أَحْمَقُ ← حَمْقَى
examples.translation:
Sick person → sick people
Killed person → those killed
Wounded person → wounded people
Prisoner → prisoners
Foolish person → foolish people
examples.explanation: The Key identifies مَرْضَى as a diptote and supplies parallel examples. Their final alif is written ى. Learn the plural with the singular; a familiar singular ending does not predict a regular ـون or ـات plural here.

concepts.title: Check what the idafah is linked to
concepts.rule: In these ordinary idafahs, a definite complement makes the phrase definite; an indefinite complement leaves it indefinite.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابُ هَذَا · كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ · كِتَابُهُ · كِتَابُ حَامِدٍ
كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ · بَيْتُ مُدَرِّسٍ
examples.translation:
This person’s book · the teacher’s book · his book · Hamid’s book
A student’s book · a teacher’s house
examples.explanation: The first line has definite complements: a demonstrative, an article-bearing noun, a pronoun and a name. The second line has indefinite complements, so its phrases remain indefinite. Omission of tanwin from the mudaf occurs in both lines and does not by itself prove definiteness.

concepts.title: Recognize several ways of being definite
concepts.rule: Personal pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, relative pronouns, and nouns with الـ are definite categories in this source.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا · أَنْتَ · هُوَ
أَحْمَدُ · بِلَالٌ · مَكَّةُ
هَذَا · ذَلِكَ · أُولَئِكَ
الَّذِي · الَّذِينَ · الَّتِي
الْكِتَابُ · الرَّجُلُ
examples.translation:
I · you · he
Ahmad · Bilal · Makkah
This · that · those
Relative pronouns: who/which
The book · the man
examples.explanation: The first five definite categories listed are personal pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, relative pronouns, and nouns bearing الْـ. Relative مَا and مَنْ also belong to the relative category when used in that function. A proper name can take tanwin and still be definite.

concepts.title: A sound feminine plural uses kasrah for nasb
concepts.rule: Kasrah can mark a sound feminine plural object.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُ السَّيَّارَاتِ.
خَرَجَ النَّاسُ مِنَ السَّيَّارَاتِ.
examples.translation:
I saw the cars.
The people came out of the cars.
examples.explanation: السَّيَّارَاتِ is an object in the first example and follows a preposition in the second. Both take kasrah, but only the second is majrur. The first is mansub with a secondary sign: kasrah instead of fathah. The article’s sun-letter assimilation still applies in pronunciation.

concepts.title: A diptote uses fathah for jarr in these examples
concepts.rule: Do not call every fathah-ending noun an object.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابُ زَيْنَبَ.
سَأَلْتُ زَيْنَبَ.
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى زَيْنَبَ.
examples.translation:
This is Zainab’s book.
I asked Zainab.
I went to Zainab.
examples.explanation: زَيْنَبَ is majrur as mudaf ilayhi and after إِلَى, but mansub as an object. The diptote’s fathah replaces kasrah in the illustrated jarr forms. It has no tanwin. Later conditions involving the article and idafah refine this rule.

concepts.title: The five nouns need conditions for their long endings
concepts.rule: Use the long case signs only when their conditions are met.

examples.arabic:
أَبٌ · أَخٌ · حَمٌ · فَمٌ · ذُو
مَاذَا قَالَ أَبُو بِلَالٍ؟
أَعْرِفُ أَبَا بِلَالٍ.
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى أَبِي بِلَالٍ.
examples.translation:
Father · brother · male in-law · mouth · having
What did Bilal’s father say?
I know Bilal’s father.
I went to Bilal’s father.
examples.explanation: In the forms taught here, these nouns take waw for raf, alif for nasb and ya for jarr when they are mudaf to something other than first-person singular ya. حَمٌ refers to a husband’s male relative. Keep the long vowels: abū, abā, abī.

concepts.title: “My brother” keeps the same visible ending
concepts.rule: Distinguish possession by “my” from the ordinary unpossessed noun.

examples.arabic:
يَدْرُسُ أَخِي بِالْجَامِعَةِ.
أَتَعْرِفُ أَخِي؟
خُذِ الْعُنْوَانَ مِنْ أَخِي.
هُوَ أَخٌ. · رَأَيْتُ أَخًا. · هَذَا مِنْ أَخٍ.
examples.translation:
My brother studies at the university.
Do you know my brother?
Take the address from my brother.
He is a brother. · I saw a brother. · This is from a brother.
examples.explanation: أَخِي has subject, object and prepositional roles without an audible case change. Without idafah, أَخٌ follows the ordinary short-vowel signs instead. These are two separate reasons not to use أَخُو / أَخَا / أَخِي mechanically.

concepts.title: “Mouth” has two case patterns
concepts.rule: Check whether mim is present before choosing the case ending.

examples.arabic:
فَمُكَ نَظِيفٌ. · اِفْتَحْ فَمَكَ. · مَاذَا فِي فَمِكَ؟
فُوكَ صَغِيرٌ. · اِفْتَحْ فَاكَ. · مَاذَا فِي فِيكَ؟
examples.translation:
Your mouth is clean. · Open your mouth. · What is in your mouth?
Your mouth is small. · Open your mouth. · What is in your mouth?
examples.explanation: With mim, فَم uses the primary short-vowel signs. Without mim, it follows the five-noun pattern: فُو / فَا / فِي. The attached كَ still means “your”; it does not itself determine which pattern is used.

concepts.title: Sound masculine plurals use ūna and īna
concepts.rule: Only the mudaf loses its sound-plural nun.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلَ الْمُدَرِّسُونَ.
مَا سَأَلْتُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ.
أَيْنَ غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ؟
أَيْنَ مُدَرِّسُو الْقُرْآنِ؟
أَرَأَيْتَ مُدَرِّسِي الْقُرْآنِ؟
examples.translation:
The teachers entered.
I did not ask the teachers.
Where is the teachers’ room?
Where are the Quran teachers?
Did you see the Quran teachers?
examples.explanation: Waw marks marfu; ya marks mansub and majrur. In مُدَرِّسُو الْقُرْآنِ and مُدَرِّسِي الْقُرْآنِ, the teachers are the mudaf, so nun drops. Being mudaf ilayhi, as in غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ, does not cause that omission.

concepts.title: The dual uses āni and ayni
concepts.rule: Dual case is carried by alif or ya, even after nun is omitted.

examples.arabic:
أَجَاءَ الْمُدَرِّسَانِ الْجَدِيدَانِ؟
أَرَأَيْتَ الْمُدَرِّسَيْنِ؟
أَسْأَلُ عَنِ الْمُدَرِّسَيْنِ.
أَيْنَ تَدْرُسُ أُخْتَا بِلَالٍ؟
أَتَعْرِفِينَ أُخْتَيْ بِلَالٍ؟
examples.translation:
Have the two new teachers come?
Did you see the two teachers?
I am asking about the two teachers.
Where do Bilal’s two sisters study?
Do you know Bilal’s two sisters?
examples.explanation: Alif marks raf and ya marks nasb/jarr. As a mudaf, أُخْتَانِ becomes أُخْتَا and أُخْتَيْنِ becomes أُخْتَيْ. Keep this distinct from sound masculine plural ū / ī.

concepts.title: An ā-ending noun can hide every case sign
concepts.rule: No audible case vowel does not mean no grammatical case.

examples.arabic: قَتَلَ الْفَتَى الْأَفْعَى بِالْعَصَا.
examples.translation: The young man killed the viper with the stick.
examples.explanation: الْفَتَى is the subject, الْأَفْعَى the object and الْعَصَا follows بِـ. All end in long ā, so none pronounces an added u, a or i. Their grammatical jobs still differ. الْإِعْرَابُ التَّقْدِيرِيُّ means that the ending is understood rather than visibly expressed.

concepts.title: First-person possession can hide case signs
concepts.rule: Use syntax to analyse a noun attached to “my.”

examples.arabic:
دَعَا جَدِّي أُسْتَاذِي مَعَ زُمَلَائِي.
دَعَا جَدُّكَ أُسْتَاذَكَ مَعَ زُمَلَائِكَ.
examples.translation:
My grandfather invited my teacher with my classmates.
Your grandfather invited your teacher with your classmates.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, جَدِّي is subject, أُسْتَاذِي object and زُمَلَائِي mudaf ilayhi. Their case signs are latent. With كَ instead, جَدُّكَ, أُسْتَاذَكَ and زُمَلَائِكَ show the three case vowels.

concepts.title: A manqus noun shows a, but hides u and i
concepts.rule: Manqus hides raf and jarr vowels but expresses the nasb fathah.

examples.arabic: سَأَلَ الْقَاضِي الْمُحَامِيَ عَنِ الْجَانِي.
examples.translation: The judge asked the advocate about the culprit.
examples.explanation: الْقَاضِي is marfu and الْجَانِي majrur, with latent case vowels. The mansub الْمُحَامِيَ pronounces its final a. This differs from the maqsur, which hides all three. The ya here belongs to the noun, not a possessive “my” suffix.

concepts.title: When does a manqus retain its ya?
concepts.rule: Look for الْـ, idafah or nasb before deciding whether to retain ya.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا قَاضٍ. · سَأَلْتُ قَاضِيًا. · هَذَا بَيْتُ قَاضٍ.
الْقَاضِي · قَاضِي مَكَّةَ
عَبَرْتُ وَادِيًا.
examples.translation:
This is a judge. · I asked a judge. · This is a judge’s house.
The judge · the judge of Makkah
I crossed a valley.
examples.explanation: An indefinite non-mudaf manqus loses final ya in the marfu and majrur forms, giving قَاضٍ. Ya remains with الْـ, as mudaf, and when mansub. The tanwin in قَاضٍ does not mean it must be majrur: the first example is marfu.

concepts.title: Fixed nouns occupy case positions
concepts.rule: A fixed word can occupy a subject, object or genitive position.

examples.arabic:
نَحْنُ طُلَّابٌ. · أَرَأَيْتَنَا؟ · هَذَا بَيْتُنَا.
رَأَيْتُ بِلَالًا. · رَأَيْتُ هَذَا.
examples.translation:
We are students. · Did you see us? · This is our house.
I saw Bilal. · I saw this.
examples.explanation: Pronouns have separately learned subject, object and possessive forms, so they remain classed as indeclinable. For هَذَا as object, say فِي مَحَلِّ نَصْبٍ, “in the position of nasb,” rather than giving it a new final vowel. Contrast the visibly mansub بِلَالًا.

concepts.title: Recognise the fixed groups and their exceptions
concepts.rule: Learn fixed groups together with their stated dual and twelve exceptions.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا · ذَلِكَ · هَؤُلَاءِ
الَّذِي · الَّتِي · الَّذِينَ
مَنْ · أَيْنَ · مَتَى · كَيْفَ
إِذَا · حَيْثُ · أَمْسِ · الْآنَ
آمِينَ · آهِ · أُفٍّ
examples.translation:
This · that · these
Who/which (relative forms)
Who · where · when · how
When · where · yesterday · now
Accept · expression of pain · expression of annoyance
examples.explanation: The Key lists demonstratives, relative pronouns, some question words, some adverbs, verb-nouns, and compound numbers 11–19. The dual demonstratives هَذَانِ / هَاتَانِ and dual relatives اللَّذَانِ / اللَّتَانِ are declinable. In twelve, only the first part declines. An ism fil such as آمِينَ is not a masdar.

concepts.title: Why أَشْيَاءُ is a diptote
concepts.rule: Learn the actual form together with its diptote behaviour.

examples.arabic:
أَشْيَاءُ
أَغْنِيَاءُ · أَنْبِيَاءُ · أَصْدِقَاءُ
examples.translation:
Things
Rich people · prophets · friends
examples.explanation: The Key connects the diptote behaviour of أَشْيَاءُ with the plural pattern illustrated by أَغْنِيَاءُ, أَنْبِيَاءُ and أَصْدِقَاءُ. Learn the actual form أَشْيَاءُ without tanwin.

concepts.title: مَعَانٍ follows the manqus pattern
concepts.rule: Learn the plural’s retained and omitted ya forms.

examples.arabic:
مَعْنًى ← مَعَانٍ · الْمَعَانِي
جَارِيَةٌ ← جَوَارٍ · الْجَوَارِي
لَيْلَةٌ ← لَيَالٍ · اللَّيَالِي
نَادٍ ← نَوَادٍ · النَّوَادِي
أَعْرِفُ لِلْوَاوِ مَعَانِيَ كَثِيرَةً.
examples.translation:
Meaning → meanings
Girl → girls
Night → nights
Club → clubs
I know many meanings of waw.
examples.explanation: The indefinite marfu and majrur forms shown end in ـٍ without the final ya. Ya returns with الْـ and appears in the mansub form مَعَانِيَ. Use the manqus analysis from Lesson 1 rather than assuming every kasrah-shaped tanwin means jarr.

concepts.title: A collective can form its unit with ـِيّ or ة
concepts.rule: A ة ending can mark one unit of a collective, not a female member.

examples.arabic:
عَرَبٌ ← عَرَبِيٌّ
تُرْكٌ ← تُرْكِيٌّ
تُفَّاحٌ ← تُفَّاحَةٌ
شَجَرٌ ← شَجَرَةٌ
سَمَكٌ ← سَمَكَةٌ
examples.translation:
Arabs → an Arab
Turks → a Turk
Apples → an apple
Trees → a tree
Fish → a fish
examples.explanation: These are examples of اِسْمُ الْجِنْسِ الْجَمْعِيّ. Some form an individual member with ـِيّ, others with ة. The unit-forming ya here is distinguished in the Key from the nisbah process introduced earlier. Learn whether a noun denotes the class or a single item.

concepts.title: Count units from the individual form
concepts.rule: Build the dual from the individual-member noun.

examples.arabic:
أُحِبُّ الْمَوْزَ.
آكُلُ مَوْزَةً.
عَرَبِيَّانِ · مَوْزَتَانِ
examples.translation:
I like bananas.
I eat one banana.
Two Arabs · two bananas
examples.explanation: The collective الْمَوْز names bananas as a kind. مَوْزَةً names one banana. Form the dual from عَرَبِيّ or مَوْزَة, not by simply adding a dual suffix to عَرَب or مَوْز.

concepts.title: “Both” uses كِلَا and كِلْتَا
concepts.rule: Use the singular predicate in the illustrated كِلَا / كِلْتَا construction.

examples.arabic:
كِلَا الطَّالِبَيْنِ فِي الْمَكْتَبَةِ.
كِلْتَا السَّيَّارَتَيْنِ أَمَامَ الْبَيْتِ.
كِلَا الطَّالِبَيْنِ تَخَرَّجَ.
كِلْتَا السَّاعَتَيْنِ جَمِيلَةٌ.
examples.translation:
Both students are in the library.
Both cars are in front of the house.
Both students graduated.
Both watches are beautiful.
examples.explanation: Use كِلَا for masculine and كِلْتَا for feminine. In the pattern taught here, their predicate is singular: تَخَرَّجَ, not a dual verb, and جَمِيلَةٌ, not a dual adjective. This follows their singular grammatical form despite the meaning “both.”

concepts.title: “Both” changes case only with a pronoun here
concepts.rule: Check whether the complement is a noun or a pronoun.

examples.arabic:
أَعْرِفُ كِلَا الرَّجُلَيْنِ.
بَحَثْتُ عَنْ كِلَا الرَّجُلَيْنِ.
رَأَيْتُ كِلَيْهِمَا.
سَأَلْتُ كِلْتَيْهِمَا.
بَحَثْتُ عَنْ كِلَيْهِمَا.
examples.translation:
I know both men.
I looked for both men.
I saw both of them (male).
I asked both of them (female).
I looked for both of them (male).
examples.explanation: With an expressed noun, كِلَا and كِلْتَا retain their final ā in nasb and jarr. With a pronoun, they decline like the dual: كِلَاهُمَا becomes كِلَيْهِمَا, and كِلْتَاهُمَا becomes كِلْتَيْهِمَا.

concepts.title: Two more broken-plural patterns
concepts.rule: Recognise the complete plural shape.

examples.arabic:
طَالِبٌ ← طَلَبَةٌ
نُسْخَةٌ ← نُسَخٌ
examples.translation:
Student → students
Copy → copies
examples.explanation: طَلَبَةٌ follows فَعَلَةٌ; نُسَخٌ follows فُعَلٌ. A ta marbutah in a plural does not by itself mean the people are female. These are lexical plural patterns, not endings to attach to every noun.

concepts.title: Some plurals have another plural
concepts.rule: A second plural may be a separate vocabulary item.

examples.arabic:
طَرِيقٌ ← طُرُقٌ ← طُرُقَاتٌ
مَكَانٌ ← أَمْكِنَةٌ ← أَمَاكِنُ
أَيْدٍ · أَيَادٍ
بُيُوتٌ · بُيُوتَاتٌ
examples.translation:
Road → roads → roads
Place → places → places
Hands · favours
Houses · respectable families
examples.explanation: The Key calls this a plural of a plural. It often has the same general plural meaning, but some words develop a distinct meaning. Other examples include أَسْوِرَةٌ → أَسَاوِرُ. Learn the lexical contrast rather than adding a plural ending freely.

concepts.title: Dhu has plural forms dhawoo and dhawii
concepts.rule: Read the waw/ya ending as a case sign.

examples.arabic:
ذَوُو الْقُرْبَى أَحَقُّ بِمُسَاعَدَتِكَ.
سَاعِدْ ذَوِي الْعِلْمِ.
سَأَلْتُ عَنْ ذَوِي الْحَاجَاتِ.
examples.translation:
Relatives deserve your help more.
Help people of knowledge.
I asked about needy people.
examples.explanation: ذَوُو marks raf; ذَوِي marks nasb or jarr. They mean people possessing the following quality. In these idafah examples the following noun is majrur.

concepts.title: Final plural patterns can shorten long words
concepts.rule: Learn the attested plural; shortening is not arbitrary spelling.

examples.arabic:
بَرْنَامَجٌ ← بَرَامِجُ
عَنْكَبُوتٌ ← عَنَاكِبُ
مُسْتَشْفًى ← مَشَافٍ
دَكَاكِينُ · مَفَاتِيحُ
examples.translation:
Programme → programmes
Spider → spiders
Hospital → hospitals
Shops · keys
examples.explanation: فَعَالِلُ and فَعَالِيلُ belong to muntaha al-jumu. Longer singulars may drop letters when forming this pattern: برنامج loses nun and the singular alif. The Key also gives سَفَارِجُ and عَنَادِلُ. Hospitals additionally has the sound feminine plural مُسْتَشْفَيَاتٌ.

concepts.title: Recognise the khataya family of plurals
concepts.rule: Recognise aya as part of these plural words.

examples.arabic:
خَطِيئَةٌ ← خَطَايَا
هَدِيَّةٌ ← هَدَايَا
مَنِيَّةٌ ← مَنَايَا
زَاوِيَةٌ ← زَوَايَا
examples.translation:
Sin → sins
Gift → gifts
Fate/death → fates
Angle → angles
examples.explanation: The Key groups these plural examples by their form. They are whole-word broken plurals. Do not add a sound-plural ending to produce them.

concepts.title: Nouns on فُعْلَةٌ change their middle vowel in the plural
concepts.rule: Read the internal vowel as well as the plural suffix.

examples.arabic:
حُجْرَةٌ ← حُجُرَاتٌ
غُرْفَةٌ ← غُرُفَاتٌ
خُطْوَةٌ ← خُطُوَاتٌ
examples.translation:
Room → rooms
Room → rooms
Step → steps
examples.explanation: For the فُعْلَةٌ pattern illustrated, the second consonant has sukun in the singular and dammah in the sound feminine plural. The plural is not made by attaching at while leaving every internal vowel unchanged.

concepts.title: Final-weak doer nouns can have فُعَلَةٌ plurals
concepts.rule: Learn the actual plural with the manqus singular.

examples.arabic:
مَاشٍ ← مُشَاةٌ
قَاضٍ ← قُضَاةٌ
حَافٍ ← حُفَاةٌ
عَارٍ ← عُرَاةٌ
وَالٍ ← وُلَاةٌ
examples.translation:
Pedestrian → pedestrians
Judge → judges
Barefoot → barefoot people
Unclothed → unclothed people
Ruler → rulers
examples.explanation: The Key explains these through فُعَلَةٌ with contraction of aya. The plural ta marbutah is part of a broken-plural pattern, not a feminine marker for the people.

concepts.title: Fala plurals end in alif and take no tanwin
concepts.rule: A hidden ending does not make the noun outside the case system.

examples.arabic:
مَيِّتٌ ← مَوْتَى
أَسِيرٌ ← أَسْرَى
مَرِيضٌ ← مَرْضَى
جَرِيحٌ ← جَرْحَى
examples.translation:
Dead → the dead
Captive → captives
Ill → patients
Wounded → wounded people
examples.explanation: The Key groups these under فَعْلَى and identifies them as diptotes. Their final alif also hides ordinary case vowels. Keep the actual plural spelling and avoid adding tanwin.

concepts.title: Some state plurals serve both masculine and feminine
concepts.rule: A shared plural shape can serve both genders and more than one noun function.

examples.arabic:
نَائِمٌ · نَائِمَةٌ ← نِيَامٌ
قَائِمٌ · قَائِمَةٌ ← قِيَامٌ
قَاعِدٌ · قَاعِدَةٌ ← قُعُودٌ
جَالِسٌ · جَالِسَةٌ ← جُلُوسٌ
examples.translation:
Sleeping → plural
Standing → plural
Seated → plural
Sitting → plural
examples.explanation: These broken plurals can describe groups of either gender. The source illustrates women with نِسْوَةٌ جُلُوسٌ. Several of the same words are also masdars, so context identifies the plural adjective meaning here.

concepts.title: A plural can reveal an extra copy of a consonant
concepts.rule: A broken plural may reveal a fuller consonant structure.

examples.arabic:
دِينَارٌ ← دَنَانِيرُ
دِيوَانٌ ← دَوَاوِينُ
قِيرَاطٌ ← قَرَارِيطُ
examples.translation:
Dinar → dinars
Poetry collection → collections
Carat → carats
examples.explanation: The Key highlights the consonant restoration/doubling in this plural family, also listing دِيمَاسٌ. Learn the whole plural rather than copying the singular’s visible consonants unchanged.

concepts.title: Diptotes are declinable nouns without ordinary tanwin
concepts.rule: No tanwin does not mean no declension.

examples.arabic: إِبْرَاهِيمُ · فَاطِمَةُ · أَحْمَرُ · مَسَاجِدُ · زُمَلَاءُ
examples.translation: Ibrahim · Fatimah · red · mosques · colleagues
examples.explanation: A diptote is muarab, not mabni. It has case roles, even when two cases share a visible ending. Some structural patterns alone suffice; proper nouns and adjectives need their category plus another qualifying feature.

concepts.title: Added feminine alif can make a word diptote
concepts.rule: The origin of the ending matters, not just its appearance.

examples.arabic:
مَرْضَى · دُنْيَا · حُبْلَى · هَدَايَا
صَحْرَاءُ · حَمْرَاءُ · أَصْدِقَاءُ
فَتًى · عَصًا · أَسْمَاءٌ
examples.translation:
Patients · world · pregnant · gifts
Desert · red female · friends
Young man · stick · names
examples.explanation: Both short/maqsur feminine alif and elongated alif-hamza must be extra beyond the root for this cause. Fata and asa have a root-final alif and are not diptotes for this reason. Asma and the other afal plurals listed have root hamza, so they accept tanwin.

concepts.title: Ultimate plural shapes independently cause diptote behaviour
concepts.rule: Use the complete Arabic form rather than its English number.

examples.arabic:
مَسَاجِدُ · مَدَارِسُ · مَفَاتِيحُ · أَسَابِيعُ
تَلَامِذَةٌ · دَكَاتِرَةٌ · أَسَاتِذَةٌ
سَرَاوِيلُ · طَبَاشِيرُ
examples.translation:
Mosques · schools · keys · weeks
Pupils · doctors · teachers
Trousers · chalk
examples.explanation: The Key gives mafail/mafail-like ultimate patterns. Words with the additional ta marbutah accept tanwin. Even non-plural nouns with the same structural shapes can be diptote, such as trousers and chalk. Tomatoes/potatoes are treated as collective common nouns despite plural English meanings.

concepts.title: Feminine proper names are normally diptote
concepts.rule: Keep the short-name option alongside the general feminine-name rule.

examples.arabic:
آمِنَةُ · زَيْنَبُ · حَمْزَةُ
هِنْدُ / هِنْدٌ
examples.translation:
Aminah · Zaynab · Hamzah
Hind (two permitted declensions)
examples.explanation: Hamzah is a man’s name ending in feminine ta marbutah. The Key permits either diptote or ordinary declension for three-letter feminine proper names whose middle letter is sakin, preferring diptote. It lists Hind, Dad and Rim.

concepts.title: Non-Arabic proper names have stated exceptions
concepts.rule: Foreign origin alone is not an exceptionless rule.

examples.arabic:
إِبْرَاهِيمُ · وِلْيَمُ · بَاكِسْتَانُ
نُوحٌ · لُوطٌ · شِيثٌ
جَوْهَرٌ
examples.translation:
Ibrahim · William · Pakistan
Nuh · Lut · Shith
Jawhar
examples.explanation: A masculine non-Arabic name of three letters with a sakin middle accepts tanwin in the Key. Feminine names remain diptote, including the listed city names. A borrowed common noun later used as a name, such as Persian jawhar “gem”, accepts tanwin.

concepts.title: Altered fual names and extra an endings are diptote
concepts.rule: Recover the root before deciding whether an ending is additional.

examples.arabic:
عُمَرُ · زُحَلُ · زُفَرُ
رَمَضَانُ · مَرْوَانُ · عُثْمَانُ
حَسَّانٌ
examples.translation:
Umar · Saturn · Zufar
Ramadan · Marwan · Uthman
Hassan
examples.explanation: The Key lists madul proper names on فُعَلُ and names ending in extra alif plus nun. Hassan accepts tanwin in its stated analysis because nun is the third radical of ح س ن, not an extra suffix.

concepts.title: Verb-shaped and fused compound names can be diptote
concepts.rule: Classify the whole proper name before applying its endings.

examples.arabic:
أَحْمَدُ · يَزِيدُ
مَعْدِيكَرِبُ · حَضْرَمَوْتُ
examples.translation:
Ahmad · Yazid
Madikarib · Hadramawt
examples.explanation: Ahmad and Yazid resemble verb shapes; the latter examples combine two nouns into fused names. This is not the ordinary two-word idafah construction. The Key treats the listed structural families as additional causes alongside being a proper name.

concepts.title: Afal and falan adjectives are diptote under their conditions
concepts.rule: A masculine adjective’s shape alone may not settle its declension.

examples.arabic:
أَكْبَرُ · أَحْمَرُ
أَرْمَلٌ · أَرْمَلَةٌ
جَوْعَانُ · شَبْعَانُ · عَطْشَانُ
examples.translation:
Greater · red
Widower · widow
Hungry · full · thirsty
examples.explanation: The Key’s afal condition is that the feminine is not formed with ta marbutah: kubra and hamra qualify, while armal/armalah does not. It also lists falan adjectives such as hungry and thirsty. Learn the adjective family with its feminine form.

concepts.title: Distributive numbers and ukhar are altered adjectives
concepts.rule: Recognise distributive number forms separately from ordinary counted numbers.

examples.arabic:
ثُلَاثُ · رُبَاعُ · مَثْنَى · مَثْلَثُ
أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ
examples.translation:
Three at a time · four at a time · two at a time · three at a time
Other days
examples.explanation: The Key lists distributive patterns فُعَالُ and مَفْعَلُ under madul adjectives. It also gives أُخَرُ, plural of أُخْرَى. In أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ, the adjective is majrur in role but shows the diptote fathah ending.

concepts.title: A bare diptote uses fathah for jarr
concepts.rule: Case role and the particular noun’s visible case sign are different things.

examples.arabic:
دَرَسْتُ فِي مَدَارِسَ كَثِيرَةٍ.
هَذِهِ كُتُبُ زَيْنَبَ.
examples.translation:
I studied in many schools.
These are Zaynab’s books.
examples.explanation: A diptote has raf with dammah, nasb with fathah, and jarr with fathah in the bare construction. Its ordinary adjective still follows the actual jarr role and can show kasrah, as كثيرة does. The second example places Zaynab as mudaf ilayhi, not as mudaf.

concepts.title: Al or being mudaf restores kasrah for jarr
concepts.rule: Check al and idafah role before choosing the diptote jarr sign.

examples.arabic:
نَزَلْتُ فِي هَذِهِ الْفَنَادِقِ.
اُكْتُبْ بِالْقَلَمِ الْأَحْمَرِ.
دَرَّسْتُ فِي مَدَارِسِ الْمَدِينَةِ.
هُوَ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ الطُّلَّابِ.
examples.translation:
I stayed in these hotels.
Write with the red pen.
I taught in Madinah’s schools.
He is one of the best students.
examples.explanation: A diptote takes regular kasrah in jarr when it has al or is itself mudaf. Tanwin does not return because al/idafah independently exclude it. Being mudaf ilayhi alone does not restore kasrah; the diptote must be the possessing first term for that condition.

concepts.title: Manqus ultimate plurals have special surface endings
concepts.rule: Learn the raf/jarr short form and the nasb ya form as one paradigm.

examples.arabic:
مَعَانٍ · الْمَعَانِي
لَهَا مَعَانٍ كَثِيرَةٌ.
أَعْرِفُ مَعَانِيَ كَثِيرَةً.
تُسْتَعْمَلُ بِمَعَانٍ كَثِيرَةٍ.
examples.translation:
Meanings · the meanings
It has many meanings.
I know many meanings.
It is used with many meanings.
examples.explanation: The Key combines manqus rules with the ultimate plural family: final ya is absent in indefinite raf/jarr and restored with al. In indefinite nasb it remains with fathah and without tanwin. جوار and نواد follow the same family. This explicit qualification prevents treating every ultimate plural as visibly tanwin-free in every form.

concepts.title: A little word for “this”
concepts.rule: Write هَذَا. Keep its first vowel long when you read it.

examples.arabic: هَذَا كِتَابٌ
examples.translation: This is a book.
examples.explanation: The first “a” sound in هَذَا is long, even though a full alif is not written there. The small alif above the letter helps show that long sound.

concepts.title: From “this” to “that”
concepts.rule: هَذَا points near; ذَلِكَ points farther away.

examples.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ وَذَلِكَ مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation: This is a house and that is a mosque.
examples.explanation: Like هَذَا, ذَلِكَ has a long “a” sound that is not written with a full alif. The small alif in a fully marked text helps you read it. Both words refer to masculine nouns in this lesson.

concepts.title: “He” and “she” can also mean “it”
concepts.rule: Choose هُوَ or هِيَ according to the Arabic noun’s gender.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ الْكِتَابُ؟ هُوَ عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ
أَيْنَ السَّاعَةُ؟ هِيَ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
examples.translation:
Where is the book? It is on the table.
Where is the watch? It is on the bed.
examples.explanation: Arabic nouns have grammatical gender. كِتَابٌ is masculine, so use هُوَ. سَاعَةٌ is feminine, so use هِيَ. Most feminine nouns end in ة, but some do not. Learn a noun’s gender along with its meaning.

concepts.title: A feminine word for “this”
concepts.rule: Match “this” to the noun: هَذَا for masculine, هَذِهِ for feminine.

examples.arabic: هَذَا وَلَدٌ وَهَذِهِ بِنْتٌ
examples.translation: This is a boy and this is a girl.
examples.explanation: وَلَدٌ is masculine, so it goes with هَذَا. بِنْتٌ is feminine, so it goes with هَذِهِ. Like هَذَا, هَذِهِ has a long first “a” sound without a full alif in its spelling.

concepts.title: A feminine word for “that”
concepts.rule: For feminine singular nouns: هَذِهِ means “this,” and تِلْكَ means “that.”

examples.arabic:
هَذَا بِلَالٌ، وَذَلِكَ حَامِدٌ
هَذِهِ آمِنَةُ، وَتِلْكَ مَرْيَمُ
examples.translation:
This is Bilal, and that is Hamid.
This is Aminah, and that is Maryam.
examples.explanation: You now have two pairs: هَذَا and ذَلِكَ for masculine nouns, and هَذِهِ and تِلْكَ for feminine nouns. The first word in each pair points near; the second points farther away. Match the demonstrative to the Arabic noun’s gender.

concepts.title: “This is a book” or “this book”?
concepts.rule: هَذَا الْكِتَابُ means “this book”; it is not yet a full sentence.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابٌ
هَذَا الْكِتَابُ
examples.translation:
This is a book.
This book
examples.explanation: هَذَا كِتَابٌ is a complete statement. هَذَا الْكِتَابُ points out a particular book but does not yet say anything about it. In this lesson’s construction, the definite noun joins with “this” to make one phrase.

concepts.title: Introduce yourself with أَنَا
concepts.rule: Use أَنَا for “I,” whoever is speaking.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا مُحَمَّدٌ
أَنَا آمِنَةُ
examples.translation:
I am Muhammad.
I am Aminah.
examples.explanation: There is still no separate word for “am” in these Arabic sentences. The pronoun أَنَا followed by a name is enough. Notice that the two names keep the different endings introduced in Chapter 4.

concepts.title: One person, one form of “you”
concepts.rule: Use أَنْتَ when addressing one male person.

examples.arabic: أَنَا   ·   أَنْتَ
examples.translation: I · you (one male person)
examples.explanation: English uses “you” in many situations. Arabic distinguishes whom you are addressing. This lesson introduces only the masculine singular form أَنْتَ. The feminine and plural forms will come later.

concepts.title: Identify someone with “who…”
concepts.rule: Use the “who…” clause to identify the person before giving the main information.

examples.arabic: الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي خَرَجَ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْآنَ تَاجِرٌ شَهِيرٌ
examples.translation: The man who went out of the mosque just now is a famous merchant.
examples.explanation: الرَّجُلُ names the person. الَّذِي خَرَجَ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْآنَ tells you which man. تَاجِرٌ شَهِيرٌ tells you something about him. Take the sentence in those three pieces to understand its structure.

concepts.title: The same الَّذِي can mean “which”
concepts.rule: Translate الَّذِي according to what it refers to: “who” for a person, “which” for a thing.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ الَّذِي أَمَامَ الْمَسْجِدِ لِلْإِمَامِ
examples.translation: The house which is in front of the mosque belongs to the imam.
examples.explanation: الَّذِي أَمَامَ الْمَسْجِدِ identifies which house. لِلْإِمَامِ gives the main information: it belongs to the imam. كِتَابٌ and بَيْتٌ are grammatically masculine, so a masculine form can refer to a thing. Other relative-pronoun forms come later.

concepts.title: Attach “your,” “his,” and “her”
concepts.rule: Attached pronouns can fill the owner’s place: كِتَابُكَ, كِتَابُهُ, كِتَابُهَا. The first noun has no الـ or tanwin.

examples.arabic: كِتَابُكَ   ·   كِتَابُهُ   ·   كِتَابُهَا
examples.translation: Your book (one male person) · his book · her book
examples.explanation: ـكَ means “your” when addressing one male person, ـهُ means “his,” and ـهَا means “her.” These are attached pronouns, rather than separate words. They fill the owner’s place in the idafah pattern, so the noun has neither الـ nor tanwin.

concepts.title: Use the long ī ending for “my”
concepts.rule: كِتَابِي means “my book.” Read a long final ī rather than the u heard before some other owner endings.

examples.arabic: كِتَابِي
examples.translation: My book
examples.explanation: The ending is read as a long “ee”: kitabi. The “u” you heard in كِتَابُكَ is not pronounced before this ي. Like the other attached owners, “my” makes the noun part of an idafah, without الـ or tanwin.

concepts.title: Say “in it” without repeating the noun
concepts.rule: Use فِيهِ to refer back to something grammatically masculine.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ فِي الْبَيْتِ؟
فِيهِ أَبِي وَأُمِّي
examples.translation:
Who is in the house?
My father and my mother are in it.
examples.explanation: فِيهِ joins فِي (“in”) to an attached pronoun. The pronoun refers back to الْبَيْتِ, so you do not need to repeat “the house.” Notice that the attached form here is pronounced hi, rather than the hu you met in كِتَابُهُ.

concepts.title: For a feminine noun, say فِيهَا
concepts.rule: Choose فِيهِ or فِيهَا according to the place being referred to.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ فِي الْغُرْفَةِ؟
فِيهَا أَخِي
examples.translation:
Who is in the room?
My brother is in it.
examples.explanation: The pronoun refers to the room, not to the brother. غُرْفَةٌ is feminine, so the answer uses فِيهَا even though the person inside is male. Match the attached pronoun to the thing it replaces.

concepts.title: A feminine form of “you”
concepts.rule: One male person: أَنْتَ. One female person: أَنْتِ.

examples.arabic: مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ يَا آمِنَةُ؟
examples.translation: Where are you from, Aminah?
examples.explanation: The final vowel distinguishes أَنْتَ (anta) from أَنْتِ (anti). The question combines مِنْ (“from”), أَيْنَ (“where”), and the pronoun. Use the form that matches the person you are speaking to.

concepts.title: “Your” changes from ـكَ to ـكِ
concepts.rule: Match the owner being addressed: ـكِ for her, ـكَ for him.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ بَيْتُكِ يَا مَرْيَمُ؟
أَيْنَ بَيْتُكَ يَا بِلَالُ؟
examples.translation:
Where is your house, Maryam?
Where is your house, Bilal?
examples.explanation: The house is the same noun in both sentences. The attached pronoun changes to match the person being addressed, not the thing owned. Listen for baytuki versus baytuka.

concepts.title: A feminine form of “who” or “which”
concepts.rule: Use الَّتِي with a feminine singular noun, whether a person or a thing.

examples.arabic:
الطَّالِبَةُ الَّتِي جَلَسَتْ أَمَامَ الْمُدَرِّسَةِ مِنْ أَلْمَانِيَا
السَّاعَةُ الَّتِي عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ لِلْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
The female student who sat in front of the female teacher is from Germany.
The watch which is on the table belongs to the teacher.
examples.explanation: الَّتِي جَلَسَتْ أَمَامَ الْمُدَرِّسَةِ identifies the student. الَّتِي عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ identifies the watch. Choose الَّتِي because الطَّالِبَةُ and السَّاعَةُ are feminine. The final part of each sentence supplies the main information.

concepts.title: One word for “these” people
concepts.rule: For these groups of people, use هَؤُلَاءِ for “these.”

examples.arabic:
هَؤُلَاءِ تُجَّارٌ
هَؤُلَاءِ مُدَرِّسَاتٌ
examples.translation:
These are merchants.
These are female teachers.
examples.explanation: Use the same demonstrative with masculine or feminine groups of people. The Key says this is chiefly a human plural form; Chapter 16 gives the basic pattern for groups of things and animals.

concepts.title: From هُوَ to هُمْ
concepts.rule: Use هُمْ with the masculine human groups in this lesson.

examples.arabic:
هُوَ مُدَرِّسٌ
هُمْ مُدَرِّسُونَ
examples.translation:
He is a teacher.
They are teachers.
examples.explanation: Unlike singular هُوَ, which can mean “it,” this plural pronoun is taught here for people. Use the plural describing word too: مُدَرِّسُونَ. Chapter 16 explains why non-human plurals take a different basic agreement pattern.

concepts.title: Attach ـهُمْ for “their”
concepts.rule: Attached to a noun, ـهُمْ means “their.”

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ بَيْتُهُمْ؟
أَبُوهُمْ تَاجِرٌ شَهِيرٌ
examples.translation:
Where is their house?
Their father is a famous merchant.
examples.explanation: Compare كِتَابُهُ (“his book”) with بَيْتُهُمْ (“their house”). هُمْ stands alone for “they” or attaches for “their”; its job depends on where it appears. أَبُوهُمْ also keeps the special و in this possession form.

concepts.title: A feminine plural “they” and “their”
concepts.rule: هُنَّ for “they”; ـهُنَّ for “their,” referring to females.

examples.arabic:
هُمْ إِخْوَتِي وَهُنَّ أَخَوَاتِي
هُنَّ زَمِيلَاتِي، وَهَذَا بَيْتُهُنَّ
examples.translation:
They are my brothers, and they are my sisters.
They are my female classmates, and this is their house.
examples.explanation: Contrast هُمْ with هُنَّ. The shaddah in هُنَّ doubles the ن. As with هُمْ, the independent and attached forms look alike, but one is the subject “they” and the other expresses ownership.

concepts.title: “Those” for a group of people
concepts.rule: The و in أُولَئِكَ is written but silent.

examples.arabic: أُولَئِكَ
examples.translation: Those
examples.explanation: The written و is not pronounced. Read the word as “ulāʾika,” with an initial short “u,” rather than a long “ū.” The same plural serves the masculine and feminine forms of “that”; connect it with هَؤُلَاءِ, “these.”

concepts.title: Address a group with أَنْتُمْ
concepts.rule: أَنْتُمْ = you; ـكُمْ = your, addressing this group.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ أَنْتُمْ؟
أَيْنَ بَيْتُكُمْ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
examples.translation:
Who are you?
Brothers, where is your house?
examples.explanation: Compare singular أَنْتَ and ـكَ with plural أَنْتُمْ and ـكُمْ. The pronoun changes with the people being addressed, not with the number of houses they own.

concepts.title: One “we” for male and female speakers
concepts.rule: Use نَحْنُ for “we,” and match the following description to the group.

examples.arabic:
نَحْنُ مُسْلِمُونَ
نَحْنُ مُسْلِمَاتٌ
examples.translation:
We are Muslims. (male group)
We are Muslims. (female group)
examples.explanation: The pronoun stays نَحْنُ. The noun describing the group changes to its appropriate masculine or feminine plural. Like أَنَا, نَحْنُ is not divided into separate masculine and feminine words.

concepts.title: Attach ـنَا for “our”
concepts.rule: ـنَا after a noun expresses “our.”

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُنَا
اللَّهُ رَبُّنَا
الْإِسْلَامُ دِينُنَا
examples.translation:
Our house
Allah is our Lord.
Islam is our religion.
examples.explanation: Compare بَيْتِي (“my house”) with بَيْتُنَا (“our house”). The possessive ending is the same for a male or female group. The main noun remains a mudaf, without الـ or tanwin.

concepts.title: Address a female group with أَنْتُنَّ
concepts.rule: أَنْتُنَّ addresses a female group.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ أَنْتُنَّ يَا أَخَوَاتِي؟
نَحْنُ بَنَاتُ الْإِمَامِ
examples.translation:
Who are you, sisters?
We are the imam’s daughters.
examples.explanation: Use أَنْتُنَّ when speaking to a group of females. Their reply uses نَحْنُ, the same “we” you already know. Contrast this with masculine plural أَنْتُمْ.

concepts.title: “Your” for a female group
concepts.rule: ـكُنَّ means “your” for the female group addressed.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ بَيْتُكُنَّ يَا سَيِّدَاتُ؟
بَيْتُنَا قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ
examples.translation:
Where is your house, ladies?
Our house is near the mosque.
examples.explanation: Compare ـكِ for one female person, ـكُنَّ for a female group, and ـكُمْ for the masculine group. The reply uses ـنَا, “our,” which does not change with the speakers’ gender.

concepts.title: Point to two with هَذَانِ or هَاتَانِ
concepts.rule: Masculine dual هَذَانِ; feminine dual هَاتَانِ.

examples.arabic:
هَذَانِ كِتَابَانِ
هَاتَانِ سَيَّارَتَانِ
examples.translation:
These are two books.
These are two cars.
examples.explanation: Choose the demonstrative according to the noun’s gender. Notice that سَيَّارَةٌ shows an open ت before the dual ending, just as attached forms can reveal the ت of ta marbutah.

concepts.title: هُمَا means “they two”
concepts.rule: هُمَا serves both genders; dual descriptions match dual nouns.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ هَذَانِ الْوَلَدَانِ؟ هُمَا طَالِبَانِ جَدِيدَانِ
أَيْنَ الْأُخْتَانِ؟ هُمَا فِي الْغُرْفَةِ
examples.translation:
Who are these two boys? They are two new students.
Where are the two sisters? They are in the room.
examples.explanation: The same هُمَا refers to the two boys or the two sisters. In طَالِبَانِ جَدِيدَانِ, both the noun and its adjective have the dual ending.

concepts.title: A shorter form of “that”
concepts.rule: Recognise ذَاكَ when you already know ذَلِكَ.

examples.arabic: ذَاكَ = ذَلِكَ
