examples.translation: That (masculine singular)
examples.explanation: Connect this word with the demonstratives you already know. This card records the form supplied in the Key; it is not a new sentence pattern or a replacement for the book’s test exercises.

concepts.title: A subject may be named or understood
concepts.rule: The تْ in “she went” is a feminine marker, not a subject pronoun.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ بِلَالٌ
ذَهَبَتْ آمِنَةُ
examples.translation:
Bilal went.
Aminah went.
examples.explanation: Without a following named subject, ذَهَبَ and ذَهَبَتْ have a hidden pronoun, called ضَمِيرٌ مُسْتَتِرٌ. In ذَهَبَتْ, the تْ marks femininity; it is not itself the subject pronoun. This differs from the attached subject endings in the next cards.

concepts.title: The plural ending can be the subject
concepts.rule: Plural subject endings here: و for the male group, ن for the female group.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبُوا إِلَى السُّوقِ
ذَهَبْنَ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ
examples.translation:
They went to the market. (male group)
They went to the school. (female group)
examples.explanation: The first form is read dhahabū, with a silent final ا. The second is dhahabna, with a short final vowel. The attached ending identifies who acted, rather than merely decorating the verb.

concepts.title: A possessive ending does not hide the noun’s case vowel
concepts.rule: Read the object ending before the possessive pronoun.

examples.arabic:
سَأَلَ الْوَلَدُ أُمَّهُ
رَأَيْتُ بَيْتَكَ
فَتَحَ الطَّالِبُ كِتَابَهُ
examples.translation:
The boy asked his mother.
I saw your house.
The student opened his book.
examples.explanation: The object noun has fathah: أُمَّ, بَيْتَ, or كِتَابَ. The attached ـهُ or ـكَ identifies the owner. Read kitab-a-hu, not kitabu-hu, when the book is the object in this sentence.

concepts.title: An object can be an attached pronoun
concepts.rule: In سَأَلْتُهُ: تُ is the subject; هُ is the object.

examples.arabic: رَأَيْتُ بِلَالًا وَسَأَلْتُهُ
examples.translation: I saw Bilal and asked him.
examples.explanation: In سَأَلْتُهُ, ـتُ expresses the subject “I,” while ـهُ expresses the object “him.” This differs from كِتَابُهُ, where ـهُ expresses an owner after a noun. The same pronoun shape can have different jobs depending on where it attaches.

concepts.title: Keep subject and object endings apart
concepts.rule: Read who saw from the subject ending; read whom they saw from the object pronoun.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُهُ
رَأَيْتَهُ
رَأَيْتِهِ
examples.translation:
I saw him.
You saw him. (one male person)
You saw him. (one female person)
examples.explanation: The vowels on ت distinguish “I,” masculine “you,” and feminine “you.” The final attached pronoun supplies the object “him.” In the last form, that object pronoun is pronounced hi after the preceding i sound.

concepts.title: ـهُ becomes ـهِ in these sound environments
concepts.rule: The vowel can change to hi while the pronoun’s reference stays the same.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُهُ   ·   فِي بَيْتِهِ
مِنْهُ   ·   فِيهِ
رَأَيْتَهُ   ·   رَأَيْتِهِ
examples.translation:
His house · in his house
From him · in him/it
You saw him (male addressee) · you saw him (female addressee)
examples.explanation: Compare the preceding vowel or long ī in each pair. The change is pronunciation harmony, not a change from “him” to a different person. The same attached pronoun still refers to a masculine singular person or thing.

concepts.title: The pronoun vowel can be long or short
concepts.rule: Listen to the sound immediately before the attached ه pronoun.

examples.arabic:
لَهُ   ·   مِنْهُ
بِهِ   ·   فِيهِ
examples.translation:
Belonging to him · from him
With him/it · in him/it
examples.explanation: In the textbook’s examples, read lahū and bihī with the pronoun vowel lengthened after a short vowel. After an unvowelled consonant or a long vowel, it is short: minhu and fīhi. This card records the connected pronunciation illustrated here; pronunciation at a pause is a separate matter.

concepts.title: Add a connecting و after ـتُمْ before an object pronoun
concepts.rule: ـتُمْ + an object pronoun becomes ـتُمُو… in these forms.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُمُوهُ   ·   رَأَيْتُمُوهَا
رَأَيْتُمُوهُمْ   ·   رَأَيْتُمُوهُنَّ
سَأَلْتُمُوهَا
examples.translation:
You saw him · you saw her
You saw them (male group) · them (female group)
You asked her.
examples.explanation: Compare رَأَيْتُمْ on its own with رَأَيْتُمُوهُ. The connection is read raʾaytumūhu. The و here connects the subject ending to the object; it is not the “they” subject ending of رَأَوْا.

concepts.title: Review the past-tense subject endings
concepts.rule: Check person, number, and gender before choosing a past-tense ending.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ   ·   ذَهَبَتْ
ذَهَبُوا   ·   ذَهَبْنَ
ذَهَبْتَ   ·   ذَهَبْتِ
ذَهَبْتُمْ   ·   ذَهَبْتُنَّ
ذَهَبْتُ   ·   ذَهَبْنَا
examples.translation:
He went · she went
They went (male group) · they went (female group)
You went (one male) · you went (one female)
You went (male group) · you went (female group)
I went · we went
examples.explanation: This is a review collection of forms introduced in earlier Key lessons, not a new table printed on page 25. Focus on the subject ending and the vowels before it. The Key postpones the full dual verb forms until Lesson 30.

concepts.title: Use ـنِي for “me” after a verb
concepts.rule: After these verbs, “me” appears as ـنِي.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتَنِي
خَلَقَنِي اللَّهُ
سَأَلَنِي الْمُدَرِّسُ
examples.translation:
You saw me.
Allah created me.
The teacher asked me.
examples.explanation: The ن is called نُونُ الْوِقَايَةِ, “the nun of protection.” It stands between the verb and the first-person ي. Compare the owner ending in كِتَابِي with the object ending after a verb: here the complete attached sequence is ـنِي.

concepts.title: The protecting ن keeps the subject vowel audible
concepts.rule: Listen before نِي: “ta” and “ti” still identify the addressee.

examples.arabic: رَأَيْتَنِي   ·   رَأَيْتِنِي
examples.translation: You saw me (one male addressee) · you saw me (one female addressee)
examples.explanation: The a in رَأَيْتَ and the i in رَأَيْتِ remain before نِي. The Key explains that joining directly to the long ī would remove that distinction. The added ن protects the verb’s ending.

concepts.title: الَّذِينَ identifies a masculine plural group
concepts.rule: For this masculine plural “who…” clause, use الَّذِينَ.

examples.arabic: الرِّجَالُ الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا مِنْ مَكْتَبِ الْمُدِيرِ مُدَرِّسُونَ جُدُدٌ
examples.translation: The men who left the headmaster’s office are new teachers.
examples.explanation: الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا مِنْ مَكْتَبِ الْمُدِيرِ identifies which men. خَرَجُوا has a plural subject pronoun referring to them. مُدَرِّسُونَ جُدُدٌ provides the main information about the group.

concepts.title: اللَّاتِي identifies a feminine plural group
concepts.rule: Use اللَّاتِي with the female group in this relative-clause pattern.

examples.arabic: الطَّالِبَاتُ اللَّاتِي جَلَسْنَ أَمَامَ الْمُدَرِّسَةِ بَنَاتُ الْمُدِيرَةِ
examples.translation: The female students who sat in front of the female teacher are the headmistress’s daughters.
examples.explanation: The clause with اللَّاتِي identifies the students. جَلَسْنَ is the female plural verb form. The main information is بَنَاتُ الْمُدِيرَةِ. Compare singular الَّتِي with plural اللَّاتِي.

concepts.title: مَا can mean “what” inside a statement
concepts.rule: Relative مَا introduces “that which …”, rather than asking a question or making a negative.

examples.arabic:
نَسِيتُ مَا قُلْتَ لِي.
أَشْرَبُ مَا تَشْرَبُ.
لَا أَعْبُدُ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ.
examples.translation:
I forgot what you told me.
I will drink what you drink.
I do not worship what you worship.
examples.explanation: This is مَا الْمَوْصُولَةُ. It is different from question مَا in مَا اسْمُكَ؟ and negative مَا in مَا فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْسَ. The words after relative مَا tell us which thing is meant. Decide its job from the whole sentence, not from the word alone.

concepts.title: Dual possessors and objects use ـهُمَا and ـكُمَا
concepts.rule: The dual suffix stays the same across these possessive and object uses.

examples.arabic:
أَبُوهُمَا · أَبُوكُمَا · أَبُونَا
رَأَيْتُهُمَا · رَأَيْتُكُمَا
رَآنَا الْمُدِيرُ.
examples.translation:
Their father (two) · your father (two) · our father
I saw them two · I saw you two
The headmaster saw us.
examples.explanation: The third-person dual suffix is ـهُمَا, and the second-person suffix is ـكُمَا, in both the possessive and object roles shown here. First-person ـنَا serves two or more people. The suffix’s function comes from what it attaches to: a noun gives possession; the illustrated verbs give an object.

concepts.title: Point to two distant things
concepts.rule: Distant dual: ذَانِكَ / ذَيْنِكَ and تَانِكَ / تَيْنِكَ.

examples.arabic:
ذَانِكَ طَالِبَانِ. · تَانِكَ مُمَرِّضَتَانِ.
اِفْتَحْ ذَيْنِكَ الْبَابَيْنِ وَتَيْنِكَ النَّافِذَتَيْنِ.
مَنْ يَسْكُنُ فِي تَيْنِكَ الْفِلَّتَيْنِ؟
examples.translation:
Those two are students. · Those two are nurses.
Open those two doors and those two windows.
Who lives in those two villas?
examples.explanation: ذَانِكَ and تَانِكَ are the marfu forms. Nasb and jarr use ذَيْنِكَ and تَيْنِكَ. Unlike singular ذَلِكَ and تِلْكَ, these dual forms show case changes. The nouns following them also take the required dual case.

concepts.title: Possessive ya takes a after alif or sakin ya
concepts.rule: Read the final -ya or doubled -yya in these attachments.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابِي
بِنْتَايَ
غَسَلْتُ رِجْلَيَّ.
examples.translation:
My book
My two daughters
I washed my two feet.
examples.explanation: The possessive ya is normally sakin in كِتَابِي. After alif, as in بِنْتَايَ, it takes fathah. After a sakin ya, the two ya sounds join with shaddah and the possessive ya takes fathah, as in رِجْلَيَّ.

concepts.title: Demonstrative kaf may match the listener
concepts.rule: Distinguish the listener from the thing being indicated.

examples.arabic:
لِمَنْ ذَلِكَ الْبَيْتُ يَا بِلَالُ؟
لِمَنْ ذَلِكُمْ الْبَيْتُ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
تِلْكِ السَّاعَةُ جَمِيلَةٌ يَا مَرْيَمُ.
examples.translation:
Whose is that house, Bilal?
Whose is that house, brothers?
That watch is beautiful, Maryam.
examples.explanation: The kaf of ذَلِكَ، تِلْكَ، أُولَئِكَ can become ki, kum or kunna according to the addressee. It marks whom you speak to, while the demonstrative’s main form identifies what you point to. The Key labels this variation optional.

concepts.title: First-person ya has different protective-nun rules
concepts.rule: Learn laytani and laalli as distinct first-person patterns.

examples.arabic:
لَيْتَنِي طِفْلٌ.
إِنِّي · إِنَّنِي
لَعَلِّي لَا أَرَاكَ مُدَّةً طَوِيلَةً.
examples.translation:
Would that I were a child.
Indeed I (two forms)
I fear I will not see you for a long time.
examples.explanation: The Key requires nun al-wiqaya with layta plus first-person ya; permits it or its omission with inna, anna, kaanna and lakinna; and uses no protective nun with laalla. These are particle-specific attachment rules.

concepts.title: A demonstrative can follow the noun it describes
concepts.rule: Keep idafah intact, then add the demonstrative.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ إِبْرَاهِيمُ هَذَا؟
سَيَّارَةُ الْمُدِيرِ هَذِهِ جَمِيلَةٌ.
أَرِنِي سَاعَتَكَ هَذِهِ.
examples.translation:
Who is this Ibrahim?
This car of the headmaster is beautiful.
Show me this watch of yours.
examples.explanation: The Key analyses the following demonstrative as a naat. It describes the proper name or the whole possessed noun phrase; it does not break the idafah by inserting itself between its parts. The cited فَأَلْقِهْ uses the shortened object-pronoun pronunciation noted in the footnote.

concepts.title: A separating pronoun makes the predicate clear
concepts.rule: Match the pronoun to the subject; do not add it mechanically everywhere.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا هُوَ الرَّجُلُ.
هَؤُلَاءِ هُمُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ.
هَذِهِ هِيَ السَّيَّارَةُ.
حَامِدٌ هُوَ اللَّاعِبُ.
examples.translation:
This is the man.
These are the criminals.
This is the car.
Hamid is the player.
examples.explanation: Without the separating pronoun, a definite noun after a demonstrative or proper name may be heard as a description awaiting a predicate. The matching pronoun clarifies the predication. The Key says its use is optional when no ambiguity is expected.

concepts.title: Pronouns change form rather than case vowels
concepts.rule: Identify the pronoun’s role and its allowed form.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا مُسْلِمٌ.
مَنْ أَنْتَ؟ · أَسْأَلُكَ.
رَأَيْتُكَ.
examples.translation:
I am a Muslim.
Who are you? · I ask you.
I saw you.
examples.explanation: A separate pronoun stands independently; an attached pronoun needs another word. Anta is a raf form while ka is nasb in the example. In رأيتك, tu is the subject and ka the object. Pronouns are fixed forms with grammatical case positions, not ordinary nouns whose final vowels decline.

concepts.title: Review separate subject pronouns
concepts.rule: Choose the form by referent and grammatical role.

examples.arabic:
هُوَ · هُمَا · هُمْ / هِيَ · هُمَا · هُنَّ
أَنْتَ · أَنْتُمَا · أَنْتُمْ / أَنْتِ · أَنْتُمَا · أَنْتُنَّ
أَنَا · نَحْنُ
examples.translation:
He · they two · they male / she · they two · they female
You male singular/dual/plural / you female singular/dual/plural
I · we
examples.explanation: These are the independent pronouns of raf. The dual forms serve either gender; first person has no male/female distinction. A separate subject pronoun may occur after illa as well as at the beginning of a statement.

concepts.title: Six attached subject forms mark who acts
concepts.rule: Separate the subject suffix from extra spelling letters and mood endings.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبْتُ · ذَهَبْتُمَا · ذَهَبْتُمْ · ذَهَبْتِ · ذَهَبْتُنَّ
ذَهَبَا · ذَهَبُوا · تَذْهَبِينَ · ذَهَبْنَ · ذَهَبْنَا
examples.translation:
I/you went (moving-ta forms)
They two went · they male went · you female go · they female went · we went
examples.explanation: The six groups are moving ta, dual alif, plural waw, female listener ya, female plural nun and first-person na. Attached raf pronouns function as subjects or equivalent ism positions; the final silent spelling alif after plural waw is not another pronoun.

concepts.title: Some subject pronouns are hidden
concepts.rule: A verb marker is not necessarily a subject pronoun.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ · ذَهَبَتْ
يَذْهَبُ · تَذْهَبُ · أَذْهَبُ · نَذْهَبُ
examples.translation:
He went · she went
He goes · you/she go(es) · I go · we go
examples.explanation: The Key lists hidden pronouns in the two unsuffixed past forms and four bare present forms. In ذَهَبَتْ, ta indicates feminine gender while the subject pronoun is hidden. If an explicit subject is present, analyse that noun in the sentence rather than adding a second independent fail.

concepts.title: Independent object pronouns use iyya
concepts.rule: Use the correct independent set for subject or object.

examples.arabic:
إِيَّاهُ · إِيَّاهُمَا · إِيَّاهُمْ / إِيَّاهَا · إِيَّاهُمَا · إِيَّاهُنَّ
إِيَّاكَ · إِيَّاكُمَا · إِيَّاكُمْ / إِيَّاكِ · إِيَّاكُمَا · إِيَّاكُنَّ
إِيَّايَ · إِيَّانَا
examples.translation:
Him · them two · them male / her · them two · them female
You male/female singular, dual and plural
Me · us
examples.explanation: The separate nasb set combines iyya with the familiar person endings. These can stand where an object pronoun must be independent. Anta and huwa belong to the separate raf set and do not substitute for iyyaka and iyyahu in those positions.

concepts.title: Object and jarr suffixes share forms
concepts.rule: Read the host word before assigning a suffix’s role.

examples.arabic:
سَأَلَهُ · سَأَلَكَ · سَأَلَنِي · سَأَلَنَا
مِنْهُ · مِنْكَ · مِنِّي · مِنَّا
examples.translation:
He asked him · you · me · us
From him · you · me · us
examples.explanation: Nasb suffixes attach to verbs or inna and its sisters. Jarr pronouns have only attached forms, used after prepositions or as possessors. The first-person pronoun is ya itself; nun in verbal ni is protective nun. The same suffix shape can therefore have different case positions.

concepts.title: A fronted pronoun object must be independent
concepts.rule: Word order changes the required pronoun form without changing its role.

examples.arabic: نَعْبُدُكَ. ← إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ.
examples.translation: We worship You → It is You that we worship.
examples.explanation: Ka cannot stand alone before the verb, so the fronted object becomes iyyaka. It remains the object even though it comes first. Do not use anta, which is a raf pronoun, for this object slot.

rows: We worship You → It is You that we worship.

concepts.title: A masdar can have an independent pronoun object
concepts.rule: A noun-form masdar may still have a doer and object in meaning.

examples.arabic:
نَنْتَظِرُ زِيَارَةَ الْمُدِيرِ إِيَّانَا.
مُسَاعَدَتُكَ إِيَّايَ كَانَتْ قَبْلَ مُسَاعَدَتِي إِيَّاكَ.
examples.translation:
We await the headmaster’s visit to us.
Your helping me was before my helping you.
examples.explanation: The headmaster is the visitor associated with the masdar زيارة, while iyyana is the person visited. In the second example the possessive suffix identifies the helper and iyya the person helped.

concepts.title: Conjunction and illa require separate object forms
concepts.rule: Illa does not by itself decide the pronoun’s case; its sentence role does.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُكَ وَإِيَّاهُ.
إِنِّي وَإِيَّاكَ نَاجِحَانِ.
لَا نَعْبُدُ إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ.
examples.translation:
I saw you and him.
Indeed I and you have passed.
We worship none but Him.
examples.explanation: A coordinated nasb pronoun uses the iyya set, including one coordinated with inna’s ism. After illa, an object pronoun is also separate. Compare the raf pronoun after illa when the role is subject, as earlier on page 163.

concepts.title: Two object pronouns may need separation
concepts.rule: Check grammatical person, not only gender, before combining object suffixes.

examples.arabic:
أَعْطَيْتُهُ إِيَّاهَا.
أَعْطَيْتُكَ إِيَّاهُ. · أَعْطَيْتُكَهُ.
examples.translation:
I gave it (the magazine) to him.
I gave it to you (two forms).
examples.explanation: Both third-person objects in the first example cannot be combined into the rejected double suffix; the second is separate. With different grammatical persons, as you and it, either attached or separate is allowed, with attached preferred in the Key.

concepts.title: Put the thing before its owner
concepts.rule: In an ordinary possessive idafah, put the thing first and the owner second: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ
examples.translation:
Bilal’s book
The imam’s house
examples.explanation: The first word is the thing possessed, called the mudaf. The second is the possessor, called the mudaf ilayhi. Together they form an idafah, a possession or “of” construction. There is no separate apostrophe or word for “of.”

concepts.title: Put the adjective after its noun
concepts.rule: In a describing phrase, place the noun before its adjective: بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ, “a new house.”

examples.arabic: بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ
examples.translation: A new house
examples.explanation: بَيْتٌ is the noun: a house. جَدِيدٌ describes it: new. The describing adjective is called naʿt, and the noun it describes is called manʿut. This phrase is not the same as الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ, “The house is new.”

concepts.title: Make a description stronger
concepts.rule: In this pattern, say the description first and جِدًّا after it.

examples.arabic: هَذَا كَبِيرٌ جِدًّا
examples.translation: This is very big.
examples.explanation: كَبِيرٌ means “big.” Adding جِدًّا makes it “very big.” Notice the different order: English places “very” before “big,” while the Arabic example places جِدًّا after كَبِيرٌ.

concepts.title: Ask about “the new teacher”
concepts.rule: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ stays together as the person you are asking about.

examples.arabic: أَيْنَ الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ؟
examples.translation: Where is the new teacher?
examples.explanation: أَيْنَ asks about the location of الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ, “the new teacher.” Both the noun and adjective have الـ and a dammah here. You are asking where a particular teacher is, rather than saying that the teacher is new.

concepts.title: Leave الـ and tanwin off the first noun
concepts.rule: In the ordinary possessive idafah taught here, the first noun has neither الـ nor tanwin.

examples.arabic: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ
examples.translation: Bilal’s book
examples.explanation: Write كِتَابُ here, not كِتَابٌ and not الْكِتَابُ. The connection to Bilal tells you which book is meant, so the first noun is definite through this relationship. Later, other kinds of idafah will add detail to this rule.

concepts.title: Give the complement its majrur role
concepts.rule: The second part of an idafah is majrur. Ordinary declinable nouns show kasrah, with or without tanwin.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُ بِلَالٍ
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ
examples.translation:
Bilal’s house
The imam’s house
examples.explanation: Compare بِلَالٌ on its own with بِلَالٍ after بَيْتُ. Compare الْإِمَامُ with الْإِمَامِ. Unlike the first word, the second may have tanwin, as in بِلَالٍ, or الـ, as in الْإِمَامِ.

concepts.title: Match the noun’s grammatical gender
concepts.rule: A describing adjective agrees with its noun in grammatical gender, even when the noun has no ة.

examples.arabic:
وَلَدٌ صَغِيرٌ   ·   بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ
كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ   ·   سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ
examples.translation:
A small boy · a small girl
A new book · a new car
examples.explanation: صَغِيرٌ becomes صَغِيرَةٌ with بِنْتٌ. جَدِيدٌ becomes جَدِيدَةٌ with سَيَّارَةٌ. Notice that بِنْتٌ is feminine without ة, while its adjective still uses the feminine form.

concepts.title: Match definiteness in a describing phrase
concepts.rule: A describing adjective follows its noun and matches its definiteness. For an ordinary noun made definite with الـ, its describing adjective takes الـ too.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is a new teacher.
The new teacher is in the classroom.
examples.explanation: مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ has no الـ on either word. الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ has الـ on both. Compare الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ: that is the statement “The teacher is new,” rather than the phrase “the new teacher.”

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ.
الْكِتَابُ الْجَدِيدُ سَهْلٌ.
examples.translation:
This is a new book.
The new book is easy.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, كِتَابٌ and جَدِيدٌ are both indefinite. In the second, الْكِتَابُ and الْجَدِيدُ are both definite. سَهْلٌ is the predicate, not another definite adjective inside “the new book.” This final chapter reviews four dimensions of adjective agreement.

concepts.title: Distinguish a description from a statement
concepts.rule: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ means “the new teacher”; الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ means “the teacher is new.”

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is a new teacher.
The new teacher is in the classroom.
examples.explanation: مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ has no الـ on either word. الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ has الـ on both. Compare الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ: that is the statement “The teacher is new,” rather than the phrase “the new teacher.”

examples.arabic:
الْبَابُ مَفْتُوحٌ
الْقَلَمُ مَكْسُورٌ
examples.translation:
The door is open.
The pen is broken.
examples.explanation: مَفْتُوحٌ describes something as “open,” and مَكْسُورٌ describes something as “broken.” Both have tanwin, but English does not say “a open” or “a broken” here. Translate the meaning of the whole sentence.

concepts.title: “With you” can mean “you have”
concepts.rule: عِنْدَكَ can express “you have,” not just a location.

examples.arabic: أَعِنْدَكَ قَلَمٌ؟
examples.translation: Do you have a pen? (addressing one male person)
examples.explanation: Literally, this asks whether there is a pen “with you.” أَ makes it a yes-or-no question, and ـكَ identifies the person being addressed. In English, the natural translation is “Do you have a pen?”

concepts.title: For family and body parts, use لِي here
concepts.rule: Use لِي أَخٌ for “I have a brother” in this lesson’s pattern.

examples.arabic:
لِي أَخٌ
لِي فَمٌ
examples.translation:
I have a brother.
I have a mouth.
examples.explanation: Literally, these say “A brother belongs to me” and “A mouth belongs to me.” The lesson distinguishes these relationships and body parts from separate things such as a pen or car, for which it teaches عِنْدَ.

concepts.title: Say “some of them”
concepts.rule: بَعْضُهُمْ means “some of them.”

examples.arabic: بَعْضُهُمْ مُدَرِّسُونَ، وَبَعْضُهُمْ مُهَنْدِسُونَ
examples.translation: Some of them are teachers, and some of them are engineers.
examples.explanation: بَعْضُهُمْ selects part of a group already understood. The attached pronoun identifies the whole group; the rest of each statement tells us about that part. Notice that بَعْضُ loses tanwin when linked to its attached pronoun.

concepts.title: From “some” to “all of us”
concepts.rule: كُلّ plus an attached pronoun can express “all of” that group.

examples.arabic: كُلُّهُمْ   ·   كُلُّكُمْ   ·   كُلُّنَا
examples.translation: All of them · all of you · all of us
examples.explanation: Compare بَعْضُهُمْ (“some of them”) from Chapter 13. The attached endings have the same meanings you already know: ـهُمْ, ـكُمْ, and ـنَا. These entries reinforce attached pronouns rather than introducing a new sentence construction.

concepts.title: Compare with أَفْعَل + مِنْ
concepts.rule: Comparative + مِنْ introduces what you compare it with.

examples.arabic:
حَامِدٌ أَطْوَلُ مِنْ بِلَالٍ
أَحْسَنُ   ·   أَجْمَلُ   ·   أَصْغَرُ   ·   أَقْدَمُ
examples.translation:
Hamid is taller than Bilal.
Better · more beautiful · smaller · older
examples.explanation: These comparative adjectives are diptotes, so the forms shown have no tanwin. The noun after مِنْ is majrur because مِنْ is a preposition. The Arabic term for the comparative/superlative form is afʿal al-tafdil.

concepts.title: This comparative form stays the same
concepts.rule: In this comparative pattern, keep the أَفْعَل form unchanged.

examples.arabic:
آمِنَةُ أَطْوَلُ مِنْ بِلَالٍ
الْأَبْنَاءُ أَطْوَلُ مِنَ الْبَنَاتِ
الْبَنَاتُ أَطْوَلُ مِنَ الْأَبْنَاءِ
examples.translation:
Aminah is taller than Bilal.
The sons are taller than the daughters.
The daughters are taller than the sons.
examples.explanation: Do not apply the ordinary adjective agreement pattern from Book 1 mechanically to this bare comparative construction. It uses the same أَطْوَلُ in all these examples. Other constructions can behave differently.

concepts.title: Attach pronouns to مِنْ for “than me/you/us”
concepts.rule: Notice the shaddah in مِنِّي and مِنَّا.

examples.arabic:
أَنْتَ أَحْسَنُ مِنِّي
أَنَا أَقْصَرُ مِنْكَ
هُمْ أَكْبَرُ مِنَّا سِنًّا
examples.translation:
You are better than me.
I am shorter than you.
They are older than us.
examples.explanation: مِنِّي has a doubled ن. So does مِنَّا, formed from مِنْ plus نَا. Other listed forms include مِنْهُ, مِنْهَا, مِنْكَ, and مِنْهُمْ, without this doubling. سِنًّا specifies age: literally “greater in age.”

concepts.title: An idafah can express “the best” or “the oldest”
concepts.rule: Use the linked majrur noun to specify “best/oldest of what.”

examples.arabic:
إِبْرَاهِيمُ أَحْسَنُ طَالِبٍ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ
فَاطِمَةُ أَكْبَرُ طَالِبَةٍ فِي فَصْلِنَا
examples.translation:
Ibrahim is the best student in the school.
Fatimah is the eldest student in our class.
examples.explanation: أَحْسَنُ طَالِبٍ and أَكْبَرُ طَالِبَةٍ are idafah phrases. The noun after the superlative is majrur. The Key also gives الْأَزْهَرُ أَقْدَمُ جَامِعَةٍ فِي الْعَالَمِ, “Al-Azhar is the oldest university in the world,” as a grammar example.

concepts.title: A feminine partner for جَوْعَانُ
concepts.rule: For this adjective class, use the فَعْلَى feminine pattern.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ جَوْعَانُ
آمِنَةُ جَوْعَى
examples.translation:
Bilal is hungry.
Aminah is hungry.
examples.explanation: You met جَوْعَانُ, عَطْشَانُ, and غَضْبَانُ in Book 1. These do not form their feminine simply by adding ة. Learn the feminine pattern illustrated by جَوْعَى. Its final ى is read as a long “ā.”

concepts.title: One plural form can serve both genders
concepts.rule: The plural form may be shared by both genders; learn its actual pattern.

examples.arabic:
الرِّجَالُ جِيَاعٌ
النِّسَاءُ جِيَاعٌ
كَسْلَانُ / كَسْلَى ← كُسَالَى
examples.translation:
The men are hungry.
The women are hungry.
Lazy (masculine/feminine) → lazy people
examples.explanation: The same جِيَاعٌ describes male or female groups. The Key separately notes كُسَالَى as the plural of كَسْلَانُ and كَسْلَى, illustrated with the Quranic phrase in 4:142. Learn this noted plural rather than forcing it into جِيَاعٌ’s pattern.

concepts.title: Track each noun’s reason for its ending
concepts.rule: In عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ, the first noun is majrur after عَلَى; the second is majrur as the idafah complement.

examples.arabic: عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation: On the teacher’s table
examples.explanation: مَكْتَبِ is majrur because it follows عَلَى, “on.” الْمُدَرِّسِ is majrur because it is the owner in the idafah. مَكْتَبِ is also the first word of that idafah, so it has neither الـ nor tanwin.

concepts.title: Match the adjective’s case to its noun
concepts.rule: A describing adjective takes the case of the noun it describes. In longer phrases, use this to identify which noun is described.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ
أَنَا فِي بَيْتٍ جَدِيدٍ
مَنْ فِي الْبَيْتِ الْجَدِيدِ؟
examples.translation:
This is a new house.
I am in a new house.
Who is in the new house?
examples.explanation: بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ ends in “un” on both words. After فِي, the phrase becomes بَيْتٍ جَدِيدٍ, with “in” on both. In الْبَيْتِ الْجَدِيدِ, both words have الـ and a single kasrah. Gender, definiteness, and case work together.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدُ
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدِ
examples.translation:
The imam’s new house
The new imam’s house
examples.explanation: In the first, الْجَدِيدُ matches بَيْتُ in case. In the second, الْجَدِيدِ matches الْإِمَامِ, the majrur owner. Both descriptions are definite, but their last vowels tell you which noun they qualify.

examples.arabic:
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
سَأَلْتُ الْمُدَرِّسَ الْجَدِيدَ.
قُلْتُ لِلْمُدَرِّسِ الْجَدِيدِ.
examples.translation:
The new teacher is in the classroom.
I asked the new teacher.
I spoke to the new teacher.
examples.explanation: Both words are marfu in the first sentence, mansub in the second, and majrur in the third. The adjective follows the noun’s case even though it does not itself immediately follow the governing verb or preposition.

examples.arabic:
أَحَضَرَ الطَّالِبُ الْجَدِيدُ؟
يَطْلُبُ الْمُدِيرُ الطَّالِبَ الْجَدِيدَ.
هَذَا دَفْتَرُ الطَّالِبِ الْجَدِيدِ.
examples.translation:
Did the new student attend?
The headmaster wants the new student.
This is the new student’s notebook.
examples.explanation: The naat الْجَدِيد follows the manut الطَّالِب in raf, nasb and jarr. Its case depends on the described noun; it does not acquire an independent sentence role as a second subject or object.

concepts.title: Extend agreement to non-human plurals
concepts.rule: In the basic rule taught here, non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ.

examples.arabic: هَؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابٌ جُدُدٌ، هُمْ صِغَارٌ
examples.translation: These are new students; they are small.
examples.explanation: Humans, angels, and similar beings belong to the first class. Things, animals, and concepts belong to the second. Human plurals use plural agreement, as in هَؤُلَاءِ, هُمْ, جُدُدٌ, and صِغَارٌ here. The important new difference is in the plural.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ، هُوَ صَغِيرٌ
هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ، هِيَ صَغِيرَةٌ
examples.translation:
This is a new book; it is small.
These are new books; they are small.
examples.explanation: كُتُبٌ is plural, but the demonstrative is هَذِهِ, the adjective جَدِيدَةٌ is feminine singular, and the pronoun is هِيَ. English naturally uses “these” and “they” in the translation. This is the basic rule; the Key notes that exceptions are learned later.

concepts.title: Make these colour words feminine
concepts.rule: These colour pairs use أَفْعَلُ / فَعْلَاءُ rather than a simple ة ending.

examples.arabic:
أَبْيَضُ · بَيْضَاءُ
أَسْوَدُ · سَوْدَاءُ
أَحْمَرُ · حَمْرَاءُ
هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةُ خَضْرَاءُ.
السَّمَاءُ زَرْقَاءُ.
examples.translation:
White (male · female)
Black (male · female)
Red (male · female)
This tree is green.
The sky is blue.
examples.explanation: Do not simply add ة to these masculine colour forms. Learn their feminine partners. Both the masculine and feminine forms in this group are diptotes: they do not take tanwin. Match the colour to the grammatical gender of the noun.

concepts.title: One colour plural for both genders
concepts.rule: Learn the shared plural as well as the two singular colour forms.

examples.arabic: مَنْ هَؤُلَاءِ الرِّجَالُ السُّودُ، وَأُولَئِكَ النِّسَاءُ السُّمْرُ؟
examples.translation: Who are these black men and those brown women?
examples.explanation: السُّودُ describes the men, and السُّمْرُ describes the women. The plural pattern itself serves both genders; it does not add a feminine singular ending. Keep this plural pattern distinct from the feminine singular فَعْلَاءُ just introduced.

concepts.title: Say “another” with آخَرُ or أُخْرَى
concepts.rule: Match “another” to gender and case; do not add tanwin to these forms.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي قَلَمٌ آخَرُ.
سَأَلْتُ مُدَرِّسَنَا وَمُدَرِّسًا آخَرَ.
زَيْنَبُ مِنْ أَمْرِيكَا، وَفِي الْفَصْلِ طَالِبَةٌ أُخْرَى مِنْ أَمْرِيكَا.
حَفِظْتُ سُورَةَ الرَّحْمَنِ وَسُورَةً أُخْرَى.
examples.translation:
I have another pen.
I asked our teacher and another teacher.
Zainab is from America, and there is another female student from America in the class.
I memorised Surat al-Rahman and another surah.
examples.explanation: Both forms are diptotes. Notice آخَرُ with قَلَمٌ and آخَرَ with مُدَرِّسًا: the adjective shares the noun’s case, but does not copy its tanwin. أُخْرَى keeps the same visible ending in these examples.

concepts.title: Compare things with كَـ
concepts.rule: كَـ + a majrur noun means “like …”.

examples.arabic:
سَاعَتِي كَسَاعَتِكَ.
هَذَا الْبَيْتُ كَالْمَسْجِدِ.
هَذِهِ الْقَهْوَةُ كَالْمَاءِ.
examples.translation:
My watch is like yours.
This house is like a mosque.
This coffee is like water.
examples.explanation: The noun after كَـ is majrur: سَاعَتِكَ, الْمَسْجِدِ and الْمَاءِ. In كَالْمَسْجِدِ, the comparison prefix joins to a noun beginning with الْـ. Read the complete phrase smoothly as one attached preposition and its noun.

concepts.title: With a pronoun, insert مِثْل
concepts.rule: For these pronoun comparisons, use كَمِثْلِهِ or كَمِثْلِي.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا كَمِثْلِهِ.
هُوَ كَمِثْلِي.
examples.translation:
I am like him.
He is like me.
examples.explanation: Do not attach the pronoun directly to كَـ in this lesson’s pattern. Insert مِثْل between the preposition and the pronoun: كَ + مِثْلِ + هِ. مِثْلِ is majrur after كَـ and connects to the pronoun as an idafah.

concepts.title: Put “this” after a definite idafah
concepts.rule: Complete the idafah first, then add the matching هَذَا or هَذِهِ.

examples.arabic:
عُلْبَةُ الْحَلْوَى هَذِهِ
كِتَابُ التَّارِيخِ هَذَا
قَلَمُ الرَّصَاصِ هَذَا
غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ هَذِهِ
سَاعَتُكَ هَذِهِ جَمِيلَةٌ.
خُذْ كِتَابِي هَذَا.
examples.translation:
This tin of sweets
This history book
This pencil
This bedroom
This watch of yours is beautiful.
Take this book of mine.
examples.explanation: With هَذَا الْكِتَابُ, the noun has الْـ. But the first noun of an idafah is mudaf and cannot take الْـ, so the Key places the demonstrative after the complete phrase: كِتَابُ التَّارِيخِ هَذَا. The demonstrative matches the thing pointed to: feminine عُلْبَةُ uses هَذِهِ, and masculine كِتَابُ uses هَذَا. The same order works with a possessive pronoun.

concepts.title: Keep dual adjectives in agreement
concepts.rule: Match a dual adjective to the noun’s gender, number and case.

examples.arabic:
فِي بَيْتِي غُرْفَتَانِ كَبِيرَتَانِ.
جَاءَ مُدَرِّسَانِ جَدِيدَانِ.
examples.translation:
There are two large rooms in my house.
Two new teachers came.
examples.explanation: غُرْفَتَانِ and كَبِيرَتَانِ are both feminine dual and marfu. مُدَرِّسَانِ and جَدِيدَانِ are masculine dual and marfu. The adjective does not stay singular when it describes these two rooms or teachers.

concepts.title: أَقَلُّ means “less”
concepts.rule: A shaddah can represent two identical root consonants brought together.

examples.arabic: قَلِيلٌ ← أَقَلُّ
examples.translation: Little / few → less / fewer
examples.explanation: The underlying comparative model is أَفْعَلُ, here illustrated by أَقْلَلُ before assimilation. The identical second and third root letters combine as لّ, giving أَقَلُّ. The expanded form explains the pattern; use أَقَلُّ in ordinary speech.

concepts.title: A plural can describe one item belonging to each of two people
concepts.rule: Do not translate the plural mechanically as several items per person.

examples.arabic:
مَا أَسْمَاؤُكُمَا؟
اِغْسِلَا وُجُوهَكُمَا.
حَلَقَ الْوَلَدَانِ رُؤُوسَهُمَا.
examples.translation:
What are your names (you two)?
Wash your faces (you two)!
The two boys shaved their heads.
examples.explanation: Each person has one of the item concerned in these examples, yet the shared expression uses a plural noun with the dual suffix. أَسْمَاءُكُمَا does not mean each person has several names here. Read the possessed plural together with its dual possessor.

concepts.title: Match number in these human-noun examples
concepts.rule: For these human nouns, match singular, dual or plural number.

examples.arabic:
لِي أَخٌ كَبِيرٌ.
بِلَالٌ لَهُ أَخَوَانِ كَبِيرَانِ.
حَامِدٌ لَهُ إِخْوَةٌ كِبَارٌ.
examples.translation:
I have an elder brother.
Bilal has two elder brothers.
Hamid has elder brothers.
examples.explanation: The examples move from كَبِيرٌ to كَبِيرَانِ to كِبَارٌ. The plural adjective here is a broken plural. Keep the earlier non-human plural rule in mind: these examples concern people and do not cancel the feminine singular agreement learned for non-human plurals.

concepts.title: Match the noun’s gender
concepts.rule: Before moving on, check all four dimensions of adjective agreement.

examples.arabic: لِي أَخٌ كَبِيرٌ، وَأُخْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ.
examples.translation: I have an elder brother and a younger sister.
examples.explanation: كَبِيرٌ agrees with masculine أَخٌ; صَغِيرَةٌ agrees with feminine أُخْتٌ. When reviewing any adjective, check the four dimensions from this chapter: definiteness, case, number and gender, using the special patterns and exceptions learned earlier. This is the final concept chapter of the Book 2 Key.

concepts.title: Finish the idafah before describing the first noun
concepts.rule: An adjective describing the first noun follows the complete idafah. In the definite examples here, that adjective is definite.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدُ
بَيْتُهُ الْجَدِيدُ
examples.translation:
The imam’s new house
His new house
examples.explanation: بَيْتُ is definite through its owner, although it has no الـ itself. Its adjective is definite: الْجَدِيدُ. The adjective follows the complete idafah rather than interrupting the link between the thing and its owner.

concepts.title: Other people: آخَرُونَ and أُخَرُ
concepts.rule: Match the “other” form to the noun and retain the non-human plural qualification.

examples.arabic:
غَابَ الْيَوْمَ بِلَالٌ وَطُلَّابٌ آخَرُونَ.
غَابَتْ زَيْنَبُ وَطَالِبَاتٌ أُخَرُ.
فِي أَيَّامٍ أُخْرَى
examples.translation:
Bilal and other male students were absent today.
Zainab and other female students were absent.
On other days
examples.explanation: آخَرُونَ is the plural of masculine آخَرُ; أُخَرُ is the diptote plural of feminine أُخْرَى. With a non-human plural such as أَيَّام, feminine singular أُخْرَى is also used. The Key also illustrates أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ, where أُخَرَ has diptote jarr.

concepts.title: Idafah removes dual and sound-plural nun
concepts.rule: Omit nun, but retain the case-carrying dual or plural letter.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ بِنْتَا بِلَالٍ؟
رَأَيْتُ بِنْتَيْ بِلَالٍ.
أَبْحَثُ عَنْ بِنْتَيْ بِلَالٍ.
جَاءَ مُدَرِّسُو الْحَدِيثِ.
سَأَلْتُ مُدَرِّسِي الْحَدِيثِ.
examples.translation:
Where are Bilal’s two daughters?
I saw Bilal’s two daughters.
I am looking for Bilal’s two daughters.
The hadith teachers came.
I asked the hadith teachers.
examples.explanation: The dual retains ā for raf and ay for nasb/jarr, while the sound masculine plural retains ū or ī. Only nun is removed. The following noun is the majrur complement; it does not restore nun or change the mudaf into a singular noun.

concepts.title: Ma after an indefinite noun can mean “some”
concepts.rule: Read noun plus ma as an unspecified member of that kind.

examples.arabic:
أَعْطِنِي كِتَابًا مَا.
رَأَيْتُهُ فِي مَكَانٍ مَا.
سَتَفْهَمُ هَذَا يَوْمًا مَا.
examples.translation:
Give me some book.
I saw him somewhere.
You will understand this someday.
examples.explanation: The Key calls this the completely indefinite and vague ma. It follows the noun as an adjective-like qualifier: a certain book, place, day or reason. It is not the negative ma or a question asking “what?”.

concepts.title: Colours and defects share a plural across genders
concepts.rule: Learn the masculine, feminine and shared plural together.

examples.arabic:
أَعْرَجُ · عَرْجَاءُ ← عُرْجٌ
أَحْمَرُ · حَمْرَاءُ ← حُمْرٌ
أَبْيَضُ · بَيْضَاءُ ← بِيضٌ
examples.translation:
Male/female person with a limp → plural
Red male/female forms → plural
White male/female forms → plural
examples.explanation: The Key gives the same plural for masculine and feminine adjectives of these colour/defect patterns. In بِيضٌ the expected dammah changes to kasrah because of ya. Do not confuse colour afal with comparative afal.

rows: Male/female person with a limp → plural

concepts.title: A whole sentence can follow yawm in idafah
concepts.rule: A clause can fill a noun position without changing every internal ending.

examples.arabic:
وُلِدْتُ يَوْمَ مَاتَ جَدِّي.
سَافَرْتُ يَوْمَ ظَهَرَتِ النَّتَائِجُ.
examples.translation:
I was born the day my grandfather died.
I travelled the day the results appeared.
examples.explanation: يَوْمَ is the mudaf time expression. The following past clause supplies its mudaf ilayhi and occupies the position of jarr. Its internal verb and subject retain their own grammar; they do not all acquire kasrah.

concepts.title: Masculine agreement can cover a mixed group
concepts.rule: Mixed-group agreement can use masculine forms.

examples.arabic:
أَبْنَائِي وَبَنَاتِي يَدْرُسُونَ.
الْمَسْجِدُ وَالْمَدْرَسَةُ قَرِيبَانِ.
examples.translation:
My sons and daughters are studying.
The mosque and school are near.
examples.explanation: The plural verb is masculine even though the group contains males and females. Likewise a masculine dual can refer jointly to a grammatically masculine and feminine noun, as the mosque/school and sun/moon examples show.

groups.title: Sentences & grammatical roles
groups.subtitle: Understand the job each part does

concepts.title: You can leave “is” unsaid
concepts.rule: Two words can make a complete Arabic sentence.

examples.arabic: هَذَا كِتَابٌ
examples.translation: This is a book.
examples.explanation: هَذَا means “this” and كِتَابٌ means “a book.” Together they already make a complete statement. English needs “is” in the translation; this Arabic sentence does not.

concepts.title: A noun’s ending tells you its job
concepts.rule: Pay attention to the final vowel, not just the letters of the word.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ
examples.translation: The house is new.
examples.explanation: الْبَيْتُ ends with a dammah, the short “u” vowel. The Key calls a noun in this state marfuʿ. For now, notice this ending; in the next card, you will see how a preposition changes it.

concepts.title: Give “this book” something to say
concepts.rule: Point out the thing, then tell the reader something about it.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ
تِلْكَ الْمُمَرِّضَةُ مِنَ الْيَابَانِ
examples.translation:
This book is new.
That nurse is from Japan.
examples.explanation: جَدِيدٌ tells us something about this book. مِنَ الْيَابَانِ tells us something about that nurse. The same construction works with all four demonstratives you have learned: هَذَا, هَذِهِ, ذَلِكَ, and تِلْكَ. Another example is هَذِهِ السَّاعَةُ جَمِيلَةٌ, “This watch is beautiful.”

concepts.title: Say what something is under
concepts.rule: The idafah pattern can express a relationship such as “under the table.”

examples.arabic:
تَحْتَ الْمَكْتَبِ
تَحْتَ الْكِتَابِ
examples.translation:
Under the table
Under the book
examples.explanation: Read the final kasrah in الْمَكْتَبِ and الْكِتَابِ. The Key explains this using the possession construction you just learned: تَحْتَ is linked to the noun that follows it. The meaning is location rather than ownership.

concepts.title: Behind or in front of?
concepts.rule: After خَلْفَ or أَمَامَ, use the following noun’s majrur form.

examples.arabic:
الْبَيْتُ خَلْفَ الْمَسْجِدِ
حَامِدٌ أَمَامَ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
The house is behind the mosque.
Hamid is in front of the teacher.
examples.explanation: Like تَحْتَ in Chapter 5, these location words form a relationship with the noun that follows. الْمَسْجِدِ and الْمُدَرِّسِ are majrur, so each has a kasrah ending in these examples.

concepts.title: Say someone is “with” someone
concepts.rule: After عِنْدَ, use the following noun’s majrur form.

examples.arabic: الْمُدَرِّسُ عِنْدَ الْمُدِيرِ
examples.translation: The teacher is with the headmaster.
examples.explanation: عِنْدَ الْمُدِيرِ tells you where the teacher is: with the headmaster, or at his place. The kasrah on الْمُدِيرِ follows the same relationship pattern you learned with تَحْتَ, خَلْفَ, and أَمَامَ.

concepts.title: Two ways of saying “with”
concepts.rule: مَعَ expresses company; عِنْدَ in this comparison includes the idea of someone’s place.

examples.arabic:
الْمُدَرِّسُ عِنْدَ الْمُدِيرِ
الْمُدَرِّسُ مَعَ الْمُدِيرِ
examples.translation:
The teacher is with the headmaster (at his place).
The teacher is with the headmaster (not specifying where).
examples.explanation: In the first example, the teacher is at the headmaster’s office or place. The second says they are together and could be anywhere. The noun after مَعَ is majrur because it is a mudaf ilayhi: الْمُدِيرِ.

concepts.title: The object gets an “a” ending here
concepts.rule: An object’s role can change its ending; possession and adjective agreement still apply.

examples.arabic:
أُحِبُّ اللَّهَ
أُحِبُّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ
أُحِبُّ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ
examples.translation:
I love Allah.
I love the Messenger of Allah.
I love the Arabic language.
examples.explanation: اللَّهَ and رَسُولَ are objects, so each ends in “a” here. In رَسُولَ اللَّهِ, the second word stays majrur because it is a mudaf ilayhi. In اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ, the adjective matches its noun’s mansub ending. With “my,” as in أَبِي, this object ending is not visible.

concepts.title: “Before” and “after” link to a noun
concepts.rule: قَبْلَ (“before”) and بَعْدَ (“after”) link to a following noun as mudaf; that complement is majrur.

examples.arabic:
بَعْدَ الدَّرْسِ
قَبْلَ الصَّلَاةِ
examples.translation:
After the lesson
Before the prayer
examples.explanation: In these phrases, قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ are mudaf, and الدَّرْسِ and الصَّلَاةِ are mudaf ilayhi. This expands the short note on بَعْدَ in Chapter 12.

examples.arabic: بَعْدَ
examples.translation: After
examples.explanation: The vocabulary entry gives the word and its grammar rule, without a full example phrase. Connect it with تَحْتَ, أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ, and عِنْدَ: each links to a following noun through an idafah relationship, so that noun is majrur.

concepts.title: Two familiar reasons for majrur
concepts.rule: Grammatical case is a role; its visible ending depends on the word’s class.

examples.arabic:
مِنْ بِلَالٍ
كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ
كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ
examples.translation:
From Bilal
The teacher’s book
Bilal’s book
examples.explanation: You have followed this rule since Chapters 4 and 5. The kasrah may appear alone or with tanwin, depending on the word and construction. The new step is that a special word class can be majrur without using kasrah.

concepts.title: Give familiar sentences their grammar names
concepts.rule: Mubtada is the starting topic; khabar tells you about it.

examples.arabic:
الْكِتَابُ سَهْلٌ
خَرَجَ بِلَالٌ
examples.translation:
The book is easy.
Bilal went out.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, الْكِتَابُ is the mubtada, the topic you start with. سَهْلٌ is its khabar, the information given about it. The second sentence starts with خَرَجَ, so it is a verbal sentence. You have used both types in Book 1.

concepts.title: The verbal subject is called fāʿil
concepts.rule: Find who did the action: a named noun or a subject pronoun.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ بِلَالٌ
ذَهَبُوا   ·   ذَهَبْتَ   ·   ذَهَبْنَا
examples.translation:
Bilal went.
They went · you went · we went
examples.explanation: بِلَالٌ is the named fāʿil. A subject can also be an attached pronoun: و in ذَهَبُوا, تَ in ذَهَبْتَ, or نَا in ذَهَبْنَا. These pronouns have the subject’s grammatical role even though they do not show a noun-style dammah ending.

concepts.title: Before a named plural subject, keep the verb singular
concepts.rule: Verb first + named plural subject: singular verb, matching gender.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ الطُّلَّابُ
ذَهَبَتِ الْبَنَاتُ
examples.translation:
The male students went.
The girls went.
examples.explanation: الطُّلَّابُ or الْبَنَاتُ supplies the named subject. The preceding verb is singular, matching gender. Do not add the “they” subject ending and then another named subject in this construction. The short “i” in ذَهَبَتِ connects the feminine marker to الـ.

concepts.title: With the noun first, the sentence has a different structure
concepts.rule: Noun first: plural topic plus a predicate sentence with a plural verb.

examples.arabic:
الطُّلَّابُ ذَهَبُوا
الطَّالِبَاتُ ذَهَبْنَ
examples.translation:
The male students went.
The female students went.
examples.explanation: Here the verb’s attached subject pronoun refers back to the starting topic. Compare ذَهَبَ الطُّلَّابُ with الطُّلَّابُ ذَهَبُوا: both translate naturally as “The students went,” but their Arabic structures differ.

concepts.title: The action’s object is mafʿūl bihi
concepts.rule: Ask what or whom the action affects to locate the object.

examples.arabic:
فَتَحَ الْوَلَدُ الْبَابَ
رَأَيْتُ حَامِدًا
سَأَلَتِ الْمُدِيرَةُ زَيْنَبَ
شَرِبَ الرَّجُلُ الْمَاءَ
examples.translation:
The boy opened the door.
I saw Hamid.
The headmistress asked Zaynab.
The man drank water.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, الْوَلَدُ is the marfuʿ subject and الْبَابَ is the mansub object. حَامِدًا keeps tanwin as an object, while زَيْنَبَ has no tanwin because of its name class. The role and the word class work together.

concepts.title: بَيْنَ means “between”
concepts.rule: With these attached pronouns, repeat بَيْنَ for each side.

examples.arabic:
جَلَسَ حَامِدٌ بَيْنَ بِلَالٍ وَفَيْصَلٍ
هَذَا بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ
examples.translation:
Hamid sat between Bilal and Faisal.
This is between you and me.
examples.explanation: بِلَالٍ is majrur after بَيْنَ, and فَيْصَلٍ is joined to it. In the pronoun example, Arabic says بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ, rather than using بَيْنَ only once before two independent pronouns.

concepts.title: A noun can say when the action happens
concepts.rule: Mansub can mark when an action occurs, not only its object.

examples.arabic:
رَجَعَ بِلَالٌ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى السُّوقِ صَبَاحًا
رَجَعْتُ مِنَ الْجَامِعَةِ مَسَاءً
examples.translation:
Bilal returned on Saturday.
I went to the market in the morning.
I returned from the university in the evening.
examples.explanation: يَوْمَ, صَبَاحًا, and مَسَاءً tell you the time of the action, rather than the thing receiving it. English adds words such as “on” or “in,” but these Arabic examples use a mansub time expression.

concepts.title: Read the case inside a time phrase
concepts.rule: A time phrase has an overall role and its own internal noun relationships.

examples.arabic:
أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَةِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ
سَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الطَّائِفِ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبُ هَذَا الْمَسَاءَ؟
examples.translation:
I go to the library every day.
I will go to Taif on Thursday.
Where will you go this evening?
examples.explanation: كُلَّ is mansub as the time expression and يَوْمٍ is its mudaf ilayhi. Likewise يَوْمَ is mansub while الْخَمِيسِ is majrur. In “this evening,” the noun الْمَسَاءَ shows the mansub case of the demonstrative phrase.

concepts.title: An indefinite topic after a question particle
concepts.rule: After an interrogative particle, an indefinite noun can serve as the topic in this pattern.

examples.arabic:
أَعَقْرَبٌ فِي الْفَصْلِ؟
أَإِلَهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ؟
examples.translation:
Is there a scorpion in the classroom?
Is there a god with Allah?
examples.explanation: The question particle أَ precedes an indefinite noun: عَقْرَبٌ or إِلَهٌ. That noun can be the mubtada here. The following phrase supplies the predicate. Keep the noun marfu, as the final ـٌ shows; being indefinite does not itself make it an object.

concepts.title: Name someone again with a badal
concepts.rule: A badal shares the grammatical case of the noun it identifies.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ أَخُوكَ الْحُسَيْنُ؟
بِنْتُهُ زَيْنَبُ طَبِيبَةٌ.
رَأَيْتُ زَمِيلَكَ عَبَّاسًا.
كَتَبْنَا إِلَى أُسْتَاذِنَا الدُّكْتُورِ بِلَالٍ.
examples.translation:
Where is your brother Husain?
His daughter, Zainab, is a doctor.
I saw your classmate, Abbas.
We wrote to our professor, Dr Bilal.
examples.explanation: الْحُسَيْنُ identifies أَخُوكَ and shares its case. The original noun is called الْمُبْدَلُ مِنْهُ, and the substitute is الْبَدَلُ. The same relationship appears in other cases: عَبَّاسًا is mansub with زَمِيلَكَ. In the last example, الدُّكْتُورِ is a badal of أُسْتَاذِنَا, and بِلَالٍ is a badal of الدُّكْتُورِ.

concepts.title: Match the verb to a female subject
concepts.rule: For these female subjects, use the feminine past or present-future form.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلَ مُحَمَّدٌ.
دَخَلَتْ آمِنَةُ.
ذَهَبَتْ مَرْيَمُ.
خَرَجَتِ الْبَقَرَةُ.
يَدْرُسُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ اللُّغَةَ الْأَلْمَانِيَّةَ، وَتَدْرُسُ مَرْيَمُ اللُّغَةَ الْفَرَنْسِيَّةَ.
examples.translation:
Muhammad entered.
Aminah entered.
Maryam went.
The cow went out.
Ibrahim studies German, and Maryam studies French.
examples.explanation: In the past examples, the feminine marker is ـتْ. In the present-future examples, يَدْرُسُ becomes تَدْرُسُ. The kasrah in خَرَجَتِ الْبَقَرَةُ is the familiar linking vowel before hamzat al-wasl; the feminine marker is still the final ت.

concepts.title: Grammatical gender allows another pattern
concepts.rule: Distinguish a female subject from a noun that is feminine only in grammar.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجَتِ السَّيَّارَةُ.
خَرَجَ السَّيَّارَةُ.
بَقِيَ ثَلَاثُ دَقَائِقَ.
examples.translation:
The car went out.
The car went out.
There are three minutes left.
examples.explanation: With the following grammatically feminine subject السَّيَّارَةُ, the Key allows either feminine خَرَجَتْ or masculine خَرَجَ. It also points to masculine بَقِيَ in the lesson’s minutes expression. This qualification concerns the verb-first constructions illustrated here; do not use it as a rule that feminine agreement can always be ignored. Further details come later.

concepts.title: Review nominal and verbal sentences
concepts.rule: Recognise the sentence’s opening and then identify its parts.

examples.arabic:
الْجُمْلَةُ الِاسْمِيَّةُ
الْجُمْلَةُ الْفِعْلِيَّةُ
examples.translation:
The nominal sentence
The verbal sentence
examples.explanation: A nominal sentence begins with an ism; a verbal sentence begins with a verb. Recall the nominal topic and predicate, and the verbal action and subject. This is a revision pointer rather than a new rule or a new set of printed examples. Review the Lesson 1 cards if these sentence patterns feel unfamiliar.

concepts.title: مِنْ قَبْلُ and مِنْ بَعْدُ keep a final u
concepts.rule: When the understood complement is omitted here, قَبْلُ and بَعْدُ have a fixed u.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ قَبْلَ الْأَذَانِ، وَرَجَعْتُ بَعْدَ الصَّلَاةِ.
أَبِي الْآنَ مُدِيرٌ، وَكَانَ مِنْ قَبْلُ مُدَرِّسًا.
أَذْهَبُ الْآنَ إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَةِ، وَسَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ مِنْ بَعْدُ.
examples.translation:
I went to the mosque before the adhan and returned after the prayer.
My father is now a headmaster; before that he was a teacher.
I am going to the library now and will go to the mosque afterwards.
examples.explanation: With an expressed complement, قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ are mudaf. In the omitted-but-understood construction here, they become mabni with final dammah. مِنْ قَبْلُ stands for “before that”; مِنْ بَعْدُ for “after that.” Do not change the fixed u to i after مِنْ in this construction.

concepts.title: ظَنَّ can take two mansub objects
concepts.rule: Compare أَظُنُّ الْجَوَّ جَمِيلًا with أَظُنُّ أَنَّ الْجَوَّ جَمِيلٌ.

examples.arabic:
الْجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ. ← أَظُنُّ الْجَوَّ جَمِيلًا.
الْبَابُ مُغْلَقٌ. ← أَظُنُّ الْبَابَ مُغْلَقًا.
أَظُنُّكَ طَيِّبًا.
أَظُنُّ أَنَّ الْجَوَّ جَمِيلٌ.
examples.translation:
The weather is fine. → I think the weather is fine.
The door is closed. → I think the door is closed.
I think you are good.
I think that the weather is fine.
examples.explanation: In the two-object construction, both the former topic and predicate become mansub. In أَظُنُّكَ, the attached كَ is the first object. The alternative with أَنَّ has a different structure: أَنَّ makes its noun mansub, while its predicate جَمِيلٌ is marfu. Do not mix the two ending patterns.

concepts.title: حَيْثُ can introduce “where”
concepts.rule: حَيْثُ links a place to a following clause.

examples.arabic: اِجْلِسْ حَيْثُ تَشَاءُ.
examples.translation: Sit where you wish.
examples.explanation: حَيْثُ introduces the place-related clause تَشَاءُ, “you wish.” Translate the phrase together as “where you wish,” rather than treating حَيْثُ as the question word أَيْنَ.

concepts.title: Another لَمَّا means “when”
concepts.rule: Temporal لَمَّا links past events as “when.” It differs from negative لَمَّا (“not yet”), which governs a majzum mudari.

examples.arabic:
لَمَّا سَمِعْتُ الْجَرَسَ دَخَلْتُ الْفَصْلَ.
لَمَّا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى مَكَّةَ زُرْتُ صَدِيقِي.
عِنْدَمَا أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ أَجْلِسُ فِي الصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ.
examples.translation:
When I heard the bell, I entered the classroom.
When I went to Makkah, I visited my friend.
When I go to the mosque, I sit in the first row.
examples.explanation: The “when” use of لَمَّا taught here accompanies the past verb. For the present-future example, the Key uses عِنْدَمَا. Compare لَمَّا يَرْجِعْ, “he has not yet returned”: that negative لَمَّا takes a majzum mudari and is a different construction.

examples.arabic: لَمَّا سَمِعْتُ الْأَذَانَ ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ.
examples.translation: When I heard the adhan, I went to the mosque.
examples.explanation: Lamma al-hiniyyah is a time adverb connecting two past events. It differs from governing لَمَّا meaning “not yet”, which takes a majzum mudari. The following verb form helps identify the construction.

concepts.title: Case describes a noun’s job
concepts.rule: Find the job first, then choose the sign for that noun group.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلَ الْمُدَرِّسُ.
سَأَلْتُ الْمُدَرِّسَ.
هَذِهِ سَيَّارَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِ.
examples.translation:
The teacher entered.
I asked the teacher.
This is the teacher’s car.
examples.explanation: The subject is marfu, the object mansub, and the mudaf ilayhi majrur. Dammah, fathah and kasrah are the primary case signs. Other noun groups use secondary signs, so a grammatical case is not simply the name of one visible vowel.

concepts.title: Six familiar roles take raf
concepts.rule: Recognise the role before selecting a raf sign.

examples.arabic:
اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ.
كَانَ الْبَابُ مَفْتُوحًا.
إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ.
خَلَقَنَا اللَّهُ.
خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ مِنْ طِينٍ.
examples.translation:
Allah is greatest.
The door was open.
Allah is forgiving.
Allah created us.
The human being was created from clay.
examples.explanation: Mubtada, khabar, the noun of kana, the predicate of inna, fail and naib al-fail take raf. In the passive final example, الْإِنْسَانُ is naib al-fail, the subject of a passive verb; Lesson 3 develops it. Keep inna’s noun distinct from its predicate.

concepts.title: Nasb includes more than direct objects
concepts.rule: Do not label every mansub word a direct object.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ.
كَانَ الطَّعَامُ لَذِيذًا.
فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْسَ.
سَافَرَ أَبِي لَيْلًا.
جَلَسَ الْمُدَرِّسُ عِنْدَ الْمُدِيرِ.
examples.translation:
Allah is forgiving.
The food was delicious.
I understood the lesson.
My father travelled at night.
The teacher sat at the headmaster’s.
examples.explanation: اللَّهَ is ism inna; لَذِيذًا khabar kana; الدَّرْسَ a direct object. لَيْلًا and عِنْدَ are maful fihi, expressions of time or place. الْمُدِيرِ is still majrur as the complement of عِنْدَ.

concepts.title: Reason, accompaniment and verbal-noun emphasis
concepts.rule: Identify the meaning of the construction, not just its final a.

examples.arabic:
مَا خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ خَوْفًا مِنَ الْحَرِّ.
سِرْتُ وَالْجَبَلَ.
ذَهَبْتُ وَخَالِدًا إِلَى السُّوقِ.
اذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ ذِكْرًا كَثِيرًا.
examples.translation:
I did not leave the house for fear of the heat.
I walked along the mountain.
I went to the market along with Khalid.
Remember Allah much.
examples.explanation: خَوْفًا gives the reason: maful lahu. A noun after waw meaning “along with,” such as الْجَبَلَ or خَالِدًا, is maful maahu. ذِكْرًا is maful mutlaq, a masdar of the verb in the sentence; كَثِيرًا describes it. These are introductory labels; fuller lessons come later.

concepts.title: Manner, specification, exception and calling
concepts.rule: These are case-role previews with their illustrated constructions.

examples.arabic:
جَدِّي يُصَلِّي قَاعِدًا.
أَنَا أَحْسَنُ مِنْكَ خَطًّا.
حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ كُلُّهُمْ إِلَّا حَامِدًا.
يَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ!
examples.translation:
My grandfather prays sitting.
I am better than you in handwriting.
All the students attended except Hamid.
O Abdullah!
examples.explanation: قَاعِدًا is hal, describing the state during the action. خَطًّا is tamyiz, specifying the field of comparison. حَامِدًا is the exception (mustathna) here. عَبْدَ is the mudaf vocative. The list does not mean every exception or every vocative always displays fathah; learn the conditions in their later lessons.

concepts.title: Two basic paths to jarr
concepts.rule: Jarr comes from a relationship, not merely the sound i.

examples.arabic:
الْقُرْآنُ كِتَابُ اللَّهِ.
الطُّلَّابُ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
examples.translation:
The Quran is the book of Allah.
The students are in the classroom.
examples.explanation: اللَّهِ completes the idafah after كِتَابُ. الْفَصْلِ follows فِي. Identify these relationships even when the noun’s group uses a secondary or latent jarr sign instead of an audible kasrah.

concepts.title: A badal identifies a noun in the same case
concepts.rule: A fixed demonstrative can be followed by a visibly declining badal.

examples.arabic:
أَنَجَحَ أَخُوكَ هَاشِمٌ؟
أَعْرِفُ أَخَاكَ هَاشِمًا.
أَيْنَ غُرْفَةُ أَخِيكَ هَاشِمٍ؟
أَنَجَحَ هَذَا الطَّالِبُ؟
أَعْرِفُ هَذَا الطَّالِبَ.
examples.translation:
Has your brother Hashim passed?
I know your brother Hashim.
Where is your brother Hashim’s room?
Has this student passed?
I know this student.
examples.explanation: هَاشِم shares the case of “your brother.” In هَذَا الطَّالِب, the demonstrative is fixed but its sentence position determines the following badal’s case. The Key refers ahead to Lesson 21 for fuller treatment.

concepts.title: لَدَى has a meaning like عِنْدَ
concepts.rule: Use لَدَى with a noun, but لَدَيْـ before a pronoun suffix.

examples.arabic:
مَاذَا لَدَيْكَ؟
لَدَى الْبَابِ · لَدَيْكَ
examples.translation:
What do you have?
At the door · with you / in your possession
examples.explanation: لَدَى is a zarf, an adverbial noun of location or possession here. Before an attached pronoun its final alif becomes ya: لَدَيْكَ. Compare the unaltered لَدَى before an expressed noun.

concepts.title: A time noun can be mansub without a preposition
concepts.rule: An Arabic time expression need not copy English “in” or “on.”

examples.arabic:
وُلِدْتُ عَامَ سَبْعَةٍ وَسِتِّينَ وَتِسْعِمِائَةٍ وَأَلْفٍ لِلْمِيلَادِ.
كُنْتُ فِي مَكَّةَ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ.
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ هَذَا الْمَسَاءَ؟
examples.translation:
I was born in 1967 CE.
I was in Makkah on Friday.
Where are you going this evening?
examples.explanation: عَامَ and يَوْمَ give the time and are mansub. They have no tanwin when mudaf to the expression following them. In هَذَا الْمَسَاءَ, the demonstrative occupies the time position and the following noun shows nasb. The date example names the CE calendar.

concepts.title: A nominal sentence can begin with more than a plain noun
concepts.rule: Identify the structure, not just the first printed word’s appearance.

examples.arabic:
هَذِهِ مَدْرَسَةٌ.
أَنَا مُجْتَهِدٌ.
أَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ.
إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ.
examples.translation:
This is a school.
I am hardworking.
That you fast is better for you.
Allah is forgiving and merciful.
examples.explanation: The أَنْ clause functions as a masdar, here “fasting,” and occupies the topic position. Inna and its sisters are particles resembling verbs; they do not turn the underlying nominal construction into a verbal sentence merely by coming first.

concepts.title: A verbal sentence can have a complete or incomplete verb
concepts.rule: Distinguish incomplete-verb syntax from naqis root morphology.

examples.arabic:
طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ.
كَانَ الْجَوُّ بَارِدًا.
صَارَ الْمَاءُ ثَلْجًا.
examples.translation:
The sun rose.
The weather was cold.
The water became ice.
examples.explanation: A complete verb takes a fail, as in the first example. An incomplete verb needs an ism and khabar, as كَانَ and صَارَ do here. “Incomplete” describes its grammatical requirement; it does not mean a weak final root letter.

concepts.title: A topic names what you want to speak about
concepts.rule: Recognise the topic by function, not only by its position.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مَرِيضٌ.
الْقِرَاءَةُ مُفِيدَةٌ.
نَحْنُ طُلَّابٌ.
أَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ.
examples.translation:
Bilal is sick.
Reading is useful.
We are students.
That you fast is better for you.
examples.explanation: A topic can be a noun, pronoun or masdar muawwal clause. It is normally definite, whether by a name, pronoun, demonstrative, relative pronoun, article or definite idafah. Both topic and ordinary noun predicate are marfu. The following cards explain exceptions to the usual definite-topic pattern.

concepts.title: Put a phrase predicate before an indefinite topic
concepts.rule: For this indefinite-topic pattern, present the phrase predicate first.

examples.arabic:
فِي الْغُرْفَةِ رَجُلٌ.
لِي أَخٌ.
تَحْتَ الْمَكْتَبِ سَاعَةٌ.
عِنْدَنَا سَيَّارَةٌ.
examples.translation:
There is a man in the room.
I have a brother.
There is a watch under the desk.
We have a car.
examples.explanation: A shibh jumlah predicate is either a prepositional phrase or a zarf expression. With the indefinite topic in this construction, it comes first. تَحْت and عِنْد are Arabic nouns, not preposition particles: their following nouns are mudaf ilayhi. Reversing the first example can produce a descriptive phrase rather than the intended complete statement.

concepts.title: A question noun can be the topic
concepts.rule: A question word’s role depends on the sentence that follows it.

examples.arabic:
مَا بِكَ؟
مَنْ مَرِيضٌ؟
كَمْ طَالِبًا فِي الْفَصْلِ؟
examples.translation:
What is wrong with you?
Who is sick?
How many students are in the classroom?
examples.explanation: مَا, مَنْ and كَمْ are the topics in these examples. بِكَ, مَرِيضٌ and فِي الْفَصْلِ supply the respective predicates. In كَمْ طَالِبًا, طَالِبًا specifies the count but is not itself the topic. The Key notes that other permissions for indefinite topics are learned later.

concepts.title: Some order changes are optional; others are required
concepts.rule: Identify topic and predicate independently of their printed order.

examples.arabic:
أَنْتَ مُدَرِّسٌ. ← أَمُدَرِّسٌ أَنْتَ؟
عَجِيبٌ هَذَا.
مَنْ مَرِيضٌ؟ · مَا اسْمُكَ؟
فِي الْمَسْجِدِ رِجَالٌ.
examples.translation:
You are a teacher. → Are you a teacher?
This is strange.
Who is sick? · What is your name?
There are men in the mosque.
examples.explanation: A normal definite topic usually comes first, but a predicate can be fronted. If the topic is a question noun, it leads; if the predicate is a question noun, that predicate leads instead. A phrase predicate must lead an indefinite topic in the pattern just learned. The summary table also analyses أَنْ تَصُومُوا as a definite noun-like clause meaning “your fasting.”

concepts.title: An understood topic or predicate may be omitted
concepts.rule: Recover the omitted part from the question.

examples.arabic:
مَا اسْمُكَ؟ — حَامِدٌ.
مَنْ يَعْرِفُ؟ — أَنَا.
examples.translation:
What is your name? — Hamid.
Who knows? — I do.
examples.explanation: حَامِدٌ is the predicate of the understood اسْمِي: اسْمِي حَامِدٌ. أَنَا is the topic of the understood أَنَا أَعْرِفُ. Context supplies the missing part, so a one-word answer is not necessarily missing grammatical sense.

concepts.title: A mufrad predicate is not a clause
concepts.rule: Mufrad predicate means a non-clausal predicate in this classification.

examples.arabic: الْمُؤْمِنُ مِرْآةُ الْمُؤْمِنِ.
examples.translation: The believer is the mirror of the believer.
examples.explanation: The predicate is the noun expression مِرْآةُ الْمُؤْمِنِ; it is not a sentence. The Key explains the metaphor as one believer helping another recognise faults. A mufrad predicate can include idafah, so it need not be just one isolated written token.

concepts.title: A whole sentence can be the predicate
concepts.rule: Keep outer and inner sentence roles separate.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ أَبُوهُ وَزِيرٌ.
الْمُدِيرُ مَا اسْمُهُ؟
الطُّلَّابُ دَخَلُوا.
examples.translation:
Bilal’s father is a minister.
What is the headmaster’s name?
The students entered.
examples.explanation: In the first, بِلَالٌ is the outer topic; أَبُوهُ وَزِيرٌ is a nominal predicate clause. The attached هُ links it back to Bilal. In the second, مَا اسْمُهُ is another nominal clause. In the third, دَخَلُوا is a verbal clause serving as the predicate of الطُّلَّابُ.

concepts.title: A phrase can fill the predicate’s raf position
concepts.rule: Phrase-level position and word-level endings are different layers.

examples.arabic:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ.
الْجَنَّةُ تَحْتَ أَقْدَامِ الْأُمَّهَاتِ.
examples.translation:
Praise belongs to Allah.
Paradise is under the feet of mothers.
examples.explanation: لِلَّهِ is a prepositional predicate in the place of raf. تَحْتَ is a mansub zarf, but the whole location expression serves as predicate in the raf position. Do not change the internal kasrah or fathah to dammah merely because the expression is a predicate.

concepts.title: Predicates agree in number and gender in these examples
concepts.rule: Match the noun predicate using the agreement pattern appropriate to the topic.

examples.arabic:
الْمُدَرِّسُ وَاقِفٌ، وَالطُّلَّابُ جَالِسُونَ.
بَابَا الْفَصْلِ مُغْلَقَانِ، وَنَافِذَتَاهُ مَفْتُوحَتَانِ.
حَامِدٌ مُهَنْدِسٌ، وَزَوْجَتُهُ طَبِيبَةٌ.
examples.translation:
The teacher is standing and the students are sitting.
The classroom’s two doors are closed and its two windows are open.
Hamid is an engineer and his wife is a doctor.
examples.explanation: The examples compare singular, plural, masculine dual and feminine dual predicates. Their forms follow the topic’s number and gender. Retain the earlier qualifications for non-human plurals rather than extending the human plural example to every noun.

concepts.title: A zarf locates an action in time or space
concepts.rule: Distinguish the mansub zarf from its majrur complement.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجْتُ لَيْلًا.
سَأُسَافِرُ غَدًا.
نِمْتُ بَعْدَ نَوْمِكَ.
مَشَيْتُ مِيلًا.
نِمْتُ تَحْتَ شَجَرَةٍ.
examples.translation:
I went out at night.
I will travel tomorrow.
I slept after you slept.
I walked a mile.
I slept under a tree.
examples.explanation: Time expressions are zarf zaman; space or distance expressions are zarf makan. The zarf is mansub when declinable. A following noun in an idafah remains majrur, as نَوْمِكَ and شَجَرَةٍ show.

concepts.title: Some adverbs have fixed endings
concepts.rule: A fixed adverb’s final vowel does not change to match its syntactic position.

examples.arabic:
مَتَى خَرَجْتَ؟ · أَيْنَ تَدْرُسُ؟
لَمْ أَغِبْ أَمْسِ.
لَمْ أَذُقْ هَذِهِ الْفَاكِهَةَ قَطُّ.
اِجْلِسْ هُنَا. · اِجْلِسْ حَيْثُ شِئْتَ.
examples.translation:
When did you go out? · Where do you study?
I was not absent yesterday.
I have never tasted this fruit.
Sit here. · Sit where you like.
examples.explanation: أَيْنَ is fixed on fathah, أَمْسِ on kasrah, and حَيْثُ / قَطُّ on dammah. هُنَا and مَتَى end in a long alif, classed as sakin. Analyse each as mabni in the place of nasb for its adverbial job. ظُرُوف is the plural of ظَرْف.

concepts.title: “All,” “part,” and fractions can stand as adverbs
concepts.rule: Find the unit after the amount word to recognise the adverbial use.

examples.arabic:
سَافَرْنَا كُلَّ النَّهَارِ.
بَقِيتُ فِي الْمُسْتَشْفَى بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ.
انْتَظَرْتُكَ رُبْعَ سَاعَةٍ.
مَشَيْتُ نِصْفَ كِيلُومِتْرٍ.
examples.translation:
We travelled the whole day.
I stayed in the hospital for part of a day.
I waited for you a quarter of an hour.
I walked half a kilometre.
examples.explanation: كُلَّ, بَعْضَ, رُبْعَ and نِصْفَ take nasb because they represent the time or distance expression. Their actual time or space unit is the majrur mudaf ilayhi. The word “all” is not always tawkid after a noun; here it heads the adverbial phrase.

concepts.title: An adjective or demonstrative can stand for a time expression
concepts.rule: A time expression’s grammatical job can pass to another word.

examples.arabic:
جَلَسْتُ وَقْتًا طَوِيلًا. ← جَلَسْتُ طَوِيلًا.
جِئْتُ هَذَا الْأُسْبُوعَ.
examples.translation:
I sat for a long time. → I sat for long.
I came this week.
examples.explanation: After وَقْتًا is omitted, its adjective طَوِيلًا represents the time expression. In the second example, هَذَا occupies the zarf position and الْأُسْبُوعَ is its badal. هَذَا remains fixed while the following noun visibly shows nasb.

concepts.title: Numbers and كَمْ can represent duration or distance
concepts.rule: Determine what كَمْ measures before assigning its role.

examples.arabic:
مَكَثْتُ فِي بَغْدَادَ أَرْبَعَةَ أَيَّامٍ.
سِرْنَا مِائَةَ كِيلُومِتْرٍ.
كَمْ لَبِثْتَ؟ · كَمْ مَشَيْتَ؟
examples.translation:
I stayed in Baghdad four days.
We travelled one hundred kilometres.
How long did you stay? · How far did you walk?
examples.explanation: أَرْبَعَةَ and مِائَةَ stand for time and distance expressions and take nasb. كَمْ has the same adverbial function when the understood unit is days, hours or distance. It is not automatically an object just because it asks “how many.”

concepts.title: Review omitted complements after “before” and “after”
concepts.rule: Keep the i with an expressed complement and fixed u in the illustrated omission construction.

examples.arabic:
كُنْتُ مُدِيرًا مِنْ قَبْلِ ذَلِكَ.
كُنْتُ مُدِيرًا مِنْ قَبْلُ.
لَمْ أَرَهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ.
لَمْ أَرَهُ مِنْ بَعْدُ.
examples.translation:
I was a headmaster before that.
I was a headmaster earlier.
I did not see him after that.
I did not see him later.
examples.explanation: With ذَلِكَ expressed, قَبْلِ and بَعْدِ are declining nouns after مِنْ and take kasrah. When the understood complement is omitted in this construction, they become mabni with dammah: قَبْلُ, بَعْدُ. This makes the earlier Book 2 rule explicit by contrast.

concepts.title: Some paired time words form a fixed compound
concepts.rule: Learn the paired time expressions as fixed compounds.

examples.arabic:
أَعْمَلُ لَيْلَ نَهَارَ.
نَعْبُدُ اللَّهَ صَبَاحَ مَسَاءَ.
examples.translation:
I work day and night.
We worship Allah morning and evening.
examples.explanation: لَيْلَ نَهَارَ and صَبَاحَ مَسَاءَ combine two nouns as a mabni expression. They are not ordinary idafah phrases requiring a majrur second noun here. This final grammar point completes the Book 3A Key; the remaining pages are vocabulary.

concepts.title: Giving can take two objects
concepts.rule: Keep track of both objects, even inside one written word.

examples.arabic:
أَعْطَيْتُ بِلَالًا سَاعَةً.
مَنْ أَعْطَاكَهُ؟
أَعْطَانِيهِ الْمُدَرِّسُ.
examples.translation:
I gave Bilal a watch.
Who gave it to you?
The teacher gave it to me.
examples.explanation: أَعْطَى يُعْطِي has masdar إِعْطَاءٌ and command أَعْطِ. Its active/passive participles are مُعْطٍ / مُعْطًى. The two objects can be nouns or attached pronouns: ka/ni identify the recipient; hu/hi identifies the gift.

concepts.title: “We” can be followed by a mansub specification
concepts.rule: Do not read the specifying noun as an ordinary marfu predicate.

examples.arabic:
نَحْنُ الطُّلَّابَ
نَحْنُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ لَا نَأْكُلُ لَحْمَ الْخِنْزِيرِ.
examples.translation:
We, the students
We Muslims do not eat pork.
examples.explanation: The specified noun is makhsus and mansub, understood as the object of an omitted أَخُصُّ, “I specify”. Its adjective follows its case, and it can itself be an idafah phrase, as the chapter’s heirs example shows.

concepts.title: Badal may rename a whole or select a part
concepts.rule: First identify the relationship, then match the case.

examples.arabic:
نَجَحَ أَخُوكَ مُحَمَّدٌ.
أَكَلْتُ الدَّجَاجَةَ نِصْفَهَا.
examples.translation:
Your brother Muhammad passed.
I ate the chicken, half of it.
examples.explanation: Total badal identifies the same referent: Muhammad is your brother. Partial badal names a part: half of the chicken. The original expression is mubdal minhu. The pronoun in نِصْفَهَا links the part back to the whole.

concepts.title: Badal can specify a quality or correct a word
concepts.rule: Use the relation in meaning to distinguish the four kinds.

examples.arabic:
أَعْجَبَنِي هَذَا الْكِتَابُ أُسْلُوبُهُ.
أَعْطِنِي الْكِتَابَ الدَّفْتَرَ.
examples.translation:
I like this book, its style.
Give me the book—I mean the notebook.
examples.explanation: Badal ishtimal specifies something associated with the original, such as a book’s style. Dissimilar badal corrects the first expression spoken by mistake. In the first example, style is not the whole book or a physical portion of it.

concepts.title: Badal need not match definiteness
concepts.rule: Do not reduce badal to adjective agreement or proper names.

examples.arabic:
أَعْرِفُ لُغَتَيْنِ: الْفَرَنْسِيَّةَ وَالْإِسْبَانِيَّةَ.
نَتَسَاءَلُ عَنِ الِامْتِحَانِ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ؟
examples.translation:
I know two languages: French and Spanish.
We ask one another about the examination: how will it be?
examples.explanation: Unlike a naat, badal need not agree in being definite or indefinite. The chapter illustrates noun-for-noun, verb-for-verb, sentence-for-sentence and a clause explaining a noun. The question clause can supply comprehensive specification.
