concepts.title: Zanna takes two objects from a nominal statement
concepts.rule: Two objects here express a judgement about one subject.

examples.arabic:
الِامْتِحَانُ قَرِيبٌ. ← أَظُنُّ الِامْتِحَانَ قَرِيبًا.
أَظُنُّ الْمُدِيرَ يَأْتِي غَدًا.
examples.translation:
The examination is near → I think it is near.
I think the headmaster is coming tomorrow.
examples.explanation: The original mubtada becomes the first object and original khabar the second. A word second object is visibly mansub; a verb clause such as يَأْتِي غَدًا occupies the position of nasb while retaining its internal grammar.

concepts.title: Zanna may instead take an or anna clauses
concepts.rule: Keep outer content and inner clause government distinct.

examples.arabic:
أَظُنُّ أَنَّ الِامْتِحَانَ سَهْلٌ.
مَا ظَنَنْتُ أَنْ يَرْسُبَ أَحْمَدُ.
examples.translation:
I think the examination is easy.
I did not think Ahmad would fail.
examples.explanation: With anna, the examination is its ism and easy its khabar. With an plus mudari, an governs the verb’s nasb. This masdar muawwal supplies the content that otherwise appears as the two objects; do not make anna’s khabar mansub as if it were directly governed by zanna.

concepts.title: Raa can mean seeing or judging
concepts.rule: Use meaning and context to resolve identical-looking verb forms.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ.
أَرَى حَامِدًا عَالِمًا.
أَرَاهُ جَاهِلًا.
examples.translation:
I saw Ibrahim.
I think Hamid is a scholar.
I think he is ignorant.
examples.explanation: Visual raa takes one object. Mental raa takes two objects originally functioning as mubtada and khabar, like zanna. In أَرَاهُ, hu is the first object and جَاهِلًا the second. This أَرَى is first-person basic raa here, not Form IV “I show”.

concepts.title: Jaala can make or deem something to be something
concepts.rule: Meaning distinguishes a real transformation from a judgement.

examples.arabic:
سَأَجْعَلُ هَذِهِ الْغُرْفَةَ دُكَّانًا.
أَجَعَلْتَنِي مُدِيرًا؟
examples.translation:
I will make this room a shop.
Have you deemed me a headmaster?
examples.explanation: In the first sense jaala causes a change; in the second it judges or supposes. The thing/person is the first object and the resulting or judged description the second. Both objects occupy nasb.

concepts.title: Opening idh can depend on an omitted “remember”
concepts.rule: Recover the implied verb from the cited narrative construction.

examples.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ
examples.translation: Remember when Ibrahim said…
examples.explanation: For the verse openings discussed, the Key supplies omitted اُذْكُرُوا, “remember”. Idh then occupies its object position. This explains an apparently standalone time clause without treating every idh in Arabic as requiring an omitted command.

concepts.title: A cognate masdar can emphasise the action
concepts.rule: An absolute object describes or reinforces the action itself.

examples.arabic:
ضَرَبَنِي بِلَالٌ ضَرْبًا.
وَكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ مُوسَى تَكْلِيمًا.
examples.translation:
Bilal gave me a real beating.
Allah spoke to Musa directly.
examples.explanation: Maful mutlaq is the action’s masdar used with its verb. Here it confirms that the action actually happened rather than being loosely or figuratively described. It is distinct from maful bihi, the person or thing affected.

concepts.title: The absolute object can specify count or kind
concepts.rule: Ask whether the masdar confirms, counts or describes the action.

examples.arabic:
طُبِعَ الْكِتَابُ طَبْعَتَيْنِ.
مَاتَ مَوْتَ الشُّهَدَاءِ.
اُكْتُبْ كِتَابَةً وَاضِحَةً.
examples.translation:
The book was printed twice.
He died the death of martyrs.
Write clearly.
examples.explanation: A count masdar can be dual or qualified by a number. Type can be specified by idafah or an adjective. The maful mutlaq remains mansub; its following mudaf ilayhi is majrur and its adjective agrees.

concepts.title: A masdar can replace its omitted verb
concepts.rule: A familiar short expression may contain an understood verb.

examples.arabic: صَبْرًا! · شُكْرًا!
examples.translation: Have patience! · Thank you!
examples.explanation: صَبْرًا stands for an instruction such as اِصْبِرْ; شُكْرًا stands for “I thank”. The verb need not be spoken for the masdar to occupy the absolute-object role. This is different from an ism fil, which is its own word class.

concepts.title: Kull, baad and ayy can stand for the action masdar
concepts.rule: The substitute carries nasb; its possessed masdar carries jarr.

examples.arabic:
أَعْرِفُهُ كُلَّ الْمَعْرِفَةِ.
أَيَّ نَوْمٍ تَنَامُ؟
examples.translation:
I know him fully well.
What sort of sleep do you sleep?
examples.explanation: These specifying words take the absolute-object role and nasb. The following masdar is their majrur mudaf ilayhi. The Key also illustrates بَعْضَ الْمُؤَاخَذَةِ for punishment to some extent.

concepts.title: A number can represent how often the action occurs
concepts.rule: Do not force the counted noun into nasb just because the number is mansub.

examples.arabic: طُبِعَ الْكِتَابُ ثَلَاثَ طَبَعَاتٍ.
examples.translation: The book was printed three times.
examples.explanation: The number takes nasb as the absolute-object substitute. The action noun supplies the count specification: after three it is plural majrur. The footnote reminds that numeric tamyiz can be majrur or mansub, depending on the number.

concepts.title: An adjective can remain after the masdar is omitted
concepts.rule: An -an adverb-like word may represent an omitted action noun.

examples.arabic:
فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْسَ جَيِّدًا.
فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْسَ فَهْمًا جَيِّدًا.
examples.translation:
I understood the lesson well.
I understood the lesson with good understanding.
examples.explanation: The shorter expression leaves out فَهْمًا and retains its adjective جَيِّدًا as the substitute. The word describes the understanding, not the learner’s state as a hal.

concepts.title: Ism al-masdar can substitute for the fuller masdar
concepts.rule: Related action nouns need not have the full derived masdar pattern.

examples.arabic:
كَلَامٌ · تَكْلِيمٌ
قُبْلَةٌ · تَقْبِيلٌ
كَلَّمَنِي كَلَامًا شَدِيدًا.
examples.translation:
Speech · speaking
A kiss · kissing
He spoke harsh words to me.
examples.explanation: The Key distinguishes the shorter action noun from the pattern masdar. Both can name the relevant action; the shorter noun can occupy the absolute-object role. Do not confuse ism al-masdar with ism fil.

concepts.title: A related masdar may come from another verb form
concepts.rule: Cognate meaning can link a verb with another form’s masdar.

examples.arabic:
اِشْتَرَيْتُ هَذِهِ السَّيَّارَةَ شِرَاءً مُبَاشِرًا.
تَبَسَّمْتُ اِبْتِسَامًا.
examples.translation:
I bought this car directly.
I smiled.
examples.explanation: The first uses the basic-root masdar شراء with Form VIII اشترى instead of its own اشتراء. The second uses Form VIII ابتسام with Form V تبسم. The Key also pairs تحبون with حب and تبتل with تبتيلا. The verbs share the action meaning in these examples.

concepts.title: A demonstrative or pronoun can refer to the action
concepts.rule: Identify what a pronoun or demonstrative points back to.

examples.arabic:
أَتَسْتَقْبِلُنِي هَذَا الِاسْتِقْبَالَ؟
اِجْتَهَدْتُ اِجْتِهَادًا لَمْ يَجْتَهِدْهُ غَيْرِي.
examples.translation:
Do you give me this kind of reception?
I worked hard in a way nobody else did.
examples.explanation: In the first, hadha is the absolute-object substitute and الاستقبال its badal. In the second, hu refers back to the masdar اجتهادا rather than to a person or direct object. Both are in a nasb position despite fixed pronunciation.

concepts.title: A synonym can stand for the verb’s own masdar
concepts.rule: Absolute-object substitutes can be linked by meaning as well as root.

examples.arabic: عِشْتُ حَيَاةً سَعِيدَةً.
examples.translation: I lived a happy life.
examples.explanation: حَيَاةً is synonymous with the masdar عِيشَةً from عاش. It can therefore occupy the absolute-object role and take nasb. The root letters need not match when the action meaning does.

concepts.title: Maful lahu gives the reason for an action
concepts.rule: Ask why the action occurs to distinguish reason from manner or emphasis.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ أَخْرُجْ خَوْفًا مِنَ الْمَطَرِ.
حَضَرْتُ حُبًّا لِلنَّحْوِ.
خَشْيَةَ إِمْلَاقٍ
examples.translation:
I did not go out for fear of rain.
I attended for love of grammar.
For fear of poverty
examples.explanation: Also called maful li-ajlihi, this masdar explains why the action is done. Common meanings include fear, love, desire and respect. It usually has tanwin, but may be mudaf, losing tanwin while its following noun is majrur.

concepts.title: Hal describes a state during an action
concepts.rule: Ask “in what state?” to identify hal.

examples.arabic:
جَاءَ بِلَالٌ رَاكِبًا.
جَاءَتْنِي الطِّفْلَةُ بَاكِيَةً وَرَجَعَتْ ضَاحِكَةً.
examples.translation:
Bilal came riding.
The girl came to me weeping and returned laughing.
examples.explanation: Bilal or the girl is sahib al-hal, the one whose state is described. The hal word is mansub and states the circumstance at the time of the action, rather than a permanent identifying adjective.

concepts.title: Waw al-hal describes the surrounding situation
concepts.rule: Waw plus a nominal clause can express “while,” rather than another separate event.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلْتُ الْمَسْجِدَ وَالْإِمَامُ يَرْكَعُ.
مَاتَ أَبِي وَأَنَا صَغِيرٌ.
جَاءَنِي الْوَلَدُ وَهُوَ يَبْكِي.
لَا تَأْكُلْ وَأَنْتَ شَبْعَانُ.
examples.translation:
I entered the mosque while the imam was bowing.
My father died when I was small.
The boy came to me crying.
Do not eat when you are full.
examples.explanation: The clause after waw describes the circumstances of the main action. It begins with a noun or pronoun. If its predicate is a verb, the Key uses mudari: يَرْكَعُ or يَبْكِي, even when the main event is past.

concepts.title: Waw al-hal can introduce a completed past action
concepts.rule: Wa-qad plus past can mean “when…had already…”.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلْتُ الْمَسْجِدَ وَالْإِمَامُ يَقْرَأُ الْفَاتِحَةَ.
دَخَلْتُ الْمَسْجِدَ وَقَدْ قَرَأَ الْإِمَامُ الْفَاتِحَةَ.
examples.translation:
I entered while the imam was reading al-Fatihah.
I entered after the imam had read al-Fatihah.
examples.explanation: The nominal hal clause describes an ongoing circumstance. The verbal past hal clause takes qad and places the completed event before the main action. Waw is not simply joining two equal past actions here.

concepts.title: The owner of hal is not always the subject
concepts.rule: Find the word being described before analysing its case.

examples.arabic:
اِشْتَرَيْتُ الدَّجَاجَةَ مَذْبُوحَةً.
يُسْمَعُ الْأَذَانُ وَاضِحًا.
الطِّفْلُ فِي الْغُرْفَةِ نَائِمًا.
examples.translation:
I bought the chicken slaughtered.
The adhan is heard clearly.
The child is in the room sleeping.
examples.explanation: The Key lists fail, passive naib al-fail, object, mubtada and khabar as possible sahib al-hal. The examples show an object, passive subject and topic. The described word keeps its own case; hal has nasb independently.

concepts.title: Sahib al-hal is usually definite, with stated alternatives
concepts.rule: Keep both the normal conditions and the source’s explicit exception.

examples.arabic:
جَاءَنِي طَالِبٌ مُجْتَهِدٌ مُسْتَأْذِنًا.
جَاءَنِي سَائِلًا طَالِبٌ.
جَاءَنِي وَلَدٌ وَهُوَ يَبْكِي.
examples.translation:
A hardworking student came seeking permission.
A student came asking.
A boy came crying.
examples.explanation: The indefinite sahib can be qualified by an adjective or have an indefinite idafah complement. Otherwise the Key fronts the hal or uses a nominal hal clause with waw. It also cites an attested indefinite example outside these requirements, so the list is not presented as exceptionless.

concepts.title: Hal may be a word or an entire clause
concepts.rule: Do not assign nasb to every word inside a hal clause.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلَ الْمُدَرِّسُ الْفَصْلَ حَامِلًا كُتُبًا كَثِيرَةً.
جَلَسْتُ أَسْتَمِعُ.
حَفِظْتُ الْقُرْآنَ وَأَنَا صَغِيرٌ.
examples.translation:
The teacher entered carrying many books.
I sat listening.
I memorised the Qur’an while I was young.
examples.explanation: A single-word hal may itself govern an object, as حاملا does. Verbal hal can have a present verb or a past wa-qad clause. A nominal clause such as وأنا صغير occupies the hal position even though its internal predicate is marfu.

concepts.title: A hal clause needs a link to the main sentence
concepts.rule: Look for the link that makes the second clause a circumstance.

examples.arabic:
جَاءَتِ الْأَخَوَاتُ يَضْحَكْنَ.
دَخَلْتُ مَكَّةَ وَالشَّمْسُ تَغْرُبُ.
رَجَعَ الطُّلَّابُ وَهُمْ مُتْعَبُونَ.
examples.translation:
The sisters came laughing.
I entered Makkah while the sun was setting.
The students returned tired.
examples.explanation: Nun in يضحكن links the clause to the sisters. Waw alone connects the sunset circumstance, whose subject is different. Both waw and hum link the students’ nominal hal clause. This connecting element is rabit.

concepts.title: Hal agrees in number and gender
concepts.rule: Use hal’s case and the owner’s gender/number together.

examples.arabic:
جَاءَ الطَّالِبَانِ ضَاحِكَيْنِ.
جَاءَ الطُّلَّابُ ضَاحِكِينَ.
جَاءَتِ الطَّالِبَتَانِ ضَاحِكَتَيْنِ.
جَاءَتِ الطَّالِبَاتُ ضَاحِكَاتٍ.
examples.translation:
The two male students came laughing.
The male students came laughing.
The two female students came laughing.
The female students came laughing.
examples.explanation: Dual and masculine sound-plural hal use ya endings. Sound feminine plural hal has kasrah for nasb. The owner may be marfu while its agreeing hal is mansub: agreement in gender/number does not mean the same case role.

concepts.title: The verb can already tell you “he”
concepts.rule: When the following noun names the subject, use that name in the translation.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ
ذَهَبَ بِلَالٌ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ
examples.translation:
He went to the mosque.
Bilal went to the mosque.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, translate ذَهَبَ as “he went.” In the second, بِلَالٌ names the person who went, so translate “Bilal went,” rather than “he went Bilal.” The book also introduces خَرَجَ, “he went out.”

concepts.title: A new action: “he sat”
concepts.rule: Use جَلَسَ for “he sat,” and add a location to say where.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ جَلَسَ مُحَمَّدٌ؟
جَلَسَ أَمَامَ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
Where did Muhammad sit?
He sat in front of the teacher.
examples.explanation: أَيْنَ asks “where.” In the question, مُحَمَّدٌ names the person who sat. In the answer, جَلَسَ already carries the meaning “he sat,” so there is no need to repeat the name. This follows the verb pattern introduced with ذَهَبَ in Lesson 4a.

concepts.title: Change the verb to say “you went” or “I went”
concepts.rule: The last vowel matters: ذَهَبْتَ = you went; ذَهَبْتُ = I went.

examples.arabic:
أَذَهَبْتَ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ الْيَوْمَ؟
نَعَمْ، ذَهَبْتُ
examples.translation:
Did you go to the school today? (one male person)
Yes, I went.
examples.explanation: ذَهَبْتَ ends in ـتَ for “you went,” addressing one male person. ذَهَبْتُ ends in ـتُ for “I went,” whether the speaker is male or female. Notice the sukun on ب in both forms.

concepts.title: A new verb for “I love”
concepts.rule: أُحِبُّ already includes the meaning “I.”

examples.arabic: أُحِبُّ أَبِي وَأُمِّي وَأَخِي وَأُخْتِي
examples.translation: I love my father, my mother, my brother, and my sister.
examples.explanation: This sentence brings together the new verb, the joining word وَ, and the possessive ending for “my.” Read it in pieces: أُحِبُّ, then each person joined by وَ. What the speaker loves is the object of the verb.

concepts.title: Add تْ to say “she went”
concepts.rule: ذَهَبَتْ means “she went”; ذَهَبْتَ means “you went” to one male person.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَتْ إِلَى الْجَامِعَةِ
ذَهَبَتْ مَرْيَمُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ
examples.translation:
She went to the university.
Maryam went to the school.
examples.explanation: The first sentence does not need a separate هِيَ. In the second, مَرْيَمُ names the subject, so translate “Maryam went,” rather than adding another “she.” Compare ذَهَبَ (“he went”), ذَهَبْتَ (“you went,” male), and ذَهَبْتُ (“I went”).

concepts.title: A long “ū” for “they went”
concepts.rule: Write the final ا in ذَهَبُوا, but do not pronounce it.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبُوا إِلَى الْجَامِعَةِ
examples.translation: They went to the university.
examples.explanation: The verb ends in ـُوا. Pronounce the و as a long “ū”; the final ا is written but not pronounced. This extends ذَهَبَ, ذَهَبْتَ, and ذَهَبْتُ from the earlier lessons.

concepts.title: A feminine plural “they went”
concepts.rule: Female group: ذَهَبْنَ. Masculine group: ذَهَبُوا.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبْنَ إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَةِ
examples.translation: They went to the library.
examples.explanation: Compare ذَهَبُوا for the masculine group with ذَهَبْنَ for the female group. The latter ends in a short “na.” This ending is different from the long “nā” of “we went,” introduced in Chapter 14.

concepts.title: “You went” for a group
concepts.rule: Use ـتُمْ for this plural “you” in the past-tense example.

examples.arabic: أَيْنَ ذَهَبْتُمْ يَا أَبْنَائِي؟
examples.translation: Where did you go, my sons?
examples.explanation: Compare singular ذَهَبْتَ with plural ذَهَبْتُمْ. The ending identifies the people being addressed, so a separate أَنْتُمْ is not required.

concepts.title: “We went” has a long final vowel
concepts.rule: ذَهَبْنَا = we went; ذَهَبْنَ = they went, feminine.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبْنَا   ·   ذَهَبْنَ
examples.translation: We went · they went (female group)
examples.explanation: The difference is the last vowel: long “nā” for “we,” short “na” for the female “they.” The extra written ا in ذَهَبْنَا helps you see the long sound.

concepts.title: “You went” for a female group
concepts.rule: Female singular ذَهَبْتِ becomes plural ذَهَبْتُنَّ.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ ذَهَبْتُنَّ يَا أَخَوَاتُ؟
أَيْنَ ذَهَبْتُمْ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
examples.translation:
Where did you go, sisters?
Where did you go, brothers?
examples.explanation: The Key compares the female ending ـتُنَّ with the masculine plural ـتُمْ. The feminine singular is ذَهَبْتِ. Group and gender both affect the ending.

concepts.title: A new action: “he returned”
concepts.rule: Reuse familiar past-tense endings with رَجَعَ.

examples.arabic:
أَرَجَعَ الْإِمَامُ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ؟
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ قَبْلَ الْأَذَانِ وَرَجَعْتُ بَعْدَ الصَّلَاةِ
examples.translation:
Has the imam returned from the mosque?
I went to the mosque before the adhan and returned after the prayer.
examples.explanation: The second example changes رَجَعَ to رَجَعْتُ for “I returned,” just like ذَهَبَ becomes ذَهَبْتُ. The words after قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ have majrur endings.

concepts.title: “We love” and “we love him”
concepts.rule: Read the pronoun’s job from its attachment: نُحِبُّهُ means “we love him.”

examples.arabic: نُحِبُّ   ·   نُحِبُّهُ
examples.translation: We love · we love him
examples.explanation: Compare أُحِبُّ (“I love”) from Chapter 11. In نُحِبُّهُ, the verb identifies “we,” and attached ـهُ is the object “him.” An attached pronoun after a verb can be an object, while after a noun it can express an owner.

concepts.title: The past-tense form is called māḍī
concepts.rule: Recognise the basic past form before learning its attached endings.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبَ   ·   رَجَعَ
examples.translation: He went · he returned
examples.explanation: The Key calls this tense الْمَاضِي. You have already used it in Book 1. New endings are attached to this basic form to express different subjects; the process is called isnad. Later lessons explain more verb patterns.

concepts.title: The vowel on ت tells you who went
concepts.rule: ذَهَبْتَ = you; ذَهَبْتُ = I. Read the final vowel carefully.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبْتَ   ·   ذَهَبْتُ
examples.translation: You went (one male person) · I went
examples.explanation: The “ta” form addresses one male person. The “tu” form refers to the speaker, male or female. Compare these attached subject pronouns with the feminine marker تْ of ذَهَبَتْ: the forms and grammatical jobs differ.

concepts.title: “You went” when speaking to one female person
concepts.rule: One female addressee: ذَهَبْتِ, ending in “ti.”

examples.arabic: ذَهَبْتِ
examples.translation: You went (one female person)
examples.explanation: Compare ذَهَبْتَ for a male addressee with ذَهَبْتِ for a female addressee. The ending is an attached subject pronoun. This lesson brings the feminine form into the past-tense system studied in Chapters 4 and 5.

concepts.title: The same written letters can have four readings
concepts.rule: Read the vowels and the context, not only the consonant letters.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَتْ
ذَهَبْتَ
ذَهَبْتِ
ذَهَبْتُ
examples.translation:
She went.
You went. (one male person)
You went. (one female person)
I went.
examples.explanation: In “she went,” ب has a vowel and the final ت has sukun. In the other three, ب has sukun, while the final ت has a, i, or u. When marks are absent, the sentence context helps determine the intended reading.

concepts.title: Address a male group with ـتُمْ
concepts.rule: Reuse ـتُمْ with the past-tense verbs you learn.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبْتُمْ   ·   أَكَلْتُمْ
مَاذَا أَكَلْتُمْ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
examples.translation:
You went · you ate
What did you eat, brothers?
examples.explanation: This is the same ending introduced with ذَهَبَ in Book 1, now applied to another verb. أَكَلَ is “he ate”; أَكَلْتُمْ is “you ate.” The attached ending is the subject.

concepts.title: Address a female group with ـتُنَّ
concepts.rule: Female group addressed: ـتُنَّ, with a doubled ن.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبْتُنَّ   ·   قَرَأْتُنَّ
أَقَرَأْتُنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَجَلَّةَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ؟
examples.translation:
You went · you read
Did you read this magazine, sisters?
examples.explanation: The question uses أَ before the verb. هَذِهِ الْمَجَلَّةَ is the thing read; the named noun shows the object’s fathah. Compare قَرَأْتُنَّ with masculine plural قَرَأْتُمْ.

concepts.title: Use ـنَا for “we” in the past
concepts.rule: ـنَا keeps its “we” meaning when the past sentence is negative.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبْنَا   ·   سَمِعْنَا
مَا سَمِعْنَا الْأَذَانَ
examples.translation:
We went · we heard
We did not hear the adhan.
examples.explanation: مَا negates the past action without changing its personal ending. In سَمِعْنَا, نَا is the subject “we”; الْأَذَانَ is the object in the full sentence.

concepts.title: A form for present or future actions
concepts.rule: Translate the مُضَارِع according to the sentence context, not as only “is doing.”

examples.arabic: كَتَبَ ← يَكْتُبُ
examples.translation: He wrote. → He writes / is writing / will write.
examples.explanation: The lesson distinguishes past الْمَاضِي, present-future الْمُضَارِع, and imperative الْأَمْر. You already know the past. The present-future form adds one of ي، ت، أ، ن at the beginning; later cards explain which subject each prefix identifies. The imperative is studied in Lesson 14.

rows: He wrote. → He writes / is writing / will write.

concepts.title: “They go” for a male group ends in ـُونَ
concepts.rule: Male group: يَـ…ـُونَ in these present-future forms.

examples.arabic:
يَذْهَبُ ← يَذْهَبُونَ
إِخْوَتِي يَدْرُسُونَ بِالْجَامِعَةِ
examples.translation:
He goes → they go
My brothers are studying at the university.
examples.explanation: The يَ prefix remains and the ending becomes ـُونَ. The و supplies the plural subject pronoun in this form; the ن is part of the ending taught here. Apply the pattern to يَدْرُسُونَ, “they study.”

concepts.title: “She goes” begins with تَـ
concepts.rule: For “she,” replace initial يَـ with تَـ in this pattern.

examples.arabic:
مَاذَا تَكْتُبُ آمِنَةُ الْآنَ؟
تَكْتُبُ رِسَالَةً إِلَى أُمِّهَا
examples.translation:
What is Aminah writing now?
She is writing a letter to her mother.
examples.explanation: Compare يَكْتُبُ, “he writes,” with تَكْتُبُ, “she writes.” The basic internal verb pattern remains the same; the prefix identifies the subject in these examples. In the question, آمِنَةُ supplies the named subject.

concepts.title: “They go” for a female group has ـنَ
concepts.rule: Female group: يَـ…ـْنَ, as in يَدْرُسْنَ.

examples.arabic: إِخْوَتِي يَدْرُسُونَ بِالْجَامِعَةِ، وَأَخَوَاتِي يَدْرُسْنَ بِالْمَدْرَسَةِ
examples.translation: My brothers study at the university, and my sisters study at the school.
examples.explanation: Compare يَدْرُسُونَ with يَدْرُسْنَ. The female-group form begins with يَـ, even though the feminine singular “she” form begins with تَـ. Learn the complete person-and-number pattern rather than treating every يَ prefix as “he.”

concepts.title: تَذْهَبُ can also mean “you go”
concepts.rule: Read تَذْهَبُ in context; أَذْهَبُ identifies “I.”

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبُ يَا بِلَالُ؟
أَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوقِ
examples.translation:
Where are you going, Bilal?
I am going to the market.
examples.explanation: The address يَا بِلَالُ makes “you” clear in the question. The answer changes the prefix to أَ for the speaker. A noun, pronoun, or conversational context tells you which meaning of تَذْهَبُ is intended.

concepts.title: “You go” to a male group begins with تَـ and ends in ـُونَ
concepts.rule: Male group addressed: تَـ…ـُونَ.

examples.arabic: مَاذَا تَشْرَبُونَ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
examples.translation: What are you drinking, brothers?
examples.explanation: Compare يَشْرَبُونَ, “they drink,” with تَشْرَبُونَ, “you drink.” The plural ending is shared, but the first letter distinguishes the group being discussed from the group being addressed.

concepts.title: سَـ makes the future meaning explicit
concepts.rule: Use سَـ to mark the future explicitly in these statements.

examples.arabic:
سَيَذْهَبُ أَبِي إِلَى مَكَّةَ غَدًا
سَأَكْتُبُ لَكَ رِسَالَةً إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ
مَتَى تَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْهِنْدِ؟
examples.translation:
My father will go to Makkah tomorrow.
I will write you a letter, God willing.
When will you go to India?
examples.explanation: سَـ is called حَرْفُ الِاسْتِقْبَالِ, the particle of futurity. In the question pattern practised by this Key, the future meaning is expressed without سَـ, as in مَتَى تَذْهَبُ. Do not assume a future translation always requires adding it.

concepts.title: “You go” to one female person has ـِينَ
concepts.rule: One female addressee: تَـ…ـِينَ.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبُ يَا بِلَالُ؟
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبِينَ يَا آمِنَةُ؟
examples.translation:
Where are you going, Bilal?
Where are you going, Aminah?
examples.explanation: Both begin with تَـ, but the female addressee form adds ـِينَ. Compare the masculine singular تَذْهَبُ, which can also mean “she goes.” The complete form identifies the meaning more reliably than the prefix alone.

concepts.title: “You go” to a female group has ـنَ
concepts.rule: Female group addressed: تَـ…ـْنَ.

examples.arabic:
أَتَفْهَمُونَ الْإِنْكِلِيزِيَّةَ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
أَتَفْهَمْنَ الْفَرَنْسِيَّةَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ؟
examples.translation:
Do you understand English, brothers?
Do you understand French, sisters?
examples.explanation: The masculine plural form has ـُونَ. The feminine plural has a sukun before ـنَ: تَفْهَمْنَ. Both are second-person because they begin with تَـ in these questions.

concepts.title: نَـ expresses “we” in the present-future form
concepts.rule: Use نَـ for “we,” regardless of the speakers’ gender.

examples.arabic:
مَاذَا تَكْتُبُونَ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟ نَكْتُبُ رَسَائِلَ
مَاذَا تَكْتُبْنَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ؟ نَكْتُبُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ
examples.translation:
What are you writing, brothers? We are writing letters.
What are you writing, sisters? We are writing homework.
examples.explanation: The questions use different address forms, but the answers both use نَكْتُبُ. Compare أَكْتُبُ, “I write,” with نَكْتُبُ, “we write.”

concepts.title: Review the present-future pronoun forms
concepts.rule: Review both the prefix and the ending, not just the verb root.

examples.arabic:
هُوَ يَذْهَبُ · هِيَ تَذْهَبُ
هُمْ يَذْهَبُونَ · هُنَّ يَذْهَبْنَ
أَنْتَ تَذْهَبُ · أَنْتِ تَذْهَبِينَ
أَنْتُمْ تَذْهَبُونَ · أَنْتُنَّ تَذْهَبْنَ
أَنَا أَذْهَبُ · نَحْنُ نَذْهَبُ
examples.translation:
He goes · she goes
They go (male · female)
You go (male · female singular)
You go (male · female plural)
I go · we go
examples.explanation: This review collection brings together the forms taught earlier; it is not a table printed in this revision lesson. Notice that تَذْهَبُ can accompany either هِيَ or أَنْتَ. Use the pronoun or context to distinguish them. Read the forms aloud and identify who is acting before moving on.

concepts.title: Build a command from “you”
concepts.rule: For this pattern: remove تَ, end with sukun, then supply the helping beginning.

examples.arabic: تَكْتُبُ ← كْتُبْ ← اُكْتُبْ
examples.translation: You write → intermediate stem → Write!
examples.explanation: For this basic masculine singular pattern, start with the second-person present-future form. Remove its initial تَ and replace the final short u with sukun. The intermediate stem begins with a consonant without a vowel, so it needs a helping beginning: hamzat al-wasl. This example becomes اُكْتُبْ. Other verb types need their own patterns.

concepts.title: Match “give/bring!” to the person addressed
concepts.rule: Learn the four address forms as a set.

examples.arabic:
يَا أَحْمَدُ هَاتِ
يَا إِخْوَانُ هَاتُوا
يَا زَيْنَبُ هَاتِي
يَا أَخَوَاتُ هَاتِينَ
examples.translation:
Ahmad, bring it!
Brothers, bring it!
Zaynab, bring it!
Sisters, bring it!
examples.explanation: The forms are هَاتِ for one male, هَاتُوا for a male group, هَاتِي for one female, and هَاتِينَ for a female group. The English “it” is understood in these natural translations, rather than an object pronoun written in the source examples.

concepts.title: Recognise خُذْ as “take!”
concepts.rule: خُذْ gives an instruction; the full imperative system comes later.

examples.arabic: خُذْ
examples.translation: Take! (addressing one male person)
examples.explanation: The Key introduces this form here and postpones the fuller imperative, called أَمْر, until Lesson 14. For now, recognise its meaning without trying to derive a complete command system from one word.

concepts.title: Choose the command’s opening vowel
concepts.rule: Middle u gives opening u; middle i or a gives opening i in these examples.

examples.arabic:
تَكْتُبُ ← اُكْتُبْ
تَجْلِسُ ← اِجْلِسْ
تَفْتَحُ ← اِفْتَحْ
examples.translation:
You write → Write!
You sit → Sit!
You open → Open!
examples.explanation: In the basic pattern taught here, use an initial u when the second radical has u. Otherwise use i: both the i of تَجْلِسُ and the a of تَفْتَحُ lead to an i opening. Learn the present-future form accurately so that you can form the command.

concepts.title: Join a command smoothly to the word before it
concepts.rule: Keep the alif in writing; omit its opening sound when joining.

examples.arabic:
اُكْتُبْ
يَا بِلَالُ اكْتُبْ
اِقْرَأْ وَاكْتُبْ
اُكْتُبْ وَاقْرَأْ
examples.translation:
Write!
Bilal, write!
Read and write!
Write and read!
examples.explanation: Beginning alone, اُكْتُبْ is uktub. After يَا بِلَالُ, connect as yā Bilālu-ktub. Likewise, وَاكْتُبْ is wa-ktub. The alif stays in writing. Do not add the hamzat al-qatʿ mark: write اُكْتُبْ and اِجْلِسْ, rather than أُكْتُبْ or إِجْلِسْ.

concepts.title: Two short commands: eat and take
concepts.rule: Eat! is كُلْ; Take! is خُذْ.

examples.arabic:
تَأْكُلُ ← كُلْ
تَأْخُذُ ← خُذْ
examples.translation:
You eat → Eat!
You take → Take!
examples.explanation: Memorise كُلْ and خُذْ as exceptions to the regular steps just introduced. They do not need an extra opening alif: their first remaining consonant already has a vowel.

concepts.title: A linking kasrah before “the”
concepts.rule: In connected speech, these commands take a linking i before الْـ.

examples.arabic:
اِشْرَبِ الْمَاءَ
اِفْتَحِ الْبَابَ
خُذِ الْكِتَابَ
examples.translation:
Drink the water!
Open the door!
Take the book!
examples.explanation: The isolated commands are اِشْرَبْ, اِفْتَحْ and خُذْ. When joined to الْـ here, the opening hamza is not pronounced. A kasrah on the command’s final consonant prevents two vowelless consonants from meeting: الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. This is a joining adjustment.

concepts.title: Match the command to your listener
concepts.rule: Choose the command ending for the listener’s gender and number.

examples.arabic:
اُكْتُبْ يَا مُحَمَّدُ
اُكْتُبُوا يَا إِخْوَانُ
اُكْتُبِي يَا آمِنَةُ
اُكْتُبْنَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ
examples.translation:
Write, Muhammad!
Write, brothers!
Write, Aminah!
Write, sisters!
examples.explanation: The masculine singular ends with sukun. The masculine plural has ـُوا, with a silent written alif after the waw. The feminine singular has ـِي, and the feminine plural has ـْنَ. Compare these with the corresponding second-person present-future forms; the masculine plural and feminine singular commands have no final nun.

concepts.title: “You don’t go” versus “Don’t go!”
concepts.rule: لَا تَذْهَبُ is a statement; لَا تَذْهَبْ is an instruction.

examples.arabic:
تَذْهَبُ
لَا تَذْهَبُ
لَا تَذْهَبْ
examples.translation:
You go.
You do not go.
Do not go!
examples.explanation: Negative لَا النَّافِيَةُ states that an action does not happen. Prohibitive لَا النَّاهِيَةُ tells someone not to do it. In this regular masculine singular example, the prohibition replaces the final dammah with sukun. Compare the ending carefully: the meaning changes even though the consonants look the same.

concepts.title: Use prohibitions in everyday instructions
concepts.rule: Recognise the prohibition even when connected speech adds a linking vowel.

examples.arabic:
لَا تَجْلِسْ هُنَا
لَا تَكْتُبْ بِالْقَلَمِ الْأَحْمَرِ
لَا تَخْرُجْ مِنَ الْفَصْلِ
لَا تَعْبُدِ الشَّيْطَانَ
examples.translation:
Do not sit here!
Do not write with the red pen!
Do not leave the classroom!
Do not worship Satan!
examples.explanation: The first three verbs clearly end with sukun. In the last example, تَعْبُدِ has a linking kasrah before the following hamzat al-wasl, to avoid two vowelless consonants meeting. That pronunciation adjustment does not turn the prohibition into an ordinary negative statement.

concepts.title: Address different listeners with “don’t”
concepts.rule: Drop the final nun in the masculine plural and feminine singular forms, but keep the feminine plural nun.

examples.arabic:
لَا تَذْهَبْ يَا بِلَالُ
لَا تَذْهَبُوا يَا إِخْوَانُ
لَا تَذْهَبِي يَا آمِنَةُ
لَا تَذْهَبْنَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ
examples.translation:
Do not go, Bilal!
Do not go, brothers!
Do not go, Aminah!
Do not go, sisters!
examples.explanation: For the masculine plural, تَذْهَبُونَ becomes لَا تَذْهَبُوا. For the feminine singular, تَذْهَبِينَ becomes لَا تَذْهَبِي. Their final nun drops. The feminine plural لَا تَذْهَبْنَ keeps its nun: do not remove every nun simply because you see a prohibition.

concepts.title: Say what you want
concepts.rule: Choose the person form of يُرِيدُ, then name what is wanted.

examples.arabic:
مَاذَا تُرِيدُ يَا بِلَالُ؟
أُرِيدُ مَاءً.
مَاذَا تُرِيدُونَ يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
نُرِيدُ أَقْلَامًا.
مَاذَا تُرِيدِينَ يَا لَيْلَى؟
examples.translation:
What do you want, Bilal?
I want water.
What do you want, brothers?
We want some pens.
What do you want, Layla?
examples.explanation: Use أُرِيدُ for “I want” and نُرِيدُ for “we want.” When addressing someone, distinguish تُرِيدُ, تُرِيدِينَ and تُرِيدُونَ. The thing wanted is an object, as the mansub endings of مَاءً and أَقْلَامًا show. Practise this verb with the pronoun patterns already learned.

concepts.title: Notice the u in يُرِيدُ
concepts.rule: Remember أَرَادَ with يُرِيدُ, and keep the present-future prefix vowel u.

examples.arabic:
يُرِيدُ · تُرِيدُ · أُرِيدُ · نُرِيدُ
أَرَادَ · أَرَدْتُ · أَرَدْتَ
examples.translation:
He wants · you want · I want · we want
He wanted · I wanted · you wanted (male)
examples.explanation: The Key links the u on يـ، تـ، أـ، نـ to verbs whose past form has four letters; fuller treatment comes in Book 3. Here that past form is أَرَادَ. Notice also أَرَدْتُ and أَرَدْتَ: the long ā of أَرَادَ is absent in these forms. Learn the actual forms rather than adding a suffix to an unchanged word.

concepts.title: Connect “want” to an action with أَنْ
concepts.rule: After أَنْ, use the mansub form of the action verb.

examples.arabic:
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ.
أَتُرِيدُ أَنْ تَأْكُلَ؟
مَاذَا تُرِيدُ أَنْ تَشْرَبَ؟
نُرِيدُ أَنْ نَجْلِسَ أَمَامَكَ.
تُرِيدُ زَيْنَبُ أَنْ تَطْبُخَ اللَّحْمَ.
examples.translation:
I want to go.
Do you want to eat?
What do you want to drink?
We want to sit in front of you.
Zainab wants to cook meat.
examples.explanation: أَنْ makes the following mudari mansub. In these forms, its final u changes to a: أَذْهَبُ becomes أَذْهَبَ. The first verb still matches the person who wants; the second matches the person doing the intended action. This أَنْ is different from أَنَّ learned earlier.

concepts.title: Four verb shapes change u to a after أَنْ
concepts.rule: For these four shapes, mansub changes the final short u to a.

examples.arabic:
يَذْهَبُ ← أَنْ يَذْهَبَ
تَذْهَبُ ← أَنْ تَذْهَبَ
أَذْهَبُ ← أَنْ أَذْهَبَ
نَذْهَبُ ← أَنْ نَذْهَبَ
examples.translation:
He goes → that he go
You go / she goes → that you / she go
I go → that I go
We go → that we go
examples.explanation: The normal marfu forms end in dammah, and the mansub forms after أَنْ end in fathah. The Key identifies four written shapes; تَذْهَبُ serves two pronouns. The same mansub change applies after the purpose lam from the previous lesson.

rows: You go / she goes → that you / she go

concepts.title: Some mansub verbs drop their final nun
concepts.rule: Only the verb governed by أَنْ loses its final nun here.

examples.arabic:
تَذْهَبِينَ ← أَنْ تَذْهَبِي
تَذْهَبُونَ ← أَنْ تَذْهَبُوا
يَذْهَبُونَ ← أَنْ يَذْهَبُوا
مَاذَا تُرِيدِينَ أَنْ تَشْرَبِي يَا آمِنَةُ؟
أَيْنَ تُرِيدُونَ أَنْ تَذْهَبُوا يَا إِخْوَانُ؟
examples.translation:
You go (female singular) → that you go
You go (male plural) → that you go
They go (male plural) → that they go
What do you want to drink, Aminah?
Where do you want to go, brothers?
examples.explanation: The presence of nun marks the marfu form in these examples; its omission marks the mansub. Notice that تُرِيدِينَ and تُرِيدُونَ keep their nun before أَنْ, while the action verb after it loses its nun. A silent written alif follows the final plural waw.

concepts.title: Keep the feminine plural nun
concepts.rule: Do not drop the feminine plural nun after أَنْ.

examples.arabic:
أَتُرِدْنَ أَنْ تَسْمَعْنَ الْأَخْبَارَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ؟
تُرِيدُ الطَّالِبَاتُ أَنْ يَجْلِسْنَ فِي الْحَدِيقَةِ.
examples.translation:
Do you want to listen to the news, sisters?
The female students want to sit in the garden.
examples.explanation: تَسْمَعْنَ and يَجْلِسْنَ keep the feminine plural ending ـْنَ. This nun is not the final nun removed from تَذْهَبِينَ or يَذْهَبُونَ in the previous card. The role after أَنْ does not require a visible change in these fixed forms.

concepts.title: Review the three mudari moods
concepts.rule: Review the whole pattern, including the forms whose spelling does not change.

examples.arabic:
يَذْهَبُ · أَنْ يَذْهَبَ · لَمْ يَذْهَبْ
يَذْهَبُونَ · أَنْ يَذْهَبُوا · لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا
يَذْهَبْنَ · أَنْ يَذْهَبْنَ · لَمْ يَذْهَبْنَ
examples.translation:
He goes · that he go · he did not go
They go (male) · that they go · they did not go
They go (female) · that they go · they did not go
examples.explanation: This review collection uses previously learned examples; the Key gives a revision instruction rather than this printed table. Compare three patterns: a changing final vowel, a removable nun, and an unchanged feminine plural ending. Identify the governing particle before deciding the verb’s mood.

concepts.title: Say “Show!” with أَرِ
concepts.rule: Learn the command forms here without guessing the later conjugations.

examples.arabic:
أَرِ يَا مُحَمَّدُ · أَرُوا يَا إِخْوَانُ
أَرِي يَا آمِنَةُ · أَرِينَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ
أَرِنِي · أَرِنَا · أَرِهِ
examples.translation:
Show, Muhammad! · Show, brothers!
Show, Aminah! · Show, sisters!
Show me! · Show us! · Show him!
examples.explanation: The opening hamza is written and pronounced as hamzat al-qatʿ. Keep the listener endings distinct from the object suffixes: أَرِي addresses one woman, while أَرِنِي asks someone to show me. The Key postpones this verb’s past and present forms.

concepts.title: Use dual past forms for two people
concepts.rule: Two addressed people share أَنْتُمَا and ذَهَبْتُمَا.

examples.arabic:
الرَّجُلَانِ ذَهَبَا.
الطَّالِبَتَانِ ذَهَبَتَا.
أَنْتُمَا ذَهَبْتُمَا.
examples.translation:
The two men went.
The two female students went.
You two went (male or female).
examples.explanation: Third-person masculine uses ـَا, and feminine uses ـَتَا. Second-person ذَهَبْتُمَا serves both genders. Arabic has no separate first-person dual: “we” نَحْنُ and its plural verb form also cover two speakers.

concepts.title: Dual mudari forms end in ـَانِ
concepts.rule: Dual marfu mudari has ـَانِ, with يـ or تـ chosen for the subject.

examples.arabic:
الطَّالِبَانِ يَذْهَبَانِ.
الطَّالِبَتَانِ تَذْهَبَانِ.
أَنْتُمَا تَذْهَبَانِ.
examples.translation:
The two male students go.
The two female students go.
You two go (male or female).
examples.explanation: يَذْهَبَانِ is third-person masculine. تَذْهَبَانِ serves both third-person feminine and second-person dual; context or the pronoun distinguishes them. The ending nun is part of the marfu pattern, not a permanent root consonant.

concepts.title: The dual completes the five verb forms
concepts.rule: For all five forms, presence or omission of nun marks the mood.

examples.arabic:
يُرِيدُ الطَّالِبَانِ أَنْ يَذْهَبَا.
الطَّالِبَانِ لَمْ يَذْهَبَا.
أَتُرِيدَانِ أَنْ تَذْهَبَا يَا أَخَوَانِ؟
أَلَمْ تَذْهَبَا يَا أُخْتَانِ؟
examples.translation:
The two students want to go.
The two students did not go.
Do you two brothers want to go?
Did you two sisters not go?
examples.explanation: The five written patterns are يَفْعَلَانِ, تَفْعَلَانِ, يَفْعَلُونَ, تَفْعَلُونَ and تَفْعَلِينَ, called الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ. They retain nun when marfu and omit it when mansub or majzum. The same shortened dual form after أَنْ and لَمْ has different meanings because the particles differ.

concepts.title: The dual command is shared by both genders
concepts.rule: Use اِذْهَبَا for either gender when there are two listeners.

examples.arabic:
اِذْهَبَا يَا أَخَوَانِ.
اِذْهَبَا يَا أُخْتَانِ.
هُمَا · أَنْتُمَا · نَحْنُ
examples.translation:
Go, brothers (two)!
Go, sisters (two)!
They two · you two · we
examples.explanation: هُمَا is the independent third-person dual pronoun for both genders, and أَنْتُمَا is the shared second-person form. The first person uses نَحْنُ. In the attached subject forms, alif appears in ذَهَبَا, ذَهَبَتَا, يَذْهَبَانِ and تَذْهَبَانِ; the past second person uses ـتُمَا.

concepts.title: Verb moods belong to the mudari
concepts.rule: Use majrur for nouns and majzum for verbs.

examples.arabic:
يَكْتُبُ · لَنْ يَكْتُبَ · لَمْ يَكْتُبْ
تَكْتُبُ · أَكْتُبُ · نَكْتُبُ
examples.translation:
He writes · he will not write · he did not write
You/she write(s) · I write · we write
examples.explanation: The four regular shapes have u in marfu, a in mansub and sukun in majzum. Do not confuse mood with changing subject suffixes. Raf and nasb apply to both nouns and verbs; jarr belongs to nouns, while jazm belongs to verbs.

concepts.title: Feminine plural mudari forms are fixed
concepts.rule: Keep feminine plural nun separate from removable mood nun.

examples.arabic:
الْأَخَوَاتُ يَكْتُبْنَ.
مَاذَا تَكْتُبْنَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ؟
examples.translation:
The sisters are writing.
What are you writing, sisters?
examples.explanation: With feminine plural nun, the mudari is mabni. This gives the formal explanation for the unchanged endings encountered in Book 2. The nun is the subject pronoun here, not the mood-marking nun of the five forms.

concepts.title: The five forms mark mood through nun
concepts.rule: Nun presence marks raf; nun omission marks nasb or jazm in these five forms.

examples.arabic:
يَكْتُبَانِ · تَكْتُبَانِ · يَكْتُبُونَ · تَكْتُبُونَ · تَكْتُبِينَ
لَنْ يَكْتُبَا · لَمْ يَكْتُبَا
لَنْ يَكْتُبُوا · لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا
لَنْ تَكْتُبِي · لَمْ تَكْتُبِي
examples.translation:
The five marfu writing forms
They two will not / did not write
They (male plural) will not / did not write
You (female singular) will not / did not write
examples.explanation: Dual, masculine plural and feminine singular patterns use secondary mood signs. Their mansub and majzum spellings match, but the governing particle supplies the mood and meaning. The dual and plural long letters remain when nun drops.

concepts.title: The passive leaves the doer unmentioned
concepts.rule: Passive changes both the verb and the former object’s grammatical role.

examples.arabic:
قَتَلَ الْجُنْدِيُّ الْجَاسُوسَ.
قُتِلَ الْجَاسُوسُ.
examples.translation:
The soldier killed the spy.
The spy was killed.
examples.explanation: The active sentence names the doer and the object. In the passive, the doer is omitted and الْجَاسُوسُ takes the subject position. The Key’s construction does not add an English-style “by the soldier” agent phrase. Learn it as an omitted-agent pattern.

concepts.title: Regular passive past: u then i
concepts.rule: The regular passive past follows فُعِلَ.

examples.arabic:
قَتَلَ ← قُتِلَ
شَرِبَ ← شُرِبَ
سَمِعَ ← سُمِعَ
examples.translation:
He killed → he was killed
He drank → it was drunk
He heard → it was heard
examples.explanation: In the simple past pattern, give the first radical dammah and the second kasrah. If the middle radical already has kasrah, keep it. The final past ending remains appropriate to its subject; passive formation is separate from subject conjugation.

concepts.title: Regular passive mudari: prefix u, middle a
concepts.rule: Passive formation can restore a weak letter missing in the active.

examples.arabic:
يَقْتُلُ ← يُقْتَلُ
يَفْتَحُ ← يُفْتَحُ
يَقْرَأُ ← يُقْرَأُ
يَجِدُ ← يُوجَدُ
يَلِدُ ← يُولَدُ
examples.translation:
He kills → he is killed
He opens → it is opened
He reads → it is read
He finds → it is found
He begets → he is born
examples.explanation: The mudari prefix takes dammah and the second radical fathah. Initial root waw, lost in active يَجِدُ or يَلِدُ, returns in يُوجَدُ and يُولَدُ. The prefix letters أ، ت، ي، ن are letters of mudaraah; the Key’s mnemonic combines them as أَتَيْنَ.

concepts.title: Passive subjects still control agreement
concepts.rule: Convert the pronoun’s grammatical form as well as the verb’s vowels.

examples.arabic:
عَمَّ سُئِلَتْ آمِنَةُ؟
تُقْرَأُ سُورَةُ الْفَاتِحَةِ فِي كُلِّ رَكْعَةٍ.
قَتَلَهُمُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ. ← قُتِلُوا.
سَأَلَنِي الْمُدِيرُ. ← سُئِلْتُ.
examples.translation:
What was Aminah asked about?
Surat al-Fatihah is read in every rakah.
The criminals killed them. → They were killed.
The headmaster asked me. → I was asked.
examples.explanation: A feminine naib al-fail takes the feminine verb form in these examples. When the active object is هُمْ or نِي, use the passive subject suffix waw or تُ respectively. Do not keep an object suffix while calling it the passive subject.

concepts.title: صَلِّ بِنَا means “Lead us in prayer”
concepts.rule: Use صَلِّ بِنَا to ask someone to lead the prayer.

examples.arabic:
صَلَّى · يُصَلِّي · صَلِّ
صَلَّى بِنَا. · صَلِّ بِنَا.
examples.translation:
He prayed · he prays · Pray!
He led us in prayer. · Lead us in prayer!
examples.explanation: صَلَّى بِنَا says he served as the imam. The command صَلِّ drops its final weak letter, while بِـ attaches to نَا, “us.” This phrase has a more specific meaning than simply reporting that someone prayed.

concepts.title: Hollow verbs have special passive forms
concepts.rule: Hollow passive: قِيلَ / يُقَالُ, بِيعَ / يُبَاعُ.

examples.arabic:
قَالَ ← قِيلَ · يَقُولُ ← يُقَالُ
بَاعَ ← بِيعَ · يَبِيعُ ← يُبَاعُ
زَادَ ← زِيدَ · يَزِيدُ ← يُزَادُ
هُنَا تُبَاعُ الصُّحُفُ وَالْمَجَلَّاتُ.
examples.translation:
Said → was said · says → is said
Sold → was sold · sells → is sold
Increased → was increased · increases → is increased
Newspapers and magazines are sold here.
examples.explanation: The regular passive vowel rules interact with the weak middle radical. Learn the resulting forms rather than leaving a separate waw or ya in the middle. تُبَاعُ agrees with the non-human plural subject in the example.

concepts.title: تَعَالَ is the command “Come!”
concepts.rule: Keep the command meaning separate from the related verb’s other meanings.

examples.arabic:
تَعَالَ يَا وَلَدُ · تَعَالَوْا يَا إِخْوَانُ
تَعَالَيْ يَا خَدِيجَةُ · تَعَالَيْنَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ
تَعَالَيَا يَا وَلَدَانِ · تَعَالَيَا يَا بِنْتَانِ
examples.translation:
Come, boy! · Come, brothers!
Come, Khadijah! · Come, sisters!
Come, boys (two)! · Come, girls (two)!
examples.explanation: In the meaning “come,” the Key uses this verb only as a command. For past or present “come,” use جَاءَ يَجِيءُ or أَتَى يَأْتِي. The related past/present forms of تَعَالَى have the different sense of rising or being exalted.

concepts.title: “Come!” changes when joined to a preceding word
concepts.rule: Pronunciation and spelling depend on whether this command begins or continues speech.

examples.arabic:
اِيتِ
وَأْتِ · فَأْتِ
examples.translation:
Come!
And come! · So come!
examples.explanation: The command of أَتَى يَأْتِي begins underlyingly with two hamzas. At the beginning of speech, vowelled hamza plus sakin hamza becomes long ī. After وَ or فَ, hamzat al-wasl drops, so the root hamza returns. The extra written alif is omitted in وَأْتِ and فَأْتِ to avoid adjacent alifs. The Key also illustrates analogous long ā and ū contractions.

concepts.title: Command someone indirectly with لِـ
concepts.rule: Lam of command takes majzum, unlike the purpose lam’s mansub.

examples.arabic:
لِيَكْتُبْ كُلُّ طَالِبٍ اسْمَهُ فِي هَذِهِ الْوَرَقَةِ.
لِتَجْلِسْ كُلُّ طَالِبَةٍ فِي مَكَانِهَا.
لِنَأْكُلْ.
examples.translation:
Let every student write his name on this paper.
Let every female student sit in her place.
Let us eat.
examples.explanation: The usual imperative addresses the listener directly. لَامُ الْأَمْرِ lets a speaker command or request an action by a third person, and also gives “let us” with first-person plural. It can govern other person forms as listed in the Key. Retain the usual majzum patterns, including nun omission for dual and masculine plural.

concepts.title: Command lam loses its kasrah after وَ, فَ and ثُمَّ
concepts.rule: Say wa-l-, fa-l- and thumma-l- in these command constructions.

examples.arabic:
لِيَجْلِسْ كُلُّ طَالِبٍ وَلْيَكْتُبْ.
فَلْنَخْرُجْ.
لِنَقْرَأْ قَلِيلًا ثُمَّ لْنَنَمْ.
examples.translation:
Let every student sit and write.
So let us go out.
Let us read for a while, then sleep.
examples.explanation: The lam begins as لِـ, but has sukun after the three words listed. This affects the lam’s pronunciation, not the verb’s majzum government. نَنَمْ also shows the familiar hollow-verb shortening.

concepts.title: Prohibitive لَا also applies to the third person
concepts.rule: Check both mood and subject before translating لَا.

examples.arabic:
لَا يَخْرُجْ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْفَصْلِ.
لَا تَدْخُلُ سَيَّارَةُ الْأُجْرَةِ الْجَامِعَةَ.
لَا تَدْخُلْ سَيَّارَةُ الْأُجْرَةِ الْجَامِعَةَ.
examples.translation:
Let no one leave the classroom.
A taxi does not enter the university.
A taxi should not enter the university.
examples.explanation: Negative لَا leaves the mudari marfu, as تَدْخُلُ shows. Prohibitive لَا makes it majzum, as تَدْخُلْ shows. Here the feminine prefix refers to سَيَّارَة, not a woman being directly addressed.

concepts.title: Review four particles that govern jazm
concepts.rule: Recognise the governor before interpreting the ending.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ · لَمَّا · لَا النَّاهِيَةُ · لَامُ الْأَمْرِ
لَا تَحْزَنْ.
فَلْيَنْظُرِ الْإِنْسَانُ إِلَى طَعَامِهِ.
examples.translation:
Did not · not yet · prohibitive do not · command lam
Do not grieve.
Let the human being look at his food.
examples.explanation: The Key groups these as جَوَازِمُ الْمُضَارِعِ. Earlier chapters supplied لَمْ and لَمَّا; this lesson adds command lam to the review. The linking kasrah in يَنْظُرِ before الْـ does not remove the verb’s majzum role. Conditional governors introduced next affect a two-part construction.

concepts.title: These majzum forms of يَكُونُ may lose root nun
concepts.rule: Distinguish this optional root deletion from normal mood-nun omission.

examples.arabic:
يَكُنْ ← يَكُ
تَكُنْ ← تَكُ
أَكُنْ ← أَكُ
نَكُنْ ← نَكُ
قَالُوا لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ.
examples.translation:
He be → shortened form
You/she be → shortened form
I be → shortened form
We be → shortened form
They said: We were not among those who prayed.
examples.explanation: The omitted nun is the third root radical, not the mood nun of the five forms. The regular يَكُنْ form is still valid. The Key illustrates the shortened forms with Quran and poetry; its poetry footnote separately explains a metrically added alif on الزُّلَالَا. Do not generalise root-nun deletion to other verbs.

concepts.title: Separate direct objects from subjects
concepts.rule: Ask who does the action, then whether it directly affects an object.

examples.arabic:
قَتَلَ الْجُنْدِيُّ الْجَاسُوسَ.
فَرِحَ الْمُدَرِّسُ.
خَرَجَ الطُّلَّابُ.
examples.translation:
The soldier killed the spy.
The teacher was happy.
The students went out.
examples.explanation: A mutaaddi verb takes a direct object: the soldier is fail and the spy maful bihi. A lazim verb such as فَرِحَ or خَرَجَ does not need a direct object. Do not label the subject as an object just because it experiences a change.

concepts.title: Some complements need a preposition
concepts.rule: Do not replace a required preposition with a direct-object ending.

examples.arabic:
نَظَرْنَا إِلَى الْجَبَلِ.
ذَهَبْتُ بِالْمَرِيضِ إِلَى الْمُسْتَشْفَى.
رَغِبَ فِي الشَّيْءِ · رَغِبَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ
examples.translation:
We looked at the mountain.
I took the patient to hospital.
Liked the thing · disliked the thing
examples.explanation: The Key calls the prepositional complement an inexplicit object: visibly majrur because of the preposition, in the position of nasb. Learn verbs with their prepositions, such as غضب على, نظر إلى and اطلع على. رَغِبَ فِي and رَغِبَ عَنْ have opposite meanings.

concepts.title: Forms II and IV can make an action causative
concepts.rule: A useful causative pattern is not a licence to invent either form for every root.

examples.arabic:
نَزَلْتُ مِنَ السَّيَّارَةِ ثُمَّ نَزَّلْتُ الطِّفْلَ.
جَلَسْتُ فِي الصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ وَأَجْلَسْتُ الطِّفْلَ بِجَانِبِي.
examples.translation:
I got out of the car, then took the child down.
I sat in the first row and seated the child beside me.
examples.explanation: Doubling the middle radical is tadif; Form IV’s added hamza is the transitive hamza. Some roots use both forms, such as نَزَّلَ and أَنْزَلَ; most use one. The Key says to learn the actual choice from books and dictionaries.

concepts.title: A causative can add a second object
concepts.rule: Count objects from the sentence meaning as well as its endings.

examples.arabic:
دَرَسْتُ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ.
دَرَّسْتُكَ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ.
أَفْهَمَ بِلَالٌ إِبْرَاهِيمَ الدَّرْسَ.
examples.translation:
I studied Arabic.
I taught you Arabic.
Bilal explained the lesson to Ibrahim.
examples.explanation: The basic verb دَرَسَ already has one object. Its causative دَرَّسَ takes the person taught and what is taught. أَفْهَمَ similarly means making someone understand something. Identify both objects separately.

concepts.title: Review the shortened “show” command
concepts.rule: Listener endings and object pronouns do different jobs.

examples.arabic:
أَرَى يُرِي أَرِ
أَرِنِي · أَرِينِي · أَرُونِي · أَرِينَنِي
examples.translation:
He showed · shows · show!
Show me! (male singular · female singular · male plural · female plural)
examples.explanation: The Key explains أَرَى as Form IV from رَأَى, with the root hamza omitted. The commands change with the listener; the attached ni is the person shown. Keep feminine plural أَرِينَنِي distinct from feminine singular أَرِينِي.

concepts.title: A present-form statement can carry a command
concepts.rule: Meaning and context can supply the force of a request.

examples.arabic: تُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ
examples.translation: Believe in Allah and His messenger.
examples.explanation: The Key reads تُؤْمِنُونَ in Qur’an 61:11 as an instruction equivalent to آمِنُوا. It points to the following يَغْفِرْ as majzum because it answers that request. Do not assume this imperative meaning for every ordinary mudari statement.

concepts.title: Dakhala uses fi differently for places and other meanings
concepts.rule: Do not insert or omit fi mechanically with every dakhala.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلْتُ الْبَيْتَ.
دَخَلْتُ فِي الِامْتِحَانِ.
دَخَلْتُ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ.
examples.translation:
I entered the house.
I entered the examination.
I entered Islam.
examples.explanation: The Key uses a direct object for entering a place such as a house, room or mosque. For entering a test, religion or similar non-place domain it uses fi. Its quoted heart example also uses fi.

concepts.title: Review the four direct nasb particles
concepts.rule: Review function and conditions, not just the four names.

examples.arabic:
أَنْ يَتُوبَ · لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ
كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ · إِذَنْ أَنْتَظِرَكَ
examples.translation:
To turn in forgiveness · you will not be able
So that we glorify You · in that case I will wait for you
examples.explanation: An and kay are infinitive particles with future force; lan negates a future action; idhan answers a statement and governs nasb under its stated conditions. The chapter calls them nawasib al-mudari. Other constructions learnt earlier may involve an understood an.

concepts.title: Name the three root positions
concepts.rule: Use fa / ayn / lam to identify which root position changes.

examples.arabic:
فَعَلَ
وَقَفَ · وَزَنَ · وَضَعَ
examples.translation:
The root-position model: fa, ayn, lam
He stopped · he weighed · he placed
examples.explanation: The first radical is called fa, the second ayn and the third lam, even when the actual letters differ. A root containing و or ي is weak (مُعْتَلّ). Weakness in the first position is مِثَال, in the second أَجْوَف, and in the third نَاقِص. Two weak radicals give لَفِيف. These are root classifications, not counts of letters visible in every conjugated form.

concepts.title: Learn the middle vowel of the basic past verb
concepts.rule: A three-radical past verb’s middle vowel is part of what you learn.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ   ·   دَخَلَ   ·   خَرَجَ
شَرِبَ   ·   حَفِظَ   ·   فَهِمَ
كَرُمَ   ·   كَبُرَ   ·   بَعُدَ
examples.translation:
He went · entered · went out
He drank · memorised · understood
He was noble/generous · became big · was far away
examples.explanation: These illustrate فَعَلَ, فَعِلَ, and فَعُلَ. In كَتَبَ, for example, ك is the first radical, ت the second, and ب the third. Learn the middle vowel with the verb; do not assume every past form uses three a-sounds.

concepts.title: Look inside كَتَبَ and يَكْتُبُ
concepts.rule: Separate the prefix from the three radicals, then notice their vowels.

examples.arabic: كَتَبَ   ·   يَكْتُبُ
examples.translation: He wrote · he writes
examples.explanation: ك is the first radical, ت the second, and ب the third. In يَكْتُبُ, يَ is the prefix, كْ has sukun, and the plain indicative form ends in dammah. The middle radical’s vowel must be learned with the verb; it is not always u.

concepts.title: The a–u vowel group
concepts.rule: a–u means middle a in the past, middle u in the present-future.

examples.arabic:
كَتَبَ ← يَكْتُبُ
قَتَلَ ← يَقْتُلُ
سَجَدَ ← يَسْجُدُ
examples.translation:
He wrote → he writes
He killed → he kills
He prostrated → he prostrates
examples.explanation: The group name refers to the middle root vowel, not the first prefix or the final case/mood ending. Learn kataba–yaktubu as a pair. This lesson introduces four of the six groups mentioned by the Key.

concepts.title: The a–i vowel group
concepts.rule: In a–i verbs, listen for the middle i after the first root consonant.

examples.arabic:
جَلَسَ ← يَجْلِسُ
ضَرَبَ ← يَضْرِبُ
غَسَلَ ← يَغْسِلُ
examples.translation:
He sat → he sits
He struck → he strikes
He washed → he washes
examples.explanation: The final vowel is still u in the plain present-future forms here. It is the middle radical that has i: yajlisu, yadribu, yaghsilu. Do not confuse the group label with the final vowel.

concepts.title: The a–a vowel group
concepts.rule: a–a keeps the middle a, not the whole word unchanged.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ ← يَذْهَبُ
فَتَحَ ← يَفْتَحُ
قَرَأَ ← يَقْرَأُ
examples.translation:
He went → he goes
He opened → he opens
He read → he reads
examples.explanation: The past and present-future still differ in prefix, the first radical’s vowel, and the final ending. Only the middle radical’s vowel stays a. These familiar verbs make a useful starting set for the group.

concepts.title: The i–a group—and why to learn verb pairs
concepts.rule: Learn past + present-future as one vocabulary pair.

examples.arabic:
فَهِمَ ← يَفْهَمُ
شَرِبَ ← يَشْرَبُ
حَفِظَ ← يَحْفَظُ
examples.translation:
He understood → he understands
He drank → he drinks
He memorised → he memorises
examples.explanation: The Key advises learning each new verb’s past and present-future together, because the correct group cannot simply be guessed from the past form. Dictionaries provide this information. For “to write,” the book’s model answer is the pair كَتَبَ يَكْتُبُ.

concepts.title: A maṣdar names the action itself
concepts.rule: A maṣdar names an action as a noun.

examples.arabic:
دَخَلَ   ·   يَدْخُلُ   ·   دُخُولٌ
خُرُوجٌ   ·   سُجُودٌ   ·   رُكُوعٌ   ·   جُلُوسٌ
examples.translation:
He entered · he enters · entry
Exit · prostration · bowing · sitting
examples.explanation: دُخُولٌ is a noun for entry, unlike the verbs that identify a subject and time. The examples here follow فُعُولٌ. Arabic has many maṣdar patterns, so learn this form with the verb rather than assuming all verbal nouns use one pattern.

concepts.title: A verbal noun behaves like a noun
concepts.rule: Apply noun rules to a maṣdar, including case and idafah.

examples.arabic:
الدُّخُولُ مَمْنُوعٌ
الرُّكُوعُ قَبْلَ السُّجُودِ
خَرَجْنَا مِنَ الْفَصْلِ قَبْلَ خُرُوجِ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
Entry is forbidden.
Bowing is before prostration.
We left the classroom before the teacher’s exit.
examples.explanation: خُرُوجِ is majrur after قَبْلَ and is itself a mudaf before الْمُدَرِّسِ. The first two examples use الـ on the verbal nouns. The action meaning does not stop a maṣdar from having ordinary noun grammar.

concepts.title: Initial waw disappears in these present forms
concepts.rule: For these verbs, recognise the root waw even when it is absent in the mudari.

examples.arabic:
وَزَنَ ← يَزِنُ
وَقَفَ ← يَقِفُ
وَجَدَ ← يَجِدُ
وَضَعَ ← يَضَعُ
examples.translation:
He weighed → he weighs
He stopped → he stops
He found → he finds
He placed → he places
examples.explanation: The first root waw is absent from these mudari forms. The Key illustrates يَزِنُ from an underlying يَوْزِنُ; the latter explains the change and is not the ordinary form to use. وَضَعَ يَضَعُ belongs to the a–a group, so learn the actual verb pair rather than guessing its middle vowel.

concepts.title: Short commands can need no opening alif
concepts.rule: Use زِنْ and ضَعْ without a helping alif.

examples.arabic:
تَزِنُ ← زِنْ
تَضَعُ ← ضَعْ
examples.translation:
You weigh → Weigh!
You place → Place!
examples.explanation: The initial root waw was already absent in the mudari. Removing تَ and the final dammah gives زِنْ and ضَعْ. No hamzat al-wasl is needed, because neither command starts with a vowelless consonant. Do not add an alif simply because the word is a command.

concepts.title: Diminutives can express smallness or affection
concepts.rule: فُعَيْلٌ can mark smallness or affection.

examples.arabic:
وَلَدٌ ← وُلَيْدٌ
زَهْرٌ ← زُهَيْرٌ
نَهْرٌ ← نُهَيْرٌ
عَبْدٌ ← عُبَيْدٌ
حَسَنٌ ← حُسَيْنٌ
examples.translation:
Boy → little/dear boy
Flower → diminutive flower form
River → little river
Servant → diminutive servant form
Hasan → Husain
examples.explanation: A diminutive is not only about physical size; it can convey endearment and occurs in personal names. Notice the opening u and the middle ay in the pattern. Learn these examples without assuming that every name is a literal description of size.

concepts.title: More verbal nouns: فَعَالٌ and فِعَالٌ
concepts.rule: Do not force every masdar into فُعُولٌ.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ ← ذَهَابٌ
نَجَحَ ← نَجَاحٌ
آبَ يَؤُوبُ ← إِيَابٌ
نَكَحَ يَنْكِحُ ← نِكَاحٌ
examples.translation:
He went → going
He succeeded → success
He returned / returns → return
He married / marries → marriage
examples.explanation: Earlier فُعُولٌ examples included خُرُوجٌ and نُزُولٌ. Here ذَهَابٌ and نَجَاحٌ follow فَعَالٌ, while إِيَابٌ and نِكَاحٌ follow فِعَالٌ. Learn each masdar with its verb; there is more than one pattern.

concepts.title: Hollow verbs have a weak middle radical
concepts.rule: Identify hollow verbs by their roots and learn the past–present pair.

examples.arabic:
قَالَ يَقُولُ · زَارَ يَزُورُ
بَاعَ يَبِيعُ · سَارَ يَسِيرُ
نَامَ يَنَامُ · خَافَ يَخَافُ
examples.translation:
Say · visit
Sell · travel/walk
Sleep · fear (past + present pairs)
examples.explanation: The middle root letter is waw or ya, even when the past form shows alif. The Key explains قَالَ from قَوَلَ, سَارَ from سَيَرَ, and نَامَ from نَوِمَ. Such underlying forms explain the changes; they are not replacements for the ordinary forms.

concepts.title: The long middle vowel shortens with certain past suffixes
concepts.rule: Compare قَالَ with قُلْتُ, سَارَ with سِرْتُ, and نَامَ with نِمْتُ.

examples.arabic:
قَالَ · قَالُوا · قَالَتْ
قُلْتُ · قُلْتَ · قُلْتُمْ · قُلْنَا
سِرْتُ · سِرْتُمْ · سِرْنَا
نِمْتُ · نِمْتُمْ · نِمْنَا
examples.translation:
He said · they said · she said
I said · you said · you all said · we said
I travelled · you all travelled · we travelled
I slept · you all slept · we slept
examples.explanation: For the a–u group, the first radical has u in these shortened forms: قُلْتُ. For a–i and i–a groups, it has i: سِرْتُ, نِمْتُ. The long vowel remains in قَالَ, قَالُوا and قَالَتْ. The suffix type matters; do not shorten every past form.

concepts.title: What is a mutaharrik pronoun suffix?
concepts.rule: The suffix’s structure can trigger shortening independently of verb mood.

examples.arabic:
تُ · تَ · تِ · نَ
يَقُلْنَ · تَقُلْنَ
يَسِرْنَ · تَسِرْنَ
يَنَمْنَ · تَنَمْنَ
examples.translation:
Vowelled suffix examples
They say · you say (female plural)
They travel · you travel (female plural)
They sleep · you sleep (female plural)
examples.explanation: A mutaharrik suffix carries a vowel, such as تُ or the feminine plural نَ. The plural waw in ذَهَبُوا is sakin. Among the mudari suffixes discussed here, feminine plural nun is mutaharrik. That is why the hollow middle vowel is omitted in these marfu feminine plural forms even without لَمْ.

concepts.title: Hollow verbs shorten in these majzum forms
concepts.rule: Use لَمْ يَقُلْ, not a long-vowel form with a final sukun.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ يَقُلْ · لَمْ تَقُلْ · لَمْ أَقُلْ · لَمْ نَقُلْ
لَمْ يَسِرْ · لَمْ تَسِرْ · لَمْ أَسِرْ · لَمْ نَسِرْ
لَمْ يَنَمْ · لَمْ تَنَمْ · لَمْ أَنَمْ · لَمْ نَنَمْ
examples.translation:
He / you or she / I / we did not say
He / you or she / I / we did not travel
He / you or she / I / we did not sleep
examples.explanation: The Key explains the change through الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. For example, the middle waw in يَقُولُ is omitted when the final lam receives sukun after لَمْ. This adds four shortened shapes to the feminine plural forms already discussed.

concepts.title: Hollow commands: قُلْ, سِرْ, نَمْ
concepts.rule: Learn each listener form; do not remove the long vowel from every hollow command.

examples.arabic:
قُلْ · قُولُوا · قُولِي · قُلْنَ
سِرْ · سِيرُوا · سِيرِي · سِرْنَ
نَمْ · نَامُوا · نَامِي · نَمْنَ
examples.translation:
Say! (male singular · male plural · female singular · female plural)
Travel! (same order)
Sleep! (same order)
examples.explanation: For the masculine singular, removing تـ and final u from the mudari leads to shortening to avoid two vowelless consonants meeting. No opening hamzat al-wasl is needed because قُـ, سِـ and نَـ already have vowels. The feminine plural also shortens; the male plural and female singular retain the long vowel.

concepts.title: Hamza spelling changes when the long ya drops
concepts.rule: Compare yajīʾu with lam yajiʾ: the long ī disappears.

examples.arabic:
يَجِيءُ
لَمْ يَجِئْ
examples.translation:
He comes.
He did not come.
examples.explanation: In يَجِيءُ, the ya and following hamza are both pronounced. In لَمْ يَجِئْ, the long vowel has been omitted; the ya-shaped element is the seat of the hamza rather than a pronounced long ī. The final hamza has sukun.

concepts.title: مَاتَ has two recorded vowel groups
concepts.rule: Recognise both مِتُّ and مُتُّ; learn which verb group supplies each form.

examples.arabic:
مَاتَ يَمَاتُ: مِتُّ · مِتْنَا
مَاتَ يَمُوتُ: مُتُّ · مُتْنَا
examples.translation:
He died / dies: I died · we died (i forms)
He died / dies: I died · we died (u forms)
examples.explanation: With a vowelled past suffix, the i–a pattern gives i and the a–u pattern gives u. The Key notes that both مِتُّ and مُتُّ occur in the Quran, nine and two times respectively, while its present-future form there is يَمُوتُ. These are recorded variants, not random interchangeable vowels in every verb.

concepts.title: Final-weak verbs can end in ا or ى
concepts.rule: Compare دَعَا / بَكَى with نَسِيَ / بَقِيَ.

examples.arabic:
دَعَا · بَكَى
نَسِيَ · بَقِيَ
examples.translation:
He invited / prayed · he wept
He forgot · he remained
examples.explanation: In دَعَا and بَكَى, the final weak radical becomes an ā sound, written ا for the waw-root example and ى for the ya-root example. With middle kasrah, as in نَسِيَ and بَقِيَ, the final ya remains pronounced. Do not assume every final-weak past ends in ā.

concepts.title: Final-weak past endings change with “they” and “she”
concepts.rule: The final weak radical may disappear; the remaining waw can instead be a pronoun suffix.

examples.arabic:
دَعَوْا · بَكَوْا · نَسُوا
دَعَتْ · بَكَتْ
نَسِيَتْ · بَقِيَتْ
examples.translation:
They invited · they wept · they forgot (male plural)
She invited · she wept
She forgot · she remained
examples.explanation: The male plural waw is the subject suffix, not the restored third radical. نَسُوا has u before that waw, replacing the singular’s i. In دَعَتْ and بَكَتْ, the final ā drops before تْ to avoid two vowelless sounds meeting. With middle kasrah, نَسِيَتْ and بَقِيَتْ retain their ya.

concepts.title: Some past suffixes restore the weak radical
concepts.rule: Learn the restored waw/ya forms alongside the ā-ending past.

examples.arabic:
دَعَوْنَ · دَعَوْتَ · دَعَوْتُ · دَعَوْنَا
بَكَيْنَ · بَكَيْتَ · بَكَيْتُ · بَكَيْنَا
examples.translation:
They invited (female) · you invited · I invited · we invited
They wept (female) · you wept · I wept · we wept
examples.explanation: Compare دَعَا with دَعَوْتُ and بَكَى with بَكَيْتُ. These forms reveal the root waw or ya hidden by the singular ā ending. The female plural ending also belongs to this group of vowelled subject suffixes.

concepts.title: A marfu final-weak verb may have no audible final u
concepts.rule: Mood can be present grammatically even when its short vowel is not heard.

examples.arabic:
يَدْعُو · تَدْعُو · أَدْعُو · نَدْعُو
يَبْكِي · تَبْكِي · أَبْكِي · نَبْكِي
examples.translation:
He / you or she / I / we invite
He / you or she / I / we weep
examples.explanation: The Key explains يَدْعُو from an underlying يَدْعُوُ and يَبْكِي from يَبْكِيُ. Those expanded forms illustrate the hidden ending rather than ordinary spelling to copy. An inaudible dammah does not make the verb majzum.

concepts.title: Distinguish root letters from pronoun endings
concepts.rule: After the root letter drops, identify the suffix that remains.

examples.arabic:
يَدْعُونَ · يَبْكُونَ · يَنْسَوْنَ
تَدْعِينَ · تَبْكِينَ · تَنْسَيْنَ
examples.translation:
They invite · they weep · they forget (male plural)
You invite · you weep · you forget (female singular)
examples.explanation: The waw in the male plural forms and ya in the female singular forms are pronoun suffixes, not the original third radical. The preceding vowel adjusts: يَبْكُونَ uses u before waw, while تَدْعِينَ uses i before ya. The forget forms keep the preceding a from their own pattern.

concepts.title: Two different structures can look identical
concepts.rule: Use the subject to interpret the ending, especially with final-weak verbs.

examples.arabic:
الرِّجَالُ يَدْعُونَ · النِّسَاءُ يَدْعُونَ
أَنْتِ تَبْكِينَ · أَنْتُنَّ تَبْكِينَ
examples.translation:
The men invite · the women invite
You weep (female singular) · you weep (female plural)
examples.explanation: For the men, the waw in يَدْعُونَ is a subject suffix after the root waw was omitted. For the women, the root waw remains and نَ is the subject suffix. Similarly, the ya in singular تَبْكِينَ is a pronoun suffix, but in the feminine plural it belongs to the root. Identical spelling does not guarantee identical grammar.

concepts.title: Mansub shows a on waw and ya, but not final alif
concepts.rule: An unchanged alif-ending form can still be mansub.

examples.arabic:
لَنْ يَدْعُوَ
لَنْ يَبْكِيَ
لَنْ يَنْسَى
examples.translation:
He will not invite.
He will not weep.
He will not forget.
examples.explanation: The fathah is pronounced after the final waw or ya in يَدْعُوَ and يَبْكِيَ. The alif-ending يَنْسَى cannot show an added pronounced fathah, so its visible form stays the same. All three are mansub after لَنْ.

concepts.title: Majzum and basic commands drop the final weak letter
concepts.rule: Final-weak majzum forms and these commands lose the final root letter.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ يَدْعُ · لَمْ يَبْكِ · لَمْ يَنْسَ
اُدْعُ · اِبْكِ · اِنْسَ
examples.translation:
He did not invite · he did not weep · he did not forget
Invite! · Weep! · Forget!
examples.explanation: After لَمْ, the final waw, ya or alif is omitted. The masculine singular commands also omit the final weak letter. Their opening hamzat al-wasl is needed because, after removing the present prefix, their first root consonant has no vowel. Contrast the shortened hollow commands قُلْ and نَمْ, which need no opening alif.

concepts.title: Recognise رَأَى and يَرَى
concepts.rule: Learn رَأَى يَرَى and لَمْ يَرَ as a set.

examples.arabic:
رَأَى · يَرَى
تَرَى · أَرَى · نَرَى
لَمْ يَرَ · لَمْ تَرَ
اُنْظُرْ
examples.translation:
He saw · he sees
You/she see(s) · I see · we see
He did not see · you/she did not see
Look!
examples.explanation: The Key explains يَرَى from an underlying يَرْأَى: the middle hamza drops. In the majzum, the final weak letter also drops, giving يَرَ. For the command meaning “look,” the Key directs the learner to اُنْظُرْ rather than forming a command from رَأَى.

concepts.title: Doubled verbs repeat the second root letter
concepts.rule: Compare the joined حَجَّ with the separated حَجَجْتُ.

examples.arabic:
حَجَّ · مَرَّ · شَمَّ
حَجَّ · حَجُّوا · حَجَّتْ
حَجَجْنَ · حَجَجْتَ · حَجَجْتُ · حَجَجْنَا
examples.translation:
He performed hajj · he passed · he smelled
He performed hajj · they performed hajj · she performed hajj
They performed hajj (female) · you performed hajj · I performed hajj · we performed hajj
examples.explanation: حَجَّ represents the root ح ج ج. In the joined form the two jims are written as جّ. With vowelled subject suffixes, the two consonants separate and the second radical’s vowel returns: حَجَجْتُ. Do not simply attach تُ to an unchanged حَجَّ.

concepts.title: Doubled mudari forms can join or separate
concepts.rule: The suffix determines whether the doubled consonants join.

examples.arabic:
يَحُجُّ · تَحُجُّ
يَحْجُجْنَ · تَحْجُجْنَ
examples.translation:
He performs hajj · you/she perform(s) hajj
They perform hajj · you perform hajj (female plural)
examples.explanation: The Key explains يَحُجُّ through an underlying يَحْجُجُ. In the feminine plural forms, the second radical retains its vowel before the vowelled nun suffix, so the two jims remain separate. The visible shaddah is not preserved in every conjugation.

concepts.title: A doubled majzum form can end with fathah
concepts.rule: A final a alone does not identify mood; check the governing particle and verb type.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ يَحُجَّ · لَمْ تَحُجَّ · لَمْ أَحُجَّ · لَمْ نَحُجَّ
لَمْ تَحُجِّي · لَمْ يَحُجُّوا
حُجَّ
examples.translation:
He / you or she / I / we did not perform hajj
You did not perform hajj (female singular) · they did not perform hajj (male plural)
Perform hajj!
examples.explanation: After لَمْ, the joined doubled form would bring two strong consonants without vowels together. In the pattern taught here, the final consonant receives fathah. This does not make it mansub: لَمْ still governs majzum. Other forms use nun omission normally. The command حُجَّ likewise has a final fathah and needs no hamzat al-wasl.

concepts.title: The middle i reappears in شَمِمْتُ
concepts.rule: Learn the vowel group as well as the doubled root.

examples.arabic:
شَمَّ · شَمِمْتَ · شَمِمْتُ
يَشَمُّ
شَمَّ
examples.translation:
He smelled · you smelled · I smelled
He smells
Smell!
examples.explanation: شَمَّ and مَسَّ belong to the i–a group. The hidden middle kasrah reappears when the consonants separate before a vowelled past suffix. The command شَمَّ has the same written and vowelled form as the past “he smelled”; context supplies the meaning.

concepts.title: Classify sound, hamzated and doubled roots
concepts.rule: Root structure determines the category.

examples.arabic:
سَجَدَ · دَخَلَ · كَتَبَ
أَكَلَ · سَأَلَ · قَرَأَ
حَجَّ · مَرَّ · شَمَّ
examples.translation:
He prostrated · entered · wrote
He ate · asked · read
He performed hajj · passed · smelled
examples.explanation: سَالِم has no root hamza, waw or ya, and no identical second/third radicals. مَهْمُوز has a root hamza, which may be first, middle or last. مُضَعَّف has identical second and third radicals. Examine root letters, not extra conjugation prefixes: a first-person أَ prefix alone does not make a root hamzated.

concepts.title: Review the three single-weak-position types
concepts.rule: Locate the weak radical before choosing the conjugation pattern.

examples.arabic:
وَضَعَ · وَقَفَ · وَزَنَ · يَئِسَ
قَالَ يَقُولُ · سَارَ يَسِيرُ · نَامَ يَنَامُ
دَعَا يَدْعُو · بَكَى يَبْكِي · نَسِيَ يَنْسَى
examples.translation:
Placed · stopped · weighed · despaired
Said / says · travelled / travels · slept / sleeps
Invited / invites · wept / weeps · forgot / forgets
examples.explanation: مِثَال is weak in the first radical (مُعْتَلُّ الْفَاءِ). أَجْوَف is weak in the second (مُعْتَلُّ الْعَيْنِ). نَاقِص is weak in the third (مُعْتَلُّ اللَّامِ). The appendix brings together the patterns from Chapters 26–28 for comparison.

concepts.title: Two weak radicals give لَفِيف
concepts.rule: The one-consonant commands قِ and عِ still come from three-radical roots.

examples.arabic:
كَوَى يَكْوِي
وَقَى يَقِي · وَعَى يَعِي
قِ · عِ
examples.translation:
He ironed / irons
He protected / protects · he understood / understands
Protect! · Understand!
examples.explanation: لَفِيف مَقْرُون has weak second and third radicals, as in كَوَى. لَفِيف مَفْرُوق has weak first and third radicals, as in وَقَى and وَعَى.
