In the basic commands of the separated type, the first weak letter is already absent from the mudari and the last drops for the command, leaving only the middle radical.

concepts.title: Final-weak verbs show mood in different ways
concepts.rule: Distinguish a hidden vowel from an omitted weak letter.

examples.arabic:
يَتْلُو ← لَمْ يَتْلُ
يَبْكِي ← لَمْ يَبْكِ
يَنْسَى ← لَمْ يَنْسَ
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَمْشِيَ.
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتْلُوَ.
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنْسَى.
examples.translation:
He recites → he did not recite
He weeps → he did not weep
He forgets → he did not forget
I want to walk.
I want to recite.
I want to forget.
examples.explanation: The marfu u is latent after final ya, waw or alif. In mansub, a is pronounced after ya or waw but remains latent after alif. In majzum, the weak letter drops, shortening the long vowel to the corresponding short one.

concepts.title: A doubled majzum can have a visible a
concepts.rule: Read mood from its governor and verb pattern together.

examples.arabic: لَمْ أَحُجَّ.
examples.translation: I did not perform hajj.
examples.explanation: The final dammah of أَحُجُّ is removed after لَمْ. Two vowelless strong consonants would meet, so fathah is added in the joined form taught here. The word is still in the majzum position; the a does not turn it into a mansub form.

concepts.title: Nisbah adds an association ending
concepts.rule: Do not confuse the association ending with grammatical nasb.

examples.arabic:
الْهِنْدُ ← هِنْدِيٌّ
أَخٌ ← أَخَوِيٌّ
أَبٌ ← أَبَوِيٌّ
نَبِيٌّ ← نَبَوِيٌّ
examples.translation:
India → Indian
Brother → brotherly
Father → fatherly
Prophet → prophetic
examples.explanation: The process is called نَسَب and the resulting adjective مَنْسُوب. Some forms are irregular, as the last three examples show. مَنْسُوب with س is different from مَنْصُوب with ص, the accusative case term.

concepts.title: An active participle names the doer
concepts.rule: Recognise the doer pattern فَاعِلٌ.

examples.arabic:
كَتَبَ ← كَاتِبٌ
سَرَقَ ← سَارِقٌ
عَبَدَ ← عَابِدٌ
خَلَقَ ← خَالِقٌ
examples.translation:
Wrote → writer
Stole → thief
Worshipped → worshipper
Created → creator
examples.explanation: اِسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ is a derived noun describing the one doing the action. The first radical is followed by long ā and the second by short i. This noun is not the finite past verb and can take ordinary noun case endings.

concepts.title: A passive participle names what receives the action
concepts.rule: Distinguish فَاعِلٌ, the doer, from مَفْعُولٌ, the affected entity.

examples.arabic:
قَتَلَ ← مَقْتُولٌ
خَلَقَ ← مَخْلُوقٌ
سَرَّ ← مَسْرُورٌ
كَسَرَ ← مَكْسُورٌ
examples.translation:
Killed → killed person
Created → created being
Pleased → pleased
Broke → broken
examples.explanation: اِسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ adds ma- before the root and long ū after the second radical. It describes the affected person or thing. Compare خَالِقٌ “creator” with مَخْلُوقٌ “created being”: root agreement does not imply the same role.

concepts.title: Active participles adjust doubled and hollow roots
concepts.rule: Learn حَاجٌّ and قَائِلٌ as adjusted فَاعِل forms.

examples.arabic:
حَجَّ ← حَاجٌّ
قَالَ ← قَائِلٌ
زَادَ ← زَائِدٌ
examples.translation:
Performed hajj → pilgrim
Said → speaker
Increased → additional / more
examples.explanation: In حَاجٌّ, the identical final radicals assimilate rather than staying as the explanatory expanded حَاجِجٌ. In the hollow examples, the weak middle radical becomes hamza after the long ā. The Key distinguishes waw-root and ya-root hollow verbs, but both show this active-participle shape.

concepts.title: Final-weak active participles become manqus nouns
concepts.rule: Apply manqus rules to the derived participle.

examples.arabic:
نَجَا يَنْجُو ← نَاجٍ · النَّاجِي
سَقَى يَسْقِي ← سَاقٍ · السَّاقِي
examples.translation:
Escaped / escapes → one who escaped
Gave / gives drink → cup-bearer
examples.explanation: Both waw-root and ya-root final-weak verbs produce an active participle ending in ya. The indefinite marfu form drops ya and has kasrah-shaped tanwin, while the article-bearing form retains it. This is noun declension after derivation.

concepts.title: Doubled passive participles keep the regular pattern
concepts.rule: Do not carry the finite verb’s shaddah unchanged into every derived noun.

examples.arabic:
سَرَّ ← مَسْرُورٌ
عَدَّ ← مَعْدُودٌ
صَبَّ ← مَصْبُوبٌ
حَلَّ ← مَحْلُولٌ
examples.translation:
Pleased → pleased
Counted → counted
Poured → poured out
Solved → solved
examples.explanation: Unlike حَاجٌّ in the active participle, these passive participles have no adjacent doubled root letters: the pattern’s long ū falls between them. The footnote notes that the passive participle is related to the passive verb; the Key supplies active dictionary forms to make the root easier to recognise.

concepts.title: Hollow passive participles shorten the pattern
concepts.rule: Compare مَقُولٌ with مَزِيدٌ to distinguish the two hollow-root types.

examples.arabic:
قَالَ ← مَقُولٌ
لَامَ ← مَلُومٌ
زَادَ ← مَزِيدٌ
كَالَ ← مَكِيلٌ
examples.translation:
Said → said
Blamed → blamed / blameworthy
Increased → additional
Measured → measured
examples.explanation: The weak second radical drops. In the ya-root examples, the pattern’s waw also changes to ya, giving long ī: مَزِيدٌ and مَكِيلٌ. In the waw-root examples, long ū remains. The expanded forms in the Key explain the changes; use the shorter resulting forms.

concepts.title: Final-weak passive participles end in a doubled weak letter
concepts.rule: Keep the final shaddah in مَدْعُوٌّ and مَبْنِيٌّ.

examples.arabic:
دَعَا ← مَدْعُوٌّ
تَلَا ← مَتْلُوٌّ
بَنَى ← مَبْنِيٌّ
شَوَى ← مَشْوِيٌّ
examples.translation:
Invited → invited
Recited → recited
Built → built
Grilled → grilled
examples.explanation: For a final waw root, the two waws combine with shaddah: مَدْعُوٌّ. For a final ya root, the pattern’s waw changes to ya and combines: مَبْنِيٌّ. The same change applies in the double-weak شَوَى example, not only simple naqis roots.

concepts.title: A derived noun can name a time or place
concepts.rule: Choose the place/time pattern using root type and the mudari vowel.

examples.arabic:
مَلْعَبٌ · مَكْتَبٌ · مَطْبَخٌ
جَرَى يَجْرِي ← مَجْرًى
لَهَا يَلْهُو ← مَلْهًى
دَخَلَ يَدْخُلُ ← مَدْخَلٌ
examples.translation:
Playground · writing place/desk · kitchen
Ran / runs → course
Amused himself / does so → entertainment place
Entered / enters → entrance
examples.explanation: The مَفْعَل pattern is used for naqis verbs regardless of their middle mudari vowel. For the non-naqis regular examples here, a middle a or u in the mudari also gives مَفْعَل. Learn both the root type and the mudari pair.

concepts.title: مَفْعِل is the other place/time pattern
concepts.rule: The noun can preserve a root letter absent from the finite mudari.

examples.arabic:
وَقَفَ يَقِفُ ← مَوْقِفٌ
وَضَعَ يَضَعُ ← مَوْضِعٌ
جَلَسَ يَجْلِسُ ← مَجْلِسٌ
نَزَلَ يَنْزِلُ ← مَنْزِلٌ
examples.translation:
Stopped / stops → stopping place
Placed / places → place
Sat / sits → sitting room
Descended / descends → lodging
examples.explanation: Mithal verbs use مَفْعِل regardless of the middle mudari vowel. For the remaining non-mithal, non-naqis examples, a middle i in the mudari gives مَفْعِل. Notice that the initial root waw appears in مَوْقِفٌ even though it was lost in يَقِفُ.

concepts.title: Learn the place-name exceptions
concepts.rule: Use the general pattern, but retain the listed exceptions.

examples.arabic:
مَنْزِلَةٌ · مَدْرَسَةٌ
مَغْرِبٌ · مَشْرِقٌ · مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation:
Position · school
Sunset place/time · sunrise place/time · mosque
examples.explanation: Ta marbuta may be added to either place/time pattern. The Key lists مَغْرِبٌ, مَشْرِقٌ and مَسْجِدٌ as exceptions: their associated mudari forms would predict the a pattern under the regular rule. Memorise these common i forms rather than treating the rule as exception-free.

concepts.title: Instrument nouns have three introduced patterns
concepts.rule: Compare the full word shape, not just the initial mim.

examples.arabic:
مِنْشَارٌ · مِحْرَاثٌ
مِصْعَدٌ · مِثْقَبٌ
مِكْنَسَةٌ · مِقْلَاةٌ · مِكْوَاةٌ
examples.translation:
Saw · plough
Lift · drill
Broom · frying pan · iron
examples.explanation: The three patterns are مِفْعَالٌ, مِفْعَلٌ and مِفْعَلَةٌ. They all begin with mi-, but the long vowel and final ة distinguish them. Learn the instrument with its verb and pattern; a shared opening does not make all three patterns identical.

concepts.title: Why مِيزَانٌ has a long ī
concepts.rule: Recognise the weighing root inside مِيزَانٌ.

examples.arabic:
فَتَحَ ← مِفْتَاحٌ
رَأَى ← مِرْآةٌ
وَزَنَ ← مِيزَانٌ
examples.translation:
Opened → key
Saw → mirror
Weighed → balance
examples.explanation: The Key derives مِيزَانٌ from an underlying مِوْزَانٌ: the iw combination changes to long ī. The waw disappears from the surface form but still belongs to the root و ز ن. This is a sound change within the instrument pattern.

concepts.title: A long ā can conceal a final-weak instrument pattern
concepts.rule: Allow for weak-letter changes when recognising a derived pattern.

examples.arabic:
قَلَى ← مِقْلَاةٌ
كَوَى ← مِكْوَاةٌ
صَفَا يَصْفُو ← مِصْفَاةٌ
examples.translation:
Fried → frying pan
Ironed → iron
Filtered → strainer
examples.explanation: The Key explains the ā through contraction of aya or awa. Thus the long vowel does not prove that the word follows مِفْعَال. The final ة and the underlying root arrangement identify the مِفْعَلَة pattern.

concepts.title: Remove ة before adding nisbah ya
concepts.rule: Do not insert the base’s ta marbuta before nisbah ـِيّ.

examples.arabic:
مَكَّةُ ← مَكِّيٌّ
مَدْرَسَةٌ ← مَدْرَسِيٌّ
جَامِعَةٌ ← جَامِعِيٌّ
examples.translation:
Makkah → Makkan
School → school-related
University → university-related
examples.explanation: Drop ta marbuta before adding the association ending. In مَكِّيٌّ the root consonant doubling remains; the ة does not remain as an extra t. Compare the earlier straightforward سُودَانِيٌّ from السُّودَان.

concepts.title: Three diminutive patterns refine the earlier rule
concepts.rule: Match the diminutive pattern to the base rather than adding one fixed suffix.

examples.arabic:
جَبَلٌ ← جُبَيْلٌ
زَهْرٌ ← زُهَيْرٌ
دِرْهَمٌ ← دُرَيْهِمٌ
كِتَابٌ ← كُتَيِّبٌ
فِنْجَانٌ ← فُنَيْجِينٌ
examples.translation:
Mountain → small mountain
Flower → diminutive flower form
Dirham → small dirham
Book → booklet
Cup → small cup
examples.explanation: The three patterns are فُعَيْلٌ, فُعَيْعِلٌ and فُعَيْعِيلٌ. All begin with u and an ay sequence after the second consonant, but differ in their later vowels and length. In كُتَيِّبٌ the base’s alif changes to ya and combines with the pattern’s ya.

concepts.title: Find the root before counting added letters
concepts.rule: Four letters do not automatically mean an augmented three-letter root.

examples.arabic:
كَتَبَ · جَلَسَ · شَرِبَ
تَرْجَمَ · بَسْمَلَ · هَرْوَلَ
examples.translation:
He wrote · sat · drank
He translated · said Bismillah · walked fast
examples.explanation: Three-radical verbs are thulathi; four-radical verbs are rubai. Vowels are not radicals. A mujarrad verb has only its root consonants; a mazid verb adds letters to modify meaning. زَلْزَلَ is a basic four-radical verb, even though it has four letters.

concepts.title: Added letters create related verb forms
concepts.rule: Recognise the added pattern without treating every derived meaning as predictable.

examples.arabic:
سَلِمَ ← سَلَّمَ · سَالَمَ · تَسَلَّمَ · أَسْلَمَ · اِسْتَسْلَمَ
زَلْزَلَ ← تَزَلْزَلَ
examples.translation:
He was safe → saved · made peace · received · became Muslim · surrendered
He shook it → it shook
examples.explanation: The examples add doubling, alif, ta, hamza or combinations. Each derived pattern is a bab; its plural is abwab. Four-radical roots can also take additions, as in تَزَلْزَلَ. Learn the meaning of each actual word with its pattern.

rows: He was safe → saved · made peace · received · became Muslim · surrendered

concepts.title: Review all six basic verb groups
concepts.rule: The basic groups and derived forms are two different uses of bab.

examples.arabic:
سَجَدَ يَسْجُدُ · جَلَسَ يَجْلِسُ · فَتَحَ يَفْتَحُ
فَهِمَ يَفْهَمُ · قَرُبَ يَقْرُبُ · وَرِثَ يَرِثُ
examples.translation:
Prostrated · sat · opened
Understood · came near · inherited
examples.explanation: The six mujarrad groups are a-u, a-i, a-a, i-a, u-u and i-i. These describe the root’s second consonant vowels, not the final grammatical ending. Learn a verb with its mudari.

concepts.title: Form II doubles the middle root letter
concepts.rule: Use yu-faʿʿilu, with kasrah before the final radical.

examples.arabic:
قَبَّلَ يُقَبِّلُ · دَرَّسَ يُدَرِّسُ
سَجَّلَ يُسَجِّلُ · رَتَّبَ يُرَتِّبُ
examples.translation:
Kissed · taught
Recorded · arranged
examples.explanation: The pattern is فَعَّلَ يُفَعِّلُ. Shaddah represents two consonants, making the past stem four letters. Its mudari prefix has dammah. The Key’s footnote clarifies the general rule: four-letter past stems use u; three-, five- and six-letter stems use a. ي، ت، أ، ن are the mudari prefixes.

concepts.title: Form II commands need no opening hamza
concepts.rule: Keep the Form II stem when making the command.

examples.arabic:
تُقَبِّلُ ← قَبِّلْ
تُدَرِّسُ ← دَرِّسْ
examples.translation:
You kiss → kiss!
You teach → teach!
examples.explanation: The remaining consonant already has a vowel, so no helping hamza is required. Keep the doubled second radical and its kasrah. These examples address one male listener; familiar listener suffixes apply to other forms.

concepts.title: Derived forms have characteristic masdars
concepts.rule: Do not force basic-verb masdars into the derived-form rule.

examples.arabic:
قَبَّلَ تَقْبِيلٌ · سَجَّلَ تَسْجِيلٌ · دَرَّسَ تَدْرِيسٌ
قَتْلٌ · كِتَابَةٌ · دُخُولٌ · شُرْبٌ
examples.translation:
Kissing · recording · teaching
Killing · writing · entry · drinking
examples.explanation: Form II’s regular masdar pattern is تَفْعِيلٌ. In contrast, basic three-radical verbs have several masdar patterns that must be learnt with the word. A masdar names the action rather than its doer or tense.

concepts.title: Final weak letters and hamza use tafilah here
concepts.rule: Learn these masdars with their weak or hamza-ending verbs.

examples.arabic: سَمَّى تَسْمِيَةٌ · رَبَّى تَرْبِيَةٌ · هَنَّأَ تَهْنِئَةٌ
examples.translation: Naming · education · congratulation
examples.explanation: For the final-weak verbs and final-hamza example taught here, the masdar is on تَفْعِلَةٌ rather than regular tafil. Keep the actual spellings and hamza seat in تَهْنِئَةٌ.

concepts.title: Replace the present prefix with mu
concepts.rule: Mu plus the present stem gives the active participle.

examples.arabic:
يُسَجِّلُ ← مُسَجِّلٌ
يُدَرِّسُ ← مُدَرِّسٌ
examples.translation:
He records → a recorder
He teaches → a teacher
examples.explanation: The pattern is مُفَعِّلٌ. The resulting word is a noun and can take tanwin. A participle may name a person or an instrument, as مُسَجِّلٌ does in the Key.

concepts.title: A small vowel change switches doer to receiver
concepts.rule: Kasrah identifies the doer; fathah identifies the receiver in this pair.

examples.arabic:
مُجَلِّدٌ · مُجَلَّدٌ
مُحَمِّدٌ · مُحَمَّدٌ
examples.translation:
Book binder · bound volume
One who praises much · one praised much
examples.explanation: The passive pattern is مُفَعَّلٌ; the active is مُفَعِّلٌ. This active/passive contrast applies across the derived forms, with their own stems. Watch the vowel of the doubled consonant here.

concepts.title: Derived place and time nouns share the passive pattern
concepts.rule: A shared pattern can have different noun functions.

examples.arabic: يُصَلِّي ← مُصَلًّى
examples.translation: He prays → a place of prayer
examples.explanation: For mazid verbs, the Key gives the same shape as the passive participle for nouns of place and time. مُصَلًّى illustrates a prayer place; its final alif also makes it a maqsur noun.

rows: He prays → a place of prayer

concepts.title: Add two basic masdar patterns to your vocabulary
concepts.rule: Keep the verb, present form and masdar together.

examples.arabic:
شَرَحَ يَشْرَحُ شَرْحٌ
غَابَ يَغِيبُ غِيَابٌ
examples.translation:
Explained → explanation
Was absent → absence
examples.explanation: شَرْحٌ illustrates فَعْلٌ and غِيَابٌ illustrates فِعَالٌ. Both name actions or states. The shared function does not require identical word patterns.

concepts.title: Form IV adds an opening hamza
concepts.rule: The prefix vowel distinguishes these basic and derived present forms.

examples.arabic:
نَزَلَ ← أَنْزَلَ
خَرَجَ ← أَخْرَجَ
examples.translation:
Came down → brought down
Went out → brought out
examples.explanation: Bab afala follows أَفْعَلَ. These pairs show a causative meaning. Its mudari is يُفْعِلُ: the added hamza drops, but the prefix keeps dammah because the past stem has four letters. Compare يَنْزِلُ with يُنْزِلُ.

concepts.title: Form IV restores hamza in the command
concepts.rule: Do not form Form IV commands by simply removing yu from the visible form.

examples.arabic:
أَنْزِلْ · أَخْرِجْ
إِنْزَالٌ · إِخْرَاجٌ · إِسْلَامٌ
examples.translation:
Bring down! · bring out!
Sending down · bringing out · becoming Muslim
examples.explanation: The Key derives the command from the underlying mudari stem, restoring the added hamza: أَفْعِلْ. This is a pronounced hamzat al-qat, not a helping wasl hamza. The regular masdar is إِفْعَالٌ.

concepts.title: Form IV uses mufil and mufal
concepts.rule: Read participle vowels carefully even when consonants match.

examples.arabic:
مُسْلِمٌ · مُمْكِنٌ
مُرْسِلٌ · مُرْسَلٌ
مُغْلِقٌ · مُغْلَقٌ
مُتْحَفٌ
examples.translation:
Muslim · possible
Sender · one sent
One closing · closed
Museum
examples.explanation: Replace the mudari prefix with mu for the active participle مُفْعِلٌ; change the second radical’s vowel to a for the passive مُفْعَلٌ. The place/time noun shares the passive pattern, as مُتْحَفٌ illustrates.

concepts.title: Weak, hamza and doubled roots keep their special changes
concepts.rule: The pattern explains the family; the weak-root rules explain its spelling.

examples.arabic:
أَقَامَ يُقِيمُ إِقَامَةٌ مُقِيمٌ مُقَامٌ
آمَنَ يُؤْمِنُ إِيمَانٌ مُؤْمِنٌ مُؤْمَنٌ
أَوْجَبَ يُوجِبُ إِيجَابٌ مُوجِبٌ مُوجَبٌ
examples.translation:
Made stand; its present, masdar and participles
Believed; its related forms
Made obligatory; its related forms
examples.explanation: The hollow example has iqamah rather than a mechanically written ifal. Adjacent hamzas merge in آمَنَ and إِيمَانٌ. In إِيجَابٌ the initial root waw changes after kasrah. Keep these root-specific changes together with the general Form IV pattern.

concepts.title: Final-weak participles may be manqus or maqsur
concepts.rule: Derived participles retain the noun-ending rules already learned.

examples.arabic:
أَتَمَّ يُتِمُّ إِتْمَامٌ مُتِمٌّ مُتَمٌّ
أَلْقَى يُلْقِي إِلْقَاءٌ مُلْقٍ مُلْقًى
الْمُلْقِي · الْمُلْقَى
examples.translation:
Completed; its related forms
Put down; its related forms
The one putting down · the thing put down
examples.explanation: أَتَمَّ keeps the doubled root. أَلْقَى gives a manqus active participle مُلْقٍ, with ya restored in الْمُلْقِي, and a maqsur passive مُلْقًى. Its masdar is إِلْقَاءٌ.

concepts.title: Form II can describe repeated or widespread action
concepts.rule: Read Form II in context: it can signal repetition or scale.

examples.arabic:
فَتَحْتُ الْبَابَ.
فَتَّحْتُ أَبْوَابَ الْفُصُولِ.
عَدَّدَ الرَّجُلُ مَالَهُ.
examples.translation:
I opened the door.
I opened the classroom doors.
The man repeatedly counted his money.
examples.explanation: The action may affect many objects or one object many times. The Key contrasts this extensive meaning with ordinary فتح and عد. It is another Form II use alongside causative meaning.

concepts.title: Form II can intensify one action
concepts.rule: A doubled stem can add intensity without adding another object.

examples.arabic:
كَسَرْتُ الْكُوبَ. ← كَسَّرْتُ الْكُوبَ.
قَطَعْتُ الْحَبْلَ. ← قَطَّعْتُ الْحَبْلَ.
examples.translation:
I broke the glass → smashed it.
I cut the rope → cut it to pieces.
examples.explanation: The Key distinguishes thorough or forceful action on one object from extensive action affecting many objects or repeated occasions. Both can use the same doubled pattern. The lexical meaning and context select the reading.

rows: I broke the glass → smashed it.
I cut the rope → cut it to pieces.

concepts.title: Faal is another basic masdar pattern
concepts.rule: A single short vowel can distinguish word patterns.

examples.arabic:
ذَهَبَ ← ذَهَابٌ
نَجَحَ ← نَجَاحٌ
examples.translation:
Went → going
Succeeded → success
examples.explanation: These masdars follow فَعَالٌ, with fathah on the first radical. Compare the preceding فُعَالٌ ailment words. The spelling may look similar without vowel marks, so learn the vowels too.

concepts.title: Form III adds alif after the first radical
concepts.rule: Distinguish the long alif of Form III from Form II doubling.

examples.arabic:
قَابَلَ يُقَابِلُ قَابِلْ
سَاعَدَ يُسَاعِدُ · حَاوَلَ يُحَاوِلُ
لَاقَى يُلَاقِي لَاقِ
examples.translation:
Met · meets · meet!
Helped · tried
Met · meets · meet!
examples.explanation: The patterns are فَاعَلَ يُفَاعِلُ فَاعِلْ. The four-letter past stem gives a dammah mudari prefix. Remove that prefix for the command; a final-weak command also loses ya, as لَاقِ shows.

concepts.title: Form III uses mufaalah masdars
concepts.rule: Retain ta marbutah after the long alif in these weak masdars.

examples.arabic:
مُسَاعَدَةٌ · مُقَابَلَةٌ · مُحَاوَلَةٌ
مُلَاقَاةٌ · مُبَارَاةٌ
examples.translation:
Help · meeting · trying
Meeting · match
examples.explanation: The first masdar pattern is مُفَاعَلَةٌ. The Key explains مُلَاقَاةٌ and مُبَارَاةٌ through contraction of the final-weak sequence. Learn these spellings with their verbs rather than keeping the underlying ya.

concepts.title: Some Form III masdars use fial
concepts.rule: Learn both available patterns without assuming both for every verb.

examples.arabic:
جَاهَدَ جِهَادٌ · نَافَقَ نِفَاقٌ
نَادَى نِدَاءٌ
examples.translation:
Strived → striving · was hypocritical → hypocrisy
Called → calling
examples.explanation: The second pattern is فِعَالٌ. In the final-weak example نِدَاءٌ, ya changes to hamza after the long alif. A verb’s vocabulary entry tells you which masdar or masdars are used.

concepts.title: Form III participles keep the long alif
concepts.rule: Keep the added alif and read the vowel before the last radical.

examples.arabic:
مُرَاسِلٌ · مُشَاهِدٌ
مُرَاقِبٌ · مُرَاقَبٌ
مُنَادٍ · مُنَادًى
مُهَاجَرٌ
examples.translation:
Correspondent · viewer
Observer · one observed
Caller · one called
Place of migration
examples.explanation: Use مُفَاعِلٌ for the active and مُفَاعَلٌ for the passive. The final-weak pair follows manqus/maqsur endings. Place/time nouns share the passive shape; context separates the place from a person acted upon.

concepts.title: Fialah is another basic masdar pattern
concepts.rule: Vocabulary meaning and masdar pattern belong together.

examples.arabic:
عَادَ عِيَادَةٌ
قَرَأَ قِرَاءَةٌ
examples.translation:
Visited a sick person → visiting the sick
Read → reading
examples.explanation: These examples follow فِعَالَةٌ. Learn عِيَادَةٌ with this meaning of عَادَ, rather than assuming every meaning of the same spelling shares the same masdar.

concepts.title: Weak-root changes explain mudiyy
concepts.rule: Do not lose the root when a weak vowel changes the pattern’s appearance.

examples.arabic: مَضَى ← مُضِيٌّ
examples.translation: Passed → passing or lapse
examples.explanation: The Key derives مُضِيٌّ from a fuul shape with waw before final ya. Waw becomes ya, the two yas combine, and the preceding dammah becomes kasrah. The surface shape therefore differs from a regular fuul masdar.

concepts.title: Form V adds ta to Form II
concepts.rule: An omitted ta may hide a Form V present verb.

examples.arabic:
تَعَلَّمَ يَتَعَلَّمُ · تَكَلَّمَ يَتَكَلَّمُ
تَلَقَّى يَتَلَقَّى
examples.translation:
Learned · spoke
Received
examples.explanation: The pattern is تَفَعَّلَ يَتَفَعَّلُ. Its five-letter past stem gives a fathah mudari prefix. When mudari ta meets the pattern’s ta, one may be omitted in literary usage: تَنَزَّلُ for تَتَنَزَّلُ, and لَا تَجَسَّسُوا for لَا تَتَجَسَّسُوا.

concepts.title: Form V commands start directly with ta
concepts.rule: Keep command deletion separate from noun-ending changes.

examples.arabic:
تَكَلَّمْ · تَغَدَّ
تَحَدُّثٌ · تَذَكُّرٌ
تَلَقٍّ · التَّلَقِّي
examples.translation:
Speak! · have lunch!
Speaking · remembering
Receiving · the receiving
examples.explanation: Remove the mudari prefix for the command; final-weak تَغَدَّ loses its alif. The masdar pattern is تَفَعُّلٌ. With final ya, the preceding dammah changes to kasrah, producing manqus تَلَقٍّ with ya restored after al.

concepts.title: Form V participles change the middle vowel
concepts.rule: Mu replaces only the mudari prefix, not the whole beginning of the stem.

examples.arabic:
مُتَعَلِّمٌ · مُتَزَوِّجٌ
مُتَكَلَّمٌ
مُتَوَضَّأٌ · مُتَنَفَّسٌ
examples.translation:
Learner · married person
Something spoken
Place of wudu · breathing space
examples.explanation: Replace the mudari prefix with mu, using kasrah for the active participle and fathah for the passive. Place/time nouns follow the passive pattern. Preserve the ta of the derived stem after mu.

concepts.title: Form V can express the result of another action
concepts.rule: Result meaning is one use of Form V, not its only possible meaning.

examples.arabic:
عَلَّمَنِي بِلَالٌ السِّبَاحَةَ.
تَعَلَّمْتُ السِّبَاحَةَ.
زَوَّجَنِي أَبِي زَيْنَبَ.
تَزَوَّجْتُ زَيْنَبَ.
examples.translation:
Bilal taught me swimming.
I learned swimming.
My father married me to Zaynab.
I married Zaynab.
examples.explanation: This relationship is mutawaa. In the derived result sentence, the person previously acted on becomes the subject; the former agent drops out. A remaining object may stay, as swimming or Zaynab does here.

concepts.title: Form VI adds ta to Form III
concepts.rule: Look for both added ta and long alif when identifying Form VI.

examples.arabic:
تَكَاسَلَ يَتَكَاسَلُ · تَثَاءَبَ يَتَثَاءَبُ
تَنَاوَلْ · تَبَاكَ
examples.translation:
Was lazy · yawned
Take! · pretend to cry!
examples.explanation: The pattern is تَفَاعَلَ يَتَفَاعَلُ. Its five-letter stem gives a fathah prefix. Commands drop that prefix; final-weak commands drop alif. One of two initial tas may be omitted in literary forms such as تَعَارَفُوا for تَتَعَارَفُوا and لَا تَعَاوَنُوا for لَا تَتَعَاوَنُوا.

concepts.title: Form VI masdars use tafaul
concepts.rule: The familiar manqus rule applies to this derived masdar too.

examples.arabic:
تَنَاوُلٌ · تَشَاؤُمٌ
تَبَاكٍ · التَّبَاكِي
examples.translation:
Taking · pessimism
Pretending to cry · the pretending to cry
examples.explanation: The masdar pattern is تَفَاعُلٌ. A final-weak root changes the preceding dammah to kasrah, producing a manqus noun. The indefinite form loses final ya in raf/jarr; al restores it, as in التَّبَاكِي.

concepts.title: Form VI uses mutafail and mutafaal
concepts.rule: Interpret the shared noun shape in its sentence context.

examples.arabic:
مُتَنَاوِلٌ · مُتَنَاوَلٌ
فِي مُتَنَاوَلِ أَيْدِي الْأَطْفَالِ
examples.translation:
One taking · what is taken
Within reach of children’s hands
examples.explanation: Replace the mudari prefix with mu. Kasrah on the second radical marks the active participle; fathah marks the passive. The place/time noun shares the passive shape, as مُتَنَاوَلٌ “reach” illustrates.

concepts.title: Form VI can mean “one another” or “pretend”
concepts.rule: Context distinguishes reciprocal action from pretence and other lexical meanings.

examples.arabic:
تَسَاءَلَ النَّاسُ. · تَعَاوَنَ النَّاسُ.
تَمَارَضَ · تَنَاوَمَ · تَعَامَى
examples.translation:
People asked one another · cooperated
Pretended to be ill · asleep · blind
examples.explanation: The Key lists reciprocal participation, musharaka, and displaying a state that is not actually present. Form VI also has vocabulary meanings such as taking and yawning, so these two uses do not exhaust the form.

concepts.title: Some initial-waw verbs have paired masdars
concepts.rule: Compensatory ة explains the shortened masdar family.

examples.arabic:
وَصْفٌ · صِفَةٌ
وَعْظٌ · عِظَةٌ
وُثُوقٌ · ثِقَةٌ
examples.translation:
Description
Admonition
Trust or confidence
examples.explanation: The Key pairs a masdar retaining root waw with one omitting it and adding ة. These examples belong to initial-waw roots. Keep both attested forms and their vowels rather than dropping waw from any arbitrary masdar.

concepts.title: Form VII begins with in
concepts.rule: Recognise the added nun and the joining behaviour of wasl.

examples.arabic:
اِنْكَسَرَ يَنْكَسِرُ
سَقَطَ الْفِنْجَانُ وَانْكَسَرَ.
اِنْصَرِفْ
examples.translation:
It broke · breaks
The teacup fell and broke.
Leave/return!
examples.explanation: The pattern is اِنْفَعَلَ يَنْفَعِلُ. The mudari prefix has fathah. After waw, read wan-kasara, not wa in-kasara. The command needs hamzat al-wasl because removing the present prefix leaves a consonant with sukun.

concepts.title: Form VII masdars use infial
concepts.rule: Keep the root while applying the masdar pattern.

examples.arabic:
اِنْكِسَارٌ · اِنْقِلَابٌ
اِنْشَقَّ ← اِنْشِقَاقٌ
اِنْجَلَى ← اِنْجِلَاءٌ
examples.translation:
Breaking · overturning
Split → splitting
Cleared → clearing
examples.explanation: The regular masdar pattern is اِنْفِعَالٌ. A doubled root separates its merged consonants in اِنْشِقَاقٌ. A final-weak ya changes to hamza after long alif in اِنْجِلَاءٌ.

concepts.title: Form VII is mostly intransitive
concepts.rule: Do not manufacture a passive meaning just because a pattern can be written.

examples.arabic:
مُنْكَسِرٌ · مُنْشَقٌّ
مُنْعَطَفٌ · مُنْحَنًى
examples.translation:
Broken · split
Road bend · curve
examples.explanation: Replace the mudari prefix with mu for the active participle. Doubled مُنْشَقٌّ merges the last radicals. Since these verbs are mostly intransitive, the Key does not form ordinary passive participles from them; the passive-shaped pattern can nevertheless name place/time, as مُنْعَطَفٌ does.

concepts.title: Form VII expresses the result of a basic action
concepts.rule: Match the result form to the original action and track the changed role.

examples.arabic:
كَسَرْتُ الْكُوبَ. ← اِنْكَسَرَ الْكُوبُ.
كَسَّرْتُ الزُّجَاجَ. ← تَكَسَّرَ الزُّجَاجُ.
examples.translation:
I broke the tumbler → the tumbler broke.
I smashed the glass → the glass broke to pieces.
examples.explanation: This is mutawaa. Form VII commonly pairs with the basic فَعَلَ, while Form V pairs with Form II فَعَّلَ. In each result sentence the formerly mansub object is now a marfu fail. These are active-form result verbs, not the morphological passive.

rows: I broke the tumbler → the tumbler broke.
I smashed the glass → the glass broke to pieces.

concepts.title: Form VIII inserts ta after the first radical
concepts.rule: Find the radicals before naming the bab.

examples.arabic:
نَظَرَ ← اِنْتَظَرَ
مَحَنَ ← اِمْتَحَنَ
examples.translation:
Looked → waited
Tested → examined
examples.explanation: Bab iftaala adds opening wasl i and ta after root consonant one. اِنْتَظَرَ is not Form VII: nun is its first root letter, and ta is extra. A surface opening in does not by itself identify the form.

concepts.title: Form VIII ta becomes dal after dal, dhal and zay
concepts.rule: A doubled consonant may hide an inserted ta.

examples.arabic:
دَعَا ← اِدَّعَى
ذَكَرَ ← اِدَّكَرَ
زَحَمَ ← اِزْدَحَمَ
examples.translation:
Called → claimed
Remembered → remembered
Crowded → became crowded
examples.explanation: With د، ذ، ز as first radical, the inserted ta becomes dal. The Key shows additional assimilation in اِدَّعَى and اِدَّكَرَ. These altered spellings still belong to Form VIII.

concepts.title: Emphatic first radicals change ta to taa
concepts.rule: Emphatic assimilation changes the added consonant, not the root family.

examples.arabic:
صَبَرَ ← اِصْطَبَرَ
ضَرَبَ ← اِضْطَرَبَ
طَلَعَ ← اِطَّلَعَ
ظَلَمَ ← اِظْطَلَمَ
examples.translation:
Was patient → had patience
Struck → was in unrest
Rose → became informed
Wronged → endured wrong
examples.explanation: After ص، ض، ط، ظ, the added ta becomes ط. With ط itself, the two letters merge as اِطَّلَعَ. Preserve the source’s attested spelling rather than restoring an ordinary ta.

concepts.title: Initial root waw can merge into the added ta
concepts.rule: Recover the original root when reading an assimilated form.

examples.arabic:
وَحَدَ ← اِتَّحَدَ
وَقَى ← اِتَّقَى
examples.translation:
Was one → united
Protected → protected himself
examples.explanation: The first radical waw assimilates into Form VIII’s extra ta, leaving doubled ta. This hides the root’s initial weak consonant. Do not treat both written tas as root letters.

concepts.title: Form VIII uses yaftailu and iftial
concepts.rule: Use the stem pattern together with weak-root rules.

examples.arabic:
اِنْتَظَرَ يَنْتَظِرُ اِنْتَظِرْ اِنتِظَارٌ
اِخْتَارَ يَخْتَارُ اِخْتِيَارٌ
اِلْتَقَى اِلْتِقَاءٌ
examples.translation:
Waited · waits · wait! · waiting
Selected · selects · selection
Met · meeting
examples.explanation: The mudari prefix has fathah. Removing it for the command leaves a sakin consonant, so wasl is needed. The masdar is اِفْتِعَالٌ; hollow اختيار and final-weak التقاء show their own changes.

concepts.title: Some active and passive participles look identical
concepts.rule: When forms coincide, sentence meaning identifies active, passive or place.

examples.arabic:
مُمْتَحِنٌ · مُمْتَحَنٌ
مُشْتَقٌّ · مُخْتَارٌ
مُجْتَمَعٌ · الْمُلْتَزَمُ
examples.translation:
Examiner · examinee
Deriving/derived · choosing/chosen
Society/gathering place · place of embracing
examples.explanation: The regular active/passive difference is kasrah versus fathah on the second radical. In doubled مُشْتَقٌّ and hollow مُخْتَارٌ, changes produce the same visible form for both. Place/time nouns share the passive shape; the Key explains al-Multazam as the named place beside the Kaaba’s door.

concepts.title: Faal intensifies an active-participle meaning
concepts.rule: Word function matters as much as the doubled root letter.

examples.arabic:
غَافِرٌ ← غَفَّارٌ
رَازِقٌ ← رَزَّاقٌ
آكِلٌ ← أَكَّالٌ
examples.translation:
One forgiving → one forgiving much
Provider → one providing much
Eater → one eating much
examples.explanation: فَعَّالٌ is one of the intensive active-participle patterns, sigh mubalaghat ism al-fail. Its shaddah belongs to this noun pattern; it does not make the word a Form II past verb.

concepts.title: Four other patterns also express intensity
concepts.rule: Recognise the family of intensive nouns rather than one suffix.

examples.arabic:
عَلِيمٌ · سَمِيعٌ
غَفُورٌ · شَكُورٌ · عَبُوسٌ · أَكُولٌ
حَذِرٌ · مِعْطَاءٌ
examples.translation:
Knowing/hearing much
Forgiving · thankful · frowning · eating much
Very cautious · giving much
examples.explanation: Alongside faal, the Key gives فَعِيلٌ, فَعُولٌ, فَعِلٌ and مِفْعَالٌ. The noun’s lexical meaning determines the natural English translation. These patterns do not all imply the same kind of repetition in every context.

concepts.title: Form IX describes colours and defects
concepts.rule: Identify which radical is doubled before naming the form.

examples.arabic:
اِحْمَرَّ يَحْمَرُّ اِحْمِرَارٌ
اِعْوَجَّ
مُحْمَرٌّ
examples.translation:
Became red · becomes red · reddening
Became crooked
Reddening (active participle)
examples.explanation: The pattern is اِفْعَلَّ. The Key restricts it to colours and defects and states that it has no passive participle. Its active participle and masdar follow the examples, with the merged last consonants separating in اِحْمِرَارٌ.

concepts.title: The Key also gives an extended Form IX pattern
concepts.rule: A similar visible ending can come from a different root structure.

examples.arabic:
اِحْمَارَّ يَحْمَارُّ اِحْمِيرَارٌ
اِدْهَامَّ
اِشْتَدَّ
examples.translation:
Became red gradually · its present and masdar
Became dark green
Became intense
examples.explanation: The variant اِفْعَالَّ is numbered ixa in this Key. Its active participle is مُحْمَارٌّ. Do not confuse اِشْتَدَّ with Form IX: its root is ش د د and the added ta makes it Form VIII. The two dals are original radicals.

concepts.title: Form X adds ista before the root
concepts.rule: Keep the root-specific changes inside the Form X stem.

examples.arabic:
اِسْتَغْفَرَ يَسْتَغْفِرُ اِسْتَغْفِرْ
اِسْتَقَالَ اِسْتَقِلْ
اِسْتَلْقَى اِسْتَلْقِ
اِسْتَحَمَّ اِسْتَحِمَّ
examples.translation:
Sought forgiveness · seeks · seek!
Resigned · resign!
Lay down · lie down!
Bathed · bathe!
examples.explanation: Use اِسْتَفْعَلَ يَسْتَفْعِلُ. Commands need wasl after removing the present prefix. Hollow commands shorten the long vowel; final-weak commands lose the final weak letter. The doubled example ends in fathah to avoid two sakins while retaining assimilation.

concepts.title: Form X masdars use istifal
concepts.rule: Derived masdar patterns still undergo weak-letter changes.

examples.arabic:
اِسْتِغْفَارٌ
اِسْتِقَالَةٌ · اِسْتِشَارَةٌ
اِسْتِلْقَاءٌ
examples.translation:
Seeking forgiveness
Resignation · consultation
Lying down
examples.explanation: Regular masdars follow اِسْتِفْعَالٌ. Hollow roots have compensatory ta marbutah, as istiqalah and istisharah. In final-weak istilqa, ya becomes hamza after long alif. Learn the attested shapes alongside the general pattern.

concepts.title: Form X nouns begin musta
concepts.rule: Read the inner vowel and context, not just the prefix musta.

examples.arabic:
مُسْتَغْفِرٌ · مُسْتَغْفَرٌ
مُسْتَقْبَلٌ · مُسْتَوْصَفٌ · مُسْتَشْفًى
examples.translation:
One seeking forgiveness · one whose forgiveness is sought
Future · clinic · hospital
examples.explanation: Use kasrah on the second radical for the active participle and fathah for the passive. The place/time noun shares the passive shape, illustrated by future, clinic and hospital. Keep the final maqsur ending in hospital.

concepts.title: Form X can mean seeking the basic action
concepts.rule: Learn each derived word’s meaning with its pattern.

examples.arabic:
غَفَرَ ← اِسْتَغْفَرَ
طَعِمَ ← اِسْتَطْعَمَ
هَدَى ← اِسْتَهْدَى
examples.translation:
Forgave → sought forgiveness
Ate → asked for food
Guided → sought guidance
examples.explanation: The Key illustrates seeking through these root pairs. Other Form X words in the lesson mean waking, resigning or lying down; they should not be forced into an English “ask for” formula.

concepts.title: Basic four-radical verbs have one main pattern
concepts.rule: Count root positions, not only written stem letters.

examples.arabic:
تَرْجَمَ يُتَرْجِمُ تَرْجَمَةٌ
مُتَرْجِمٌ · كِتَابٌ مُتَرْجَمٌ
examples.translation:
Translated · translates · translation
Translator · translated book
examples.explanation: Rubai mujarrad follows فَعْلَلَ يُفَعْلِلُ with a dammah mudari prefix. The masdar is فَعْلَلَةٌ. In its participles, the third radical takes kasrah for active and fathah for passive. Unlike Form II, four different root positions are present.

concepts.title: Four-radical roots can add ta
concepts.rule: Identify four original radicals before applying the augmented pattern.

examples.arabic:
تَرَعْرَعَ يَتَرَعْرَعُ تَرَعْرُعٌ
تَمَضْمَضَ
examples.translation:
Grew up · grows up · growing up
Rinsed his mouth
examples.explanation: The first augmented rubai pattern is تَفَعْلَلَ. Its mudari has fathah and its masdar تَفَعْلُلٌ. Do not classify it as a three-radical Form V just because it begins with ta.

concepts.title: Another four-radical pattern doubles the last radical
concepts.rule: A doubled ending does not identify the root length by itself.

examples.arabic:
اِطْمَأَنَّ يَطْمَئِنُّ اِطْمِئْنَانٌ
اِشْمَأَزَّ
examples.translation:
Felt reassured · feels reassured · reassurance
Detested
examples.explanation: The Key gives اِفْعَلَلَّ as the second augmented pattern. The final two radical positions and their assimilation need careful counting. This is a four-radical family, despite its resemblance to the colour pattern.

concepts.title: An added nun gives a third four-radical pattern
concepts.rule: Separate inserted nun from the four root consonants.

examples.arabic:
اِفْرَنْقَعَ يَفْرَنْقِعُ اِفْرِنْقَاعٌ
اِفْرَنْقَعَ النَّاسُ.
examples.translation:
Dispersed · disperses · dispersal
The people dispersed.
examples.explanation: The pattern is اِفْعَنْلَلَ, with opening wasl i and inserted nun. The masdar follows اِفْعِنْلَالٌ. The root consonants remain ف ر ق ع in this example; nun is additional.

concepts.title: Doubled present verbs normally merge their last radicals
concepts.rule: The subject ending determines whether assimilation can occur.

examples.arabic:
يَحُجُّ · يَحُجُّونَ
يَحْجُجْنَ · تَحْجُجْنَ
examples.translation:
He performs hajj · they perform hajj
They female · you female plural perform hajj
examples.explanation: Idgham joins the second and third radicals in most mudari forms. It does not occur with the feminine plural moving subject pronoun. The Key explains the merged verb through the underlying unmerged form.

concepts.title: Some doubled jazm and command forms allow two shapes
concepts.rule: Do not mistake the merged final fathah for nasb in these majzum forms.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ يَحُجَّ · لَمْ يَحْجُجْ
حُجَّ · اُحْجُجْ
اُحْجُجْنَ
examples.translation:
He did not perform hajj (two forms)
Perform hajj! (two male-singular forms)
Perform hajj! (female plural)
examples.explanation: The four bare mudari forms—he, you/she, I, we—may retain assimilation with final fathah or undo it with sukun in jazm. Male singular command likewise permits both. Female plural command must remain unmerged. Undoing the merger is fakk al-idgham.

concepts.title: Fail can be a masdar pattern
concepts.rule: A word pattern does not have only one grammatical function.

examples.arabic:
رَنَّ الْجَرَسُ ← رَنِينٌ
صَفَرَ ← صَفِيرٌ
examples.translation:
The bell rang → ringing
He whistled → whistling
examples.explanation: The Key adds فَعِيلٌ to the basic masdar patterns. The same general shape may have other noun/adjective functions elsewhere, so identify the word’s meaning and source verb.

concepts.title: Masdar al-marra counts occurrences
concepts.rule: Use occurrence nouns when the number of actions matters.

examples.arabic:
ضَرْبَةٌ · ضَرْبَتَانِ
تَكْبِيرٌ ← تَكْبِيرَةٌ
إِطْلَالٌ ← إِطْلَالَةٌ
examples.translation:
One strike · two strikes
Saying Allahu akbar → one saying
Looking out → one look out
examples.explanation: The basic occurrence pattern is فَعْلَةٌ. It can be dual or plural for multiple occurrences. In derived forms the Key adds ta marbutah to the regular masdar, as تكبيرة and إطلالة show.

concepts.title: Masdar al-hayah describes manner
concepts.rule: A short-vowel change separates “one occurrence” from “manner”.

examples.arabic:
جِلْسَةٌ · مِشْيَةٌ
اِجْلِسْ جِلْسَةَ طَالِبِ عِلْمٍ.
examples.translation:
Manner of sitting · manner of walking
Sit as a student sits.
examples.explanation: The manner pattern is فِعْلَةٌ, compared with occurrence فَعْلَةٌ. The Key does not form this manner masdar from mazid forms. A possessive phrase or other qualification can identify the particular manner.

concepts.title: Masdar mimi starts with added mim
concepts.rule: The same noun pattern may name an action, receiver, place or time.

examples.arabic:
مَمَاتٌ · مَعْرِفَةٌ · مَغْفِرَةٌ
مُمَزَّقٌ · مُخْرَجٌ · مُنْقَلَبٌ
examples.translation:
Death · knowledge · forgiveness
Tearing apart · taking out · return
examples.explanation: Basic masdar mimi examples use mafal/mafil with or without ta marbutah. In mazid forms its shape matches the passive participle. Context distinguishes an action noun from a passive participle or a place/time noun sharing that shape.

concepts.title: Ful is another basic masdar pattern
concepts.rule: Store the vowelled masdar with its verb.

examples.arabic:
شَرِبَ شُرْبٌ
شَكَرَ شُكْرٌ
examples.translation:
Drank → drinking
Thanked → thanks
examples.explanation: The examples follow فُعْلٌ. These are basic masdars learned with their verbs. Their vowels distinguish them from other root-related noun patterns.

concepts.title: Fail is a basic masdar pattern too
concepts.rule: Read the written short vowels and long letters separately.

examples.arabic: لَعِبَ ← لَعِبٌ
examples.translation: He played → playing
examples.explanation: The Key adds فَعِلٌ to the masdar patterns. Do not confuse it with the longer فَعِيلٌ pattern of ringing and whistling in Chapter 27.

concepts.title: Review fal as a masdar pattern
concepts.rule: Repeated examples consolidate the same pattern across chapters.

examples.arabic: شَرَحَ ← شَرْحٌ
examples.translation: He explained → explanation
examples.explanation: The Key revisits فَعْلٌ here. The middle consonant has sukun, separating it from other short-vowel masdar patterns learned earlier.

concepts.title: Turn a statement into a question
concepts.rule: A small أَ at the start changes the statement into a question.

examples.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ ← أَهَذَا بَيْتٌ؟
examples.translation: This is a house. → Is this a house?
examples.explanation: The rest of the sentence stays the same. You can answer with نَعَمْ (“yes”) or لَا (“no”). The lesson also introduces مَا هَذَا؟ (“What is this?”) and مَنْ هَذَا؟ (“Who is this?”).

rows: This is a house. → Is this a house?

concepts.title: After “in” or “on,” the ending changes
concepts.rule: After a preposition, look for the “i” ending in these examples.

examples.arabic:
فِي الْبَيْتِ
عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ
فِي بَيْتٍ
examples.translation:
In the house
On the table
In a house
examples.explanation: Compare الْبَيْتُ with فِي الْبَيْتِ: the ending changes from “u” to “i.” An indefinite noun keeps tanwin, but “un” changes to “in”: بَيْتٌ becomes بَيْتٍ. These are the patterns for the nouns shown here.

concepts.title: Say who something belongs to
concepts.rule: Attach لِـ to the next noun and use its majrur form.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا لِبِلَالٍ، وَذَلِكَ لِحَامِدٍ
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ
examples.translation:
This belongs to Bilal, and that belongs to Hamid.
Praise belongs to Allah.
examples.explanation: The following noun is majrur: بِلَالٍ and حَامِدٍ have kasrah with tanwin. Notice the spelling لِلَّهِ: the Key explains that the initial alif of اللَّه is dropped, without adding another written lam.

concepts.title: Ask “who does this belong to?”
concepts.rule: Use لِمَنْ to ask whom something belongs to.

examples.arabic:
لِمَنْ هَذَا؟
لِمَنِ الْكِتَابُ؟
examples.translation:
Whose is this?
Whose is the book?
examples.explanation: With هَذَا, read لِمَنْ with its normal ending. Before الـ in connected speech, the final ن takes a short “i”: لِمَنِ الْكِتَابُ. Compare this question with كِتَابُ مَنْ؟ from Chapter 5: both can ask about ownership.

concepts.title: Say where something comes from or goes to
concepts.rule: مِنْ gives the starting point; إِلَى gives the destination.

examples.arabic: ذَهَبَ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ
examples.translation: He went to the mosque.
examples.explanation: إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ tells you the destination. The final kasrah in الْمَسْجِدِ follows the preposition rule you just learned. مِنْ gives a starting point instead. When مِنْ is followed by الـ in connected speech, read it as مِنَ, with a short “a.”

concepts.title: Call someone with يَا
concepts.rule: For these examples, call with يَا plus a single “u” ending.

examples.arabic:
يَا بِلَالُ
يَا شَيْخُ
يَا أُسْتَاذُ
examples.translation:
O Bilal!
O shaykh!
O teacher!
examples.explanation: In the calling forms shown here, the noun after يَا has one dammah, not tanwin. Compare بِلَالٌ on its own with يَا بِلَالُ when calling him. Other forms of direct address are taught later.

concepts.title: لِـ changes its vowel with most pronouns here
concepts.rule: Remember the set: لَكَ، لَهُ، لَهَا — but لِي.

examples.arabic: لَكَ   ·   لَهُ   ·   لَهَا   ·   لِي
examples.translation: Belonging to you (one male person) · to him · to her · to me
examples.explanation: Read laka, lahu, and laha with a fathah after ل. But لِي keeps a kasrah and is read li with a long “ee.” This is a change in the preposition’s form when it joins a pronoun.

concepts.title: A small ب attached to the next word
concepts.rule: Attach بِـ to the next word; the noun following it is majrur.

examples.arabic:
بِالْجَامِعَةِ
الْجَامِعَةُ الْإِسْلَامِيَّةُ بِالْمَدِينَةِ الْمُنَوَّرَةِ
examples.translation:
At the university
The Islamic University at Madinah Munawwarah
examples.explanation: The preposition keeps its kasrah and makes the following noun majrur. Notice بِالْجَامِعَةِ and بِالْمَدِينَةِ: ب attaches to الـ, and the alif remains in writing. This differs from the spelling rule for لِـ + الـ.

concepts.title: مَا can also make a negative statement
concepts.rule: In مَا عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ, مَا means “not,” rather than “what.”

examples.arabic: مَا عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ
examples.translation: I do not have a car.
examples.explanation: عِنْدِي expresses “I have.” With مَا before it, the example means “I do not have.” The job of مَا depends on its sentence: in مَا هَذَا؟ it asks “what,” but here it negates a statement.

concepts.title: Ask “whom?” or “what?”
concepts.rule: Some object forms stay unchanged: مَنْ and مَاذَا are indeclinable.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ تُحِبُّ؟
مَاذَا تُحِبُّ؟
أَتُحِبُّ لُغَتَكَ؟
examples.translation:
Whom do you love?
What do you love?
Do you love your language? (one male person)
examples.explanation: مَنْ and مَاذَا are objects in these questions, but they do not gain a visible “a” ending. They are indeclinable: their form stays unchanged. Compare لُغَتَكَ, whose noun has the object’s fathah. Its ة appears as ت when an attached pronoun follows.

concepts.title: “Which?” can change its ending
concepts.rule: أَيُّ، أَيِّ، أَيَّ show its role; the following noun stays majrur.

examples.arabic:
أَيُّ بَيْتٍ هَذَا؟
مِنْ أَيِّ بَلَدٍ أَنْتَ؟
أَيَّ لُغَةٍ تُحِبُّ؟
examples.translation:
Which house is this?
Which country are you from?
Which language do you like?
examples.explanation: The following noun is a mudaf ilayhi: بَيْتٍ, بَلَدٍ, لُغَةٍ. أَيُّ has dammah in the first example, becomes أَيِّ after مِنْ, and is أَيَّ as the object of تُحِبُّ. The Key also gives فِي أَيِّ فَصْلٍ جَلَسْتَ؟, “In which classroom did you sit?”

concepts.title: Add emphasis with إِنَّ
concepts.rule: إِنَّ adds emphasis and makes its following noun mansub.

examples.arabic: الْكِتَابُ سَهْلٌ ← إِنَّ الْكِتَابَ سَهْلٌ
examples.translation: The book is easy. → Indeed, the book is easy.
examples.explanation: After إِنَّ, the starting noun becomes mansub: الْكِتَابُ changes to الْكِتَابَ. It is now called ism inna, and the predicate is called khabar inna. The predicate سَهْلٌ keeps its marfuʿ form here.

rows: The book is easy. → Indeed, the book is easy.

concepts.title: Change the case, not the noun’s tanwin class
concepts.rule: Mansub does not mean every word gains tanwin.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ الْمُدَرِّسَ جَدِيدٌ
إِنَّ آمِنَةَ طَالِبَةٌ
إِنَّ حَامِدًا مَرِيضٌ
examples.translation:
Indeed, the teacher is new.
Indeed, Aminah is a student.
Indeed, Hamid is sick.
examples.explanation: الْمُدَرِّسَ keeps no tanwin because of الـ. آمِنَةَ keeps no tanwin because of its name class. حَامِدًا keeps tanwin, now with fathah. The noun is mansub in all three examples, but its spelling reflects its own class.

concepts.title: إِنَّ uses attached pronouns
concepts.rule: Attach the pronoun to إِنَّ rather than leaving أَنْتَ unchanged after it.

examples.arabic:
أَنْتَ غَبِيٌّ ← إِنَّكَ غَبِيٌّ
إِنِّي / إِنَّنِي   ·   إِنَّا / إِنَّنَا
examples.translation:
You are foolish. → Indeed, you are foolish.
Indeed I… (two forms) · indeed we… (two forms)
examples.explanation: The source example shows أَنْتَ replaced by attached ـكَ. The Key also gives two forms each for first-person singular and plural. Its full pronoun exercise is in the main book; these cards introduce only the forms given in the Key.

concepts.title: لَعَلَّ can express hope or fear
concepts.rule: لَعَلَّ changes the meaning to hope or fear, with إِنَّ-like grammar.

examples.arabic:
لَعَلَّ الْجَوَّ جَمِيلٌ
لَعَلَّ الْمُدَرِّسَ مَرِيضٌ
examples.translation:
I hope the weather is fine.
I am afraid the teacher is sick.
examples.explanation: The following noun is mansub, while the predicate remains marfuʿ in these examples. Context tells you whether لَعَلَّ expresses a hoped-for possibility or an unwelcome possibility. The Key says the lesson’s main examples focus on hope.

concepts.title: Offer two choices with أَ… أَمْ…
concepts.rule: Put the question particle next to the first option being compared.

examples.arabic:
أَطَبِيبٌ أَنْتَ أَمْ مُهَنْدِسٌ؟
أَمُدَرِّسٌ أَنْتَ أَمْ طَالِبٌ؟
أَإِلَى مَكَّةَ ذَهَبْتَ أَمْ إِلَى جُدَّةَ؟
examples.translation:
Are you a doctor or an engineer?
Are you a teacher or a student?
Did you go to Makkah or Jeddah?
examples.explanation: The Key corrects questions that put أَ before أَنْتَ or the verb while the actual choice is between professions or destinations. Place أَ before one alternative and أَمْ before the other.

concepts.title: Say “is not” with لَيْسَ
concepts.rule: لَيْسَ negates the statement; بِـ makes the following predicate noun majrur.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ ← لَيْسَ الْبَيْتُ بِجَدِيدٍ
examples.translation: The house is new. → The house is not new.
examples.explanation: الْبَيْتُ is now called ism laysa. بِجَدِيدٍ is khabar laysa. The predicate noun takes a majrur ending after بِـ in this construction. The next card explains a valid alternative without بِـ.

rows: The house is new. → The house is not new.

concepts.title: Without بِـ, the predicate is mansub
concepts.rule: With بِـ: بِجَدِيدٍ. Without it here: جَدِيدًا.

examples.arabic: لَيْسَ الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدًا
examples.translation: The house is not new.
examples.explanation: Here جَدِيدًا is khabar laysa and is mansub. Compare بِجَدِيدٍ in the main lesson example. The meaning is the same; the visible ending changes with the construction. This alternative is flagged briefly for fuller study later.

concepts.title: Use لَيْسَتْ with a feminine singular topic
concepts.rule: Feminine topic: لَيْسَتْ; before الـ, connect it with a short “i.”

examples.arabic:
لَيْسَتْ زَيْنَبُ بِمَرِيضَةٍ
لَيْسَتِ السَّيَّارَةُ بِقَدِيمَةٍ
examples.translation:
Zaynab is not sick.
The car is not old.
examples.explanation: The second sentence connects as “laysatis-sayyaratu.” This is the same linking adjustment seen in Book 1’s ذَهَبَتِ الْبِنْتُ. The predicate also agrees with the feminine noun: مَرِيضَةٍ or قَدِيمَةٍ.

concepts.title: The ending of لَسْتُ already says “I”
concepts.rule: A whole sentence can provide the information about an outer topic.

examples.arabic:
لَسْتُ بِمُهَنْدِسٍ
أَنَا لَسْتُ بِمُهَنْدِسٍ
examples.translation:
I am not an engineer.
I am not an engineer. (with explicit “I”)
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, the ـتُ pronoun is ism laysa, and بِمُهَنْدِسٍ is its predicate. In the second, أَنَا is the outer mubtada and the whole لَسْتُ بِمُهَنْدِسٍ sentence supplies its khabar.

concepts.title: Do not add بِـ before an existing prepositional phrase
concepts.rule: Keep an existing prepositional predicate; do not stack an extra بِـ on it.

examples.arabic:
لَسْتُ مِنَ الْهِنْدِ
لَيْسَ لِي إِخْوَةٌ
examples.translation:
I am not from India.
I have no brothers.
examples.explanation: مِنَ الْهِنْدِ is already a prepositional predicate. In the second example, لِي is the prepositional predicate and إِخْوَةٌ is ism laysa. The noun stays after the phrase, just as in لِي إِخْوَةٌ, “I have some brothers.”

concepts.title: إِنَّ also works with a predicate placed first
concepts.rule: Find ism inna even when a prepositional phrase comes first.

examples.arabic: لِي إِخْوَةٌ ← إِنَّ لِي إِخْوَةً
examples.translation: I have some brothers. → Indeed, I have some brothers.
examples.explanation: لِي supplies khabar inna. إِخْوَةً is ism inna, so it becomes mansub even though the prepositional phrase stands between it and إِنَّ. The rule follows the noun’s role rather than its immediate position.

rows: I have some brothers. → Indeed, I have some brothers.

concepts.title: A polite way to ask who someone is
concepts.rule: Use the intended polite meaning, rather than translating each word mechanically.

examples.arabic: مَنِ الْأَخُ؟
examples.translation: May I ask who you are?
examples.explanation: The Key describes this as a polite way to ask a stranger who he is. The kasrah on ن helps مَنْ connect to الـ, like لِمَنِ الْكِتَابُ in Book 1. The literal wording and conversational meaning are different.

concepts.title: لَكِنَّ adds a contrast
concepts.rule: لَكِنَّ contrasts ideas using the إِنَّ family’s grammar.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُجْتَهِدٌ وَلَكِنَّ حَامِدًا كَسْلَانُ
سَيَّارَتِي قَدِيمَةٌ وَلَكِنَّهَا قَوِيَّةٌ
examples.translation:
Bilal is hardworking, but Hamid is lazy.
My car is old, but it is strong.
examples.explanation: The following noun is mansub: حَامِدًا. A pronoun attaches, as in لَكِنَّهَا. The predicate remains marfuʿ in these examples. The initial وَ links the contrast to the preceding statement.

concepts.title: كَأَنَّ means “it looks as if”
concepts.rule: كَأَنَّ adds “as if,” with a mansub noun or attached pronoun.

examples.arabic:
كَأَنَّ الْإِمَامَ مَرِيضٌ
كَأَنَّهَا أُخْتُكَ
كَأَنَّكَ مِنَ الْهِنْدِ
examples.translation:
It looks as if the imam is sick.
It looks as if she is your sister.
You seem to be from India.
examples.explanation: الْإِمَامَ is mansub after كَأَنَّ. Pronouns attach in كَأَنَّهَا and كَأَنَّكَ. The predicate can be a noun or a prepositional phrase, so use the same role-finding skills as with إِنَّ.

concepts.title: Ask for confirmation with أَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ؟
concepts.rule: Recognise the confirmation question and its affirmative بَلَى.

examples.arabic:
أَنْتَ طَالِبٌ، أَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ؟
بَلَى
examples.translation:
You are a student, isn’t that right?
Yes, indeed.
examples.explanation: The Key gives بَلَى as the affirmative answer to this negative confirmation question when the person is a student. Its fuller explanation comes in Lesson 4, so this card introduces the phrase without treating بَلَى as the answer to every question.

concepts.title: Ask “which of the two?”
concepts.rule: أَيُّهُمَا asks you to choose one of a known pair.

examples.arabic: فِي الْفَصْلِ طَالِبَانِ مِنْ فَرَنْسَا، أَيُّهُمَا أَخُوكَ؟
examples.translation: There are two students from France in the class. Which of them is your brother?
examples.explanation: The question selects one person from the pair already mentioned. This links Book 1’s أَيّ, “which,” with هُمَا, “the two of them.”

concepts.title: Negate a past action with مَا
concepts.rule: مَا + past verb expresses “did not” in these examples.

examples.arabic:
مَا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى السُّوقِ
مَا خَرَجَ الْإِمَامُ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ
دَخَلَ بِلَالٌ وَلَكِنَّهُ مَا جَلَسَ
examples.translation:
I did not go to the market.
The imam did not go out of the mosque.
Bilal entered, but he did not sit.
examples.explanation: The verb keeps its past-tense form. مَا supplies the negation. The third example also reuses لَكِنَّ with an attached pronoun to connect a contrasting negative statement.

concepts.title: Answer the meaning of a negative question
concepts.rule: To overturn a negative question’s assumption, use بَلَى.

examples.arabic:
أَلَسْتَ بِمُسْلِمٍ؟
بَلَى، أَنَا مُسْلِمٌ
نَعَمْ، لَسْتُ بِمُسْلِمٍ
examples.translation:
Are you not a Muslim?
Yes, I am a Muslim.
No, I am not a Muslim.
examples.explanation: English “yes/no” does not map neatly to these Arabic answers. بَلَى affirms the positive fact: “I am.” نَعَمْ confirms the negative statement: “I am not.” Read the full reply rather than memorising a one-word English translation.

concepts.title: The ending of “which” follows its job
concepts.rule: أَيُّ، أَيَّ، أَيِّ change; the following linked noun stays majrur.

examples.arabic:
أَيُّ طَالِبٍ خَرَجَ؟
أَيَّ كِتَابٍ قَرَأْتَ؟
بِأَيِّ قَلَمٍ كَتَبْتَ؟
examples.translation:
Which student went out?
Which book did you read?
With which pen did you write?
examples.explanation: In the first, أَيُّ is the mubtada and has dammah. In the second, أَيَّ is the object and is mansub. In the third, أَيِّ follows بِـ and is majrur. The linked nouns طَالِبٍ, كِتَابٍ, and قَلَمٍ are all mudaf ilayhi.

concepts.title: Use أَنَّ after “I think”
concepts.rule: After أَظُنُّ here, use أَنَّ to introduce what you think.

examples.arabic:
أَظُنُّ أَنَّ حَامِدًا مَرِيضٌ
أَظُنُّ أَنَّ فَاطِمَةَ غَائِبَةٌ
أَظُنُّ أَنَّكَ مُتْعَبٌ
examples.translation:
I think that Hamid is sick.
I think that Fatimah is absent.
I think that you are tired.
examples.explanation: The noun of أَنَّ is mansub: حَامِدًا or فَاطِمَةَ. An attached pronoun appears in أَنَّكَ. Its predicate is marfuʿ in these examples. The opening example also gives أَظُنُّ أَنَّهَا ذَهَبَتْ إِلَى مَكَّةَ, “I think that she went to Makkah.”

concepts.title: A short word for “why?”
concepts.rule: Recognise لِمَ and its standalone form لِمَهْ.

examples.translation: Why? · Why? (standalone form with final hāʾ)
examples.explanation: The added ه is called هَاءُ السَّكْتِ, the hāʾ used at a pause. Keep this form distinct from other words beginning لم; here the word is a question about the reason.

concepts.title: Two different cases can share the same ending
concepts.rule: Work out the role first; a shared ending does not make the cases identical.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ الطَّالِبَاتِ فِي الْحَافِلَاتِ
إِنَّ الْإِخْوَةَ وَالْأَخَوَاتِ فِي الْبَيْتِ
examples.translation:
Indeed, the female students are in the buses.
Indeed, the brothers and sisters are at home.
examples.explanation: الطَّالِبَاتِ is mansub as ism inna; الْحَافِلَاتِ is majrur after فِي. Their visible endings match, but their grammatical roles differ. The second example contrasts ordinary الْإِخْوَةَ with sound feminine plural الْأَخَوَاتِ after إِنَّ.

concepts.title: A mudaf after يَا is mansub
concepts.rule: With an idafah address, the mudaf after يَا is mansub.

examples.arabic:
يَا بِنْتَ بِلَالٍ!
يَا أُخْتَ مُحَمَّدٍ!
يَا ابْنَ أَخِي!
يَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ!
examples.translation:
O daughter of Bilal!
O sister of Muhammad!
O son of my brother!
O servant of Allah!
examples.explanation: The first noun is the mudaf and takes fathah here: بِنْتَ, أُخْتَ, ابْنَ, or عَبْدَ. The owner following it remains a mudaf ilayhi. Compare the single-dammah forms يَا بِلَالُ and يَا أُسْتَاذُ learned in Book 1.

concepts.title: In direct address, أَبُو becomes أَبَا
concepts.rule: Special nouns can show case through a changing long vowel.

examples.arabic:
يَا أَبَا بَكْرٍ!
يَا رَبَّنَا!
examples.translation:
O Abu Bakr!
O our Lord!
examples.explanation: أَبَا بَكْرٍ is an idafah used in direct address, so its first word is mansub. This extends Book 1’s special “father/brother” noun forms beyond the marfuʿ أَبُو. رَبَّنَا shows that a mudaf can have an attached owner pronoun too.

concepts.title: Add a pronoun to emphasise the owner
concepts.rule: The extra pronoun stresses the owner already expressed by the attached ending.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابُكَ أَنْتَ
هَذَا قَلَمِي أَنَا
ذَلِكَ كِتَابُهَا هِيَ
examples.translation:
This is your book—yours.
This is my pen—mine.
That is her book—hers.
examples.explanation: The attached pronoun already identifies the owner. أَنْتَ, أَنَا, and هِيَ repeat that owner for emphasis. The Key also gives هَذَا بَيْتُهُ هُوَ, “This is his house—his.” You do not need to add this emphasis to every possession sentence.

concepts.title: كَانَ moves the statement into the past
concepts.rule: With a location phrase, كَانَ changes the time without changing that phrase internally.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ فِي الْفَصْلِ ← كَانَ بِلَالٌ فِي الْفَصْلِ
كَانَتْ زَيْنَبُ فِي الْمَطْبَخِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is in the class. → Bilal was in the class.
Zaynab was in the kitchen.
examples.explanation: The location phrases keep their internal form: فِي الْفَصْلِ and فِي الْمَطْبَخِ. Their nouns remain majrur because of فِي. The Key also gives كَانَ الْقَلَمُ تَحْتَ الْكِتَابِ, “The pen was under the book.”

concepts.title: A noun predicate after كَانَ becomes mansub
concepts.rule: After كَانَ here, the predicate describing word is mansub.

examples.arabic: بِلَالٌ مَرِيضٌ ← كَانَ بِلَالٌ مَرِيضًا
examples.translation: Bilal is sick. → Bilal was sick.
examples.explanation: بِلَالٌ remains marfuʿ, while the predicate مَرِيضٌ becomes مَرِيضًا. Compare this with the unchanged prepositional phrase in the previous card. The Key introduces the difference briefly and returns to it in Lesson 25.

rows: Bilal is sick. → Bilal was sick.

concepts.title: Bring a phrase forward to emphasise it
concepts.rule: An earlier position can highlight a phrase while its case still shows its role.

examples.arabic:
رَأَيْتُ بِلَالًا ← بِلَالًا رَأَيْتُ
أَإِلَى الْمُدِيرِ ذَهَبْتُمْ؟
examples.translation:
I saw Bilal. → It was Bilal that I saw.
Was it to the headmaster that you went?
examples.explanation: بِلَالًا keeps its mansub ending even when placed before the verb. إِلَى الْمُدِيرِ is also brought forward as the point being stressed. Position changes emphasis without cancelling the phrase’s grammatical role.

concepts.title: Name the hopeful and fearful uses of لَعَلَّ
concepts.rule: With لَعَلَّ, a welcome possibility expresses hope; an unwelcome possibility expresses concern. Context decides the meaning.

examples.arabic: لَعَلَّهُ يَرْجِعُ الْيَوْمَ مُتَأَخِّرًا
examples.translation: I am afraid he will come back late today.
examples.explanation: Hope is called التَّرَجِّي; apprehension is called الْإِشْفَاقُ. In this example, coming back late is the unwelcome possibility. The present-future verb يَرْجِعُ fits the possible future event. The grammatical behaviour of لَعَلَّ remains the same.

examples.arabic:
لَعَلَّهُ بِخَيْرٍ.
لَعَلَّهُ مَرِيضٌ.
لَعَلِّي لَا أَحُجُّ بَعْدَ عَامِي هَذَا.
examples.translation:
I hope he is well.
I am afraid he is sick.
I am afraid I will not perform hajj after this year of mine.
examples.explanation: A welcome possibility expresses hope (التَّرَجِّي); an unwelcome possibility expresses concern (الْإِشْفَاق). The last example is the Key’s hadith illustration of concern. The particle’s grammar remains the same in both meanings.

concepts.title: Negate the present action with لَا
concepts.rule: For the present negative statements here, use لَا + مُضَارِع.

examples.arabic:
لَا أَفْهَمُ الْفَرَنْسِيَّةَ
لَا أَشْرَبُ قَهْوَةً
examples.translation:
I do not understand French.
I do not drink coffee.
examples.explanation: Compare the past negative مَا أَكَلْتُ شَيْئًا, “I did not eat anything.” In the present examples, لَا comes before the verb and the form keeps its ending here. This is negative statement لَا; commands not to do something are a different construction studied later.

concepts.title: Contrast quoted words with “that…” content
concepts.rule: In these constructions: quoted statement إِنَّ; heard/thought content أَنَّ.

examples.arabic:
قَالَ الْمُدَرِّسُ: إِنَّ الِامْتِحَانَ غَدًا
سَمِعْتُ أَنَّ الِامْتِحَانَ غَدًا
أَظُنُّ أَنَّ الِامْتِحَانَ غَدًا
examples.translation:
The teacher said, “The examination is tomorrow.”
I heard that the examination is tomorrow.
I think that the examination is tomorrow.
examples.explanation: The information is the same, but its relationship to the opening verb changes. In all three, الِامْتِحَانَ is mansub as the noun of the particle. This reviews the إِنَّ versus أَنَّ distinction from Chapter 6 with a matched set of examples.

concepts.title: Say that something almost happens
concepts.rule: Use كَادَ / يَكَادُ with a mudari verb to express “almost” or “about to.”

examples.arabic:
كَادَ الْوَلَدُ يَضْحَكُ
كَادَ الْمُدَرِّسُ يَخْرُجُ
يَكَادُ الْجَرَسُ يَرِنُّ
يَكَادُ الْإِمَامُ يَرْكَعُ
examples.translation:
The boy almost laughed.
The teacher was about to leave.
The bell is about to ring.
The imam is about to bow.
examples.explanation: In the first example, the boy reached the point of laughing but did not laugh. The pattern shown is كَادَ or يَكَادُ, followed by a marfu noun and a present-future verb. Even after past كَادَ, the following action uses the mudari form: يَضْحَكُ or يَخْرُجُ.

concepts.title: A usual habit or what is happening now?
concepts.rule: In this lesson’s contrast: لَا for the usual situation; مَا for what is not happening now.

examples.arabic:
لَا أَفْهَمُ الْفَرَنْسِيَّةَ
لَا نَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَلْعَبِ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ
لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ
مَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ
examples.translation:
I do not understand French.
We do not go to the playground on Friday.
I do not drink coffee.
I am not drinking coffee now.
examples.explanation: In the contrast taught here, لَا describes the general habit or usual situation. مَا with the mudari refers to the present moment. These are negative statements, so the verbs retain their normal endings; neither coffee sentence is a command to stop drinking.

concepts.title: Limit the meaning with إِنَّمَا
concepts.rule: Read إِنَّمَا as restricting the statement: “only.”

examples.arabic:
إِنَّمَا أَنْظُرُ إِلَى الصُّوَرِ
أَنْتَ لَا تَكْتُبُ الدَّرْسَ، إِنَّمَا تَكْتُبُ رِسَالَةً
إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ
إِنَّمَا الصَّدَقَاتُ لِلْفُقَرَاءِ
examples.translation:
I am only looking at the pictures.
You are not writing the lesson; you are only writing a letter.
Actions are judged only by intentions.
Charity is only for the poor.
examples.explanation: إِنَّمَا narrows what is being said. In the second example, the contrast tells us what the person is actually writing. Notice الْأَعْمَالُ and الصَّدَقَاتُ keep their marfu endings in the nominal examples; do not automatically apply the mansub noun pattern of إِنَّ alone.

concepts.title: Say “nothing” with a negative and شَيْئًا
concepts.rule: مَا + past verb + شَيْئًا gives “did not … anything.”

examples.arabic:
مَا أَكَلْتُ شَيْئًا.
مَا رَأَيْتُ شَيْئًا.
مَا قَرَأْنَا شَيْئًا.
examples.translation:
I did not eat anything.
I saw nothing.
We read nothing.
examples.explanation: مَا negates the past action, while شَيْئًا means “a thing” as its mansub object. Together they give “not a thing.” The negative meaning belongs to the combination; شَيْئًا alone does not mean “nothing.”

concepts.title: Use غَيْرُ for “non-” or “not”
concepts.rule: After غَيْرُ, put the following word in the majrur case.

examples.arabic:
وَرَقٌ مُسَطَّرٌ · وَرَقٌ غَيْرُ مُسَطَّرٍ
صَحِيحٌ · غَيْرُ صَحِيحٍ
مُسْلِمٌ · غَيْرُ مُسْلِمٍ
examples.translation:
Ruled paper · unruled paper
Correct · incorrect
Muslim · non-Muslim
examples.explanation: غَيْرُ is the mudaf, so its following word is majrur: مُسَطَّرٍ, صَحِيحٍ or مُسْلِمٍ. Do not keep the original dammah after inserting غَيْرُ. The examples show its own marfu form; its grammatical role determines its own case in a sentence.

concepts.title: Say “since” with مُنْذُ
concepts.rule: مُنْذُ + a majrur time expression gives “since” or “for.”

examples.arabic:
مَا رَأَيْتُهُ مُنْذُ يَوْمِ السَّبْتِ.
بِلَالٌ غَائِبٌ مُنْذُ أُسْبُوعٍ.
examples.translation:
I have not seen him since Saturday.
Bilal has been absent for a week.
examples.explanation: The noun after مُنْذُ is majrur in these examples: يَوْمِ and أُسْبُوعٍ. With a named starting point, English uses “since”; with a duration, natural English uses “for.” The Arabic preposition is the same.

concepts.title: Emphasise “all” with كُلّ and a pronoun
concepts.rule: For this emphasis, كُلّ follows the noun, matches its case and carries a referring pronoun.

examples.arabic:
حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ كُلُّهُمْ.
خَرَجَتِ الطَّالِبَاتُ كُلُّهُنَّ.
قَرَأْتُ الْكِتَابَ كُلَّهُ.
بَحَثْتُ عَنْهُ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ كُلِّهَا.
examples.translation:
All the students attended.
All the female students went out.
I read the book completely.
I looked for him in the whole school.
examples.explanation: This emphasis is called تَأْكِيدٌ. كُلّ takes an attached pronoun referring back to the emphasised noun: هُمْ, هُنَّ, هُ or هَا. It also shares that noun’s case: كُلُّهُمْ is marfu, كُلَّهُ mansub, and كُلِّهَا majrur.

concepts.title: Call to a noun with الْـ using أَيُّهَا
concepts.rule: For the illustrated الْـ nouns, call with يَا أَيُّهَا + noun.

examples.arabic:
يَا بِلَالُ!
يَا رَجُلُ!
يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ!
يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّجُلُ!
examples.translation:
Bilal!
Man!
O people!
O man!
examples.explanation: يَا is حَرْفُ النِّدَاءِ, the vocative particle. In this construction, put أَيُّهَا between يَا and the noun beginning with الْـ. The Key gives يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ, rather than directly joining يَا to النَّاسُ. Follow the illustrated form without extending it to every type of vocative.

concepts.title: Say “will not” with لَنْ
concepts.rule: Use لَنْ + mansub mudari, without سَـ, for “will not.”

examples.arabic:
سَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الرِّيَاضِ غَدًا.
لَنْ أَذْهَبَ إِلَى الرِّيَاضِ غَدًا.
examples.translation:
I will go to Riyadh tomorrow.
I will not go to Riyadh tomorrow.
examples.explanation: لَنْ takes the mudari, but makes it mansub, like أَنْ. Here أَذْهَبُ changes to أَذْهَبَ. Omit the future prefix سَـ when using لَنْ; the future meaning is already present. Compare earlier مَا with a past verb and لَا with the present-future verb.

concepts.title: لَنْ follows the familiar ending patterns
concepts.rule: Drop nun in the illustrated ـِينَ / ـُونَ forms; keep the feminine plural ـْنَ.

examples.arabic:
يَا آمِنَةُ، أَلَنْ تَذْهَبِي إِلَى الطَّائِفِ فِي عُطْلَةِ الصَّيْفِ؟
يَا أَخَوَاتُ، أَلَنْ تَدْرُسْنَ اللُّغَةَ التُّرْكِيَّةَ فِي الْعَامِ الْمُقْبِلِ؟
examples.translation:
Aminah, will you not go to Taif during the summer holidays?
Sisters, will you not study Turkish next year?
examples.explanation: تَذْهَبِينَ becomes لَنْ تَذْهَبِي: its final nun is omitted. The masculine plural forms تَذْهَبُونَ and يَذْهَبُونَ likewise lose nun. The feminine plural forms تَذْهَبْنَ and يَذْهَبْنَ remain unchanged, as تَدْرُسْنَ shows. Initial أَ makes the negative future statement a question.

concepts.title: Emphasise “never” in the future with أَبَدًا
concepts.rule: لَنْ … أَبَدًا means “will never …”.

examples.arabic:
لَنْ أَشْرَبَ الْخَمْرَ أَبَدًا.
لَنْ أَكْتُبَ إِلَيْهِ أَبَدًا.
إِنَّ لُغَتَكَ صَعْبَةٌ جِدًّا، لَنْ أَدْرُسَهَا أَبَدًا.
examples.translation:
I will never drink wine.
I will never write to him.
Your language is very difficult; I will never study it.
examples.explanation: لَنْ supplies the negative future meaning, and أَبَدًا adds “ever,” giving “never” together. Keep the verb mansub: أَشْرَبَ, أَكْتُبَ and أَدْرُسَ. Do not treat أَبَدًا alone as the word that negates the verb.

concepts.title: For “never” in the past, notice قَطُّ
concepts.rule: In this contrast, negative past takes قَطُّ and negative future takes أَبَدًا.

examples.arabic: مَا رَأَيْتُهُ قَطُّ.
examples.translation: I never saw him.
examples.explanation: مَا makes the past verb negative; قَطُّ emphasises that it never happened. Compare لَنْ أَكْتُبَ إِلَيْهِ أَبَدًا for the future. The book points ahead to Lesson 29 for more on قَطُّ; this card introduces only the contrast given here.

concepts.title: لَمْ gives a present-form verb a past negative meaning
concepts.rule: لَمْ + majzum mudari means “did not …”.

examples.arabic:
يَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ يَذْهَبْ
تَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ تَذْهَبْ
أَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ أَذْهَبْ
نَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ نَذْهَبْ
لَمْ أَفْهَمْ هَذَا الدَّرْسَ.
examples.translation:
He goes → He did not go
You go / she goes → You / she did not go
I go → I did not go
We go → We did not go
I did not understand this lesson.
examples.explanation: The verb remains mudari in form, but لَمْ gives it a past negative meaning. Its grammatical state changes from marfu to majzum. In these regular forms, omit the final dammah and end with sukun. Compare mansub after أَنْ, which uses a final a instead.

concepts.title: Majzum also has nun patterns
concepts.rule: Keep the distinction between a removable final nun and the feminine plural nun.

examples.arabic:
تَذْهَبِينَ ← لَمْ تَذْهَبِي
تَذْهَبُونَ ← لَمْ تَذْهَبُوا
يَذْهَبُونَ ← لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا
لَا، لَمْ يَحْضُرُوا.
الطَّالِبَاتُ لَمْ يَذْهَبْنَ إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَةِ.
examples.translation:
You go (female singular) → You did not go
You go (male plural) → You did not go
They go (male plural) → They did not go
No, they did not attend.
The female students did not go to the library.
examples.explanation: The ـِينَ and ـُونَ forms lose their final nun, as they do in the mansub. Their majzum state is not shown by adding a final sukun to the written word. The feminine plural forms يَذْهَبْنَ and تَذْهَبْنَ keep their ending unchanged.

concepts.title: A majzum verb can have a linking kasrah
concepts.rule: A linking kasrah after لَمْ does not make the verb a majrur noun.

examples.arabic:
أَلَمْ تَكْتُبِ الرِّسَالَةَ؟
لَمْ تَحْفَظِ الطَّالِبَةُ الْقُرْآنَ.
examples.translation:
Did you not write the letter?
The female student did not memorise the Quran.
examples.explanation: Alone, the relevant forms end تَكْتُبْ and تَحْفَظْ. Joining to the following الْـ drops its opening hamza and would bring two vowelless consonants together. The linking i avoids الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. The verb is still majzum; this kasrah is a pronunciation adjustment.

concepts.title: Say “not yet” with لَمَّا
concepts.rule: لَمَّا + majzum mudari means “has / have not yet …”.

examples.arabic:
لَمَّا أَشْرَبِ الْقَهْوَةَ.
وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ.
ذَهَبَ أَبِي إِلَى مَكَّةَ، وَلَمَّا يَرْجِعْ.
examples.translation:
I have not yet had coffee.
Faith has not yet entered your hearts.
My father went to Makkah and has not yet returned.
examples.explanation: Use the mudari in its majzum state after لَمَّا. يَرْجِعْ clearly shows the sukun. أَشْرَبِ and يَدْخُلِ have the linking kasrah explained in the previous card, because the next word begins with hamzat al-wasl. This card covers the negative لَمَّا taught here.

concepts.title: Answer “Not yet” with لَمَّا alone
concepts.rule: In a clear context, لَمَّا alone can mean “Not yet.”

examples.arabic:
أَخَرَجَ الطُّلَّابُ؟
لَمَّا.
لَمَّا يَخْرُجُوا.
examples.translation:
Have the students gone out?
Not yet.
They have not yet gone out.
examples.explanation: The short reply لَمَّا stands for the full negative clause given in the last line. The question tells us which action is understood. This is an omission of an understood verb, not a different meaning of لَمَّا.

concepts.title: Say “neither … nor” with مَا … وَلَا
concepts.rule: مَا … item … وَلَا item denies both things.

examples.arabic:
مَا عِنْدِي قَلَمٌ وَلَا كِتَابٌ.
مَا فِي الثَّلَّاجَةِ مَاءٌ وَلَا عَصِيرٌ.
مَا فِي جَيْبِي رِيَالٌ وَلَا قِرْشٌ.
examples.translation:
I have neither a pen nor a book.
There is neither water nor juice in the fridge.
There is neither a riyal nor a qirsh in my pocket.
examples.explanation: مَا negates the first statement, and وَلَا adds the second denied item. The nouns shown retain their marfu endings: قَلَمٌ, كِتَابٌ, مَاءٌ and عَصِيرٌ. Learn this pattern as a complete construction rather than turning the second لَا into a command.

concepts.title: “Neither … nor” can negate past actions
concepts.rule: For these paired past negatives, use لَا … وَلَا.

examples.arabic:
لَا أَكَلْتُ وَلَا شَرِبْتُ.
لَا قَرَأَ وَلَا كَتَبَ.
examples.translation:
I neither ate nor drank.
He neither read nor wrote.
examples.explanation: Both verbs are past forms. This paired construction explains why لَا appears with them here. Do not mistake it for the prohibitive لَا followed by a majzum mudari: these sentences report what did not happen.

concepts.title: Use لِـ to name a book’s author
concepts.rule: Book title + لِـ + author can mean “a book by …”.

examples.arabic:
الْمُوَطَّأُ لِلْإِمَامِ مَالِكٍ
لِسَانُ الْعَرَبِ لِابْنِ مَنْظُورٍ
