examples.translation:
Al-Muwatta by Imam Malik
Lisan al-Arab by Ibn Manzur
examples.explanation: The lam introduces the author and governs a majrur noun phrase. Its translation depends on context: here it credits authorship rather than simply meaning “for.” In لِلْإِمَامِ, the preposition joins to الْـ in writing.

concepts.title: كَانَ makes the predicate mansub
concepts.rule: After كَانَ, keep its noun marfu and make a noun/adjective predicate mansub.

examples.arabic:
الْمَاءُ بَارِدٌ. ← كَانَ الْمَاءُ بَارِدًا.
زَيْنَبُ مَرِيضَةٌ. ← كَانَتْ زَيْنَبُ مَرِيضَةً.
الْجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ. ← كَانَ الْجَوُّ جَمِيلًا.
examples.translation:
The water is cold. → The water was cold.
Zainab is sick. → Zainab was sick.
The weather is fine. → The weather was fine.
examples.explanation: The former mubtada becomes اسم كان and remains marfu. The former khabar becomes خبر كان and is mansub. The new ending belongs to the predicate: بَارِدًا, مَرِيضَةً, جَمِيلًا. Match كَانَ / كَانَتْ to the subject as illustrated.

rows: The water is cold. → The water was cold.
Zainab is sick. → Zainab was sick.
The weather is fine. → The weather was fine.

concepts.title: A prepositional predicate keeps its visible form
concepts.rule: A phrase can occupy the predicate position while its preposition still governs its noun.

examples.arabic:
الْمُدَرِّسُ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
كَانَ الْمُدَرِّسُ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
examples.translation:
The teacher is in the classroom.
The teacher was in the classroom.
examples.explanation: فِي الْفَصْلِ serves as the predicate phrase. الْفَصْلِ stays majrur because it follows فِي. Do not turn it into الْفَصْلَ merely because خبر كان has a mansub grammatical position.

concepts.title: لَا يَزَالُ means “is still”
concepts.rule: لَا يَزَالُ / لَا تَزَالُ follows the كَانَ pattern and expresses continuation.

examples.arabic:
لَا يَزَالُ بِلَالٌ مَرِيضًا.
لَا تَزَالُ مَرْيَمُ طَالِبَةً.
لَا يَزَالُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ فِي الْمُسْتَشْفَى.
examples.translation:
Bilal is still sick.
Maryam is still a student.
Ibrahim is still in the hospital.
examples.explanation: The noun remains marfu and an ordinary predicate becomes mansub: مَرِيضًا, طَالِبَةً. A prepositional predicate remains visibly unchanged, as in فِي الْمُسْتَشْفَى. Translate the complete expression لَا يَزَالُ as continuation, “still.”

concepts.title: An oath emphasises an affirmative past with لَقَدْ
concepts.rule: After the illustrated oath, affirmative past takes لَقَدْ; negative past does not.

examples.arabic:
وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ رَأَيْتُهُ فِي السُّوقِ.
وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ سَمِعْتُ هَذَا الْخَبَرَ مِنْ كَثِيرٍ مِنَ النَّاسِ.
وَاللَّهِ مَا أَكَلْتُ شَيْئًا.
examples.translation:
By Allah, I saw him in the market.
By Allah, I heard this news from many people.
By Allah, I did not eat anything.
examples.explanation: The affirmative past is strengthened with لَقَدْ; the negative past example needs no such emphasis. The waw in وَاللَّهِ is an oath preposition, so اللَّهِ is majrur. Read this use separately from ordinary joining وَ meaning “and.”

concepts.title: بَعْدُ can mean “yet” in a negative sentence
concepts.rule: لَمْ … بَعْدُ means “has/have not yet …”.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ أَكْوِهِ بَعْدُ.
لَمْ يَرْجِعْ أَبِي بَعْدُ.
لَمْ أَكْتُبْ لَهُ رِسَالَةً بَعْدُ.
examples.translation:
I have not yet ironed it.
My father has not yet returned.
I have not yet written him a letter.
examples.explanation: The verb is negative with لَمْ, and بَعْدُ supplies “yet” in this context. Its final u is fixed in the expression. Compare the earlier negative لَمَّا, which itself means “not yet.”

concepts.title: Review “never” with قَطُّ and أَبَدًا
concepts.rule: Past: لَمْ … قَطُّ; future: لَنْ … أَبَدًا.

examples.arabic:
لَمْ أَكْتُبْ إِلَيْهِ قَطُّ.
لَنْ أَكْتُبَ إِلَيْهِ أَبَدًا.
examples.translation:
I never wrote to him.
I will never write to him.
examples.explanation: قَطُّ emphasises the negative past, here expressed with لَمْ. أَبَدًا emphasises the negative future after لَنْ. قَطُّ is mabni and keeps its ending. Notice also أَكْتُبْ versus أَكْتُبَ: the two negative particles govern different moods.

concepts.title: “All” and “himself” follow the emphasised noun
concepts.rule: Emphasis follows the noun in case and refers back with a pronoun.

examples.arabic:
حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ كُلُّهُمْ.
سَأَلْتُ الطُّلَّابَ كُلَّهُمْ.
سَلَّمْتُ عَلَى الطُّلَّابِ كُلِّهِمْ.
قَالَ لِي هَذَا الْمُدِيرُ نَفْسُهُ.
سَأَلْتُ الْمُدِيرَ نَفْسَهُ.
examples.translation:
All the students attended.
I asked all the students.
I greeted all the students.
The headmaster himself told me this.
I asked the headmaster himself.
examples.explanation: كُلّ and نَفْس take the case of the muakkad, the noun emphasised. Their attached pronoun refers back to that noun. This explains the changing u / a / i in كُلُّهُمْ, كُلَّهُمْ and كُلِّهِمْ.

concepts.title: Extra مِنْ strengthens “any” or “none”
concepts.rule: Use extra مِنْ only within the stated conditions.

examples.arabic:
هَلْ مِنْ سُؤَالٍ؟
مَا غَابَ مِنْ أَحَدٍ.
لَا تَكْتُبْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ.
هَلْ مِنْ جَدِيدٍ؟
examples.translation:
Any question?
No one is absent.
Do not write anything.
Anything new?
examples.explanation: مِنْ الزَّائِدَةُ occurs here with negation, prohibition or a question formed with هَلْ. The noun after it must be indefinite. “Extra” means added for grammatical emphasis; it does not mean meaningless or freely insertable anywhere.

concepts.title: Extra مِنْ changes the ending, not the original role
concepts.rule: A visibly majrur noun after extra مِنْ can still function as subject, object or topic.

examples.arabic:
مَا رَأَيْتُ أَحَدًا. ← مَا رَأَيْتُ مِنْ أَحَدٍ.
مَا حَضَرَ أَحَدٌ. ← مَا حَضَرَ مِنْ أَحَدٍ.
هَلْ مِنْ سُؤَالٍ عِنْدَكَ؟
examples.translation:
I did not see anyone (without / with emphasis).
No one attended (without / with emphasis).
Do you have any question?
examples.explanation: أَحَد remains the object in the first pair and subject in the second, despite its visible kasrah after مِنْ. In the question, سُؤَال is the topic and عِنْدَكَ the predicate. Separate visible government from the underlying sentence role.

concepts.title: Drop الْـ when calling these proper names
concepts.rule: Call the illustrated proper name with يَا حَسَنُ.

examples.arabic:
الْحَسَنُ · الْحُسَيْنُ · الزُّبَيْرُ
يَا حَسَنُ!
examples.translation:
Al-Hasan · al-Husain · al-Zubayr
Hasan!
examples.explanation: The Key removes the article when these proper names follow يَا. This is a rule for the illustrated personal names; compare the earlier يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ construction for an ordinary article-bearing noun.

concepts.title: Hijazi مَا can work like لَيْسَ
concepts.rule: Analyse the construction before deciding which مَا is present.

examples.arabic:
الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ.
مَا الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدًا.
مَا الْبَيْتُ بِجَدِيدٍ.
مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا.
examples.translation:
The house is new.
The house is not new.
The house is not new.
This is not a human being.
examples.explanation: مَا الْحِجَازِيَّةُ makes the ordinary predicate mansub, like لَيْسَ. An extra بِـ may instead give the predicate a visible majrur ending. Its grammatical predicate role remains. Distinguish this nominal-sentence مَا from relative and question مَا.

concepts.title: Calling can specify an otherwise indefinite noun
concepts.rule: The intended listener determines the specified versus unspecified vocative.

examples.arabic:
يَا رَجُلُ! · يَا وَلَدُ!
يَا رَجُلًا خُذْ بِيَدِي.
يَا بِلَالُ!
examples.translation:
Man! · Boy! (a particular listener)
Someone, take my hand.
Bilal!
examples.explanation: In the specified call, رَجُلُ becomes definite through the caller’s intention and is mabni on dammah. In the unspecified appeal, رَجُلًا remains indefinite and mansub. An already definite personal name such as بِلَال remains definite when called.

concepts.title: “Began to” uses a following mudari clause
concepts.rule: Read the first verb as beginning an action, then the mudari as the action begun.

examples.arabic:
طَفِقَ بِلَالٌ يَكْتُبُ.
أَخَذَ الْمُدَرِّسُ يَشْرَحُ الدَّرْسَ.
جَعَلْتُ آكُلُ.
examples.translation:
Bilal began to write.
The teacher began explaining the lesson.
I began to eat.
examples.explanation: These are incomplete verbs in this construction. بِلَالٌ is the ism of طَفِقَ, and the mudari clause يَكْتُبُ is its predicate. In جَعَلْتُ, تُ supplies the ism. The predicate verb is mudari; no أَنْ is inserted in the examples.

concepts.title: Nudbah expresses pain or mourning
concepts.rule: Read the form as an exclamation of pain or sorrow.

examples.arabic:
وَارَأْسَاهْ!
وَايَدَاهْ!
وَابِلَالَاهْ!
examples.translation:
Oh, my head!
Oh, my hand!
Alas for Bilal!
examples.explanation: From رَأْسِي or يَدِي, the possessive ya is omitted and the exclamatory ending ـَاهْ is added. The same construction expresses sorrow for a person’s loss. The Key calls this النُّدْبَة.

concepts.title: Opening la adds emphasis without changing case
concepts.rule: Emphatic la leaves the topic marfu.

examples.arabic:
وَلَذِكْرُ اللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ.
لَهُ · لَهَا · لَكَ · لَكُمْ
examples.translation:
Indeed the remembrance of Allah is greater.
For him · her · you · you all
examples.explanation: The emphatic lam has fathah and prefixes the mubtada without making it majrur or mansub. Prepositional لِـ normally has kasrah, though it also has fathah before these pronouns. Identify function as well as sound.

concepts.title: Asbaha works like kana
concepts.rule: Recognise the same ism/khabar structure with a new meaning.

examples.arabic:
أَصْبَحَ حَامِدٌ مَرِيضًا.
أَصْبَحْتُ نَشِيطًا.
examples.translation:
Hamid became ill in the morning.
I became active in the morning.
examples.explanation: As a sister of kana, أَصْبَحَ has a marfu ism and mansub khabar. The ism may be a noun or attached subject pronoun. Context may remove the morning meaning, as in becoming brothers by Allah’s grace.

concepts.title: Yushiku expresses “about to”
concepts.rule: Treat the an-clause as the whole predicate.

examples.arabic:
يُوشِكُ الطُّلَّابُ أَنْ يَرْجِعُوا إِلَى بِلَادِهِمْ فِي الْإِجَازَةِ.
أُوشِكُ أَنْ أَتَزَوَّجَ.
examples.translation:
The students are about to return to their countries in the holidays.
I am about to get married.
examples.explanation: أَوْشَكَ يُوشِكُ is a sister of kana. The Key specifies a masdar muawwal predicate, أَنْ plus mansub mudari. الطُّلَّابُ is the first ism; a hidden أنا is the second. Nun drops from يَرْجِعُوا after an.

concepts.title: Innama restricts the meaning to “only”
concepts.rule: Only changes the scope of meaning; it does not make the next noun mansub.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّمَا أَنَا مُدَرِّسٌ.
إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ.
إِنَّمَا يَكْذِبُ.
examples.translation:
I am only a teacher.
Actions are judged only by intentions.
He is only telling a lie.
examples.explanation: In innama, ma is kaffah: it prevents inna’s usual nasb government. الْأَعْمَالُ therefore remains marfu. Unlike inna alone, innama can also introduce a verbal sentence.

concepts.title: An oath has an answer clause
concepts.rule: Use laqad for the illustrated affirmative past oath answer.

examples.arabic:
وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ فَرِحْتُ كَثِيرًا.
وَاللَّهِ مَا رَأَيْتُهُ.
examples.translation:
By Allah, I was greatly delighted.
By Allah, I did not see him.
examples.explanation: The oath is qasam; its following statement is jawab al-qasam. An affirmative madi answer takes emphatic laqad in this lesson, while a negative madi answer does not. Oath waw is a preposition, so اللَّهِ is majrur; it is different from conjunction waw.

concepts.title: Amsa is the evening counterpart of asbaha
concepts.rule: Identify the use by whether it links an ism to a predicate.

examples.arabic: أَمْسَى الْجَوُّ لَطِيفًا.
examples.translation: The weather became pleasant in the evening.
examples.explanation: الْجَوُّ is the marfu ism of أَمْسَى and لَطِيفًا its mansub khabar. Compare أَصْبَحَ in Chapter 17. The vocabulary also distinguishes the complete verb “enter/spend the evening” from this incomplete use.

concepts.title: Describe an ailment with bi
concepts.rule: Learn the expression together with its word order and case.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ بِي صُدَاعًا شَدِيدًا.
مَاذَا بِكِ يَا زَيْنَبُ؟
صُدَاعٌ · زُكَامٌ · دُوَارٌ · سُعَالٌ
examples.translation:
I have a severe headache.
What is troubling you, Zaynab?
Headache · cold · vertigo · cough
examples.explanation: The expression uses bi for the person affected. In the first sentence, the bi phrase is the fronted predicate of inna and صُدَاعًا its delayed ism. Several disease words use فُعَالٌ; this is a vocabulary pattern, not a rule for every illness.

concepts.title: With inna, emphatic lam moves to the predicate
concepts.rule: Separate inna’s case government from the lam’s emphasis.

examples.arabic:
لَبَيْتُكَ أَجْمَلُ.
إِنَّ بَيْتَكَ لَأَجْمَلُ.
examples.translation:
Indeed your house is more beautiful.
Surely your house is indeed more beautiful.
examples.explanation: The opening emphatic lam cannot remain beside inna in its original place. It moves to the khabar and is called lam muzahlaqa. Inna still makes its ism mansub; the lam itself does not alter the predicate’s case.

concepts.title: Qad with a past verb marks certainty
concepts.rule: Identify the tense after qad before translating it.

examples.arabic:
قَدْ دَخَلَ الْمُدَرِّسُ الْفَصْلَ.
قَدْ فَاتَتْكَ دُرُوسٌ.
examples.translation:
The teacher has already entered the classroom.
You did miss lessons.
examples.explanation: The Key calls this taakkud. Qad precedes the madi verb and confirms the event. It does not function as a noun-case governor.

concepts.title: Qad with a present verb has several readings
concepts.rule: The same particle can have different force with the same tense.

examples.arabic:
قَدْ يَعُودُ الْمُدِيرُ غَدًا.
قَدْ يَصْدُقُ الْكَذُوبُ.
وَقَدْ تَعْلَمُونَ أَنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إِلَيْكُمْ
examples.translation:
The headmaster may return tomorrow.
A habitual liar sometimes tells the truth.
You know for sure that I am Allah’s messenger to you.
examples.explanation: With mudari, the Key lists doubt/possibility, rarity/paucity, and certainty. Do not translate every instance as “may”. The last source example explicitly illustrates certainty.

concepts.title: Layta expresses a difficult or impossible wish
concepts.rule: Distinguish wish (layta) from hope (laalla).

examples.arabic:
لَيْتَ النُّجُومَ قَرِيبَةٌ.
لَيْتَنِي غَنِيٌّ.
لَيْتَ الشَّبَابَ يَعُودُ.
examples.translation:
Would that the stars were near.
Would that I were rich.
Would that youth returned.
examples.explanation: Layta makes its ism mansub and leaves its khabar marfu or in the position of raf. The predicate may be a word, a verb clause or a fronted phrase. Ya may precede layta to heighten the wish, as يَا لَيْتَنِي.

concepts.title: La can deny the whole category
concepts.rule: Identify category-negating la from its noun construction.

examples.arabic:
لَا كِتَابَ عِنْدِي.
لَا دَاعِيَ لِلْخَوْفِ.
لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ.
examples.translation:
I have no book of any kind.
There is no need to fear.
There is no doubt in it.
examples.explanation: La nafiyah lil-jins excludes every member of the named kind. Its ism and khabar are indefinite in the construction taught here. The simple, non-idafah ism is mabni on fathah, as كِتَابَ; a phrase can supply the predicate. This is not prohibitive la governing a verb.

concepts.title: Review the six particles resembling verbs
concepts.rule: Keep each particle’s meaning alongside the shared case rule.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ · أَنَّ · كَأَنَّ · لَكِنَّ · لَيْتَ · لَعَلَّ
إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ.
examples.translation:
Indeed/that · as if · but · would that · perhaps
Indeed Allah is forgiving.
examples.explanation: Inna and anna emphasise; kaanna expresses resemblance or a tentative impression; lakinna corrects or qualifies; layta wishes; laalla hopes or fears. They make the former mubtada mansub as their ism and retain the khabar. The Key compares their meaning and nasb government with verbs.

concepts.title: Inna’s predicate can be a word, clause or phrase
concepts.rule: Do not demand one visible marfu noun for every predicate.

examples.arabic:
كَأَنَّ شَيْئًا لَمْ يَحْدُثْ.
إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا.
كَأَنَّكَ مِنَ الصِّينِ.
لَعَلَّ الْمُدَرِّسَ عِنْدَ الْمُدِيرِ.
examples.translation:
As if nothing had happened.
Indeed Allah forgives all sins.
It looks as if you are from China.
I hope the teacher is at the headmaster’s.
examples.explanation: The khabar may be a single expression, verbal clause, nominal clause, prepositional phrase or zarf phrase. A verbal predicate allows an indefinite ism, as شَيْئًا illustrates. The clause has the predicate role even when its internal verb or nouns have their own endings.

concepts.title: A phrase predicate can precede inna’s ism
concepts.rule: Fronting a phrase does not change which noun inna governs.

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ إِلَيْنَا إِيَابَهُمْ.
إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا.
examples.translation:
Indeed to Us is their return.
Indeed with hardship is ease.
examples.explanation: When the ism is definite, the Key permits the phrase predicate before or after it. With an indefinite ism in these constructions, the phrase must come first: يُسْرًا follows مَعَ الْعُسْرِ. Inna’s delayed ism remains mansub.

concepts.title: Asa can be an incomplete verb of hope or fear
concepts.rule: Find the separate ism before treating asa as incomplete.

examples.arabic:
عَسَى اللَّهُ أَنْ يَعْفُوَ عَنْهُمْ.
عَسَيْتُ أَنْ أَتَزَوَّجَ هَذَا الْعَامَ.
examples.translation:
It is hoped Allah will pardon them.
I hope to get married this year.
examples.explanation: As a sister of kana, asa takes an ism and khabar. Allah is the first example’s ism; the attached tu is the second’s. The predicate is an plus mudari. Like laalla, asa can express hope or fear according to context.

concepts.title: Complete asa has an-clause as its subject
concepts.rule: The same verb’s complete and incomplete analyses depend on construction.

examples.arabic:
عَسَى أَنْ يَهْدِيَنِي رَبِّي.
عَسَى أَنْ أَرْسُبَ.
examples.translation:
It is hoped my Lord will guide me.
I fear I may fail.
examples.explanation: When immediately followed by the masdar muawwal, complete asa has that whole clause as fail. Compare incomplete عَسَيْتُ أَنْ أَرْسُبَ, with tu as ism. The source’s يَهْدِيَنِ is a shortened written/pronounced object form, not a different clause role.

concepts.title: Paired la can negate two past actions
concepts.rule: Past-form la…wa-la can deny both actions together.

examples.arabic:
مَا أَكَلْتُ.
لَا أَكَلْتُ وَلَا شَرِبْتُ.
examples.translation:
I did not eat.
I neither ate nor drank.
examples.explanation: The chapter contrasts ordinary ma negating one past verb with repeated la for two past verbs negated together. This la is negative; it is not a prohibition addressed to the listener.

concepts.title: Jaala can also create or begin
concepts.rule: Choose the grammatical analysis after identifying jaala’s meaning.

examples.arabic:
وَجَعَلَ الظُّلُمَاتِ وَالنُّورَ.
جَعَلَ حَامِدٌ يَضْرِبُنِي.
examples.translation:
He created darkness and light.
Hamid began beating me.
examples.explanation: In the creation sense jaala takes one object (which may be coordinated). In the beginning sense it works like kana: Hamid is its ism and the mudari clause its khabar. The predicate is not a second direct object in this use.

concepts.title: Partitive min means part of a whole
concepts.rule: Keep min when the intended meaning is “some of” or “one of”.

examples.arabic:
كُلْ هَذَا. · كُلْ مِنْ هَذَا.
أَنْتَ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ الطُّلَّابِ.
أَنْتَ أَحْسَنُ الطُّلَّابِ.
examples.translation:
Eat this · eat some of this
You are one of the best students.
You are the best student.
examples.explanation: Min tabidiyyah selects a portion or member of the named group. It is not the extra emphatic min taught earlier. In the first comparison, leaving min out permits the whole item rather than specifying a part.

concepts.title: Question hamza comes before a conjunction
concepts.rule: The choice of question particle affects its position.

examples.arabic:
وَهَلْ جَاءَ الْمُدِيرُ؟
أَوَجَاءَ الْمُدِيرُ؟
examples.translation:
And has the headmaster come?
And has the headmaster come?
examples.explanation: The Key places waw before hal, but interrogative hamza before waw. Its Qur’anic examples also show hamza preceding thumma. Do not simply replace hal with hamza while keeping the old order.

concepts.title: “My Lord” has five calling forms
concepts.rule: Recognise the same possessive calling meaning across the variants.

examples.arabic:
يَا رَبِّي · يَا رَبِّ · يَا رَبِّيَ
يَا رَبَّ · يَا رَبَّا · يَا رَبَّاهْ
examples.translation: O my Lord (the five forms, plus final pause ha)
examples.explanation: The Key lists original ya, omitted ya with kasrah, retained ya with fathah, omitted ya with fathah, and long-alif form. The last may take ha as-sakt. These are variants of a vocative possessed by first-person ya; رَبِّ is especially frequent in the cited usage.

concepts.title: Ala can draw attention to an important statement
concepts.rule: Read the particle’s role from the whole utterance.

examples.arabic: أَلَا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ الْمُفْسِدُونَ
examples.translation: Take notice: they themselves are the mischief-makers.
examples.explanation: This ala is an opening and attention particle, harf istiftah wa-tanbih. Distinguish it from interrogative/urging uses that may look similar without context. The following statement retains its own inna construction.

concepts.title: Kana’s pronoun predicate may be attached or separate
concepts.rule: Nasb pronoun forms can represent a predicate as well as an object.

examples.arabic:
لَا، مَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَكُونَهُ.
لَا، مَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَكُونَ إِيَّاهُ.
examples.translation: No, I do not want to be one (both forms).
examples.explanation: In reply to wanting to be a judge, hu or iyyahu stands for the predicate of kana. The Key accepts both attachment and separation. This is a khabar in the position of nasb, not an ordinary direct object of kana.

concepts.title: Emphatic nun strengthens a present verb or command
concepts.rule: Identify emphatic nun separately from plural-subject nun and the five-form mood nun.

examples.arabic:
اُخْرُجَنَّ · اُخْرُجَنْ
وَاللَّهِ لَأَنْشُرَنَّ الْإِسْلَامَ فِي بَلَدِي.
examples.translation:
Do get out! (heavy · light nun)
By Allah, I shall propagate Islam in my country.
examples.explanation: Nun al-tawkid has a heavy doubled form and a less frequent light single form. The Key uses it with mudari and imperative, not madi. Its addition requires changes to the normal stem endings.

concepts.title: The vowel before emphatic nun identifies some subject forms
concepts.rule: Read yaktubanna, yaktubunna and taktubinna distinctly.

examples.arabic:
يَكْتُبُ ← يَكْتُبَنَّ
يَكْتُبُونَ ← يَكْتُبُنَّ
تَكْتُبِينَ ← تَكْتُبِنَّ
examples.translation:
He writes → emphatic he will write
They male write → emphatic they will write
You female write → emphatic you will write
examples.explanation: The four bare forms replace final dammah with fathah before heavy nun. Masculine plural loses its mood nun and written waw, retaining short u before the emphatic nun. Female singular similarly retains short i after ya drops. These vowels preserve the subject distinction.

rows: He writes → emphatic he will write
They male write → emphatic they will write
You female write → emphatic you will write

concepts.title: Dual and female plural emphatic forms retain more letters
concepts.rule: Distinguish subject nun from the newly added emphatic nun.

examples.arabic:
يَكْتُبَانِ ← يَكْتُبَانِّ
يَكْتُبْنَ ← يَكْتُبْنَانِّ
examples.translation:
They two write → emphatic dual
They female write → emphatic female plural
examples.explanation: The dual mood nun drops but alif stays, followed by heavy nun with kasrah. Female plural subject nun stays, an alif separates it from emphatic nun, and the latter again has kasrah. Keep these separate from the masculine plural u-nna form.

rows: They female write → emphatic female plural

concepts.title: Commands and prohibitions follow the same subject distinctions
concepts.rule: Add emphasis to the correctly identified subject form, restoring weak letters as taught.

examples.arabic:
لَا تَمْشِ ← لَا تَمْشِيَنَّ
لَا تَنْسَ ← لَا تَنْسَيَنَّ
اُكْتُبَنَّ · اُكْتُبَانِّ · اُكْتُبُنَّ · اُكْتُبِنَّ · اُكْتُبْنَانِّ
examples.translation:
Do not walk → emphatic prohibition
Do not forget → emphatic prohibition
Emphatic write! for male singular, dual, male plural, female singular, female plural
examples.explanation: Majzum five-form mood nuns are already absent. The same emphatic changes then apply. A final weak radical omitted in jazm or command is restored before nun, as ya in walking and forgetting. The command table preserves all listener distinctions.

concepts.title: Emphatic nun is optional in commands and request-like mudari
concepts.rule: Use the grammatical environment and intended emphasis together.

examples.arabic:
اِنْزِلَنَّ مِنَ السَّيَّارَةِ يَا وَلَدُ.
لَا تَأْكُلَنَّ وَأَنْتَ شَبْعَانُ.
هَلْ تُسَافِرَنَّ وَأَنْتَ مَرِيضٌ؟
examples.translation:
Do get out of the car, boy.
Do not eat when you are full.
Are you travelling while ill?
examples.explanation: The Key lists imperative and mudari with talab—command, prohibition or questioning—as optional uses. This does not make emphatic nun an ordinary ending to add to every report.

concepts.title: A future affirmative oath answer requires emphatic nun under conditions
concepts.rule: Do not flatten the oath rule into “every oath takes nun”.

examples.arabic:
وَاللَّهِ لَأَحْفَظَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ الْكَرِيمَ.
وَاللَّهِ لَا أَخْرُجُ.
وَاللَّهِ لَأُحِبُّكَ.
examples.translation:
By Allah, I will memorise the Qur’an.
By Allah, I will not go out.
By Allah, I love you.
examples.explanation: The Key requires affirmative meaning, future reference and lam attached to the verb. A negative answer has neither lam nor nun. A present-state answer has lam but no nun. If lam attaches to a fronted phrase or to sawfa rather than directly to the verb, nun is not used.

concepts.title: Conditional imma strongly calls for emphatic nun
concepts.rule: Identify which imma is being used before applying the emphasis rule.

examples.arabic: إِمَّا تَذْهَبَنَّ إِلَى مَكَّةَ أَذْهَبْ مَعَكَ.
examples.translation: If you go to Makkah, I will go with you.
examples.explanation: The nun of conditional in assimilates into ma, producing imma. The Key calls emphatic nun after it near-compulsory. This is different from the alternative-choice imma…wa-imma construction learned earlier. The answer retains its conditional jazm.

concepts.title: Join two ideas with “and”
concepts.rule: Write وَ together with the next word.

examples.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ وَذَلِكَ مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation: This is a house and that is a mosque.
examples.explanation: Notice وَذَلِكَ in the example. There is no space between وَ and ذَلِكَ. The joining word lets you connect two statements you already know how to make.

concepts.title: In these statements, “or” is أَوْ
concepts.rule: For these statement alternatives, use أَوْ.

examples.arabic:
خُذْ هَذَا أَوْ ذَاكَ
رَأَيْتُ ثَلَاثَةً أَوْ أَرْبَعَةً
خَرَجَ بِلَالٌ أَوْ حَامِدٌ
examples.translation:
Take this or that.
I saw three or four.
Bilal or Hamid went out.
examples.explanation: Contrast these statements with the أَ… أَمْ… choice questions in the previous card. Both words may be translated “or,” but they are not interchangeable in the constructions being taught.

concepts.title: Give a reason with لِأَنَّ
concepts.rule: لِأَنَّ introduces the reason and follows the أَنَّ pattern.

examples.arabic:
مَا خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ
ذَهَبَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ إِلَى الْمُسْتَشْفَى لِأَنَّهُ مَرِيضٌ
examples.translation:
I did not go out of the house because the weather is cold.
Ibrahim went to the hospital because he is sick.
examples.explanation: Its noun is mansub: الْجَوَّ. A pronoun attaches in لِأَنَّهُ. The predicate is marfuʿ in these examples: بَارِدٌ or مَرِيضٌ. This connects reason-giving with the إِنَّ family grammar.

concepts.title: Introduce a separate topic with أَمَّا… فَـ
concepts.rule: Pair أَمَّا with فَـ before the information about that topic.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا مِنْ أَلْمَانِيَا. أَمَّا بِلَالٌ فَهُوَ مِنْ بَاكِسْتَانَ، وَأَمَّا إِبْرَاهِيمُ فَهُوَ مِنَ الْيَابَانِ
أَمَّا أَخِي فَيَسْكُنُ مَعَ أَبِي وَأُمِّي
examples.translation:
I am from Germany. As for Bilal, he is from Pakistan; as for Ibrahim, he is from Japan.
As for my brother, he lives with my father and mother.
examples.explanation: The فَـ may attach to a pronoun, as in فَهُوَ, or directly to a verb, as in فَيَسْكُنُ. The Key also contrasts two pens with أَمَّا ذَاكَ فَبِعَشَرَةٍ, “As for that one, it costs ten.”

concepts.title: Give a reason with فَإِنَّ
concepts.rule: Read فَإِنَّ here as the reason for the instruction.

examples.arabic:
كُلْ هَذَا فَإِنَّكَ جَوْعَانُ
اُدْخُلْ فَإِنَّ الدَّرْسَ قَدْ بَدَأَ
اِغْسِلِ الْقَمِيصَ فَإِنَّهُ وَسِخٌ
examples.translation:
Eat this, because you are hungry.
Come in, for the lesson has already started.
Wash the shirt, for it is dirty.
examples.explanation: The instruction comes first; فَإِنَّ then explains why. The familiar grammar of إِنَّ still applies: الدَّرْسَ is its mansub noun, or an attached pronoun supplies its noun, as in إِنَّكَ and إِنَّهُ. Compare this way of giving a reason with لِأَنَّ from earlier lessons.

concepts.title: Give the purpose of an action with لِـ
concepts.rule: Purpose لِـ is followed by a mansub mudari.

examples.arabic:
أَدْرُسُ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ لِأَفْهَمَ الْقُرْآنَ.
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ لِأَغْسِلَ وَجْهِي.
فَتَحْتُ النَّافِذَةَ لِيَخْرُجَ الذُّبَابُ.
خَلَقَنَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى لِنَعْبُدَهُ.
examples.translation:
I study Arabic to understand the Quran.
I went to the bathroom to wash my face.
I opened the window so that the flies might go out.
Allah created us so that we may worship Him.
examples.explanation: This لِـ is لَامُ التَّعْلِيلِ, the lam of purpose. The following mudari is mansub because of a hidden أَنْ after the lam. Notice the final a in أَفْهَمَ, أَغْسِلَ and يَخْرُجَ. The person doing the purpose action can differ from the person doing the first action.

concepts.title: A coordinated noun shares case
concepts.rule: Coordinating “and” links nouns with the same case.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجَ حَامِدٌ وَصَدِيقُهُ.
طَلَبَ الْمُدِيرُ حَامِدًا وَصَدِيقَهُ.
أَيْنَ كُتُبُ حَامِدٍ وَصَدِيقِهِ؟
examples.translation:
Hamid and his friend went out.
The headmaster wanted Hamid and his friend.
Where are the books of Hamid and his friend?
examples.explanation: صَدِيق follows حَامِد in raf, nasb and jarr. The waw here means “and”; compare the different waw of accompaniment introduced in the mansub overview. The meaning and construction determine which analysis applies.

concepts.title: Waw can mean “and” or oath “by”
concepts.rule: Identify the job of waw from its construction.

examples.arabic:
أُرِيدُ كِتَابًا وَقَلَمًا.
خَرَجَ الزُّبَيْرُ وَحَامِدٌ.
وَاللَّهِ مَا رَأَيْتُهُ.
examples.translation:
I want a book and a pen.
Zubayr and Hamid went out.
By Allah, I did not see him.
examples.explanation: The first two waw words are conjunctions. The oath waw is a preposition and makes the following noun majrur. A waw inside a root, as in وَلَدٌ, is simply one of its letters rather than a separate conjunction.

concepts.title: إِمَّا … وَإِمَّا offers alternatives
concepts.rule: إِمَّا … وَإِمَّا marks alternatives.

examples.arabic:
الِاسْمُ إِمَّا مُذَكَّرٌ وَإِمَّا مُؤَنَّثٌ.
إِمَّا تَزُورُنِي وَإِمَّا أَزُورُكَ.
examples.translation:
A noun is either masculine or feminine.
Either you visit me or I visit you.
examples.explanation: Repeat إِمَّا before each alternative and join the second with وَ. The alternatives can be nouns or clauses, as the two examples show. This is different from using وَ alone to assert that both things happen.

concepts.title: An أَنْ clause can do a noun’s job
concepts.rule: Separate the clause’s overall noun role from the mood of its internal verb.

examples.arabic:
أَنْ تَدْرُسَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ أَفْضَلُ.
يَنْبَغِي أَنْ تَكْتُبَ عُنْوَانَكَ بِوُضُوحٍ.
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ.
تَعَالَ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَخْرُجَ.
لَا تَذْهَبْ إِلَى أَنْ أَرْجِعَ.
examples.translation:
Studying Arabic is better.
It is necessary that you write your address clearly.
I want to go out.
Come before you leave.
Do not go until I return.
examples.explanation: Such a clause can occupy a raf position as topic, predicate or subject; a nasb position as object; or a jarr position after a preposition or as an idafah complement. The Key also gives الْإِسْلَامُ أَنْ تُؤْمِنَ بِاللَّهِ, with the clause as predicate. The internal verb is still mansub after أَنْ.

concepts.title: Ask whether an action is possible
concepts.rule: Use يُمْكِنُ + pronoun + أَنْ + action for “can” or “may” in this pattern.

examples.arabic:
أَيُمْكِنُنِي أَنْ أَجْلِسَ هُنَا؟
نَعَمْ، يُمْكِنُكَ أَنْ تَجْلِسَ.
لَا يُمْكِنُهُ أَنْ يَخْرُجَ الْآنَ.
examples.translation:
May I sit here?
Yes, you may sit.
He cannot go out now.
examples.explanation: يُمْكِنُنِي expresses possibility for me; يُمْكِنُكَ for you; يُمْكِنُهُ for him. Follow it with أَنْ and the action in its mansub form. The first example politely asks permission by literally asking whether sitting here is possible for the speaker.

concepts.title: Say “must” with يَجِبُ عَلَى
concepts.rule: يَجِبُ عَلَى someone أَنْ + action expresses an obligation.

examples.arabic:
يَجِبُ عَلَيْنَا أَنْ نَفْهَمَ الْقُرْآنَ.
يَجِبُ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَرْجِعَ غَدًا.
يَجِبُ عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ إِلَى الرِّيَاضِ الْيَوْمَ.
examples.translation:
We should understand the Quran.
You must return tomorrow.
I must go to Riyadh today.
examples.explanation: عَلَى takes the attached person: عَلَيْنَا, عَلَيْكَ, عَلَيَّ. The action follows أَنْ, so its mudari is mansub. The Key identifies the clause أَنْ نَفْهَمَ as the subject of يَجِبُ: literally, that action is necessary for us.

concepts.title: “Should not” differs from “need not”
concepts.rule: Negate the action for “must not”; negate يَجِبُ for “need not” in this contrast.

examples.arabic:
يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ لَا يَخْرُجَ مِنَ الْفَصْلِ.
لَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْنَا أَنْ نَحْضُرَ هَذَا الدَّرْسَ.
examples.translation:
He should not leave the classroom.
We need not attend this lesson.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, leaving is the action that must not happen: the negative is with the second verb. In the second, لَا denies the necessity itself. Not being required to attend does not by itself mean attendance is forbidden.

concepts.title: لَا يَنْبَغِي means “it is not proper”
concepts.rule: لَا يَنْبَغِي لِـ someone أَنْ + action expresses what is not proper.

examples.arabic:
لَا يَنْبَغِي لِلطَّالِبِ أَنْ يَغِيبَ.
لَا يَنْبَغِي لَكَ أَنْ تَقُولَ هَذَا.
examples.translation:
It is not proper for a student to be absent.
It is not becoming of you to say this.
examples.explanation: لِـ introduces the person concerned, and أَنْ introduces the action in its mansub form. Here the expression concerns propriety, not merely whether someone is physically able to act. Compare يُمْكِنُ and يَجِبُ from earlier lessons.

concepts.title: لَوْ introduces an unfulfilled past condition
concepts.rule: Read لَوْ as a past counterfactual in this lesson, with its separate result clause.

examples.arabic:
لَوِ اجْتَهَدْتَ لَنَجَحْتَ.
لَوْ عَرَفْتُ أَنَّكَ مَرِيضٌ مَا تَأَخَّرْتُ.
لَوْ سَمِعْتَ قِصَّتَهُ لَبَكَيْتَ.
examples.translation:
Had you worked hard, you would have passed.
Had I known you were sick, I would not have been late.
Had you heard his story, you would have cried.
examples.explanation: The first example implies the effort and result did not occur. The second clause is the jawab, commonly introduced by lam in an affirmative result. That lam is usually omitted when the result is negative, as مَا تَأَخَّرْتُ shows. The kasrah on لَوِ in connected speech helps join to hamzat al-wasl.

concepts.title: A command’s result can be majzum
concepts.rule: A demand followed by its intended result can govern jazm in that result.

examples.arabic:
اِقْرَأْهُ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى تَفْهَمْهُ.
لَا تَكْسَلْ تَنْجَحْ.
examples.translation:
Read it again and you will understand it.
Do not be lazy and you will pass.
examples.explanation: The result verbs تَفْهَمْ and تَنْجَحْ are majzum because they express the consequence of the preceding request or prohibition. طَلَب covers both command and prohibition. This concerns a result relation, not any unrelated mudari that happens to follow a command.

concepts.title: إِذَا introduces a future condition
concepts.rule: Distinguish the form of the verb from the time of the condition.

examples.arabic:
إِذَا رَأَيْتَ خَالِدًا فَاسْأَلْهُ عَنِ الْكِتَابِ.
إِذَا جَاءَ رَمَضَانُ فُتِحَتْ أَبْوَابُ الْجَنَّةِ.
examples.translation:
If you see Khalid, ask him about the book.
When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise are opened.
examples.explanation: إِذَا is a zarf with conditional meaning, translated “if” or “when.” The condition is shart and the result jawab al-shart. Past forms are common but mudari can also occur in the condition or result. This differs from the unfulfilled past condition with لَوْ.

concepts.title: A nominal result clause takes فَـ
concepts.rule: Use fa before a nominal jawab al-shart.

examples.arabic:
إِذَا اجْتَهَدْتَ فَالنَّجَاحُ مَضْمُونٌ.
وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ.
examples.translation:
If you work hard, success is certain.
When My servants ask you about Me, I am near.
examples.explanation: A nominal sentence as the result takes فَـ, including one introduced by إِنَّ. The fa links the entire result; it is not a prefix changing the case of the first noun. Other result types have their own fa conditions, developed in the next chapter.

concepts.title: Requests and questions in the result take فَـ
concepts.rule: A result containing a demand or question is linked with fa.

examples.arabic:
إِذَا رَأَيْتَ حَامِدًا فَاسْأَلْهُ عَنْ مَوْعِدِ السَّفَرِ.
إِذَا وَجَدْتَ الْمَرِيضَ نَائِمًا فَلَا تُوقِظْهُ.
إِذَا رَأَيْتُ بِلَالًا فَمَاذَا أَقُولُ لَهُ؟
examples.translation:
If you see Hamid, ask him about the departure time.
If you find the patient sleeping, do not wake him.
If I see Bilal, what should I tell him?
examples.explanation: The result can direct someone to act, prohibit an action, or ask a question. All three introduced types require the linking fa in this lesson. A command formed with lam likewise uses the result fa, as فَلْيَرْكَعْ in the Key’s mosque example.

concepts.title: Conditional إِنْ can govern two majzum verbs
concepts.rule: Recognise the two-part condition before assigning jazm.

examples.arabic:
إِنْ تَذْهَبْ أَذْهَبْ.
إِنْ تَأْكُلْ طَعَامًا فَاسِدًا تَمْرَضْ.
examples.translation:
If you go, I will go too.
If you eat rotten food, you will fall sick.
examples.explanation: إِنْ and the similar conditional words are أَدَوَاتُ الشَّرْطِ الْجَازِمَةُ. In this simple mudari-plus-mudari pattern, both verbs are majzum. This إِنْ is different from emphasis إِنَّ and from infinitive أَنْ. إِنْ plus negative لَا can be written إِلَّا in the conditional example in the Key.

concepts.title: مَنْ and مَا can introduce general conditions
concepts.rule: The meaning and paired clauses distinguish conditional مَنْ / مَا from their other uses.

examples.arabic:
فَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ.
وَمَا تَفْعَلُوا مِنْ خَيْرٍ يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ.
examples.translation:
Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it.
Whatever good you do, Allah knows it.
examples.explanation: These uses govern a condition and result, unlike a simple question or relative clause. يَعْمَلْ and يَرَ show jazm, including loss of the final weak letter in يَرَهُ. تَفْعَلُوا loses its mood nun; يَعْلَمْ has sukun.

concepts.title: مَتَى and أَيْنَ can mean whenever and wherever
concepts.rule: Read these as general conditions, not direct time/place questions.

examples.arabic:
مَتَى تُسَافِرْ أُسَافِرْ.
أَيْنَ تَسْكُنْ أَسْكُنْ.
أَيْنَمَا تَكُونُوا يُدْرِكْكُمُ الْمَوْتُ.
examples.translation:
Whenever you travel, I will travel too.
Wherever you stay, I will stay too.
Wherever you may be, death will overtake you.
examples.explanation: The verbs are majzum in these conditional uses. An added مَا often strengthens أَيْنَ, giving أَيْنَمَا. That added part does not turn it into a question asking for one particular location.

concepts.title: أَيّ and مَهْمَا introduce open-ended conditions
concepts.rule: Separate the conditional word’s noun role from the verb moods it governs.

examples.arabic:
أَيَّ مُعْجَمٍ نَجِدْ فِي الْمَكْتَبَةِ نَشْتَرِهِ.
مَهْمَا تَقُلْ نُصَدِّقْكَ.
examples.translation:
Whichever dictionary we find in the bookshop, we will buy it.
Whatever you say, we believe you.
examples.explanation: أَيّ connects to a following noun as mudaf; its own case follows its job, here object of نَجِدْ. مَهْمَا does not need that noun. The hollow تَقُلْ and final-weak نَشْتَرِهِ illustrate the familiar weak-verb jazm changes.

concepts.title: Conditional form and time need not match
concepts.rule: Past morphology can express a future conditional event.

examples.arabic:
وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا نَعُدْ.
وَإِنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنَا.
مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ حَرْثَ الْآخِرَةِ نَزِدْ لَهُ فِي حَرْثِهِ.
مَنْ يَقُمْ لَيْلَةَ الْقَدْرِ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ.
examples.translation:
If you return, We shall return.
If you return, We shall return.
Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase it for him.
Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Qadr with faith and hope of reward will have past sins forgiven.
examples.explanation: Both verbs may be mudari, both madi, or one of each. A mudari in the direct conditional construction is majzum; a madi stays mabni without a new visible mood ending. The Key’s first two quotations occur in distinct contexts, so their shared grammatical pattern should not erase their contextual meanings.

concepts.title: Fa also links a fixed verb or قَدْ result
concepts.rule: Recognise the result’s opening construction when deciding whether fa is required.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ غَشَّنَا فَلَيْسَ مِنَّا.
وَمَنْ يُطِعِ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَقَدْ فَازَ فَوْزًا عَظِيمًا.
examples.translation:
Whoever deceives us is not one of us.
Whoever obeys Allah and His messenger has achieved great success.
examples.explanation: A jamid verb such as لَيْسَ lacks a normal full set of past/present/command forms; its result takes fa. A result introduced by قَدْ also takes fa. The linking kasrah in يُطِعِ joins to the following hamzat al-wasl.

concepts.title: Fa precedes results introduced by مَا, لَنْ, سَـ or سَوْفَ
concepts.rule: A fa-linked result clause does not simply inherit jazm on every verb inside it.

examples.arabic:
مَهْمَا تَكُنِ الظُّرُوفُ فَمَا أَكْذِبُ.
مَنْ لَبِسَ الْحَرِيرَ فِي الدُّنْيَا فَلَنْ يَلْبَسَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ.
إِنْ تُسَافِرْ فَسَأُسَافِرُ.
وَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ عَيْلَةً فَسَوْفَ يُغْنِيكُمُ اللَّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ.
examples.translation:
Whatever the circumstances, I do not lie.
Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter.
If you travel, I will travel too.
If you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty.
examples.explanation: The list covers negative مَا, negative future لَنْ, future سَـ and سَوْفَ. Do not force the mudari after the result fa into jazm: أَكْذِبُ and أُسَافِرُ remain marfu, while يَلْبَسَ is mansub after لَنْ.

concepts.title: A كَأَنَّمَا result takes fa too
concepts.rule: Analyse the linked clause as a whole as well as its internal words.

examples.arabic: فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ النَّاسَ جَمِيعًا.
examples.translation: Then it is as if he had killed all humanity.
examples.explanation: This is the result excerpt from the Key’s Quran 5:32 example, condemning an unjust killing by comparing it with killing everyone. Grammatically, كَأَنَّمَا is another result opening requiring fa. In the conditional construction governed by a jazm word, the entire fa-linked jawab is described as فِي مَحَلِّ جَزْمٍ, rather than making every internal verb visibly majzum.

concepts.title: حَتَّى means “until” or “so that”
concepts.rule: Identify endpoint or purpose, then keep the mansub verb.

examples.arabic:
انْتَظِرْ حَتَّى أَلْبَسَ.
دَخَلْتُ حَتَّى لَا أَشْغَلَكَ.
أَدْرُسُ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ حَتَّى أَفْهَمَ الْقُرْآنَ.
examples.translation:
Wait until I get dressed.
I entered so that I might not distract you.
I study Arabic so that I can understand the Quran.
examples.explanation: The first gives an endpoint; the others a purpose. The verb following حَتَّى is mansub in these patterns because of a latent أَنْ. A negative لَا before the action does not replace this government with a prohibition.

concepts.title: Wa-law means “even if”
concepts.rule: Use the context to translate the past form after wa-law.

examples.arabic:
اِشْتَرِ هَذَا الْمُعْجَمَ وَلَوْ كَانَ غَالِيًا.
اُحْضُرِ الِامْتِحَانَ وَلَوْ كُنْتَ مَرِيضًا.
examples.translation:
Buy this dictionary even if it is expensive.
Attend the examination even if you are ill.
examples.explanation: The Key uses وَلَوْ followed by a madi verb. Interpret the clause as a concession, not necessarily a past event. The instruction remains despite the stated obstacle.

concepts.title: Light lakin loses lakinna’s case government
concepts.rule: Check the nun before applying inna-like endings.

examples.arabic:
جَاءَ الْمُدَرِّسُ لَكِنِ الطُّلَّابُ مَا جَاءُوا.
غَابَ عَلِيٌّ وَلَكِنْ حَضَرَ أَحْمَدُ.
examples.translation:
The teacher came, but the students did not.
Ali was absent, but Ahmad attended.
examples.explanation: لَكِنَّ is a sister of inna and makes its ism mansub. لَكِنْ, without doubled nun, does not do this: الطُّلَّابُ stays marfu. Light lakin may also introduce a verbal sentence. The linking kasrah before al does not restore shaddah or government.

concepts.title: Result fa can make a present verb mansub
concepts.rule: Recognise the causal/result relationship before assigning nasb.

examples.arabic:
لَيْتَ لِي مَالًا كَثِيرًا فَأَتَصَدَّقَ.
لَا تَأْكُلْ كَثِيرًا فَتَنَامَ.
examples.translation:
I wish I had much money so I could give alms.
Do not eat too much lest you sleep.
examples.explanation: The Key includes wishing among talab, alongside commands, prohibitions and questions. A mudari connected to that preceding expression by this causal fa is mansub. Do not apply the rule to every fa; ordinary conjunction and conditional-result fa have other functions.

concepts.title: A preposition may drop before a masdar muawwal
concepts.rule: An omitted preposition need not remove the underlying relationship.

examples.arabic:
أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنْ أَنْ أَكْذِبَ.
أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ أَنْ أَكْذِبَ.
أَمَرَنَا اللَّهُ بِأَنْ نُصَلِّيَ. · أَمَرَنَا اللَّهُ أَنْ نُصَلِّيَ.
examples.translation:
I seek refuge in Allah from telling lies (both forms).
Allah commanded us to pray (both forms).
examples.explanation: The preposition preceding an plus mudari may be omitted, unlike the corresponding ordinary noun construction. Retaining it is optional here. An still governs nasb inside the clause, whether or not the preposition is visible.

concepts.title: Anna plus its sentence can act as one noun unit
concepts.rule: Analyse both the clause’s outer role and its internal grammar.

examples.arabic:
بَلَغَنِي أَنَّهُ مَاتَ.
يَسُرُّنِي أَنَّكَ تِلْمِيذِي.
يَبْدُو أَنَّكَ مُسْتَعْجِلٌ.
examples.translation:
News reached me that he died.
I am pleased that you are my student.
It appears that you are in a hurry.
examples.explanation: Anna, its ism and its khabar form a masdar muawwal. In these examples the whole clause supplies the fail of the preceding verb. Inside it, anna still makes its ism mansub and retains its predicate structure.

concepts.title: Lawla means “but for”
concepts.rule: Read the premise and prevented outcome together.

examples.arabic:
لَوْلَا الشَّمْسُ لَهَلَكَتِ الْأَرْضُ.
لَوْلَا الِاخْتِبَارُ مَا حَضَرْتُ الْيَوْمَ.
examples.translation:
But for the sun, the earth would have perished.
But for the test, I would not have attended today.
examples.explanation: The noun after lawla is a mubtada whose predicate is omitted. Its answer here is a past verbal sentence. An affirmative answer takes lam; a negative answer does not. The stated preventing fact exists, unlike a simple unreal “if” premise.

concepts.title: Lawla can take an anna-clause
concepts.rule: A clause can express the same preventing fact as a noun.

examples.arabic:
لَوْلَا أَنَّ الْجَوَّ حَارٌّ لَحَضَرْتُ الْمُحَاضَرَةَ.
لَوْلَا أَنِّي مَرِيضٌ لَسَافَرْتُ مَعَكَ.
examples.translation:
But for the hot weather, I would have attended the lecture.
But for being ill, I would have travelled with you.
examples.explanation: Instead of a single noun, the Key uses anna with its ism and khabar after lawla. The an-clause expresses the fact blocking the answer. Keep anna’s internal mansub ism and marfu predicate.

concepts.title: Ma plus a verb can act as a masdar
concepts.rule: Use the noun-like role of the whole clause to identify infinitive ma.

examples.arabic:
بَعْدَ مَا دَخَلَ الْمُدَرِّسُ = بَعْدَ دُخُولِ الْمُدَرِّسِ
بَعْدَ مَا يَخْرُجُ الْمُدَرِّسُ
examples.translation:
After the teacher entered = after the teacher’s entry
After the teacher leaves
examples.explanation: Ma masdariyyah combines with a madi or mudari verb to express a verbal noun. The whole unit can follow baad or a preposition. Unlike an, this ma does not itself make the mudari mansub.

concepts.title: An omitted amma answer can hide its fa
concepts.rule: Contextual omission does not cancel the normal amma answer rule.

examples.arabic:
أَخِي يَدْرُسُ بِالْمَدْرَسَةِ، أَمَّا أَنَا فَأَدْرُسُ بِالْجَامِعَةِ.
فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ
examples.translation:
My brother studies at school; as for me, I study at university.
It will be said to them
examples.explanation: The normal answer after amma takes fa. In the cited Qur’anic example, the Key supplies an omitted answer “it will be said to them”; the following question is the speech content, explaining why no visible answer-fa appears immediately before it.

concepts.title: Kay introduces a purpose and governs nasb
concepts.rule: Use kay/likay for purpose and keep the following verb mansub.

examples.arabic:
أَدْرُسُ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ لِكَيْ أَفْهَمَ الْقُرْآنَ الْكَرِيمَ.
اِجْتَهِدْ لِكَيْلَا تَرْسُبَ.
examples.translation:
I study Arabic so that I may understand the Qur’an.
Work hard lest you fail.
examples.explanation: Kay is an infinitive particle making mudari mansub. Purpose lam may appear or be omitted. لِكَيْ plus negative la is written لِكَيْلَا. In the train example فَاتَنِي الْقِطَارُ, Arabic makes the train the subject and me the object: literally the train missed me.

concepts.title: Idhan means “in that case” in a reply
concepts.rule: Idhan does not govern nasb automatically wherever it appears.

examples.arabic:
إِذَنْ نَسْتَقْبِلَهُ فِي الْمَطَارِ.
نَحْنُ إِذَنْ نَسْتَقْبِلُهُ.
إِذَنْ فِي الْمَطَارِ نَسْتَقْبِلُهُ.
examples.translation:
In that case we will receive him at the airport.
We, in that case, will receive him.
In that case, at the airport we will receive him.
examples.explanation: For nasb, idhan must begin the sentence, immediately precede the verb, and the verb must refer to the future. The latter examples fail the first or second condition and retain marfu. A present state such as “I fear” also stays marfu.

concepts.title: An oath or negative la may intervene after idhan
concepts.rule: Learn the stated exceptions without treating all intervening words alike.

examples.arabic:
إِذَنْ وَاللَّهِ نَسْتَقْبِلَهُ فِي الْمَطَارِ.
إِذَنْ لَا نَسْتَقْبِلَهُ فِي الْمَطَارِ.
examples.translation:
In that case, by Allah, we will receive him at the airport.
In that case we will not receive him at the airport.
examples.explanation: The Key explicitly permits an intervening oath or negative la. These do not behave like an intervening location phrase. The other conditions—initial position and future meaning—still apply.

concepts.title: Surprise idha may introduce a conditional answer
concepts.rule: Identical particles can serve different roles in one sentence.

examples.arabic: وَإِذَا ذُكِرَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ دُونِهِ إِذَا هُمْ يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ.
examples.translation: When those besides Him are mentioned, unexpectedly they rejoice.
examples.explanation: A nominal conditional answer ordinarily takes fa. The Key shows idha al-fujaiyyah replacing that fa to present a surprising response. Distinguish the first temporal/conditional idha from the second surprise idha in the example.

concepts.title: Conjunction la excludes the second item
concepts.rule: Read this la as “not [the other item]” inside a coordination.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجَ بِلَالٌ لَا حَامِدٌ.
اِسْأَلِ الْمُدِيرَ لَا الْمُدَرِّسَ.
رَغْبَةً فِي الْعِلْمِ لَا رَهْبَةً مِنَ الِامْتِحَانِ
examples.translation:
Bilal left, not Hamid.
Ask the headmaster, not the teacher.
For love of knowledge, not fear of the examination
examples.explanation: La atifah coordinates a second noun while denying the action or relationship for it. The coordinated noun follows the first noun’s case, as marfu Hamid or mansub teacher shows. It does not govern a following majzum verb like prohibitive la.

concepts.title: An exception has three elements
concepts.rule: Identify the tool before applying an ending rule.

examples.arabic: نَجَحَ الطُّلَّابُ كُلُّهُمْ إِلَّا خَالِدًا.
examples.translation: All the students passed except Khalid.
examples.explanation: Khalid is mustathna, the excepted item; students is mustathna minhu, the group from which it is excepted; illa is the tool. Illa is a particle. Ghayr and siwa are noun tools; ma ada and ma khala are verbal tools. Their grammatical class affects the following noun.

concepts.title: Tell time with “except”
concepts.rule: Read the hour first, then subtract the amount after إِلَّا.

examples.arabic:
التَّاسِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا
السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ إِلَّا عَشْرَ دَقَائِقَ
السَّاعَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ إِلَّا خَمْسَ دَقَائِقَ
السَّاعَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ إِلَّا دَقِيقَةً وَاحِدَةً
examples.translation:
Quarter to nine
Ten minutes to one
Five minutes to two
One minute to five
examples.explanation: The noun expression after إِلَّا is mansub in these examples: رُبْعًا, عَشْرَ, خَمْسَ, or دَقِيقَةً. The number phrase still keeps its internal counted-noun relationship, as in خَمْسَ دَقَائِقَ.

concepts.title: Exceptions can be connected or disconnected
concepts.rule: Connected/disconnected and complete/mufarragh are different classifications.

examples.arabic:
وَصَلَ الضُّيُوفُ إِلَّا أَمْتِعَتَهُمْ.
مَا جَاءَ إِلَّا حَامِدٌ.
examples.translation:
The guests arrived, but their baggage did not.
No one came except Hamid.
examples.explanation: A connected exception excludes a member of the group; a disconnected exception contrasts another kind, such as baggage with guests. Separately, a complete exception names the original group; mufarragh omits it. The latter occurs with negation, prohibition or questioning.

concepts.title: Complete affirmative exceptions take nasb
concepts.rule: Do not decide case from illa alone; classify the construction first.

examples.arabic:
يَغْفِرُ اللَّهُ الذُّنُوبَ كُلَّهَا إِلَّا الشِّرْكَ.
لِكُلِّ دَاءٍ دَوَاءٌ إِلَّا الْمَوْتَ.
examples.translation:
Allah forgives all sins except shirk.
Every illness has a medicine except death.
examples.explanation: The first is a connected, complete affirmative construction. The second is disconnected because death is not an illness. Both excepted nouns are mansub. A command is included in the chapter’s affirmative category when classifying an exception sentence.

concepts.title: Complete non-affirmative exceptions allow two analyses
concepts.rule: The second option follows the original group’s actual case.

examples.arabic:
مَا حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ إِلَّا حَامِدًا / حَامِدٌ.
مَا اتَّصَلْتُ بِالطُّلَّابِ إِلَّا حَامِدًا / حَامِدٍ.
examples.translation:
The students did not attend except Hamid.
I did not contact the students except Hamid.
examples.explanation: For a connected complete exception in a negative, prohibitive or interrogative sentence, the Key permits nasb or the case of mustathna minhu. Thus marfu students allows Hamid marfu; prepositional students allows Hamid majrur. When the original group is mansub, both analyses have the same visible ending.

concepts.title: In mufarragh, the noun takes its normal sentence role
concepts.rule: Use the sentence role, not an automatic nasb rule.

examples.arabic:
مَا رَسَبَ إِلَّا بِلَالٌ.
مَا رَأَيْتُ إِلَّا بِلَالًا.
مَا بَحَثْتُ إِلَّا عَنْ خَالِدٍ.
examples.translation:
No one failed except Bilal.
I saw no one except Bilal.
I looked for none except Khalid.
examples.explanation: Bilal is fail in the first, object in the second; Khalid follows a preposition in the third. Temporarily ignoring illa can help identify the slot, but it reverses the meaning, so this is an analysis aid only. A separate pronoun is required after illa, as إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ.

concepts.title: Ghayr and siwa carry the exception’s case
concepts.rule: Do not transfer ghayr’s variable case to its fixed majrur complement.

examples.arabic:
نَجَحَ الطُّلَّابُ غَيْرَ حَامِدٍ.
مَا نَجَحَ غَيْرُ حَامِدٍ.
مَا سَأَلْتُ غَيْرَ حَامِدٍ.
examples.translation:
The students passed except Hamid.
No one passed except Hamid.
I asked none except Hamid.
examples.explanation: Apply the illa construction’s corresponding role to ghayr itself: nasb, raf or jarr as appropriate. The noun after it remains majrur through idafah. Siwa follows the same case analysis, with latent endings because it is maqsur.

concepts.title: Ma ada and ma khala take a mansub exception
concepts.rule: The class of the exception tool determines the following noun’s analysis.

examples.arabic:
اِخْتَبَرْتُ الطُّلَّابَ مَا عَدَا ثَلَاثَةً.
أَلَا كُلُّ شَيْءٍ مَا خَلَا اللَّهَ بَاطِلُ
examples.translation:
I examined the students except three.
Lo, everything except Allah is untrue.
examples.explanation: After these two verbal tools the excepted noun is mansub. The poetic line’s بَاطِلُ would normally have tanwin; the Key attributes its omission to metre. Keep poetic licence separate from ordinary declension.

concepts.title: Bal can cancel or move beyond a previous idea
concepts.rule: Decide from context whether bal corrects or advances the thought.

examples.arabic:
بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ.
إِبْرَاهِيمُ كَسْلَانُ بَلْ هُوَ مُهْمِلٌ.
examples.translation:
On the contrary, they are alive.
Ibrahim is lazy; rather, he is negligent.
examples.explanation: The first has an omitted mubtada hum and cancels the preceding idea of death. The second moves from one description to another without cancelling the first. The Key calls these ibtal and intiqal. In its garden example, the later statement corrects the speakers’ first impression.

concepts.title: “One” follows the noun
concepts.rule: For one book, say كِتَابٌ وَاحِدٌ.

examples.arabic: كِتَابٌ وَاحِدٌ
examples.translation: One book
examples.explanation: The number agrees with the noun it describes. Both words here are masculine singular and have tanwin. This is a different construction from the numbers three to ten, which are introduced later in the chapter.

concepts.title: Ask “how many?” with كَمْ
concepts.rule: After كَمْ here: singular noun, mansub ending.

examples.arabic:
كَمْ كِتَابًا؟
كَمْ سَيَّارَةً؟
examples.translation:
How many books?
How many cars?
examples.explanation: English uses a plural noun, but Arabic here uses singular كِتَابًا and سَيَّارَةً. Their fathah tanwin marks the mansub ending. Do not use the plural just because the English question does.

concepts.title: The dual already tells you “two”
concepts.rule: You can say كِتَابَانِ without adding a separate word for two.

examples.arabic: كِتَابَانِ اِثْنَانِ
examples.translation: Two books (with “two” emphasised)
examples.explanation: Usually كِتَابَانِ by itself is enough: the dual ending already expresses two. The word اِثْنَانِ can be added as an agreeing adjective for emphasis.

concepts.title: For three to ten, put the number first
concepts.rule: Number first; counted noun plural and majrur for 3–10.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ
أَرْبَعَةُ بُيُوتٍ
خَمْسَةُ أَقْلَامٍ
عَشَرَةُ رِجَالٍ
examples.translation:
Three books
Four houses
Five pens
Ten men
examples.explanation: The number is the mudaf; the counted noun is the mudaf ilayhi. That counted noun is called the maʿdud. It is plural and majrur in this 3–10 construction. Notice that the number, as mudaf, does not take tanwin.

concepts.title: The number’s ending follows its own job
concepts.rule: Find the number’s role separately from the counted noun’s role.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجَ ثَلَاثَةُ طُلَّابٍ
فِي أَرْبَعَةِ بُيُوتٍ
رَأَيْتُ خَمْسَةَ رِجَالٍ
examples.translation:
Three students went out.
In four houses
I saw five men.
examples.explanation: ثَلَاثَةُ is the subject, أَرْبَعَةِ follows فِي, and خَمْسَةَ is the object of رَأَيْتُ. The words طُلَّابٍ, بُيُوتٍ, and رِجَالٍ stay majrur because each is a mudaf ilayhi.

concepts.title: An understood word can be left out
concepts.rule: An omitted counting word can still be understood from the question.

examples.arabic:
كَمْ ثَمَنُ هَذَا الْكِتَابِ؟
كَمْ رِيَالًا ثَمَنُ هَذَا الْكِتَابِ؟
examples.translation:
What is the price of this book?
How many riyals is the price of this book?
examples.explanation: The Key supplies رِيَالًا to show the omitted counted unit. Another monetary unit could be understood instead. This explains why the shorter question does not visibly show the singular mansub counting noun taught with كَمْ.

concepts.title: For 3–10, check the counted noun’s gender
concepts.rule: For these 3–10 forms, the number and counted noun have opposite gender forms.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةُ أَبْنَاءٍ   ·   ثَلَاثُ بَنَاتٍ
أَرْبَعَةُ إِخْوَةٍ   ·   أَرْبَعُ أَخَوَاتٍ
خَمْسَةُ آبَاءٍ   ·   خَمْسُ أُمَّهَاتٍ
examples.translation:
Three sons · three daughters
Four brothers · four sisters
Five fathers · five mothers
examples.explanation: This is often called opposite-gender agreement for numbers 3–10: the form with ة goes with masculine counted nouns; the form without it goes with feminine counted nouns. Identify the counted noun’s gender from its singular, rather than guessing from its plural ending.

concepts.title: Keep the same pattern as the numbers grow
concepts.rule: Keep gender, plural form, and majrur case together when counting.

examples.arabic:
سِتَّةُ رِجَالٍ   ·   سِتُّ نِسَاءٍ
سَبْعَةُ طُلَّابٍ   ·   سَبْعُ طَالِبَاتٍ
ثَمَانِيَةُ بُيُوتٍ   ·   ثَمَانِي غُرَفٍ
examples.translation:
Six men · six women
Seven male students · seven female students
Eight houses · eight rooms
examples.explanation: The 3–10 pairs are ثَلَاثَة/ثَلَاث, أَرْبَعَة/أَرْبَع, خَمْسَة/خَمْس, سِتَّة/سِتّ, سَبْعَة/سَبْع, ثَمَانِيَة/ثَمَانِي, تِسْعَة/تِسْع, عَشَرَة/عَشْر. The first form in each pair is used with a masculine counted noun. The Key specifically notes the unvowelled final ي in ثَمَانِي here.

concepts.title: The two forms of “ten” sound different
concepts.rule: Hear the short vowel in عَشَرَة and the sukun in عَشْر.

examples.arabic:
عَشَرَةُ رِجَالٍ
عَشْرُ نِسَاءٍ
examples.translation:
Ten men
Ten women
examples.explanation: This is not just removing the written ة. The internal pronunciation changes too: ʿasharah versus ʿashr. Both still form the 3–10 construction with a plural majrur counted noun.

concepts.title: One and two match feminine nouns
concepts.rule: One and two agree; three to ten use the opposite-gender number forms.

examples.arabic:
لِي أُخْتٌ وَاحِدَةٌ
لِي أُخْتَانِ اِثْنَتَانِ
examples.translation:
I have one sister.
I have two sisters.
examples.explanation: Unlike 3–10, one and two agree with the noun’s gender. اِثْنَتَانِ can emphasise the dual أُخْتَانِ, which already means two sisters. Compare the masculine وَاحِدٌ and اِثْنَانِ from Chapter 19.

concepts.title: Hundred and thousand take a singular counted noun
concepts.rule: Hundred/thousand + singular majrur counted noun.

examples.arabic:
مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ
أَلْفُ رِيَالٍ
أَلْفُ مُسْلِمَةٍ وَمِائَةُ طَالِبَةٍ
examples.translation:
One hundred books
One thousand riyals
One thousand Muslim women and one hundred female students
examples.explanation: The counted-noun pattern differs from Book 1’s 3–10: it is singular here, not plural. The same number forms serve masculine and feminine counted nouns. The ا in the spelling مِائَة is silent; مِئَة is another spelling given by the Key.

concepts.title: 11–20 use a singular mansub counted noun
concepts.rule: For the 11–20 examples here, the counted noun is singular mansub.

examples.arabic:
أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا
تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا
examples.translation:
Eleven stars
Nineteen books
examples.explanation: Compare Book 1’s three books, ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ, with eleven stars: the counted noun is singular here and has a mansub ending. The number words 11–19 are compounds; 20 is treated separately.

concepts.title: Both parts of 11 and 12 match gender
concepts.rule: With 11 and 12, both components match the counted noun’s gender.

examples.arabic:
أَحَدَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا
إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
اِثْنَا عَشَرَ طَالِبًا
اِثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Eleven male students
Eleven female students
Twelve male students
Twelve female students
examples.explanation: The Key compares both genders to explain the rule, while this lesson mainly practises masculine counted nouns. The counted noun remains singular mansub in each phrase.

concepts.title: For 13–19, the two parts follow different gender rules
concepts.rule: For 13–19: first part opposite, second part matching.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا
ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Thirteen male students
Thirteen female students
examples.explanation: With masculine طَالِبًا, the first part has ة and the second is عَشَرَ. With feminine طَالِبَةً, the first lacks ة and the second is عَشْرَةَ. The lesson practises masculine forms first; feminine practice returns in Lesson 6.

concepts.title: Most 11–19 compounds keep their form
concepts.rule: A fixed ending does not mean the phrase always has the same grammatical role.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا
أُرِيدُ ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا
هَذَا الْقَلَمُ بِثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا
examples.translation:
I have thirteen riyals.
I want thirteen riyals.
This pen costs thirteen riyals.
examples.explanation: ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ keeps the same visible form as a topic, an object, or after بِـ. Compare the changing ثَلَاثَةُ / ثَلَاثَةَ / ثَلَاثَةِ forms of the single number three.

concepts.title: The first part of twelve does change
concepts.rule: Twelve is the exception: its first part changes with case.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي اثْنَا عَشَرَ رِيَالًا
أُرِيدُ اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا
هَذَا الْكِتَابُ بِاثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا
examples.translation:
I have twelve riyals.
I want twelve riyals.
This book costs twelve riyals.
examples.explanation: The second part عَشَرَ stays fixed, but the first behaves like the changing dual. The initial hamzat al-wasl in these forms drops in connected pronunciation after a preceding word.

concepts.title: Twenty has the same gender form
concepts.rule: Use عِشْرُونَ with either gender here; keep the counted noun singular mansub.

examples.arabic:
عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا
عِشْرُونَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Twenty male students
Twenty female students
examples.explanation: The counted noun is still singular mansub. Unlike the two-part 11–19 compounds, twenty is a single word. Its other case forms and the tens 30–90 are studied later in the book.

concepts.title: Ordinal numbers tell you position
concepts.rule: Separate ordinal position (“third”) from quantity (“three”).

examples.arabic:
أَوَّلُ   ·   ثَانٍ   ·   ثَالِثٌ
رَابِعٌ   ·   خَامِسٌ   ·   سَادِسٌ
examples.translation:
First · second · third
Fourth · fifth · sixth
examples.explanation: The indefinite “second” is ثَانٍ, with the same omitted-final-ي behaviour as غَالٍ. With الـ, it is الثَّانِي. These words express order rather than how many things there are.

concepts.title: Practise eleven and twelve with feminine nouns
concepts.rule: With feminine counted nouns, use إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ or اِثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ here.

examples.arabic:
أَحَدَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا   ·   إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
اِثْنَا عَشَرَ طَالِبًا   ·   اِثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Eleven male students · eleven female students
Twelve male students · twelve female students
examples.explanation: This revisits Chapter 3 with the feminine maʿdud in focus. The counted noun remains singular mansub. The feminine number forms are not made merely by adding ة to the masculine compound: learn إِحْدَى and اِثْنَتَا.

concepts.title: For thirteen to nineteen, only the second part agrees
concepts.rule: For 13–19, apply the two gender rules separately.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا
ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
ثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا
ثَمَانِي عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Thirteen male students
Thirteen female students
Eighteen male students
Eighteen female students
examples.explanation: With طَالِبَةً, the first part lacks ة, while the second is feminine عَشْرَةَ. With طَالِبًا, the first has ة and the second is عَشَرَ. The noun itself remains singular mansub.

concepts.title: Hear the difference in عَشَرَ and عَشْرَةَ
concepts.rule: Do not read عَشْرَةَ with an extra vowel between ش and ر.

examples.arabic:
عَشَرَ   ·   عَشْرَةَ
ثَمَانِي عَشْرَةَ
examples.translation:
The masculine and feminine second parts of the compound
Eighteen (with a feminine counted noun)
examples.explanation: Read ʿashara versus ʿashrata in these compound forms. The Key also notes that the final ي in ثَمَانِي has sukun in ثَمَانِي عَشْرَةَ. Vowel differences matter as much as the written ة.

concepts.title: Fractions have a recurring pattern
concepts.rule: ثُلُثٌ and سُدُسٌ keep both short u-vowels.

examples.arabic: ثُلُثٌ   ·   سُدُسٌ
examples.translation: One-third · one-sixth
examples.explanation: The Key specifically notes that ثُلُثٌ and سُدُسٌ retain the middle dammah. Other fractions in this series often shorten to a form with the middle vowel omitted. Learn the actual fraction word and its pronunciation rather than treating it as a counting number.

concepts.title: A preposition before كَمْ allows another counted-noun ending
concepts.rule: With a preposition before كَمْ, the counted noun may be mansub or majrur here.

examples.arabic:
كَمْ رِيَالًا عِنْدَكَ؟
بِكَمْ رِيَالًا / رِيَالٍ هَذَا؟
فِي كَمْ يَوْمًا / يَوْمٍ؟
examples.translation:
How many riyals do you have?
How many riyals does this cost?
In how many days?
examples.explanation: بِـ and فِي come before كَمْ in the latter questions. In that setting, both counted-noun endings shown are permitted. This is a qualification of the earlier كَمْ rule, not a reason to use a majrur ending after every كَمْ question.

concepts.title: A number can follow the noun as an adjective
concepts.rule: Distinguish number-first idafah from a descriptive number after the noun.

examples.arabic:
الطُّلَّابُ الْجُدُدُ الْخَمْسَةُ
الْكُتُبُ الْأَرْبَعَةُ
الْأَخَوَاتُ الْخَمْسُ
examples.translation:
The five new students
The four books
The five sisters
examples.explanation: This differs from the number-first idafah, such as خَمْسَةُ طُلَّابٍ. The descriptive number is definite here, like the noun it qualifies. The number’s masculine/feminine form still follows the counting pattern taught earlier.

concepts.title: Join units and tens with وَ
concepts.rule: Say the unit, then وَ, then عِشْرُونَ.

examples.arabic:
وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا
ثَلَاثَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ
أَرْبَعَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ
تِسْعَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ
examples.translation:
Twenty-one students
Twenty-three
Twenty-four
Twenty-nine
examples.explanation: Unlike a fixed compound such as ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ, the parts here are linked by “and.” The unit forms shown have tanwin. اِثْنَانِ, used in twenty-two, does not take tanwin. This lesson practises the masculine counted-noun pattern.

concepts.title: The unit keeps its gender rule
concepts.rule: Keep the unit’s gender rule and use a singular mansub counted noun.

examples.arabic:
وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا
اِثْنَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا
ثَلَاثَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا
خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا
examples.translation:
Twenty-one men
Twenty-two men
Twenty-three men
Twenty-five men
examples.explanation: The counted noun is singular and mansub: رَجُلًا. The gender rule is applied to the unit part rather than to عِشْرُونَ, which has the same gender form. The chapter heading is numbers 21–30, with these examples concentrating on the joined unit-and-twenty forms.

concepts.title: The tens follow the sound-plural endings
concepts.rule: Change the tens for case; keep their counted noun singular mansub.

examples.arabic:
فِي الْفَصْلِ عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا.
قَرَأْتُ عِشْرِينَ كِتَابًا.
اشْتَرَيْتُهُ بِعِشْرِينَ رِيَالًا.
examples.translation:
There are twenty students in the class.
I read twenty books.
I bought it for twenty riyals.
examples.explanation: The tens have ـُونَ when marfu and ـِينَ when mansub or majrur. Their counted noun stays singular and mansub in these examples, regardless of the number’s own case. Distinguish عِشْرِينَ, governed by بِـ, from its counted noun رِيَالًا.

concepts.title: Twenty-one and twenty-two match gender
concepts.rule: In 21 and 22, match the unit to the counted noun’s gender.

examples.arabic:
وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا
إِحْدَى وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبَةً
اِثْنَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا
اِثْنَتَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Twenty-one male students
Twenty-one female students
Twenty-two male students
Twenty-two female students
examples.explanation: Use وَاحِدٌ / اِثْنَانِ with the masculine noun and إِحْدَى / اِثْنَتَانِ with the feminine noun. The joining وَ remains. عِشْرُونَ does not change for gender, and the counted noun remains singular mansub.

concepts.title: In 23–29, the unit has opposite gender
concepts.rule: Apply gender opposition to the unit, not to the tens.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا
ثَلَاثٌ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Twenty-three male students
Twenty-three female students
examples.explanation: The masculine counted noun takes ثَلَاثَةٌ, while the feminine counted noun takes ثَلَاثٌ. Apply the same principle to the other units through nine. The tens themselves use the same form for either gender.

concepts.title: Number review: one and two versus three to ten
concepts.rule: One and two agree; three to ten oppose gender.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابٌ وَاحِدٌ · كِتَابَانِ اثْنَانِ
سَيَّارَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ · سَيَّارَتَانِ اثْنَتَانِ
ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ · ثَلَاثُ نِسَاءٍ
examples.translation:
One book · two books
One car · two cars
Three men · three women
examples.explanation: One and two follow the noun as adjectives. Three to ten precede their counted noun in the illustrated idafah and use the opposite gender form. This chapter consolidates earlier rules; compare each group rather than applying one rule to every number.

concepts.title: Number review: eleven, twelve and thirteen to nineteen
concepts.rule: For 13–19: unit opposes; ten agrees. Eleven and twelve agree in both parts.

examples.arabic:
أَحَدَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا · إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
اِثْنَا عَشَرَ طَالِبًا · اِثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا · ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ طَالِبَةً
examples.translation:
Eleven male students · eleven female students
Twelve male students · twelve female students
Thirteen male students · thirteen female students
examples.explanation: In eleven and twelve, both parts agree with the noun’s gender. In thirteen through nineteen, the unit part has opposite gender while the ten part agrees. All the counted nouns here are singular mansub.

concepts.title: Unchanging gender forms and the dual nun
concepts.rule: Keep these gender forms; omit a dual mudaf’s nun before its counted noun.

examples.arabic:
خَمْسُونَ مُسْلِمًا · خَمْسُونَ مُسْلِمَةً
مِائَةُ طَالِبٍ · مِائَةُ طَالِبَةٍ
مِائَتَا رِيَالٍ · أَلْفَا دُولَارٍ
examples.translation:
Fifty male Muslims · fifty female Muslims
One hundred male students · one hundred female students
Two hundred riyals · two thousand dollars
examples.explanation: Do not change the tens, مِائَة or أَلْف for the counted noun’s gender. The dual forms مِائَتَانِ and أَلْفَانِ lose their nun when joined to an expressed counted noun as mudaf. The alif in مِائَة is silent; the Key also permits the spelling مِئَة.

concepts.title: Choose the counted noun’s number and case
concepts.rule: 3–10: plural majrur; 11–99: singular mansub; 100/1000: singular majrur.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ
أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا
أَلْفُ رِيَالٍ
examples.translation:
Three books
Eleven stars
One thousand riyals
examples.explanation: After 3–10, use a plural majrur counted noun. After 11–99, use a singular mansub counted noun. After 100 and 1000, use a singular majrur counted noun. These are rules for the counted noun, separate from the number’s own role in the sentence.

concepts.title: The number’s own case comes from its job
concepts.rule: Determine the number’s job separately from the counted noun’s pattern.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي رِيَالٌ وَاحِدٌ · أُرِيدُ رِيَالًا وَاحِدًا
عِنْدِي رِيَالَانِ اثْنَانِ · أُرِيدُ رِيَالَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ
عِنْدِي خَمْسَةُ رِيَالَاتٍ
أُرِيدُ خَمْسَةَ رِيَالَاتٍ
هَذَا الْقَلَمُ بِخَمْسَةِ رِيَالَاتٍ
examples.translation:
I have one riyal · I want one riyal
I have two riyals · I want two riyals
I have five riyals.
I want five riyals.
This pen costs five riyals.
examples.explanation: وَاحِدٌ and اِثْنَانِ follow their nouns’ case. خَمْسَة changes u / a / i according to its own sentence role, while رِيَالَاتٍ remains majrur after it. Do not give the number and counted noun the same ending automatically.

concepts.title: Most teen compounds keep their endings
concepts.rule: A fixed ending does not mean the number has the same grammatical job everywhere.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا.
أُرِيدُ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا.
هَذَا الْقَلَمُ بِخَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا.
examples.translation:
I have fifteen riyals.
I want fifteen riyals.
This pen costs fifteen riyals.
examples.explanation: خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ keeps the same visible endings even after بِـ. Its grammatical role changes, but the compound is mabni. Twelve differs: its first part changes like a dual; the next card isolates that exception.

concepts.title: Only the first part of twelve changes
concepts.rule: Twelve changes its first part for case; its second part stays fixed.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي اثْنَا عَشَرَ رِيَالًا.
أُرِيدُ اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا.
هَذَا الْقَلَمُ بِاثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رِيَالًا.
اِثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ رُوبِيَّةً · اِثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ رُوبِيَّةً
examples.translation:
I have twelve riyals.
I want twelve riyals.
This pen costs twelve riyals.
Twelve rupees (marfu · mansub/majrur)
examples.explanation: The first part follows the dual case distinction. عَشَرَ or عَشْرَةَ remains unchanged. Do not restore the dual nun inside this compound. The counted noun stays singular mansub in every example.

concepts.title: Tens and hundred/thousand have different case patterns
concepts.rule: Keep the case pattern of each number group distinct.

examples.arabic:
أَعِنْدَكَ سِتُّونَ رِيَالًا؟
أُرِيدُ سِتِّينَ رِيَالًا.
هَذَا الْكِتَابُ بِسِتِّينَ رِيَالًا.
مُرَتَّبُهُ أَلْفُ دُولَارٍ.
أَخَذْتُ أَلْفَ دُولَارٍ مِنْهُ.
اشْتَرَيْتُهُ بِأَلْفِ دُولَارٍ.
examples.translation:
Do you have sixty riyals?
I want sixty riyals.
This book costs sixty riyals.
His salary is one thousand dollars.
I took one thousand dollars from him.
I bought it for one thousand dollars.
