examples.explanation: The tens decline like a sound masculine plural. مِائَة and أَلْف decline regularly: u when marfu, a when mansub, i when majrur. Their counted nouns follow their separate rules: رِيَالًا after sixty, but دُولَارٍ after thousand.

concepts.title: Two thousand keeps the dual case distinction
concepts.rule: Use ـَا for the marfu dual mudaf and ـَيْ for its other two cases.

examples.arabic:
أُجْرَتُهُ أَلْفَا رِيَالٍ.
مَا يُرِيدُ أَلْفَيْ رِيَالٍ.
يَعْمَلُ بِأَلْفَيْ رِيَالٍ.
examples.translation:
His wages are two thousand riyals.
He does not want two thousand riyals.
He works for two thousand riyals.
examples.explanation: أَلْفَا is marfu; أَلْفَيْ is used for both mansub and majrur. مِائَتَا / مِائَتَيْ behaves the same way for two hundred. The counted noun is majrur after the dual mudaf.

concepts.title: Inside the hundreds, مِائَة is majrur
concepts.rule: Within these compounds, the first part carries case and the hundred-part remains majrur.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي ثَلَاثُمِائَةِ رِيَالٍ.
أُرِيدُ ثَلَاثَمِائَةِ رِيَالٍ.
اشْتَرَيْتُهُ بِثَلَاثِمِائَةِ رِيَالٍ.
ثَمَانِمِائَةِ
examples.translation:
I have three hundred riyals.
I want three hundred riyals.
I bought it for three hundred riyals.
Eight hundred (the hundred-part remains majrur)
examples.explanation: The first part changes u / a / i with its job. مِائَةِ remains majrur as mudaf ilayhi; the Key joins the parts in writing. In ثَمَانِمِائَة, the original ya of ثَمَانِي has been omitted, and the nun’s kasrah remains unchanged. Do not apply the visible three-hundred vowel changes mechanically to that nun.

concepts.title: Thousand can be both a count and a counted noun
concepts.rule: Read a large number in layers; each layer has its own relationship.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةُ آلَافِ رِيَالٍ
سِتَّةَ عَشَرَ أَلْفَ رِيَالٍ
ثَلَاثُونَ أَلْفَ رِيَالٍ
مِائَةُ أَلْفِ رِيَالٍ
examples.translation:
Three thousand riyals
Sixteen thousand riyals
Thirty thousand riyals
One hundred thousand riyals
examples.explanation: Relative to the preceding number, “thousand” is the counted noun: plural majrur after three, singular mansub after sixteen or thirty, and singular majrur after hundred. Relative to رِيَالٍ, it is itself the number and forms an idafah with that unit.

concepts.title: A number regains tanwin when its counted noun is omitted
concepts.rule: An omitted counted noun can restore tanwin to a number that otherwise forms idafah.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي عَشَرَةٌ. · عِنْدِي عَشَرَةُ رِيَالَاتٍ.
بِأَلْفٍ يَا أَخِي. · بِأَلْفِ رِيَالٍ.
عِشْرِينَ أَلْفًا يَا أَخِي. · أُرِيدُ عِشْرِينَ أَلْفَ رِيَالٍ.
examples.translation:
I have ten. · I have ten riyals.
For a thousand, brother. · For a thousand riyals.
Twenty thousand, brother. · I want twenty thousand riyals.
examples.explanation: With an expressed counted noun, the number is mudaf and has no tanwin. When that noun is omitted in these examples, عَشَرَةٌ, أَلْفٍ and أَلْفًا take tanwin. This does not mean every Arabic number can take tanwin: fixed teen compounds and the tens retain their own patterns.

concepts.title: Read a larger number in ordered groups
concepts.rule: Break the number into groups and keep each group’s gender and case rules.

examples.arabic:
ثَلَاثَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ وَخَمْسُمِائَةٍ وَسِتَّةُ آلَافِ رِيَالٍ
ثَلَاثٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ وَخَمْسُمِائَةٍ وَسِتَّةُ آلَافِ رُوبِيَّةٍ
examples.translation:
6,543 riyals
6,543 rupees
examples.explanation: The example reads 3 + 40 + 500 + 6,000, joining the groups with وَ. The unit changes from ثَلَاثَةٌ for masculine رِيَال to ثَلَاثٌ for feminine رُوبِيَّة. The other groups keep their appropriate internal rules. The Key presents this reading order as preferable, not as the only possible order.

concepts.title: Review the case inside three hundred
concepts.rule: Keep the two grammatical layers of the hundred compound distinct.

examples.arabic: ثَلَاثُمِائَةِ · تِسْعُمِائَةِ
examples.translation: Three hundred · nine hundred (marfu first parts)
examples.explanation: This is a cross-reference rather than a new example set. The first component follows the number’s sentence role, while مِائَةِ is majrur inside the compound. See the Book 2 hundreds card for the full marfu, mansub and majrur comparison.

concepts.title: Tamyiz specifies what a quantity measures
concepts.rule: Separate the measure’s role from the material that specifies it.

examples.arabic:
شَرِبْتُ لِتْرًا حَلِيبًا.
اِشْتَرَيْتُ مِتْرًا حَرِيرًا.
عِنْدِي كِيلُوغْرَامٌ بُرْتُقَالًا.
examples.translation:
I drank a litre of milk.
I bought a metre of silk.
I have a kilogram of oranges.
examples.explanation: Tamyiz al-dhat identifies the thing measured. The Key lists number, linear measurement, capacity/volume and weight. The measure word has its own sentence role; the specifying noun is mansub in these examples.

concepts.title: Question كَمْ differs from exclamatory كَمْ
concepts.rule: Choose the tamyiz pattern for the intended question or exclamation.

examples.arabic:
كَمْ كِتَابًا عِنْدَكَ؟
كَمْ كِتَابٍ عِنْدَكَ!
كَمْ مِنْ كِتَابٍ عِنْدَكَ!
كَمْ كُتُبٍ عِنْدَكَ!
كَمْ نَجْمٍ فِي السَّمَاءِ!
examples.translation:
How many books do you have?
How many books you have!
How many books you have!
How many books you have!
How many stars there are in the sky!
examples.explanation: Question كَمْ has singular mansub tamyiz in the pattern taught here. Exclamatory كَمْ has singular or plural majrur tamyiz, optionally preceded by مِنْ. Intonation and punctuation also differ. The Key recommends avoiding the plural-with-min variant كَمْ مِنْ كُتُبٍ, favouring the listed alternatives.

concepts.title: Numeric tamyiz has its own case and number rules
concepts.rule: Tamyiz describes a function; its numeric construction determines the ending.

examples.arabic:
أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا
ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ
مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ
examples.translation:
Eleven stars
Three books
One hundred books
examples.explanation: The specifying noun after 11–99 is singular mansub. After 3–10 it is plural majrur; after 100 and 1000 it is singular majrur. Preserve the earlier number-agreement rules as well.

concepts.title: Quantity-like words also take specification
concepts.rule: Recognise the same semantic need behind different quantity expressions.

examples.arabic:
كَمْ بِنْتًا لَكَ؟
هَلْ عِنْدَكَ كِيسٌ دَقِيقًا؟
مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا
examples.translation:
How many daughters have you?
Have you a sack of flour?
An atom’s weight of good
examples.explanation: Kam resembles a number; a sack resembles a capacity measure; an atom’s weight resembles a weight measure. The Key also gives the size of a palm as measurement-like. Their specifying nouns clarify what the quantity refers to.

concepts.title: Some quantity specification can use min or idafah
concepts.rule: Watch what governs jarr in each alternative.

examples.arabic:
اِشْتَرَيْتُ مِتْرًا حَرِيرًا.
اِشْتَرَيْتُ مِتْرًا مِنْ حَرِيرٍ.
اِشْتَرَيْتُ مِتْرَ حَرِيرٍ.
examples.translation: I bought a metre of silk (three constructions).
examples.explanation: A quantity tamyiz can instead be majrur through min or by becoming mudaf ilayhi. The measure loses tanwin in the idafah version. Numeric tamyiz retains its own rules, so do not transfer the alternatives indiscriminately to numbers.

concepts.title: Sentence tamyiz clarifies the aspect of a judgement
concepts.rule: Do not extend the quantity min/idafah alternatives to every sentence tamyiz.

examples.arabic:
حَسُنَ بِلَالٌ خُلُقًا.
حَسُنَ خُلُقُ بِلَالٍ.
وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا
examples.translation:
Bilal is good in manners.
Bilal’s manners are good.
We caused the earth to gush with springs
examples.explanation: Tamyiz al-nisbah resolves a vagueness in the whole relation, not one measured quantity. The Key shows a subject-derived analysis with manners and an object-derived analysis with springs. It teaches mansub for these examples, while its footnote explicitly reserves exceptions for later study.

concepts.title: Add another idea with “also”
concepts.rule: أَيْضًا adds “also” to the meaning.

examples.arabic: هَذَا جَمِيلٌ، وَذَلِكَ أَيْضًا جَمِيلٌ
examples.translation: This is beautiful, and that is also beautiful.
examples.explanation: You already know هَذَا, ذَلِكَ, and وَ. أَيْضًا adds the idea that the second thing shares the same description. Keep the rest of the sentence pattern you know.

concepts.title: “So” and “with me” in one sentence
concepts.rule: The subject ending and the pronoun after بِـ have separate jobs.

examples.arabic:
فَفَرِحَ بِيَ الْمُدَرِّسُ كَثِيرًا
فَرِحْتُ بِكَ
فَرِحُوا بِنَا
أَفَرِحْتَ بِهِ؟
examples.translation:
So the teacher was greatly pleased with me.
I was pleased with you.
They were pleased with us.
Were you pleased with him?
examples.explanation: The first فَ means “so,” and بِيَ means “with me” here. The other examples change the verb’s subject and the pronoun attached to بِـ independently. Match who is pleased to the verb, and whom they are pleased with to the attached pronoun.

concepts.title: A reassuring answer to a request
concepts.rule: Interpret أَبْشِرْ in its request-and-response context.

examples.arabic: أَبْشِرْ
examples.translation: Don’t worry; you will get what you want.
examples.explanation: The Key explains the intended meaning rather than translating the expression word for word. Recognise it as reassurance in response to a request, not as a generic word for every “yes.”

concepts.title: Say “How beautiful!” with مَا أَفْعَلَ…
concepts.rule: Recognise the whole exclamation pattern, not just the word مَا.

examples.arabic:
مَا أَجْمَلَ هَذِهِ السَّيَّارَةَ!
مَا أَسْهَلَ هَذَا الدَّرْسَ!
examples.translation:
How beautiful this car is!
How easy this lesson is!
examples.explanation: The pattern is مَا أَفْعَلَهُ. A mansub noun phrase can replace the attached pronoun: هَذِهِ السَّيَّارَةَ or هَذَا الدَّرْسَ. This مَا expresses wonder, rather than asking “what?” or negating a statement.

concepts.title: Exclaim about a person or a group
concepts.rule: Attached pronoun or mansub noun: both can complete the wonder pattern.

examples.arabic:
مَا أَطْيَبَكَ!
مَا أَفْقَرَهَا!
مَا أَكْثَرَ النُّجُومَ!
examples.translation:
How good you are!
How poor she is!
How numerous the stars are!
examples.explanation: ـكَ and ـهَا identify the person the exclamation concerns. النُّجُومَ is a mansub noun in the third example. Compare أَكْثَرَ here with the comparative form ending in dammah: this is a different construction despite the similar word shape.

concepts.title: A physical copy is a مُصْحَفٌ
concepts.rule: Use مُصْحَفٌ for the physical copy or edition.

examples.arabic:
عِنْدِي مُصْحَفَانِ.
هَذَا مُصْحَفٌ هِنْدِيٌّ، وَذَاكَ مُصْحَفٌ مِصْرِيٌّ.
examples.translation:
I have two copies of the Quran.
This is an Indian edition of the Quran, and that is an Egyptian edition.
examples.explanation: Use مُصْحَفٌ when counting physical copies or describing an edition’s origin. الْقُرْآنُ names the Quran itself; the Key warns against substituting it for مُصْحَفٌ in these examples. The dual مُصْحَفَانِ counts two copies.

concepts.title: Permit someone to do something
concepts.rule: سَمَحَ لِـ someone بِـ an action noun means “permitted someone to do it.”

examples.arabic:
سَمَحَ لَهُ بِالْخُرُوجِ.
اِسْمَحْ لِي بِالْجُلُوسِ هُنَا.
لَا أَسْمَحُ لَكَ بِالدُّخُولِ.
examples.translation:
He permitted him to leave.
Permit me to sit here.
I do not permit you to enter.
examples.explanation: The person appears in لَهُ, لِي or لَكَ. The permitted action is expressed with a verbal noun after بِـ: الْخُرُوجِ, الْجُلُوسِ or الدُّخُولِ. These nouns are majrur. Learn the whole construction, rather than translating the English infinitive word by word.

concepts.title: Make a request with أَرْجُو
concepts.rule: أَرْجُو introduces a request.

examples.arabic:
أَرْجُو
رَجَا · يَرْجُو
examples.translation:
I request
He requested · he requests
examples.explanation: The first-person form begins with أَ. The Key supplies رَجَا يَرْجُو as the verb pair and singles out أَرْجُو for making a request. Learn this expression now; the following chapter uses it with أَنْ to introduce what is requested. Do not confuse أَرْجُو with the noun رَجَاءٌ.

concepts.title: Some expressions have the force of a verb
concepts.rule: An اِسْمُ فِعْلٍ can express a verb’s meaning without being an ordinary conjugated verb.

examples.arabic:
هَيَّا بِنَا!
آهِ
أُفٍّ
آمِينَ
examples.translation:
Come along!
I feel pain.
I am bored / exasperated.
Accept my prayer.
examples.explanation: The Key introduces هَيَّا بِنَا as “Come along!” and groups it with expressions such as آهِ, أُفٍّ and آمِينَ. They convey a complete response or request without following the ordinary verb-conjugation pattern practised earlier. Translate their function in context.

concepts.title: Ask someone not to hurry: مَهْلًا
concepts.rule: مَهْلًا means “Slowly, please; do not hurry.”

examples.arabic: مَهْلًا!
examples.translation: Slowly, please! / Do not hurry!
examples.explanation: The Key gives this expression directly. Learn it as a useful complete utterance. Its meaning can be translated as an instruction, even though it does not use the لَا + verb prohibition pattern introduced earlier.

concepts.title: Recognise “Here it is!”
concepts.rule: هَا هُوَ ذَا and هَا هِيَ ذِي announce the sought person or thing.

examples.arabic:
هَا هُوَ ذَا!
هَا هِيَ ذِي!
هَأَنَذَا!
examples.translation:
Here he/it is!
Here she/it is!
Here I am!
examples.explanation: The Key gives a masculine form, a feminine form, and the first-person response. Match the expression to the person or thing being identified. Learn these as complete expressions rather than assembling them as an ordinary location sentence.

concepts.title: Learn a prayer for complete recovery
concepts.rule: شَفَاكَ اللَّهُ is a wish for the listener’s recovery.

examples.arabic: شَفَاكَ اللَّهُ شِفَاءً كَامِلًا.
examples.translation: May Allah grant you complete health.
examples.explanation: The Key gives this complete expression for wishing someone recovery. كَ refers to the person addressed, and كَامِلًا describes شِفَاءً. Translate the intended prayer, rather than automatically reading the past verb as a report of a completed event.

concepts.title: Say “No, thanks” with وَ
concepts.rule: For the expression taught here, say لَا، وَشُكْرًا.

examples.arabic: لَا، وَشُكْرًا.
examples.translation: No, thanks.
examples.explanation: لَا declines the offer; وَشُكْرًا adds thanks. The Key warns against omitting وَ in this expression, since the resulting phrase would deny thanks rather than politely combine refusal and gratitude. Learn the complete expression with its pause and conjunction.

concepts.title: After “he said,” the quoted sentence uses إِنَّ
concepts.rule: In this direct quote after قَالَ, begin with إِنَّ.

examples.arabic: قَالَ: إِنَّكَ أَحْسَنُ طَالِبٍ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation: He said, “You are the best student in the class.”
examples.explanation: قَالَ introduces the quoted words. The quote begins with إِنَّكَ, not أَنَّكَ, in this construction. The rest of the sentence reuses the superlative أَحْسَنُ طَالِبٍ from Chapter 3.

concepts.title: إِلَيْكَ can function as “Take!”
concepts.rule: إِلَيْكَ / إِلَيْكِ / إِلَيْكُمْ / إِلَيْكُنَّ can introduce an offered object.

examples.arabic:
إِلَيْكُمْ أَمْثِلَةً أُخْرَى.
إِلَيْكَ هَذَا الْكِتَابَ يَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ.
إِلَيْكِ الْمَلَاعِقَ يَا أُخْتِي.
إِلَيْكُنَّ هَذِهِ الدَّفَاتِرَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ.
examples.translation:
Take some more examples.
Take this book, Ibrahim.
Take the spoons, sister.
Take these notebooks, sisters.
examples.explanation: Although built from إِلَى and an attached pronoun, the expression has command force here. The pronoun changes for the listener. The thing offered is its mansub object, as أَمْثِلَةً shows. Distinguish this use from the ordinary prepositional meaning “to you.”

concepts.title: A past form can express a wish
concepts.rule: Past morphology does not always give past-time meaning.

examples.arabic:
رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ. · غَفَرَ اللَّهُ لَهُ. · شَفَاهُ اللَّهُ.
لَا أَرَاكَ اللَّهُ مَكْرُوهًا!
لَا فَضَّ اللَّهُ فَاكَ!
examples.translation:
May Allah have mercy on him. · May Allah forgive him. · May Allah grant him health.
May Allah not show you anything unpleasant!
May Allah preserve your speech!
examples.explanation: The wish use of the past is negated with لَا. The last expression literally asks that the mouth not be broken; the Key explains it as appreciation of something beautifully said. Translate the idiomatic wish rather than treating it as a literal threat.

concepts.title: دَخَلَ عَلَى can mean going in to see someone
concepts.rule: دَخَلَ عَلَى someone can mean going in to see them.

examples.arabic: دَخَلْتُ عَلَى الْمُدِيرِ.
examples.translation: I went in to the headmaster in his office.
examples.explanation: The Key gives this as a complete construction. عَلَى governs the majrur الْمُدِيرِ. The phrase concerns entering someone’s presence, rather than physically entering the person. Learn the verb with its preposition and intended meaning.

concepts.title: Announce “Here they are!”
concepts.rule: Match the whole “here” expression to the people being identified.

examples.arabic:
هَا هُوَ ذَا · هَا هِيَ ذِي
هَا هُمَا ذَانِ · هَا هُمَا تَانِ
هَا هُمْ أُولَاءِ · هَا هُنَّ أُولَاءِ
examples.translation:
Here he is · here she is
Here they two are (male · female)
Here they are (male plural · female plural)
examples.explanation: The Key sometimes writes the parts together. Read the pronoun and demonstrative together: هُمَا serves both genders but ذَانِ / تَانِ distinguishes them. The plural expression uses أُولَاءِ with هُمْ or هُنَّ.

concepts.title: Answer “Here I am” or “Here we are”
concepts.rule: Keep the first-person reply distinct from “Here he/she is.”

examples.arabic:
هَأَنَذَا · هَأَنَذِي
هَا نَحْنُ أُولَاءِ
examples.translation:
Here I am (male · female).
Here we are.
examples.explanation: The Key gives هَأَنَذَا for a male speaker and هَأَنَذِي for a female speaker. Groups of either gender use هَا نَحْنُ أُولَاءِ. The expressions answer a search or call for the speaker or group.

concepts.title: آهِ is an ism fil meaning “I feel pain”
concepts.rule: An ism fil can have an understood subject.

examples.arabic: آهِ · آهْ
examples.translation: I feel pain.
examples.explanation: The Key gives these pain expressions as verb-nouns, not ordinary conjugated verbs. Their fail is a hidden pronoun representing أَنَا. This connects to the earlier category of fixed expressions with verb-like force.

concepts.title: هَاءَ is another command-like “Take!”
concepts.rule: Ism fil forms can express a command and take an object.

examples.arabic:
هَاءَ الْكِتَابَ يَا عَلِيُّ.
هَاءِ الْكِتَابَ يَا آمِنَةُ.
هَاؤُمْ الْكِتَابَ يَا إِخْوَانُ.
هَاؤُنَّ الْكِتَابَ يَا أَخَوَاتُ.
examples.translation:
Take the book, Ali.
Take the book, Aminah.
Take the book, brothers.
Take the book, sisters.
examples.explanation: The noun الْكِتَابَ is the object of the command-like expression. The listener forms distinguish masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural and feminine plural. Learn them with the earlier إِلَيْكَ family rather than treating هَاءَ as an ordinary conjugated past verb.

concepts.title: Warn with iyyaka wa
concepts.rule: Match the warning pronoun to the listener and mark the danger mansub.

examples.arabic:
إِيَّاكَ وَالْكِلَابَ!
إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْحَسَدَ!
إِيَّاكِ · إِيَّاكُنَّ
examples.translation:
Beware of dogs!
Beware of jealousy!
Female singular · female plural warning forms
examples.explanation: This construction is tahdhir, a warning. Change the pronoun for the listener: iyyaka, iyyaki, iyyakum, iyyakunna. The waw here introduces the thing to avoid; the following noun takes nasb.

concepts.title: Adraka asks how someone came to know
concepts.rule: Read the expression as a question about knowledge or significance.

examples.arabic:
دَرَى ← أَدْرَى
وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ أَنَّهُ يَكْذِبُ؟
examples.translation:
He knew → informed
How did you come to know that he is lying?
examples.explanation: أَدْرَى is Form IV from دَرَى. The question literally asks what informed you. The Key connects this expression with وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ, where it introduces the significance of the Night of Decree.

concepts.title: Poetry illustrates sentence structure and special endings
concepts.rule: Keep poetic licence separate from the normal noun-ending rule.

examples.arabic:
أَمَّا مَذَاقُهُ فَحُلْوٌ، وَأَمَّا وَجْهُهُ فَجَمِيلُ.
وَمَا التَّأْنِيثُ لِاسْمِ الشَّمْسِ عَيْبٌ
examples.translation:
Its taste is sweet, and its face is beautiful.
Feminine gender for the word sun is no defect.
examples.explanation: The first line describes a good deed through taste and appearance; amma introduces each topic and fa its answer. جَمِيلُ would normally have tanwin here, but the Key explains its omission for metre. The alternate line says grammatical gender gives neither defect to the sun nor pride to the moon.

concepts.title: An-clause warnings omit waw
concepts.rule: Change the construction as well as the word when replacing a noun by an-clause.

examples.arabic:
إِيَّاكَ وَالنَّوْمَ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
إِيَّاكَ أَنْ تَنَامَ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
إِيَّاكِ أَنْ تَنْسَيْ.
examples.translation:
Beware of sleeping in class.
Beware lest you sleep in class.
Beware lest you forget (female).
examples.explanation: When a masdar muawwal supplies the danger, the Key drops the waw of the noun construction. The feminine تَنْسَيْ loses nun after an; masculine singular is تَنْسَى with latent nasb. Match both the warning pronoun and verb to the listener.

concepts.title: Idha can introduce a surprise
concepts.rule: Translate this idha as an unexpected discovery.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجْتُ فَإِذَا شُرْطِيٌّ بِالْبَابِ.
دَخَلْتُ الْغُرْفَةَ فَإِذَا حَيَّةٌ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ.
examples.translation:
I went out and, to my surprise, a policeman was at the door.
I entered the room and unexpectedly found a snake on the bed.
examples.explanation: Idha al-fujaiyyah presents an unexpected state. Fa is usually prefixed, and the following mubtada may be indefinite, as شرطي and حية are here. There is no conditional premise awaiting an answer.

concepts.title: La budda expresses necessity
concepts.rule: Necessity uses la budda with min or a masdar muawwal.

examples.arabic:
لَا بُدَّ مِنَ الِاخْتِبَارِ.
لَا بُدَّ أَنْ تَكْتُبَ لَهُ.
لَا بُدَّ أَنْ نُسَافِرَ.
examples.translation:
One must take the test.
You must write to him.
We must travel.
examples.explanation: La is category-negating la. An ordinary noun follows min. When an-clause replaces that noun, min may be omitted, as in the examples. An still makes the following mudari mansub.

concepts.title: Halla urges now or reproaches a missed action
concepts.rule: The tense tells you whether the action is still urged or its neglect regretted.

examples.arabic:
هَلَّا تَشْكُوهُ إِلَى الْمُدِيرِ؟
هَلَّا شَكَوْتَهُ إِلَى الْمُدِيرِ؟
examples.translation:
Should you not complain about him to the headmaster?
Should you not have complained about him to the headmaster?
examples.explanation: With mudari, halla urges someone to act. With madi, it rebukes an omitted action (tandim). The Key also lists أَلَا، أَلَّا، لَوْمَا، لَوْلَا in these urging/reproach functions. Identify use from context rather than assuming lawla always means “but for”.

concepts.title: Wonder has an afil bi construction too
concepts.rule: Interpret the construction as wonder rather than an ordinary instruction.

examples.arabic:
مَا أَكْثَرَ النُّجُومَ! = أَكْثِرْ بِالنُّجُومِ!
مَا أَفْقَرَهُ! = أَفْقِرْ بِهِ!
examples.translation:
How numerous the stars are!
How poor he is!
examples.explanation: The second verb-of-wonder construction uses أَفْعِلْ بِـ. It looks like a command but functions as exclamation here. In أَبْصِرْ بِهِ وَأَسْمِعْ, the Key explains that the repeated bihi is omitted after the second verb.

concepts.title: Uff expresses annoyance as a verb-noun
concepts.rule: An ism fil can carry verbal meaning while remaining fixed.

examples.arabic: أُفٍّ
examples.translation: An expression of annoyance or irritation
examples.explanation: The Key classifies uff as an ism fil, meaning “I am annoyed/irritated”. It is mabni. Its tanwin-like sound does not make it an ordinary freely declining noun.
